- Per-harness `modelTracking` overlay (`"provider/model" → true`, carried through both harness projections) and `settings.modelAutoUpdate { enabled, mode: notify|apply, intervalHours, maxPriceMultiplier }`. Routes: `GET/PUT /api/settings/model-auto-update`, `PUT /api/harnesses/[id]/models/tracking` (ollama refused).
- `lib/services/model-update-scheduler.ts`, registered from `instrumentation.ts` (unref'd timers, HMR guard, `MODEL_UPDATE_INTERVAL_MS` override). `GET /api/fleet/model-updates` (last persisted report), `POST .../check` (run now), `POST .../apply` (manual one-click apply of a reported successor).
- Catalog: `retired` / `deprecates` fields; `deepseek/deepseek-v3.2` flagged retired (OpenRouter expiration 2026-09-28), `google/gemini-2.5-flash` deprecates 2026-10-20. Rows are flagged, never removed, so live cascades stay readable.
- Reconciled onto the cascade-library stack: this branch's own `lib/services/cascade-write.ts` (`writeCascade`) and its tests are gone. The scheduler's auto-apply and `POST /api/fleet/model-updates/apply` call `applyCascadeToHarness` from `lib/services/cascade-writer.ts`, the stack's single validated write path. `PUT /api/harnesses/[id]/models` is exactly as the parent has it. The byte-for-byte splice pin and created-file pin from the dropped test file are ported into `cascade-writer.test.ts`.

## Why
Closes #136. Providers retire ids on a schedule and ship newer same-family versions; today nobody notices until an agent 404s. This makes freshness visible fleet-wide and, per cascade entry, lets an operator opt in to following the newest same-family version.

Policy, in one place:
- **Default OFF.** `modelAutoUpdate.enabled` is `false`; with it off the scheduler does no background network at all (manual `POST .../check` still works).
- **notify mode** reports successors, retirements and price ratios at `GET /api/fleet/model-updates`. Nothing is written.
- **apply mode** auto-bumps only *tracked* entries to a strictly-same-family newer **version** that is present in the live provider list, within the price ceiling (`maxPriceMultiplier`; no published pricing → `price-unknown` → never auto-applied), through the validated writer (`applyCascadeToHarness`: validate → render → splice → write → overlay), followed by a `quick` restart and a `cascade:auto-update` audit row `{ harness, from, to, provider, priceRatio }`. The `modelTracking` key rotates to the new id.
- **ollama / bedrock / custom never auto-apply.** Unstable (preview/beta/exp) successors never apply. A harness with a restart already in flight is skipped.
- **Snapshot-only bumps are notify-only** (a human may apply one via `POST .../apply`).
- A writer refusal (provider with no credential in the agent's `.env`, unsafe YAML scalar) writes nothing, restarts nothing, leaves tracking untouched, and audits `cascade:auto-update:blocked` with the reason.

## Verification
- `pnpm vitest run` → 119 files, 1441 tests, all green (on head `effc6be`).
- `npx tsc --noEmit 2>&1 | grep -v '^\.next/'` → clean.
- `lib/services/__tests__/model-update-scheduler.test.ts` (22 tests; `cascade-writer.test.ts` 14) runs the **real** `applyCascadeToHarness` against a tmpdir fleet with real `.env` files, so validate-before-write is exercised on the scheduler path, not mocked away. Every guard (untracked, snapshot, unstable, price ceiling, price-unknown, ollama, restart-in-flight, writer refusal, policy off) has a test asserting nothing was written and nothing was restarted.
- Rebased onto `dev/juniperbevensee/cascade-library`; the `writeCascade` extraction commit was dropped and its consumers rewritten in the same history so each commit builds.

## Risk
The scheduler rewrites a running agent's `config.yaml` with no human in the loop — but only when the operator has flipped `enabled` and chosen `apply`, only for entries they tracked, and only through the same writer the editor uses. Worst case on a bad write is the existing crash-loop, which the validator exists to prevent; the byte-identical splice pin guards against a refactor changing what lands on disk.

hits.body:
## Problem

Several service tests create their **source** fixtures correctly under `os.tmpdir()` (`fs.mkdtempSync`), but the **destination** agent dir is computed from the *real* home:

```ts
path.join(os.homedir(), `.hermes-${name}`)
```

So `importFromDir` / `createOverlay` / `duplicateOverlay` write agent dirs into the developer's actual `$HOME`. Running the suite leaves a pile of `~/.hermes-*` fixture dirs behind (observed ~10+: `~/.hermes-test-agent`, `~/.hermes-source-agent`, `~/.hermes-build-test`, `~/.hermes-minimal`, `~/.hermes-cloned-agent`, `~/.hermes-my-new-agent`, `~/.hermes-fallback-test`, `~/.hermes-image-test`, `~/.hermes-soul-test`, …). The `afterEach` cleanups miss anything left by a failed/interrupted run.

## Worse: a real parallel-test flake

`harness-create.test.ts` and `harness-e2e.test.ts` both target the **same** hardcoded `~/.hermes-soul-test` (a `detects persona from SOUL.md` test in each). When vitest runs the two files in parallel they race:

```
Error: Destination already exists: /Users/<user>/.hermes-soul-test. Remove it first or choose a different name.
 ❯ HarnessService.importFromDir lib/services/harness.ts:1436
```

Hit live on 2026-06-25 — intermittent, ordering-dependent.

## Side effect (safety)

The natural cleanup `rm -rf ~/.hermes-*` is genuinely dangerous: those names collide with **real** agent home dirs (`~/.hermes-cryptids`, `~/.hermes-cyborg`, `~/.hermes-egregore`, …) holding live `auth.json`/state. A destructive-command guard correctly blocks it — so the test cruft can't be safely bulk-cleaned. The fix below removes the cruft at the source.

## Fix

Mock `os.homedir()` per-test to a fresh tmpdir so destinations land in tmp (auto-cleaned, isolated, no cross-file collisions). The pattern already exists elsewhere in the suite — e.g. `surfaces/disconnect/route.test.ts`:

```ts
vi.spyOn(os, 'homedir').mockReturnValue('/home/test')
```

Apply the same to the agent-dir tests (pointing `homedir` at a per-test `mkdtemp` so the writes succeed in tmp), and drop the shared hardcoded `.hermes-soul-test` name.

## Likely offenders

- `lib/services/__tests__/harness-create.test.ts` (writes `~/.hermes-imported-agent`, `~/.hermes-soul-test`; no `homedir` mock)
- `lib/services/__tests__/harness-e2e.test.ts` (writes `~/.hermes-e2e-test-agent`, `~/.hermes-imported-agent`; no `homedir` mock)
- verify: `harness-duplicate.test.ts`, `deploy-route.integration.test.ts`, `agent-deploy-templates.test.ts`

## Acceptance

- After `pnpm test`, **no new `~/.hermes-*` dirs** appear in the real `$HOME`.
- No two test files share a hardcoded home destination path (kills the parallel race).

Switches the sanitization PR gate from full-tree to **diff-only**, and moves the **full-tree** audit to a **scheduled** lane. The base package (`infra/templates/**`, docs, base SOUL/skills) ships to every HSM-created agent, so it must never leak secrets/PII/use-case particulars — this keeps that protection while stopping the gate from flaky-blocking contributors on pre-existing, untouched content.

## What changed
- **`scripts/check_sanitization.py`** — new `git_changed_files(base_ref, root)` (three-dot `git diff --name-only BASE...HEAD`) + a `--diff` CLI mode. `--all` (full-tree) and `--diff` (PR range) feed the **same** two-layer, fail-closed detection; only file *selection* differs.
- **`.github/workflows/sanitization.yml`** — `pull_request` now runs `--diff` (scans only the PR's full range); `push: main` **stays on `--all`** (publish-time backstop, untouched).
- **`.github/workflows/sanitization-scheduled.yml`** (new) — daily cron (`17 9 * * *`) + `workflow_dispatch` running `--all` with **both layers, fail-closed** — the full-tree detection backstop.
- **`scripts/test_check_sanitization.py`** — added `TestDiffOnlyScope` (leak in a changed file is caught; a pre-existing leak in an unchanged file is not scanned by the PR gate but IS caught full-tree) and `TestGitChangedFiles` (three-dot range includes all PR commits, excludes base).

## Guardrails (owner-approved #77 comment) — all satisfied
1. **Scheduled full-tree gardener lane ships in this same PR** — `sanitization-scheduled.yml`, `--all`, both layers, fail-closed, on cron + dispatch. Full-tree *detection* added before/with removing full-tree *prevention* from the PR gate. ✅
2. **`push: main` kept on full-tree `--all`** — unchanged. ✅
3. **PR gate is diff-only over the full PR range** — `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD` (three-dot), via the new `--diff` mode → existing `select_sensitive_files()`. ✅
4. **Scope-only** — both layers kept, semantic layer still required, fail-closed semantics intact, **every regex/pattern byte-for-byte unchanged**. The diff touches only file-selection wiring + a new scheduled workflow + tests. ✅
5. **One-time clean cutover** — see below. ⚠️ deterministic clean; semantic blocked on a **pre-existing billing outage** (not a content leak). ⚠️

## Cutover result
- `python3 scripts/check_sanitization.py --all --deterministic-only` on current `main` → **clean** (exit 0). No pre-existing secret/PII leak is grandfathered past the now-diff-only PR gate.
- The full `--all` (semantic layer included) **cannot be confirmed clean**: on current `main` and every recent `push:main` run, the semantic step errors with `400 – Your credit balance is too low to access the Anthropic API`. This is a pre-existing infra/billing failure (the semantic gate is already red for everyone today), **not** a content finding — but per guardrail #5 the strict `--all` clean confirmation does not hold, so this PR is left for maintainer decision rather than auto-merged.

## Overview

In a multi-agent deployment where multiple Hermes agent containers share a single inference backend — whether a local Ollama instance or a cloud provider API with a shared org-level key — KV cache is not isolated between agents. This is a latent privacy and security concern worth documenting and mitigating.

## How it arises

HSM deploys multiple agent containers that each make independent inference calls to the same upstream endpoint:

- **Local models (Ollama):** All agents point to the same host Ollama instance (`host.docker.internal:11434`). Ollama has no tenant isolation — it is designed for single-user local use.
- **Cloud APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.):** These providers scope prompt cache to the API key / organization. HSM deployments typically share one org-level API key across all agents, meaning all agents share the same cache namespace at the provider.

## What leaks and how

**Prefix cache sharing (passive):**
LLM inference servers implement KV cache reuse for common prompt prefixes as a performance optimization. When two agents share an identical prefix — which is likely if they use the same base system prompt — the inference server reuses the same cached KV state for both. The model's internal attention state for the shared prefix is the same physical computation for all agents sharing that prefix.

This does not cause spontaneous content bleed (Agent B's output won't contain Agent A's private tokens), but it means the attention state is not isolated between agents.

**Stale slot memory (passive):**
In Ollama and vLLM, KV memory slots are not zeroed on release. When a slot is freed by one agent and reassigned to another, the new agent's prefill overwrites it — but there is a window where physically non-cleared prior state exists. This is a design assumption in both systems (single-user or trusted multi-tenant use).

**Timing side-channel (active/adversarial):**
Peer-reviewed research (PROMPTPEEK, NDSS 2025; Cache Me Catch You, NDSS 2026) demonstrates that an adversarial client sharing the same inference backend can reconstruct other users' recent prompts with >95% accuracy using timing oracles derived from KV cache hit/miss latency differences. This requires intentional probing (~500-1000 requests per token) but only needs API access — no elevated privileges.

The same attack class applies to shared Ollama instances and to shared-key cloud API deployments.

**Published CVEs:**
- CVE-2025-25183 / GHSA-rm76-4mrf-v9r8: vLLM prefix cache hash collision enabling cache poisoning (patched v0.7.2)
- CVE-2025-1953: vLLM/SGLang KV cache hash collision via meet-in-the-middle (NDSS 2026)
- Azure OpenAI Nov 2025: cross-tenant training data contamination via fine-tuning cache race condition (MSRC advisory)

## Risk levels

| Scenario | Passive risk | Active/adversarial risk |
|----------|-------------|------------------------|
| Shared Ollama, all first-party trusted agents | Low | Medium (if any agent ever compromised) |
| Shared cloud API key, same org | Low | Medium (same) |
| Shared Ollama with any untrusted or third-party agent | Medium | High |
| Separate API keys per agent (different orgs) | None | None |

## Mitigations

**Short term — break shared prefix matching:**
Insert a unique non-guessable token (e.g. a per-agent UUID or HMAC) in the first few tokens of each agent's system prompt. Since KV cache reuse is keyed on exact token sequence, this ensures no two agents ever share a cache block, regardless of how similar the rest of their prompts are. Low cost, no infrastructure change required.

**Medium term — per-agent key provisioning:**
Where the provider supports it, provision separate API keys per agent so caching is scoped per-key rather than per-org. Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI currently offer a sub-key/per-user key provisioning API, so this is not available today for those providers. Worth tracking as providers evolve their multi-tenant offerings.

**Longer term — inference isolation:**
For deployments with strict privacy requirements between agents, run separate inference backend instances per agent or per trust boundary. This provides full KV isolation at the cost of additional resource overhead.

## References

- arXiv:2502.07776 — Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs (Stanford/CRFM, 2025)
- PROMPTPEEK — I Know What You Asked (NDSS 2025)
- Cache Me, Catch You (NDSS 2026)
- NVIDIA Security Blog — Structuring Applications to Secure the KV Cache (Apr 2025)
- Ollama issue tracker: no documented per-caller KV isolation

Before: Swarm Map had no way to keep a tool's output out of an agent's model context, so outputs licensed under terms like the Kaitiakitanga License (Papa Reo's te reo Māori transcripts, which may not go to services that collect or use them) couldn't be handled safely, and there was no Papa Reo transcription for agents.

## What
- **Auto-seed on first contact.** A sender's card is created from *observed* platform facts only — display name, the id forms they present, first/last seen. Nothing about them is inferred. The seed happens before the read, so a first-time sender is recognized on their **first** turn, not their second.
- **Self-learned id aliases.** `pre_llm_call` supplies both id forms per turn (Signal carries a phone number *and* an ACI UUID), so the plugin learns the mapping itself and records it on the card. This works for arbitrary senders; `resolved-identities.json` only ever covers admin-entered identities and so can't cover a stranger who joins a group — it stays as a fallback.
- **`remember_person` tool.** The agent records what it *learns* about how to talk to someone, instead of a human editing frontmatter.
- `PERSON_MEMORY_READONLY=1` restores slice-1 (read-only) behavior; `PERSON_MEMORY_DISABLED=1` still disables the plugin entirely.

## Why
Slice 1 was read-only, so the adaptation layer only worked for people someone had hand-written a markdown card for — in practice, nobody. A memory layer that needs manual seeding isn't a memory layer. This makes the card set populate and improve through ordinary interaction, with no manual step and no admin configuration.

## Verification
30-case harness against the real template: auto-create on first contact, first-turn recognition, both alias directions resolving to one card (no duplicates), no rewrite across repeated turns, tool-driven enrichment reshaping the directive, read-only mode, fail-open on unknown sender / malformed event / unwritable directory, and traversal safety. Existing 0.2.0 alias tests re-run green (8/8), so the `resolved-identities.json` fallback is not regressed.

## Risk
This plugin now **writes**, where before it only read. Mitigations, all tested:
- Writes are atomic (tmp+rename) and gated on actual content change; `last_seen` is date-granular, bounding disk cost to one write per person per day.
- Every write path is fail-open — a write failure degrades to "no memory of this person", never a broken turn.
- Agent-written values are rejected if they contain anything identifier-shaped (phone/email/UUID), because these fields are echoed verbatim into shared group sessions. Writable fields are an allowlist; ids live in the filename and the non-injected `alias_ids` field.
- Untrusted platform display names are stripped of control characters and length-capped before they can reach the model's context.

Worth a second opinion on: auto-seeding means the agent keeps a durable record of everyone who ever messages it, including in groups. That's the point of the feature, but it is a new persistent-record property — `PERSON_MEMORY_READONLY=1` is the opt-out.

## Scope, stated honestly up front

A newly created agent's Google MCP previously **could not start**. After this it starts, can authenticate, and persists its tokens — but it **grants nothing** until an operator adds Drive folder IDs. That limit is deliberate (see Security below), not an oversight. The original title said "make Google MCP actually work"; that oversold it.

## Four defects, all silent

| # | Defect | Symptom |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `GOOGLE_MCP_DIR` probed only `~/Documents/GitHub/google-multiplayer-mcp`; the repo is commonly cloned as `google-mcp` | operator ticks "Google", gets **no Google** — no mount, no `mcp_servers` entry, no error |
| 2 | `--config /opt/google/config.yaml` | only `/opt/google/tokens` is mounted → `readFileSync` → **exit 1** |
| 3 | nothing wrote a permission config anywhere | no file to read even with 1 and 2 fixed |
| 4 | `GOOGLE_TOKEN_DIR` set nowhere | server fell back to `$HOME/.nimbleco-google/tokens`; with `HOME=/opt/data` the `/opt/google/tokens` mount was **dead weight** |

Plus: `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID`/`SECRET` were never provisioned and HSM never writes `~/.nimbleco-google/config.json`, so `loadGlobalConfig()` always threw and OAuth was **impossible** regardless of scoping. Now written to the agent `.env` (from the request, else inherited from HSM's own env) and referenced from the `mcp_servers` env block.

## Security: why the default grants nothing

`google-multiplayer-mcp`'s `permissions.ts`:

```ts
/** Get allowed folder IDs for a service. Empty array = no restriction. */
```

**Empty `folders` means unrestricted.** So `drive: {access: write, folders: []}` would hand every new agent unscoped read/write over an entire Google account. The wizard collects no folder IDs, so every service generates at `access: none`, with a header explaining how to scope it. A test asserts **every** generated service is `none`, not a sampled few.

## Found while fixing the above

`generateEnvContent` wrote a wizard-supplied Brave key as `BRAVE_API_KEY` only. The runtime reads **exclusively** `BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY` (`plugins/web/brave_free/provider.py`, plus the auto-detect table in `tools/web_tools.py`); nothing reads `BRAVE_API_KEY`. The key was invisible to the agent — so the `search_backend: brave-free` pin also added here would have fallen straight through to auto-detect, inert on exactly the agents it was for. Both names are now written.

## Independent audit findings, all addressed

**BLOCKING — the preflight ran after side effects.** The 400 sat below `mkdirSync` and the `.env` write and returned from inside the `try`, making the `catch`'s cleanup unreachable. A rejected deploy left a half-created agent dir **containing the resolved plaintext LLM key**, then 409'd every retry of that name forever — recoverable only by `rm -rf` from a shell. On the Letta runtime it orphaned an already-created brain agent too. The file states the correct rule two functions above: *"before a single door byte is written."* The preflight now sits above **every** side effect, including the Letta branch.

Also fixed: unvalidated `googleIdentity` interpolated into YAML (`"a: b"` breaks the parse and exits the server — reintroducing this very bug; a newline could inject permission entries past the deny-by-default); the probe now requires `node_modules` as well as `dist/index.js` (the bundle imports bare `googleapis`/`js-yaml`, so a pruned checkout passed and exited 1 at runtime); non-absolute `GOOGLE_MCP_DIR` is rejected (Docker reads a relative volume source as a **named volume**, mounting an empty dir over the bundle); the 400 carries `ok: false`; and the generated OAuth runbook now passes `GOOGLE_TOKEN_DIR` and the client creds, without which it hit EROFS on the read-only container.

## Testing

18 route-level integration tests running the **real** deploy logic and real fs writes against temp dirs — including that a rejected deploy leaves no dir, no docker start, no key-registry writes, and that the same name is still deployable afterwards.

**Mutation-verified** rather than trusted green: reverting each of the six fixes individually fails a test (preflight position → 4 failures; the other five → 1 each). `911 passed` on the real tree, `tsc --noEmit` clean.

Note for reviewers: this repo has stale `.wt-*` worktree directories that vitest collects by default and which fail for unrelated reasons — run with `--exclude '**/.wt-*/**'`.

## Not in this PR

`duplicateOverlay` recursively copies the agent data dir, so a duplicate inherits the source's `google-permissions.yaml` **and its `google-tokens/`** — sharing Google identity and OAuth tokens between agents. Same isolation concern the code already handles for surface env vars; deserves its own change.

## What & why

The base package (`infra/templates/**`, docs, base skills/soul) ships to **every** agent HSM creates, but HSM has had **no CI gate at all**. This adds a layered, fail-closed sanitization gate so the base can never ship secrets, PII, or use-case-specific particulars — **even from an automated contribution** (e.g. an agent opening a PR).

## How
- **`scripts/check_sanitization.py`** — two layers, both must pass:
  - **Deterministic** (`scan_secrets`): secret/API keys (Anthropic/OpenAI/GitHub/AWS/Google/Slack), private-key blocks, JWTs, quoted hardcoded credentials, real email addresses (placeholder domains whitelisted), phone numbers. Placeholder-aware (ignores `xxxx…` runs). **No API key needed** — enforces immediately.
  - **Semantic** (`assess`): an LLM flags use-case-specific particulars (real names, orgs tied to a case, document/dataset IDs, case codenames, specific dates/locations). **Required → fails closed** if the key is unavailable.
  - **Full-tree** (`--all`): scans the whole base surface, so a pre-existing leak can't hide in an untouched file (the diff-only gap).
- **`.github/workflows/sanitization.yml`** — runs the scanner's own unit tests + the full-tree base scan on every PR and on push to main.
- **Sanitized a real pre-existing leak**: an operator SSH target (`<user>@<host>`) in a base planning doc.

## Tests
18 scanner unit tests (RG-TDD); the current base scans **clean** on the deterministic layer.

## One setup step (admin)
Set the repo secret **`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`** to enable the semantic layer. Until then the deterministic layer (keys/PII) still enforces; the semantic step fails closed to signal the missing secret.

- CVE-2025-1953: vLLM/SGLang KV cache hash collision via meet-in-the-middle (NDSS 2026)
- Azure OpenAI Nov 2025: cross-tenant training data contamination via fine-tuning cache race condition (MSRC advisory)

## Risk levels

| Scenario | Passive risk | Active/adversarial risk |
|----------|-------------|------------------------|
| Shared Ollama, all first-party trusted agents | Low | Medium (if any agent ever compromised) |
| Shared cloud API key, same org | Low | Medium (same) |
| Shared Ollama with any untrusted or third-party agent | Medium | High |
| Separate API keys per agent (different orgs) | None | None |

## Mitigations

**Short term — break shared prefix matching:**
Insert a unique non-guessable token (e.g. a per-agent UUID or HMAC) in the first few tokens of each agent's system prompt. Since KV cache reuse is keyed on exact token sequence, this ensures no two agents ever share a cache block, regardless of how similar the rest of their prompts are. Low cost, no infrastructure change required.

**Medium term — per-agent key provisioning:**
Where the provider supports it, provision separate API keys per agent so caching is scoped per-key rather than per-org. Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI currently offer a sub-key/per-user key provisioning API, so this is not available today for those providers. Worth tracking as providers evolve their multi-tenant offerings.

**Longer term — inference isolation:**
For deployments with strict privacy requirements between agents, run separate inference backend instances per agent or per trust boundary. This provides full KV isolation at the cost of additional resource overhead.

## References

- arXiv:2502.07776 — Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs (Stanford/CRFM, 2025)
- PROMPTPEEK — I Know What You Asked (NDSS 2025)
- Cache Me, Catch You (NDSS 2026)
- NVIDIA Security Blog — Structuring Applications to Secure the KV Cache (Apr 2025)
- Ollama issue tracker: no documented per-caller KV isolation

## What

- A third harness adapter behind the door: the Claude Agent SDK (`lib/runtimes/claude-sdk/`), with the same four verbs as Pi and Letta Code (start, send, read, veto). Lab only: no launcher, no UI, nothing wired into the app.
- The model route speaks a second wire format, Anthropic Messages, with the key swap, metering and the budget cap. The OpenAI chat format is unchanged.
- A fake SDK and a scripted Anthropic model for CI, twelve shims broken on purpose, a cell image for the sealed Docker rig, and four checks that are this harness's own.
- `docs/lab/claude-sdk.md`: what is proven and what is not.

## Why

The door's promise is that the rules hold whatever the harness is. Two harnesses that both speak the OpenAI chat format were not much of a test of that. The Claude Agent SDK speaks another format, is a compiled program, and has a permission system of its own, so it tests parts of the contract the first two did not.

## Verification

Real Claude Agent SDK 0.3.325 (Claude Code 2.1.325), scripted model, no key and no account:

- **Process level: 18 of 18 checks pass.** Twelve broken shims each turned their named checks red.
- **Sealed Docker cell: 24 of 24 pass** (S0-S3, the shared checks, C8, C9, C10, and the four of its own). Eleven broken rigs each turned their named checks red.
- **Pi 1.5.2 and Letta Code 0.34.60 re-run after the shared changes:** Pi 14 of 14 at process level and 20 of 20 in its cell; Letta Code 16 of 16 and 22 of 22. All four matrix files were made again from those runs.
- **Network, by hand:** a packet capture in the cell during the Docker run. In the in-cell checks that run no probe, every packet the cell sent went to the door or to Docker's resolver. Started with its defaults instead, in the same sealed container, the SDK looked up `api.anthropic.com` ten times; every lookup failed and no packet left for anywhere but the door.
- `npx vitest run`: 255 files, all passing. `npx tsc --noEmit`: clean. Sanitize gate, deterministic layer: clean on every changed file. The semantic layer needs a key this machine does not hold, so it runs here in CI.
- **Mutation, by hand:** 89 changes to the new code, one at a time. 84 turned a named test red. Four of the other five now have a test; the fifth was a guard nothing could make refuse, and was removed.

What the real SDK did that the plan did not expect, each now with a test and a broken shim:

- Its permission callback is not asked about every call. It ran a file read in its work folder and a shell `ls` without asking. The shim tells it to ask about each tool by name.
- Its hooks do not run in its minimal mode, so the callback is the veto.
- A failed model call ends the turn as a `result` of subtype `success`, with the error as its text. The shim posts nothing unless the turn says it did not fail.
- It is a compiled program, so no tripwire can be loaded into it. Its traffic is watched through a proxy at process level, which is weaker than for the other two harnesses. Its matrix says so.

Not verified:

- **Nothing was run against Anthropic's API.** A one-turn run is written (`npm run conformance -- anthropic-live`) and needs an SDK folder and a key file. CI runs the same code with a stand-in at each end.
- Anthropic's Commercial Terms and usage policy were not read. The doc has a paragraph on what the SDK's own pages say and what is left open.

## Risk

- **Shared contracts changed, each additively:** `ModelShape` gained optional parts; the shared key check reads the key from whichever header the format uses; the credential guard takes two named exceptions and decides itself what each may hold; a harness can add a caveat to its own matrix; the scripted model has a second format; two rule statements name both formats; the Docker rig's entry picks its adapter from a table. Two other branches are changing `lib/door` and `lib/core` at the same time, so expect small merge conflicts there.
- The SDK is not open source and is not a dependency of this repo. It is pinned in `conformance/docker/claude-sdk/` for the test image only, and Dependabot's update pull requests are switched off for that folder, as for Letta Code's.
- "Ask about every tool" rests on one settings line on one pinned version. The shim sends no turn to another version, and C4q is the check that would notice.
- One gap found in the shared suite and left alone: for a harness that keeps its thread, the scripted model's OpenAI side never asks for the removed tool in the third turn of C15t. The doc says why it was not changed here.

## What

- Adds `lib/core/`: one policy record, a 35-rule catalogue, and `decide()`, the single function that says who an agent may hear and answer, which tools it may run, and when its budget is spent.
- Adds `lib/door/`: the sidecar that owns chat in, chat out and model traffic. Fake connector only. Receipts for every decision, outbound redaction that fails closed, one reply per turn, a model route that swaps a placeholder for the real key, meters tokens and keeps spend in a ledger by month.
- Adds `lib/runtimes/pi/`: the Pi shim (one `pi --mode rpc` process per session), a prompt preamble a sender cannot forge, and a tool gate extension that blocks on anything but an explicit allow.
- Adds `conformance/`: 38 scenario pairs, fake-proof guards with negative controls, a scripted model, a fake Pi for CI, fourteen shim checks, eight deliberately broken shims, and a matrix file generated from a real Pi 1.5.2 run.
- Adds `conformance/docker/`: a sealed Docker cell for Pi and the rig around it (the sidecar's side, a sink that stands in for the internet, a control that proves the sink can be hit), a probe that tries each way out, a runner that starts one rig per check and removes only what it made, and a second matrix file generated from that run.
- Adds the spec, the plan and a report under `docs/lab/`.

Nothing is wired into the app, the UI, the Hermes path or any running agent. No dependency was added.

## Why

Every harness enforces chat rules differently, so each new harness has meant re-rendering the same rules and hoping they hold. This slice tries the other shape on Pi: rules are decided once, outside the harness, and the per-harness code shrinks to "start it, send text, read text, veto a tool".

## Verification

- `npx vitest run`, after merging main (which now has #337): 211 files, 4149 passed, 1 skipped (pre-existing).
- `npx tsc --noEmit`: clean.
- Sanitization gate, deterministic layer, on the PR diff: clean. The semantic layer runs in CI only.
- `SWARMLAB_PI_BIN=... npm run conformance` against a real Pi 1.5.2 install: 23 of 23. All fourteen checks pass, and each of the eight broken shims turned its named checks red. `conformance/matrix/pi-1.5.2.process.json` was written by that run, and a CI test now fails if that file no longer matches the suite.
- `npm run conformance:docker` with real Pi 1.5.2 in a sealed cell, on Docker Desktop 4.76 for Mac (engine 29.5.2): 29 of 29. S0-S3, C8, C9 and C10 pass, and so do the thirteen process-level checks run again in the cell. Ten rigs broken on purpose (a route to the sink, an ordinary network, the key in the cell's environment, the key in a file, a writable cell, a host folder mounted, a file where a Docker socket would be, a door with a route out, a sink nobody can prove works, C10 with the gate left in) each turned its named checks red for the reason it names. A rig handed a real-looking key is refused before Docker is asked for anything, and again by the cell itself. `conformance/matrix/pi-1.5.2.docker.json` was written by that run, and a CI test fails if it no longer matches the suite.
- The Docker checks were then broken by hand twice (the sink's log ignored; the probe's answers ignored) and the must-fail tests went red both times.
- An audit of the Docker cell then tried, by hand in a live cell, ways out the probe does not: every TCP port on Docker's side of the cell network, a port another lab container published, DNS watched with a packet capture (with a control that was seen leaving), IPv6 without the cell's own setting, and the model route and the door's port poked from inside. Nothing got out and no key came back. It found the run went red on a network that answers no IPv6 DNS question (fixed), three checks with no broken rig (added), and that S1-S3 did not read what Docker actually gave the container (they now do; a cell given a shared process namespace, a published port and loosened seccomp turned S1 and S2 red when tried). These by-hand trials are not standing checks; the report says which.
- Not run: C13 (no tool verdict depends on who asked yet, so it could not fail for the reason it names), C7, C12b. The Docker run is not in CI.
- Mutation checks, run by hand and not committed: listed in `docs/lab/pi-slice.md`, "What this does not show", item 11.
- Not verified: the Docker run on any other machine, Docker version or engine, or on Linux.

## Risk

- **The wall is shown on one machine, for the ways out that were tried.** With Pi in the lab's Docker cell, a tool it ran reached nothing but the door and read no secret, also with the tool gate removed. That is Docker Desktop for Mac, one version, and a list of probes, not a proof: a way out that is not on the list was not tried. `docs/lab/pi-slice.md` lists the limits (DNS judged by its answer, no IPv6 control, wall-check lines with no broken cell behind them, the cell token readable inside the cell, no limits tested, and more). Do not read this PR as "Pi is safe to deploy".
- **These are lab images and a lab rig.** Nothing in Swarm Map starts a cell like this, and no running agent is in one. In the rig the door has no route out either; a door that talks to a real model and a real chat platform needs one, and that side is not tested.
- **The Docker run needs an internet connection for its controls.** A one-off container asks DNS for three names before a run (and, if this machine's resolver answers no IPv6 question, asks a public resolver itself), and one cell that is broken on purpose is put on an ordinary network and opens one connection from there. No public address is written in the repo.
- **At process level, "nothing left this machine" is shown for Pi's own Node runtime only.** The tripwire there does not see a program Pi starts that is not Node. The Docker cell is what covers that.
- **The key swap and the budget cap exist for one wire format** (OpenAI chat-completions). A harness that speaks another has neither; the route refuses its calls.
- **Pi is given no direct messages**, because its sessions share one folder on disk.
- **The bot loop limit is not enforced.** With bots allowed, two bots can answer each other without end.
- **The credential preflight is a list of names and shapes.** A credential it has not been taught goes through; Pi's environment is listed by hand for that reason.
- **Several check lines have no broken shim behind them** (C2, C4a, C12, C15 and parts of C1, C5v, C8p). The report lists them.
- A scripted model tests plumbing only.
- The fake Pi was wrong once already (real Pi never asks the gate about an undeclared tool). The real-Pi run caught it. The fake can drift again when Pi changes; the pin is 1.5.2.
- `tsconfig.json` gains `allowImportingTsExtensions`, and `vitest.config.ts` excludes `conformance/suites/*.real.test.ts`. Both are small, but they touch shared config.
- This is one branch rather than the four stacked PRs the plan described. It is large (about 16,100 lines, 1,600 of them a lock file, mostly tests and scenario files). The commits can be read one at a time.
- An earlier commit on this branch held a longer copy of the spec. The tip does not, but the branch history still does. Squash on merge if that matters.

## Links

- `docs/lab/pi-slice.md`: what exists, how to run it, what it does not show.
- `docs/lab/primitives.md`: the spec. `docs/lab/plan-pi.md`: the plan as written.

## Why
Adding an OpenRouter key to the fleet was impossible through the UI — the Keys vault dropdown and the per-harness key-add dropdown both omitted `openrouter` entirely (screenshot from Juniper: dropdown lists anthropic/openai/google/aws/github/brave/notion/telegram/custom, no openrouter). OpenRouter is the fleet's designated cheap-metered provider (`[intelligent-routing-cost]`, token-spend audit), and with Claude API credits exhausted the fleet is currently degrading straight to local GLM instead of a cheap metered rung.

## Root cause (deeper than the dropdown)
`openrouter` was also absent from `KeysService.PROVIDER_TO_VAR`, so it only resolved `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` via the generic fallback. That left it vulnerable to **hint-redirection**: a user-supplied name/envVar hint on the keys form silently wrote the key to the wrong var. A regression test proves the old behavior wrote `STALE_VAR=sk-or-...`. Mapping it canonically makes it immune, exactly like every other known provider (the existing brave test covers the same guarantee).

## Changes
- `app/(dashboard)/keys/page.tsx` + `app/(dashboard)/harnesses/[id]/page.tsx`: add `openrouter` to `KEY_PROVIDERS`
- `lib/services/keys.ts`: map `openrouter → OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in `PROVIDER_TO_VAR`
- `lib/model-catalog.ts`: add Kimi K2.7 Code (confirmed-live on OpenRouter, ~\$0.72/\$3.49 per M tok) as the cheap-metered workhorse rung above the local-GLM floor
- RGTDD tests for both the hint-redirection fix and the catalog rung

## Tests
`keys.test.ts` + `model-catalog.test.ts` + `harnesses/[id]/models/route.test.ts` — 67 passing. Typecheck clean on touched files.

- `zai`/GLM already mapped correctly (`GLM_API_KEY`); left untouched.
- Catalog is suggestions-only; the cascade editor accepts free-text, so per-agent cheaper picks (Qwen/DeepSeek-class) work without a catalog entry — verify the exact live slug before putting one in a cascade.

## Problem

`PUT /api/harnesses/:id/models` writes the model cascade into a live agent's `config.yaml` and the agent restarts onto it, with no validation. A model whose **provider has no configured credential for that agent** crash-loops it on restart — the motivating case: pushing `moonshotai/kimi-k2.7-code` via `openrouter` onto an agent that has no `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.

## What changed since the first revision

The original PR validated cascade models against `MODEL_CATALOG`. Review correctly rejected that: `MODEL_CATALOG` is a tiny ~2-per-provider **suggestions** list, **not** an allowlist (anthropic only lists `claude-sonnet-4-6` + `claude-haiku-4-5`). Strict membership would 400 **legitimate in-use models** — `claude-opus-4-8` (the fleet's actual model), newer gemini/gpt, etc. That's a regression. The strict-catalog check is **gone**.

## Fix — validate provider-credential PRESENCE, not catalog membership

In the `PUT` handler, before any config write:

1. **Empty/missing model id → always 400.** The unambiguous crash case; kept.
2. **Provider-credential presence.** Read the agent's configured provider keys and reject a cascade entry **only** when its provider is *definitively un-serviceable* for that agent.

New `readAgentEnvVarNames(dataDir)` (in `lib/services/harness.ts`, alongside the other `read*(dataDir)` readers the route already uses) reads the agent's `.env` and returns the set of var **names** present — never values, never logged. Same parse semantics as `keys.ts` `parseEnvFile` (skips comments, blanks, empty/`${...}` values).

`validateCascadeEntries(entries, presentEnvVars)` rejects an entry **iff**: the provider needs a known single credential, we know which env var(s), **and** none are present.

## Fail-open is the load-bearing constraint

Zero false-rejections of legitimate models is the bar — blocking a valid config is worse than missing an exotic bad one. We reject **only** when positively certain:

- **Enforced (single, unambiguous credential):** `anthropic` (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` *or* `ANTHROPIC_TOKEN`), `openai` (`OPENAI_API_KEY`), `openrouter` (`OPENROUTER_API_KEY`).
- **`ollama` / `custom` → always allowed.** Local / `base_url`, no key needed.
- **`google` / `gemini` → always allowed.** Multiple auth modes (API key, Vertex+ADC, service-account JSON); a missing `GOOGLE_API_KEY` is *not* proof of un-serviceability → fail open.
- **`bedrock` → always allowed.** AWS multi-var creds / instance role / `~/.aws` that needn't appear in the agent `.env`; absence isn't proof → fail open.
- **Unknown providers (`nous`, proxies, anything else) → always allowed.** No authoritative credential to check.
- **No env-var info → only the empty-id guard applies.**

Model ids are no longer checked against any list (only the provider's credential is). `claude-opus-4-8` and any future/exotic model id pass as long as the agent can actually serve its provider.

## Tests

- `lib/__tests__/model-catalog.test.ts` — credential-presence unit tests (provider-with-key incl. an *uncatalogued* model passes; provider-without-key rejected listing model+provider+expected var; `ANTHROPIC_TOKEN` path; multi-error reporting; `ollama`/`custom`/`google`/`gemini`/`bedrock`/`nous`/empty-provider fail-open; empty-id rejected even for no-key providers). Catalog-membership tests removed.
- `app/api/harnesses/[id]/models/route.test.ts` — route integration (provider-with-key → 200 + write; openrouter-without-key → 400 + no write; `fallback_providers` shape; `ollama` no key → 200; unknown provider fail-open → 200; empty cascade → 400; empty model id → 400). Credential reader mocked.
- **Full suite: 366 pass.** The 4 failures in `usage.test.ts` are a **pre-existing** `better-sqlite3` native ABI mismatch (NODE_MODULE_VERSION 127 vs 137), unrelated to this change. `tsc --noEmit` clean.

## For the reviewer

- **Where I chose to fail open (please sanity-check):** `google`/`gemini`, `bedrock`, and all unknown providers are **never** rejected on credential grounds. A real but exotic mis-config (e.g. an OpenAI-compatible provider behind `custom` with the wrong/absent key) won't be caught — by design, to guarantee no false-rejections of valid configs. The empty-id guard is the only universal floor.
- **`ANTHROPIC_TOKEN`:** anthropic is serviceable if *either* `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_TOKEN` is set (the keys.ts bearer-vs-apikey split), so a bearer-only agent isn't falsely rejected.
- No deploy / restart / merge performed. Code-only guard for human review.

**Task for the gardener.** Model IDs change often (Anthropic retires older ones); the create-new wizard and existing-harness cascade editor can offer models that are retired → agent crash-loops on restart. Add live freshness checking. Anthropic-first, extensible.

## Design (ready to build)
1. `lib/services/model-freshness.ts` — `fetchLiveModels('anthropic')`: find an Anthropic key via the keys service, call `GET /v1/models` (auth `x-api-key` + `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01`, **no beta header**; paginate), cache to disk with ~1h TTL. **Fail-soft**: no key / network error → return `null`, callers fall back to the static `MODEL_CATALOG` unflagged (never block the UI).
2. `GET /api/models/live?provider=anthropic` → `{ models, fetchedAt }`.
3. **Freshness signal = list membership.** Retired models simply disappear from `/v1/models` (404 on retrieve) — there is no "deprecated" flag in the response. So: catalog entries **absent** from the live list → mark `retired: true`; live IDs **not** in `MODEL_CATALOG` → offer as suggestable/new.
4. Consume in **both** the create-new wizard model step **and** the existing-harness cascade editor (`app/api/harnesses/[id]/models`) — show a "retired — pick a current model" warning on stale entries.
5. Provider-keyed so openai/google can be added later; wire **Anthropic only** now.

## Notes / guardrails
- Verify model IDs against the live list, never hardcode from training data.
- The models endpoint object carries `id`, `display_name`, `created_at`, and (since Mar 2026) `max_input_tokens`/`max_tokens`/`capabilities`.
- RGTDD + independent audit before merge, per the repo's dev flow.

Context: raised 2026-07-02; deferred here from a live session so it lands as durable, gardener-pickup-able work rather than dying in chat.

hits.body:
## Problem

Assigning a vault key stored with `provider: "custom"` writes the **wrong** env var to the agent's `.env`. `resolveEnvVar()` maps only by provider (`PROVIDER_TO_VAR`) with a `${PROVIDER}_API_KEY` fallback, so a custom key named `capsolver` resolves to **`CUSTOM_API_KEY`** instead of `CAPSOLVER_API_KEY`. The key's `name` was ignored.

Real-world impact: the CapSolver key (`provider: custom`, `name: capsolver`) is assigned to 6 agents in the vault but was **materialized to none** — the HSM "assign via API" path silently wrote `CUSTOM_API_KEY`, so the `captcha-cascade` plugin never found its credential. Discovered while wiring CapSolver onto the osint agent.

## Fix

- **`resolveEnvVar(provider, value, hints?)`** — resolution order: explicit `envVar` hint → `PROVIDER_TO_VAR[provider]` → name-derived (`"capsolver"` → `CAPSOLVER_API_KEY`; a name that's already a full identifier like `OPEN_MEASURES_API_KEY` is kept) → the old `${PROVIDER}_API_KEY` fallback.
- Threaded `EnvVarHints {name, envVar}` through `writeKeyToEnv` / `removeKeyFromEnv` and every caller (`add`, `setAssignment`, `rotateValue`, `remove`) so write and remove target the **same** var. `removeKeyFromEnv` now derives via `resolveEnvVar` instead of its own copy of the fallback.
- Added optional **`envVar`** to `Key`/`KeyInput` (persisted on add/update) and a custom-only **"Env var"** field in the keys UI for precise control when a display name differs from the target var.

## Tests

New `custom-provider env-var routing` suite: name→var derivation, full-identifier passthrough, explicit `envVar` override, and remove clearing the derived var. Full suite green (660 passed), `tsc --noEmit` clean, no new lint errors.

## Note

The existing `capsolver` vault key needs no migration — name-derivation resolves it correctly on the next assign. (The osint agent was unblocked out-of-band by writing the value directly; this makes the vault path correct for the other 5 assigned agents.)

## What & why

The base package (`infra/templates/**`, docs, base skills/soul) ships to **every** agent HSM creates, but HSM has had **no CI gate at all**. This adds a layered, fail-closed sanitization gate so the base can never ship secrets, PII, or use-case-specific particulars — **even from an automated contribution** (e.g. an agent opening a PR).

## How
- **`scripts/check_sanitization.py`** — two layers, both must pass:
  - **Deterministic** (`scan_secrets`): secret/API keys (Anthropic/OpenAI/GitHub/AWS/Google/Slack), private-key blocks, JWTs, quoted hardcoded credentials, real email addresses (placeholder domains whitelisted), phone numbers. Placeholder-aware (ignores `xxxx…` runs). **No API key needed** — enforces immediately.
  - **Semantic** (`assess`): an LLM flags use-case-specific particulars (real names, orgs tied to a case, document/dataset IDs, case codenames, specific dates/locations). **Required → fails closed** if the key is unavailable.
  - **Full-tree** (`--all`): scans the whole base surface, so a pre-existing leak can't hide in an untouched file (the diff-only gap).
- **`.github/workflows/sanitization.yml`** — runs the scanner's own unit tests + the full-tree base scan on every PR and on push to main.
- **Sanitized a real pre-existing leak**: an operator SSH target (`<user>@<host>`) in a base planning doc.

## Tests
18 scanner unit tests (RG-TDD); the current base scans **clean** on the deterministic layer.

## One setup step (admin)
Set the repo secret **`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`** to enable the semantic layer. Until then the deterministic layer (keys/PII) still enforces; the semantic step fails closed to signal the missing secret.

## What

Add an **Analytics** tab within each harness (per-agent view) plus a **fleet-wide analytics view**, showing regularly-updating operational metrics.

## Per-harness analytics tab

- Which surfaces are being used most (Signal / Telegram / Discord / Slack / Mattermost)
- Who is messaging the bot the most per surface (top users by message count in time window)
- Message volume per surface per day/week

### Not per-surface (agent-level metrics)
- **Cost tracking:** estimated spend per agent per day/week/month (model usage × per-model pricing)
- **Tool calls:** which tools the agent is calling, frequency, success/failure rates
- **Model usage breakdown:** which models in the cascade are being used, input/output tokens per model, escalation frequency (cheap → premium)

## Fleet-wide analytics view

- Total token spend across all agents, broken down by model
- Cost breakdown by agent (which agents are expensive vs cheap)
- Surface distribution across the fleet
- Model cascade efficiency (how often cheap tier handles requests vs escalating)

## Cost-calculation correctness requirement (critical)

Cost estimation **must not be independently re-implemented in every place cost is mentioned** across the codebase. Instead:

- There should be a **single source of truth** for per-model pricing (one config table / module, not scattered constants)
- The analytics tab should consume that shared variable, not compute its own estimate
- Add a **check/audit** that cost values displayed across Swarm Map (analytics tab, any existing cost displays, budget alerts, etc.) are all derived from the same source — flag any place that hardcodes or re-computes pricing independently

This prevents the maintenance trap where pricing updates in one place silently diverge from another.

## Context

- Connects to the gardener analytics handoff (`handoffs/2026-07/23-juniper-hsm-analytics-tab-harness-fleet-tools-model-tokens.md` in nimbleco-memory) — that has the full Phase 1-3 breakdown
- digicryptids already has per-request `req.llmUsage.totalTokens` tracking and a `usage_logs` table — that's the existing pattern to generalize fleet-wide
- The `[token-spend-audit]` thread (Anthropic spend is not sustainable) is the financial pressure driving this

## Open questions (for design, not blocking the issue)

- Data collection model: push (agents emit metrics to HSM) vs pull (HSM reads agent logs/DB)?
- Storage: time-series in Postgres, SQLite per-agent, or central analytics DB?
- Time granularity: real-time, hourly, daily?

## What
- Swarm Map listens on `127.0.0.1` on macOS (pm2 and `bin/dev.sh`); Linux keeps `0.0.0.0`, because there `host.docker.internal` is the Docker bridge address. `HSM_BIND_HOST` (bare IP) overrides; `HSM_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0` restores the old behaviour.
- `pnpm pm2:reapply` re-applies pm2's cached start arguments, and validates the config before it stops the running app.
- With `CF_ACCESS_TEAM_DOMAIN` and `CF_ACCESS_AUD` set, every request that arrived through Cloudflare must carry a valid Access JWT (RS256 against the team's keys, issuer, audience, expiry), pages included. Unset = off. Half set = edge requests get 503. On-host requests (agents, gates, SSH tunnel) skip this and keep the operator-session gate.
- README and AGENTS document both settings.

## Why
Listening on every interface let anyone on the local network skip the Access login, and Access was enforced only at Cloudflare's edge, so a deleted or misapplied policy would have left the dashboard open through the tunnel.

## Verification
- Rebased onto main as one commit. The agent-port loopback part of the original change landed in #344 and is dropped here; this PR now touches only the dashboard's own bind address and the Access check.
- Tests: `lib/auth/cf-access.test.ts` (signature, alg pinning, issuer, audience, expiry, key rotation, fetch backoff), `proxy.test.ts` (edge vs on-host, fail-closed, matcher), new `ecosystem.config.test.ts` (per-platform default, override, refusal of non-IP values, reapply ordering).

- The earlier semantic sanitize flag (the README copyright line) is covered by the copyright-holder exemption added to `sanitize.config.json` in #306; nothing was changed to the gate here.
- Not verified on a running host.

## Risk
- After deploy on macOS, anything that reached the dashboard over the network by IP stops connecting. A Cloudflare Tunnel on the same machine must point at `127.0.0.1` or `localhost`. Rollback: start pm2 with `HSM_BIND_HOST=0.0.0.0` and run `pnpm pm2:reapply`.
- A plain `pm2 restart` keeps the old bind; `pnpm pm2:reapply` is needed to pick up the change.
- If an Access application has bypass paths, requests on those paths arrive without a JWT and will be refused once the check is on.

## Summary

Every agent compose Swarm Map generates **unconditionally** mounts a Docker named volume at `/state` and runs a one-shot `state-init-<name>` service that symlinks `/opt/data/{state,response_store,kanban}.db` onto it. Since hermes-agent-mt commit `c3bf62ebd392` ("feat: boot authenticated session authority in ordinary gateway", 2026-09-08), the gateway refuses to boot when `Path(db.db_path).resolve().parent != home` — and `resolve()` follows the symlink to `/state`, so **the check always fails** wherever this layout applies. On native Linux, agents crash-loop from birth.

## Evidence (current main)

**swarm-map** — `lib/services/harness-compose.ts`:
- `stateInitService()` called with no guard at `:594` (`generatePlainCompose`) and `:681` (`generateVpnCompose`); the third call site at `:926` is the explicit per-harness `migrate-db` route.
- The hermes service always mounts `- hermes-state-<name>:/state` (`:624` plain, `:748` vpn) and the file always ends in the top-level named-volume trailer from `stateVolumeBlock()` (`:639`, `:763`).
- `STATE_INIT_SCRIPT` (`:397-457`) leaves the DB paths as **dangling symlinks** (`ln -sfn`) on a fresh harness — SQLite `O_CREAT` follows them onto the volume. So new agents are born symlinked; this is not limited to explicitly migrated harnesses.

**hermes-agent-mt** — `gateway/run_runtime.py:47-49`:
```python
if (await asyncio.to_thread(Path(db.db_path).resolve)).parent != home:
    raise RuntimeError(f'session authority database does not belong to the reserved profile {home}')
```
For a Swarm Map agent `home` is `/opt/data` (HERMES_HOME is pinned in the generated compose). With `state.db -> /state/state.db`, the resolved parent is `/state` — mismatch, raise, crash-loop.

## Repro (feldspar, native Linux, ext4-over-LUKS bind mount)

1. Create an agent through the UI → compose generated with the state layout.
2. Container crash-loops with `RuntimeError: session authority database does not belong to the reserved profile /opt/data`.
3. Delete the three symlinks from the host data dir and `docker start` the container → gateway boots clean. It re-breaks on any recreate (state-init re-symlinks) and every new agent is born broken.

## Why this is Linux-visible

The named-volume layout exists to escape a macOS Docker Desktop/OrbStack **VirtioFS torn-write** corruption vector (issue #204, PR2 — `docs/runbooks/db-named-volume-migration.md`). On a native Linux bind mount there is no VirtioFS, so the mechanism buys nothing — and it actively breaks the profile check. Note the check itself is platform-independent (`Path.resolve()` follows symlinks in-container on any host), so this is not strictly Linux-only; it's simply unreachable in the VirtioFS dev setup where the layout was introduced.

## Suggested direction

1. **swarm-map (this issue):** stop applying the state-volume layout unconditionally. Make it opt-in (a setting, default **off**), with the explicit `migrate-db` route remaining for hosts that actually need it. Native-Linux deployments should get plain bind mounts by default.
2. **hermes-agent-mt (complementary, separate issue):** the check's apparent intent is "the store must live inside the reserved profile dir" — comparing the **unresolved** `Path(db.db_path).parent` tolerates symlinked stores targeted within the profile, and matches that intent.

## Impact

Every Linux deployment of Swarm Map (a primary deployment target, given Docker Desktop licencing churn) ships agents that cannot boot. We worked around it on our box by deleting the symlinks by hand and are preparing the opt-in patch; filing so it stops surprising other Linux hosts.

## Summary

`person_memory` 0.3.0 (#219) made person cards **self-seeding**: every sender is
auto-recorded on first contact. That was the right fix for the problem it solved
— cards previously had to be hand-written, so in practice the adaptation layer
adapted to nobody — but it turns a hand-curated handful of cards into an
auto-accumulating record of everyone an agent has ever spoken to, across every
surface it runs on.

Three related gaps follow from that. None of them is urgent for a deployment
where every participant is trusted. All of them are load-bearing the moment an
agent sits in a room with someone who isn't. Filing this as hardening work for
that era rather than as a live incident.

## Gap 1 — person cards have no context scoping

Cards are scoped to the **agent** and keyed by `platform:id`. There is no
channel, group, or surface dimension. A card learned in a DM applies in a group
and vice versa.

The adaptation directive is appended to the user message, so in a shared session
its contents are visible to everyone present. Today that is bounded by the
writable-field allowlist and the identifier rejection added in #219, but the
structural point stands: what the agent learned about someone in one context is
applied, and shown, in another.

## Gap 2 — the person store is enumerable through general-purpose tools

Cards are files under the agent's home directory, and **the filenames are raw
platform identifiers**. Agents configured with a local (unsandboxed) terminal
backend can read that directory with ordinary file tools.

A directory listing is therefore sufficient to enumerate every person an agent
has a card for, without opening a single file. Self-seeding did not create this
property — it raises the value of the target, because the directory now fills
itself.

Worth noting explicitly: this is derivable from the public source in about a
minute, which is part of why it's being filed openly rather than quietly.

Possible directions:
- move the person store outside the agent's tool-reachable home
- mediate access through a plugin accessor that only ever returns the current
  sender, so there is no listable directory
- hash or opaque-ify filenames so a listing is not itself a contact list

## Gap 3 — no requester-tier gating on tools

`remember_person` is offered to every sender. `enabled_toolsets` /
`disabled_toolsets` are per **agent**, not per **requester**, so there is no way
to express "this tool is available to an operator but not to an arbitrary group
participant."

This generalizes well past this plugin — it is the tier question for the whole
tool registry, and it is the piece most worth designing before it is needed.

## Prior art in our own design

Earlier design work already sketched the axes this needs: a habitat/trust tier
concept (`HabitatTier`), per-tool `allowedTiers` and `risk` metadata, and a
memory-scope notion with siloed vs tag-gated strategies. The vocabulary exists;
what is missing is **enforcement keyed to the requester**. A useful reframe:
person memory is a memory scope with no tier, sitting inside an agent whose
tools also have no tier — the enumeration surface is what those two facts
produce together.

## Levers that exist today

- `PERSON_MEMORY_READONLY=1` — keeps adaptation, stops all accumulation, per agent
- `PERSON_MEMORY_DISABLED=1` — disables the plugin entirely

## Scope of this issue

Design and hardening, not a patch. Reasonable first slices, in rough order of
value:

1. Requester-tier metadata on tools + enforcement at registry exposure time
2. Non-enumerable person store (accessor-mediated or opaque filenames)
3. A scoping dimension on cards (surface, then channel/trust-context)
4. Consent/disclosure and retention: people are not told a durable card is being
   written about them, and nothing ages out

Policy decision (Juniper, 2026-08-06): **any hermes agent deployed via the swarm map on primo should get the coherence stack automatically** — the `coherence_observer` plugin + a `coherence-compute` sidecar.

Today this was done by hand for the three primo agents. The manual recipe (= the spec for automating):

1. **Observer plugin**: copy the flat `coherence_observer/` plugin dir into the agent data dir's `plugins/`, and append `coherence_observer` to `config.yaml → plugins.enabled`. Plugin dirs must be FLAT (nested packages silently fail to load) and underscore-named (dashed dirs are silently skipped by the `hermes_plugins.<dirname>` import).
2. **Compute sidecar**: one container per agent from the shared `coherence-compute:ready` image, on the agent's docker network, PLUGIN_SSE_URL/PLUGIN_POST_URL → http://<container>:7731, host-mounted COHERENCE_LOG_DIR (default is container-internal and silently ephemeral — see CHURPRIMO/coherence-compute#43), --restart unless-stopped.
3. **Dashboard**: add the agent to `OBSERVERS` in coherence-dashboard's run.sh and connect the dash container to the agent's network (CHURPRIMO/coherence-dashboard#1 made this N-agent).
4. **Identity launch gate** (from the 2026-08-06 pmf incident): seed SOUL.md identity card + memories/people roster (own Slack ID + sibling IDs) before first contact.

Suggested implementation: hook into harness compose generation / lifecycle for primo-hosted harnesses, gated by a per-host or per-harness flag (compute image is 14.6GB, CPU embeddings).

hits.body:
## Overview

In a multi-agent deployment where multiple Hermes agent containers share a single inference backend — whether a local Ollama instance or a cloud provider API with a shared org-level key — KV cache is not isolated between agents. This is a latent privacy and security concern worth documenting and mitigating.

## How it arises

HSM deploys multiple agent containers that each make independent inference calls to the same upstream endpoint:

- **Local models (Ollama):** All agents point to the same host Ollama instance (`host.docker.internal:11434`). Ollama has no tenant isolation — it is designed for single-user local use.
- **Cloud APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.):** These providers scope prompt cache to the API key / organization. HSM deployments typically share one org-level API key across all agents, meaning all agents share the same cache namespace at the provider.

## What leaks and how

**Prefix cache sharing (passive):**
LLM inference servers implement KV cache reuse for common prompt prefixes as a performance optimization. When two agents share an identical prefix — which is likely if they use the same base system prompt — the inference server reuses the same cached KV state for both. The model's internal attention state for the shared prefix is the same physical computation for all agents sharing that prefix.

This does not cause spontaneous content bleed (Agent B's output won't contain Agent A's private tokens), but it means the attention state is not isolated between agents.

**Stale slot memory (passive):**
In Ollama and vLLM, KV memory slots are not zeroed on release. When a slot is freed by one agent and reassigned to another, the new agent's prefill overwrites it — but there is a window where physically non-cleared prior state exists. This is a design assumption in both systems (single-user or trusted multi-tenant use).

**Timing side-channel (active/adversarial):**
Peer-reviewed research (PROMPTPEEK, NDSS 2025; Cache Me Catch You, NDSS 2026) demonstrates that an adversarial client sharing the same inference backend can reconstruct other users' recent prompts with >95% accuracy using timing oracles derived from KV cache hit/miss latency differences. This requires intentional probing (~500-1000 requests per token) but only needs API access — no elevated privileges.

The same attack class applies to shared Ollama instances and to shared-key cloud API deployments.

**Published CVEs:**
- CVE-2025-25183 / GHSA-rm76-4mrf-v9r8: vLLM prefix cache hash collision enabling cache poisoning (patched v0.7.2)
- CVE-2025-1953: vLLM/SGLang KV cache hash collision via meet-in-the-middle (NDSS 2026)
- Azure OpenAI Nov 2025: cross-tenant training data contamination via fine-tuning cache race condition (MSRC advisory)

## Risk levels

| Scenario | Passive risk | Active/adversarial risk |
|----------|-------------|------------------------|
| Shared Ollama, all first-party trusted agents | Low | Medium (if any agent ever compromised) |
| Shared cloud API key, same org | Low | Medium (same) |
| Shared Ollama with any untrusted or third-party agent | Medium | High |
| Separate API keys per agent (different orgs) | None | None |

## Mitigations

**Short term — break shared prefix matching:**
Insert a unique non-guessable token (e.g. a per-agent UUID or HMAC) in the first few tokens of each agent's system prompt. Since KV cache reuse is keyed on exact token sequence, this ensures no two agents ever share a cache block, regardless of how similar the rest of their prompts are. Low cost, no infrastructure change required.

**Medium term — per-agent key provisioning:**
Where the provider supports it, provision separate API keys per agent so caching is scoped per-key rather than per-org. Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI currently offer a sub-key/per-user key provisioning API, so this is not available today for those providers. Worth tracking as providers evolve their multi-tenant offerings.

**Longer term — inference isolation:**
For deployments with strict privacy requirements between agents, run separate inference backend instances per agent or per trust boundary. This provides full KV isolation at the cost of additional resource overhead.

## References

- arXiv:2502.07776 — Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs (Stanford/CRFM, 2025)
- PROMPTPEEK — I Know What You Asked (NDSS 2025)
- Cache Me, Catch You (NDSS 2026)
- NVIDIA Security Blog — Structuring Applications to Secure the KV Cache (Apr 2025)
- Ollama issue tracker: no documented per-caller KV isolation

Agents working on the software they run in (Swarm Map, Hermes instances) currently can't read logs, which makes self-debugging slow or impossible without a human pasting log excerpts.

- `POST /api/harnesses/:id/artifacts/sync` becomes the add-only, repeatable adopt route (`surface`, `packs`, `assignKeys`, `includeVision`). It rewrites inline `plugins.enabled: []` as a block list. New `GET /api/harnesses/:id/base-package/drift` only reports problems and changes nothing.

## Why
cyborg-public loads 0 of its 4 plugins because of an inline `[]`. Its web search has been broken since August. It improvises scripts that hit admin-only approval. ## What
- When a listed channel has `web-only` or `none` tools and the agent's own channel has shell or file tools, the launcher starts a second sealed cell for those channels, built with web, search and notes only, with its own networks, token, port and sessions. It shares the door, the budget and the per-room notes.
- The door sends turns from those channels (and their threads) to the second cell only, refuses a second cell whose hello declares any other tool class, refuses any non-web/search/notes call from it (`tools.cell`), and refuses a reply, end, error or tool call that one cell sends under the other cell's turn (`turn.cell`).
- Dry run checks both cells (new `S0t`), `status`/`stop` cover both, and the dashboard Status card shows a **Cells** row.
- Single-channel configs, and configs with no shell or file tools, are unchanged: one cell, same run layout, same policy and hash.

## Why
Per-channel tool limits were enforced by the door and the per-turn tool list, but the one cell still held the shell and file tools used by the agent's own channel. A separate cell makes the per-room limit a wall, as the design doc already said it would need. Matching calls to the cell that owns the turn also closes the cross-turn filing path between cells.

Found during an independent audit of #185. **Pre-existing on `main`** — not introduced by that PR, though #185 widens the set of reachable providers.

## The leak

For any provider with no `PROVIDER_TO_VAR` entry (`custom` today; `google` and any `?request=`-appended provider under #185), `resolveEnvVar` derives the env-var name from the key's **current** name hint. `removeKeyFromEnv` (`lib/services/keys.ts:455-473`) therefore resolves a *different* var after a rename, because `rotateValue` (`:611-632`) and `remove` (`:648`) pass the post-rename name.

Reproduced against the real service:

```
write google key, name="Team Key"   ->  TEAM_KEY_API_KEY=<secret>   written to agent .env
remove,           name="Renamed Key" ->  TEAM_KEY_API_KEY=<secret>   STILL PRESENT
```

The secret stays in the agent's `.env` in plaintext under the stale variable, indefinitely, after the operator has deleted the key in HSM.

## Why it matters

The code states the opposite intent — `lib/services/keys.ts:642-646` says deleting a key should strip it from the fleet. An operator who rotates or revokes a credential reasonably believes it is gone from the agents.

## Suggested fix

Persist the resolved env-var name alongside the key record at write time and use *that* for removal, rather than re-deriving it from a mutable name hint. Re-deriving can never be correct across a rename.

Related: making `PROVIDER_TO_VAR` the single source of truth (see the #185 review) shrinks the set of providers that depend on name-derived vars at all, but does not fix `custom`.

Both port allocators parse `docker ps` output for `0.0.0.0:<port>` and nothing else. On a host where containers publish on a specific address (mine bind to the host's Tailscale address on purpose; 100.100.1.2 below stands in for it), no existing agent's port is ever counted, so each new deploy is handed BASE_PORT and `docker compose up -d` fails with "Bind for 100.100.1.2:8642 failed: port is already allocated".

The two places, at c95cebb:

`app/api/setup/deploy/route.ts:22` has its own local `nextAvailablePort()` which runs `docker ps --format '{{.Ports}}'` and matches `/0\.0\.0\.0:(\d+)/g` (line 32). The wizard deploy calls this at line 275, so it also bypasses `collectUsedPorts` in `lib/services/harness.ts` entirely - no compose scan, no reserved ports, no `.env` scan, and only running containers.

`lib/services/harness.ts:97`, in `dockerPublishedPorts()`, matches `/0\.0\.0\.0:(\d+)->/g` on `docker ps -a`. The comment above it assumes 0.0.0.0 is the format docker emits.

## Repro

On a host whose compose publishes with a `host_ip`: run one agent with `host_ip: 100.100.1.2, published: 8642`, then deploy a second agent through the wizard. It is assigned 8642 as well and `compose up` fails. Quicker check: `docker ps --format '{{.Ports}}'` prints `100.100.1.2:8642->8642/tcp`, which neither regex matches.

## Suggested fix

Match any host address in both places, e.g. `/(?:\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3}|\[[0-9a-f:]+\]):(\d+)->/g`, or just `/:(\d+)->\d+\/(?:tcp|udp)/g`. And have the deploy route call the exported `nextAvailablePort` from `lib/services/harness.ts` (with `composeBaseDir` and `reservedPorts`) instead of its own copy, so the wizard sees compose files, stopped containers and `.env`-declared ports too.

One related note: when `compose up` fails, the catch at `route.ts:562` deletes the agent data dir but leaves `compose/<slug>/docker-compose.yml` and the Created containers behind, so a retry from the UI fails on the missing `env_file`. Removing those on rollback would make the retry work.

## Two asks in one

### 1. Add \"Discover existing channels\" for Discord (parity with Signal/Mattermost)

**The pain:** today, wiring an agent into a Discord channel means manually hunting down the channel snowflake ID (enable Discord developer mode → right-click channel → Copy Channel ID → paste into `DISCORD_ALLOWED_CHANNELS`). For anyone administering more than a couple of channels this is tedious and error-prone.

**The pattern that already exists:** Signal and Mattermost surfaces have a **\"Discover existing groups →\"** button on the harness page (`app/(dashboard)/harnesses/[id]/page.tsx`). It calls `app/api/surfaces/signal/groups/route.ts` (and the Mattermost equivalent), lists the groups the bot account is already a member of, and lets the operator pick which to allowlist — no manual ID copying.

**Requested:** same feature for Discord.

- New route `app/api/surfaces/discord/channels/route.ts` that lists channels across the guilds the bot is a member of (Discord REST: `GET /users/@me/guilds` → per-guild `GET /guilds/{id}/channels`)
- \"Discover existing channels →\" button on the Discord surface card, mirroring the Signal UX
- Multi-select UI filtered to text channels the bot can actually see (skip categories, voice, threads the bot can't read)
- Writes selected snowflakes into `DISCORD_ALLOWED_CHANNELS` the same way the Signal flow writes group UUIDs
- Should respect the existing Discord permission model (see below) — e.g. if `DISCORD_IGNORED_CHANNELS` is set, those channels should be marked/excluded in the picker

ROADMAP already marks this shipped for Signal + Mattermost (`docs/ROADMAP.md`: \"Discover existing groups (Signal, Mattermost)\"). Discord is the gap.

### 2. Review the default Discord permission system

Discord has the richest admission surface of any platform in `lib/surfaces/registry.ts`:

- `DISCORD_ALLOWED_USERS` — user snowflake allowlist
- `DISCORD_ALLOWED_CHANNELS` — channel allowlist
- `DISCORD_ALLOWED_ROLES` — role allowlist (OR'd with the user allowlist)
- `DISCORD_IGNORED_CHANNELS` — deny list (deny beats allow)
- `DISCORD_REQUIRE_MENTION` — only respond when @mentioned
- `DISCORD_ALLOW_BOTS` — respond to other bots
- `DISCORD_CHANNEL_SCOPED_ACCESS` — per-channel access control

Worth a design review pass on:

- **Are the defaults sensible for a fresh agent?** (Currently: closed by default — every list empty = deny all. That's safe but means Discord is the hardest surface to bring up, compounded by the missing discovery feature above.)
- **Is the allow/deny precedence documented clearly enough?** (`docs/surface-permissions.md` covers the resolver contract, but operator-facing docs for the Discord-specific OR-of-roles + deny-beats-allow semantics could be clearer)
- **Does the UI surface the permission model accurately?** (i.e. does the harness page make it obvious which knobs are Discord-only vs shared across surfaces)
- **Role-based admission UX** — `DISCORD_ALLOWED_ROLES` is powerful (\"anyone with the Moderator role can talk to the bot\") but role IDs are even more painful to find than channel IDs. If we add channel discovery, consider role discovery too (`GET /guilds/{id}/roles`).

## Why together

The permission review and the discovery feature interact: any change to the default permission posture (e.g. making Discord default-open within a guild) changes what the discovery UI should suggest. Filing as one issue so they're designed coherently; can be split if implementation prefers.

## References

It is left out of `list()` / `get()`, listed by `GET /api/harnesses/retired`, and shown on the fleet page in its own block with one action, "Forget row". A request that would change something is answered 409 when the id it carries is the stored id of such a row, matched exactly, whether the id is in the URL (`/api/harnesses/<id>/...`) or in the body (a key's `assignedTo`, a cascade or model-update `harnessId`). ## What

- A Discord connector for the lab's door (`lib/door/connectors/discord.ts`), behind the same interface as the fake connector. No new dependency: it uses Node 24's own WebSocket and fetch, so no third-party package holds a bot token.
- A launcher for one Pi agent in one Discord channel (`lib/lab/pi-discord/`): config, dry run, start, stop, status, receipts. The door runs on the machine; Pi runs in the sealed cell and reaches the door through a relay that holds nothing.
- `bots.loop` is now a real rule: the door counts bot messages delivered in a row and `decide()` stops at the limit. Two more door rules: a reply size cut (`out.size`) and "a message is read once" for edits and deletes (`in.once`).
- A runbook: `docs/lab/pi-discord.md`.
- `allowedBotIds`: name the only bots that are heard. A policy can name its bots (`bots.ids`), and `decide()` drops any bot that is not named. Every other bot and every webhook is dropped with a receipt. Each named bot has its own loop count.
- A `persona` setting (a name and one line). The launcher tells the agent what it is and, in its own fixed words, what it cannot do: no tools, text only, one channel. It replaces Pi's own introduction, which says it is a coding assistant that can run commands.

Nothing here is wired into the Swarm Map app or any running agent. This PR does not start anything.

## Why

The Pi slice proved the rules with a scripted room. The next step is one real surface, with every inbound message still going through `decide()` and every reply through the door's redaction and size limit.

## How it holds the rules

- Every gateway message becomes a door event. The connector decides nothing.
- The reply can only go to the room the message came from. The connector also refuses any post outside the one channel it was started for, before a request is made.
- Replies ping nobody (`allowed_mentions` is empty).
- The bot token and the model key are read from two files only their owner can read, named by `SMLAB_DISCORD_TOKEN_FILE` and `SMLAB_MODEL_KEY_FILE`. They are never in the config, the cell, the compose file, a receipt or a log.
- The connector asks Discord for server and server-message events only. It never asks for direct messages, and asks for message text only when the config says so.
- `createDoor()` still refuses any connector that is not the fake one, unless the surface is named as live by whoever starts the door.
