## What
- `lib/model-versions.ts`: model-id normaliser (family / version / snapshot / unstable), `findSuccessor` (strictly same family, strictly newer version or snapshot), `priceRatio`.
- `lib/services/model-freshness.ts`: live model lists for openrouter / anthropic / zai with a 1h disk cache under `DATA_DIR/model-lists/`, fail-soft (no key, network error, bad body → `null`, entries stay unflagged). Keys resolved through KeysService per request, never persisted or logged. `GET /api/models/live?provider=`.
- Per-harness `modelTracking` overlay (`"provider/model" → true`, carried through both harness projections) and `settings.modelAutoUpdate { enabled, mode: notify|apply, intervalHours, maxPriceMultiplier }`. Routes: `GET/PUT /api/settings/model-auto-update`, `PUT /api/harnesses/[id]/models/tracking` (ollama refused).
- `lib/services/model-update-scheduler.ts`, registered from `instrumentation.ts` (unref'd timers, HMR guard, `MODEL_UPDATE_INTERVAL_MS` override). `GET /api/fleet/model-updates` (last persisted report), `POST .../check` (run now), `POST .../apply` (manual one-click apply of a reported successor).
- Catalog: `retired` / `deprecates` fields; `deepseek/deepseek-v3.2` flagged retired (OpenRouter expiration 2026-09-28), `google/gemini-2.5-flash` deprecates 2026-10-20. Rows are flagged, never removed, so live cascades stay readable.
- Reconciled onto the cascade-library stack: this branch's own `lib/services/cascade-write.ts` (`writeCascade`) and its tests are gone. The scheduler's auto-apply and `POST /api/fleet/model-updates/apply` call `applyCascadeToHarness` from `lib/services/cascade-writer.ts`, the stack's single validated write path. `PUT /api/harnesses/[id]/models` is exactly as the parent has it. The byte-for-byte splice pin and created-file pin from the dropped test file are ported into `cascade-writer.test.ts`.

## Why
Closes #136. Providers retire ids on a schedule and ship newer same-family versions; today nobody notices until an agent 404s. This makes freshness visible fleet-wide and, per cascade entry, lets an operator opt in to following the newest same-family version.

Policy, in one place:
- **Default OFF.** `modelAutoUpdate.enabled` is `false`; with it off the scheduler does no background network at all (manual `POST .../check` still works).
- **notify mode** reports successors, retirements and price ratios at `GET /api/fleet/model-updates`. Nothing is written.
- **apply mode** auto-bumps only *tracked* entries to a strictly-same-family newer **version** that is present in the live provider list, within the price ceiling (`maxPriceMultiplier`; no published pricing → `price-unknown` → never auto-applied), through the validated writer (`applyCascadeToHarness`: validate → render → splice → write → overlay), followed by a `quick` restart and a `cascade:auto-update` audit row `{ harness, from, to, provider, priceRatio }`. The `modelTracking` key rotates to the new id.
- **ollama / bedrock / custom never auto-apply.** Unstable (preview/beta/exp) successors never apply. A harness with a restart already in flight is skipped.
- **Snapshot-only bumps are notify-only** (a human may apply one via `POST .../apply`).
- A writer refusal (provider with no credential in the agent's `.env`, unsafe YAML scalar) writes nothing, restarts nothing, leaves tracking untouched, and audits `cascade:auto-update:blocked` with the reason.

## Verification
- `pnpm vitest run` → 119 files, 1441 tests, all green (on head `effc6be`).
- `npx tsc --noEmit 2>&1 | grep -v '^\.next/'` → clean.
- `lib/services/__tests__/model-update-scheduler.test.ts` (22 tests; `cascade-writer.test.ts` 14) runs the **real** `applyCascadeToHarness` against a tmpdir fleet with real `.env` files, so validate-before-write is exercised on the scheduler path, not mocked away. Every guard (untracked, snapshot, unstable, price ceiling, price-unknown, ollama, restart-in-flight, writer refusal, policy off) has a test asserting nothing was written and nothing was restarted.
- Rebased onto `dev/juniperbevensee/cascade-library`; the `writeCascade` extraction commit was dropped and its consumers rewritten in the same history so each commit builds.

## Risk
The scheduler rewrites a running agent's `config.yaml` with no human in the loop — but only when the operator has flipped `enabled` and chosen `apply`, only for entries they tracked, and only through the same writer the editor uses. Worst case on a bad write is the existing crash-loop, which the validator exists to prevent; the byte-identical splice pin guards against a refactor changing what lands on disk.

Stacked on #233 — merge that first (use a merge commit, not squash, so the stack stays clean).

hits.body:
## Problem

A `mode:rebuild` shipped **stale code**. The rebuild path runs `docker compose ... up -d --build --force-recreate <service>`, and the build reads a **local checkout** (`~/Documents/GitHub/hermes-agent-mt`). That checkout was 1 commit behind `main` — missing a merged fix — and nothing pulled it first, so the build silently produced an out-of-date image.

## Fix

Before any build mode (`rebuild`/`purge`), HSM now syncs the build-source checkout to the code it's **supposed** to build, and **fails loud** rather than shipping stale.

- **`DockerService.syncBuildSource(dir)`** — `git fetch` then `merge --ff-only @{u}`. Throws on: not-a-git-repo, dirty working tree, detached HEAD, no upstream tracking branch, or non-fast-forward (diverged history). Logs the branch + commit it built from (`[rebuild] <svc>: building <dir> @ <branch> <sha> (synced to <upstream>)`).
- **`DockerService.restart(..., buildSource?)`** — runs the sync **synchronously before** the detached build spawn, so a failure surfaces to the API caller (HTTP 500 with a clear message) instead of building stale.
- **`HarnessService.restart()`** — resolves the source from the harness's own compose `build:` context (authoritative — exactly what `--build` reads, and honors any per-harness override), falling back to the global `hermesDir` setting. Returns `null` for image-only harnesses (e.g. evil-duck) so nothing is synced.
- **`readComposeBuildContext()`** (harness-compose) — parses both the long-form (`build:` / `context:`) and shorthand (`build: /path`) compose layouts in use on the Mini.
- On a failed sync, `clearRestarting()` so the harness isn't wedged in the "restarting" state — the user can retry after fixing the checkout.

### Source-of-truth note

There is **no per-harness source repo/branch/ref** in HSM config — `harnesses.json` carries only models/platform/compose-file. All local-build harnesses share one checkout + the global `hermesDir`/`useLocalBuild` settings, and there is no configured branch (the build just used whatever was checked out — the root of the bug). This change makes the ref resolution explicit (the checkout's own upstream tracking branch) and logged, and refuses to fast-forward-bypass dirty/diverged state.

## Tests

- Docker sync: ff-success, dirty→fail, non-ff→fail, no-upstream→fail, detached-HEAD→fail, non-build-mode skip, image-only skip.
- Build-context parsing: long form, shorthand, image-only (null), VPN variant.

26 tests pass; `tsc --noEmit` clean.

## Audit (read-only, Mac Mini)

Every harness's build source verified — all "set right":

| Harness | Source | Expected ref | Actual state | Set right? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cryptids, mare, nimbleco, osint, personal | `…/hermes-agent-mt` (long-form context) | main | main, clean, 0/0 | ✅ |
| cyborg, egregore, seraph-doer, seraph-generalist, seraph-thinker | `…/hermes-agent-mt` (shorthand build:) | main | main, clean, 0/0 | ✅ |
| evil-duck | `ghcr.io/nimblecoai/hermes-agent:latest` (image, no build) | — | n/a | ✅ |

All local-build harnesses share the **single** checkout `/Users/juni/Documents/GitHub/hermes-agent-mt` → on `main`, tracking `origin/main`, clean, 0 ahead / 0 behind, not detached. The stale state that triggered the bug was transient and has since been pulled current. **No mismatches, nothing ff-pulled, nothing needing a human decision.**

## Deploy note

Deploying this fix itself requires an HSM rebuild/restart on the Mini — **not done here** (per instructions, don't disrupt the running HSM/agents). Flagging for a human.

## What

- Door agents can read the web without the cell getting a route out: a `web_fetch` tool (class `network`) and a `web_search` tool (class `search`) that ask the door, which makes the request itself and hands back text marked as untrusted.
- Two fetch modes, both off by default: `allowlist` reads only listed hosts or host/path prefixes (the record's `egress.hosts`, now read); `public` reads any public address (`egress.default: 'public'`). In both: GET only, no credential or cookie, private/loopback/link-local/metadata addresses refused after every DNS answer and on every redirect, connection pinned to the checked address, size/time/hourly limits, HTML reduced to text, content to the model only, receipts with host/path/size and never content.
- Search through the Brave Search API with a key only the door holds, read from a 0600 file whose path sits with the record's other secret paths. Results are titles, addresses and snippets; a result is readable only if the current mode allows it; its own hourly count; receipts hold the query length and result count, never the query.
- Launcher config `tools.web` (`mode`, `allow`, `approval`, `search`), a web section on the dashboard's Tools card (mode, approval, suggested sites as one-click chips, search toggle and key file path), the rules in the catalogue, and ten harness-neutral conformance checks (N1+, N1 to N9).

## Why

Agents are most useful with research, and the cell cannot reach the network. This gives them a read-only way to reach the web that the door decides and bounds, like every other tool.

## Verification

- Unit suite: 5,581 tests; all pass but two compose tests that read the Docker name prefix the run set on purpose, which pass without it. `tsc`, the sanitization gate (deterministic layer) and `next build` are clean.
- Real Pi 1.5.2: 59 checks pass as a process, 60 in the sealed Docker cell, the ten web checks among them, against a fake web and a fake search provider on loopback with a fake DNS. No test reaches the internet.
- Broken on purpose: seven door rigs and gates (no list check, unchecked redirects, no address check, kept cookies, no limits, a search key when search is off, a gate whose web tool fetches by itself) each turn their named web checks red and leave the others green.
- Launcher Docker suites with a fake Discord: Pi 20 of 20, Letta Code 15 of 15. Letta Code (26 process, 34 Docker) and the Claude Agent SDK (36 process, 38 Docker) pass as before and list the web checks as not run.
- Hand mutations: 67 lines broken one at a time; 63 turned a named test red, 4 change nothing alone because a second line holds the same thing.
- An audit found and fixed, among others: Node's `http.request` with `agent: false` ignores `createConnection` and dials localhost (the request now names the checked address too); a denied approval still left a fetch ticket; an HTML stripper that went quadratic on unclosed tags.

## Risk

- New outbound traffic from the door process, off unless an operator turns it on. Under `public`, what an agent puts in an address or a query reaches that site or the provider.
- No prompt-injection scanning of pages: content is marked untrusted and goes to the model only. A scanner can plug in at the door later.
- The TLS path and the real Brave endpoint are not exercised by tests (the fakes are plain http on loopback); production is https only.
- Pi only, like the other tools. Conflicts with the command-policy PR are expected in `decide.ts`, `door.ts`, `config.ts`, the Tools card and the six matrices.

## What
- New Discord agents start with DMs closed. A first connect seeds `DISCORD_DM_ALLOWED_USERS` from explicit admins or the admins named there, never the whole allowlist. Later connects change no Discord or Signal list, set or unset.
- An explicit admin change moves that list, and recreates the container, only if it equalled the previous explicit admins. A first admin list that matches the allowlist is left alone with a warning. Allowlist edits and settings saves never move it.
- New Signal agents start `SIGNAL_ALLOWED_USERS` as their explicit admins, or `0` (nobody), including through a first connect after a page save or a Signal key. Page saves add no empty Signal list. A first Discord connect also closes an empty channel list, and removing the last channel through the policy route denies.
- The admin and connect routes warn about a listed admin who is not on `DISCORD_ALLOWED_USERS`. Help text points at the DM list, and a public-surface warning flags a `*` DM gate.
- Connect warnings now show in the UI, and the Signal setup script prints `0` with corrected notes.

## Why
hermes-agent-mt#200 added a Discord DM gate that Swarm Map did not know about, so new agents had no managed DM list. On Signal, the adapter reads an unset list as `*` and an empty one as open mode, where a stranger's group invite is accepted. On Discord, an empty channel list means every channel. So an empty line cannot mean closed on those lists.

## Verification
- `npx vitest run`: 2559 passed, 0 failed, written red first. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean. ESLint: no errors on the touched files beyond the settings route's existing ones. Merged with main.
- Ran the fleet-live Signal adapter and gateway authorization with unset, empty, `0` and a listed user. Only `0` and a real list refuse a stranger's group approval and stop pairing replies to strangers' DMs.
- Not verified on a live agent: nothing was deployed, and no real DM was sent.

## Risk
- Existing agents are not migrated. A Discord agent with no `DISCORD_DM_ALLOWED_USERS` stays closed under the adapter's unset rule, once it runs an image with #200.
- A closed agent can get stuck. If its allowlist is exactly the people who should DM, including a single person, the first admin list matches it and stays closed, and the next save no longer matches the list. To open it: disconnect and reconnect naming the admins, or choose a first list that differs from the allowlist, or set the line by hand.
- A chosen first admin list that differs from the allowlist opens an agent whose DM list is empty, including one closed on purpose.
- Disconnect strips the var, including a hand-set value. A later connect reseeds it.
- Existing Signal agents with an empty or unset list stay open to group invites until the adapter changes. That needs a hermes-agent-mt fix.

## What

- The model route now writes a receipt for every call it does not complete, and says why: refused before forwarding (`model.route`: no price, not a model call, not readable, wrong stand-in key), refused by the budget (`budget.cap`), or failed at the provider (`model.provider`: an error status, no answer in time, a cut-off reply, or a 200 stream or body that carries an error). It passes each one to the door through a new `onFailure` hook. The provider's own words are never written down.
- When a turn ends with nothing to post, the door now posts one short line in the room, under the message that started the turn: `No answer this time.` plus the reason when a model call failed during the turn, or else "finished without a reply", "something went wrong inside the agent", or "took too long, so the door stopped waiting for it" (no harness acts on a cancel). The line goes through the same outbound re-check, redaction and receipts as a reply. A message deleted mid-turn still gets nothing, and a turn a bot started gets only a receipt (`turn.to-bot`), so a failure cannot feed a bot loop. A refusal by the rules for any reason but the budget is told in one fixed sentence.
- New checks C6m, C6b and C6s (`conformance/suites/failure-checks.ts`), run for Pi with a tool in ask mode: the provider refuses the model call after a tool ran, the budget refuses it, and a model call outlasts the turn. Each needs a receipt with the reason and the right line in the room. They are red with a new broken shim link, `covers-failures`, which reports a failed turn as one that answered "All done." (C6m, C6b), and in a cell with the gate that asks nobody (C6m).
- Metering is unchanged: a call that cannot be metered is still never forwarded, and a forwarded call is charged by its reported usage, or by size when there is none. With tools on, the launcher now allows a turn ten minutes (the route's wait for one call) instead of three, since a tool turn makes at least two calls.

## Why

With tools on, a turn makes more model calls, and a slow model can take minutes for one. From the room, an agent waiting on a slow call, an agent whose call failed, and an agent whose turn ended with nothing to say all looked the same: silence. A provider error wrote no receipt, a turn that ended with no reply or with an error posted nothing, and a turn that ran past its deadline was dropped without a word. This change gives each of those a reason in the receipts and a line in the room.

A replay of OpenRouter's stream shape for a tool call (keep-alive comments, reasoning deltas, the tool call in pieces, a finish event, and a usage event that repeats the finish with one empty choice) is metered exactly from its usage figure, before and after this change. That replay is now a test.

## Verification

- `npx vitest run`: the full suite passes. On this machine, under heavy load from other work, each full run had a few timing failures in files this change does not touch (a token-broker script, worker start-up), and a different set each time. Each failed file passed when run again on its own. 13 new model-route tests, including the OpenRouter replay, and 6 new door tests. Four existing door tests that pinned the old silence (no reply, the deadline, a reply after settled, and the deadline after an approval) now expect the line in the room. The live-run rig's tests now tell a reply apart from the door's line.
- `npx tsc --noEmit`: clean. ESLint on the changed files: no errors.
- Real Pi 1.5.2 as a process (`npm run conformance`): 42 of 42, including C6m, C6b and C6s. `covers-failures` turned C6m and C6b red and left C1, C6 and C6s green. Matrix regenerated.
- Real Pi 1.5.2 in the sealed Docker cell (`npm run conformance:docker`, `pi.docker.test.ts`): 50 of 50. The gate that asks nobody turned C6m red. Docker matrix regenerated.
- Launcher Docker suite (`pi-discord.docker.test.ts`) with a fake Discord: 20 of 20, including a new end-to-end test where the provider refuses a call and the channel gets the line. With the `onFailure` wiring removed from the launcher, that test went red.
- Hand mutations: 11 lines broken one at a time in the route, the shapes and the door. Each turned a named test red once a test for a finish reason of `error` with no error object was added.
- Independent audit, on the code as it now stands: real Pi 1.5.2 42 of 42, Letta Code 0.34.60 26 of 26, Claude Agent SDK 0.3.325 36 of 36 as processes; in Docker, Pi 50 of 50, Pi launcher 20 of 20, Letta Code 34 of 34, Letta Code launcher 15 of 15, Claude Agent SDK 38 of 38. The first real Agent SDK run found that C4m no longer failed for three broken shims, because the door's line filled in for the missing reply; post counts now leave that line out. Provider error bodies holding key-, account-, URL- and path-shaped strings, across nine statuses and four body types, put none of it in a receipt or a room line. Ten hand mutations to the door, route, shapes and launcher each turned a test red.
- Sanitization gate (deterministic layer) on the diff: clean.

## Risk

- A room now sees a line where it used to see silence, on every failed turn, including when the budget is spent. A turn a bot started is never told, so a failure cannot keep a bot loop going.
- Which turn gets blamed for a failed call is decided by time alone. With two turns running at once, either may be the one that is told. The receipts name the call that failed.

## What
- `sharedVpn` is now a VPN group name (e.g. `"private"`, `"public"`) or `null`, instead of a boolean. Each group has its own gluetun container (`gluetun-<group>`), compose project (`swarm-vpn-<group>`), key file (`<dataDir>/vpn/<group>/gluetun.env`), and deny-all control-server lockdown.
- Moving an agent between groups starts the target group's gluetun first, then rewrites the compose and recreates the agent. A move to a group with no key file is refused, and the agent stays where it was.
- The settings UI offers Off / Private group / Public group.

## Why
Agents in one shared namespace can reach each other's localhost servers, so they have to be split by trust. All fleet agents except cyborg-public go in `private`; cyborg-public goes alone in `public`.

**Groups are any validated name, not a fixed list.** Which agents trust each other is the owner's policy, not code. A group only works once its key file exists (created by the owner's key script), so a typo is refused for the missing key instead of quietly creating a new namespace. The pattern `^[a-z][a-z0-9]{0,15}$` keeps the name safe in container names, project names, paths and YAML.

The #280 boolean shape is now rejected with 400. That layout was never deployed, so there is no migration shim.

## Verification
- Red-green tests:
  - group validation;
  - a separate container, project and network_mode per group;
  - a move round-trips exactly;
  - a hand-made `container:gluetun-vera` is not read as a group;
  - route: a move starts the target gluetun before recreating the agent;
  - route: a move to a group with no key file refuses and writes nothing;
  - route: a boolean or malformed group gets 400.
- `pnpm vitest run`: 2143 pass. `tsc --noEmit` is clean.

## Risk
- Members of one group still share localhost (by design). Mixing trust levels in one group brings the exposure back.
- Recreating a group's gluetun cuts off that group's agents until they are recreated. Other groups are unaffected.

The README headline still said **"Multiplayer admin and orchestrator platform for Hermes"** while the product now claims two first-class runtimes. Several other surfaces went the other way and promised Letta capability we have **not** shipped. This PR fixes the framing and, more importantly, removes the overclaims — every correction below is checkable against `main`.

**Do not merge without reading the evidence column.** The whole point of this PR is that the claims are verifiable.

---

## 1. Headline and framing (claim was contradictory)

| Claim before | Status | Now |
|---|---|---|
| "Multiplayer admin and orchestrator platform for **Hermes**" | Contradicts the two-runtime story | "…for **heterogeneous agent runtimes**" — Hermes (container-per-agent) **and** Letta (memory-first agents as rows on one shared server) |
| Headline linked `NimbleCoAI/hermes-agent` | Stale org | `NimbleCoOrg/hermes-agent-mt` |
| Letta link | absent | `letta-ai/letta` — verified live via `gh repo view letta-ai/letta` |

Also repointed three `NimbleCoAI/hermes-agent` links in `docs/migrating.md` (lines 11, 203, 206) and the Requirements bullet that pointed only at `NousResearch/hermes-agent` (now names the MT fork we actually deploy, crediting upstream).

**Not touched on purpose:** the Quick Start `git clone` URL. That is the single README change in open PR #187 — left alone so this PR does not conflict there.

## 2. Overclaims corrected

### memfs / git-backed "Context files" — was promising a feature that is off

**Evidence:** `git_enabled` has **zero** occurrences anywhere in this repository (`grep -rn "git_enabled" . --exclude-dir=node_modules --exclude-dir=.git` → no hits), and agents created by our deploy path come up `git_enabled: false`.

`components/harness/letta-agent-detail.tsx` rendered a **"Context files (memfs)"** panel headed by a paragraph describing "the agent's git-backed memory file tree", followed — for every agent we create — by an empty box and the excuse *"No context files (agent may predate memfs, or files aren't exposed on this server)"*. That reads as "your agent happens to have no files", not "this feature is not on".

Fixed:
- Heading now carries a **`not enabled`** badge whenever the list is empty.
- The git-backed-memory explanation only renders when files are actually present (so it stays useful for externally-created agents that do have memfs).
- Empty state now says git-backed memory files are not enabled for agents Swarm Map deploys, points at **Core memory (blocks)** as the real live memory surface, and states that enabling memfs is not shipped.
- `MemoryBlocks` no longer says blocks "project into `system/` files" as present tense.
- Wizard copy `app/(setup)/setup/wizard/page.tsx:590` said *"Letta agents use **memfs** memory (git-backed context files)"* → corrected to core-memory blocks, with memfs marked not enabled.
- Wizard runtime picker (line 452) dropped "(memfs memory)".
- The file's header comment now carries a `MEMFS IS NOT ENABLED — DO NOT WRITE COPY THAT PROMISES IT` note with the evidence, so the next person editing this file cannot reintroduce the claim by accident.

### The Letta API surface is read-only + send-message

**Evidence — full route inventory, reproduced from `docs/runtimes.md`:**

```
--- app/api/letta/harnesses/route.ts            8:export async function GET() {
--- app/api/letta/agents/route.ts               7:export async function GET() {
--- app/api/letta/agents/[id]/blocks/route.ts   6:export async function GET(
--- app/api/letta/agents/[id]/messages/route.ts 6:export async function POST(
--- app/api/letta/agents/[id]/files/route.ts    7:export async function GET(
```

Four GETs and one POST. **No `PATCH`, `PUT` or `DELETE` anywhere under `app/api/letta/`.** So there is no lifecycle or memory-management parity to claim:

- README now tabulates the Letta routes exactly, labelled "read-only plus send-message… there is no `PATCH`, `PUT`, or `DELETE`".
- Detail-view copy no longer says a Letta agent is "managed over REST" — it now says read-only plus sending a message, with editing memory / reconfiguring / deleting called out as not shipped.
- Stated honestly where creation *does* live: `POST /api/setup/deploy` with the Letta runtime selected (`deployLettaAgent`). The one `services.letta.deleteAgent` call is rollback-only for a failed deploy — `docs/runtimes.md` says so explicitly so nobody reads it as a user-facing delete.

### Budget does not inherit on the default path

Approval and audit **do** inherit through a Hermes front — they gate the turn before it runs. Budget does not, because streaming is on by default and a streamed turn reports **zero tokens** to the enforcement hook, so spend is never counted and a soft cap is never approached.

Every place this could be read as three-for-three inheritance now says two-for-three and names the streaming reason:
- README **Runtimes** table + a "Budget caveat, stated plainly" paragraph.
- `docs/runtimes.md` §3, with the explicit instruction *"Do not write 'the bridge inherits the door's approval, audit and budget'."*
- Wizard step 3 Letta panel — the place an operator would most naturally assume the door's guarantees carry over.

### New: `docs/runtimes.md`

The shipped/not-shipped matrix with the verification commands inline, so this stops being tribal knowledge. Linked from the README headline and the Documentation section.

## 3. Repo metadata (done via `gh`, outside this diff)

- **Description** was `Multiplayer admin and orchestration layer for Hermes agents.` → now names both runtimes and the control-plane guarantees.
- **Topics** were `agentic-ai, ai, hermes, local-ai, multiplayer` → now `agent-orchestration, agentic-ai, ai, letta, local-ai, multi-agent, multiplayer, swarm-map`. `hermes` removed (Hermes-only framing), `letta` and `swarm-map` added.

## 4. License detection — `Other/NOASSERTION` vs the AGPL v3 claim

The repo shipped an AGPL v3 `LICENSE`, but GitHub's licence API returned `{"key":"other","spdx_id":"NOASSERTION"}` — contradicting both the README and the website.

**Cause:** the file was **not** verbatim. Three lines were prepended above the licence text:

```
Hermes Swarm Map
Copyright (C) 2025-2026 Juniper Bevensee and contributors
<blank>
```

Everything from line 4 down was already byte-identical to `https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.txt` (661 lines, verified by `diff`). Only the header deviated, and that is the sole plausible reason the classifier failed.

**Fix:** dropped the three-line header, so `LICENSE` is now **byte-identical to gnu.org's `agpl-3.0.txt`** (`diff -q` clean). The project attribution moved to a new `NOTICE` file — which also records *why*, so it does not get re-prepended — plus a copyright line in the README's License section.

**Verified against GitHub's own classifier**, not just asserted — same endpoint, two refs:

```bash
$ gh api repos/NimbleCoOrg/swarm-map/license                                  # main
{"key": "other",     "spdx_id": "NOASSERTION", "url": null}

$ gh api "repos/NimbleCoOrg/swarm-map/license?ref=dev/juniperbevensee/honest-public-claims"
{"key": "agpl-3.0",  "spdx_id": "AGPL-3.0",    "name": "GNU Affero General Public License v3.0"}
```

The three-line header was the entire cause. On merge the repo sidebar and the licence API will read **AGPL-3.0**, matching the README and the website.

>
> ⚠️ **Merge-order note:** PR #187 also touches `LICENSE` — its only change there is line 1, `Hermes Swarm Map` → `Swarm Map`. That line no longer exists in this branch, so the two will conflict. **Resolution: keep this PR's `LICENSE`** (verbatim AGPL) — #187's intent is preserved, because `NOTICE` already carries the corrected `Swarm Map` name.

## 5. `docs/migrating.md` GHCR namespace

The Tier 3 image mapping already pointed at `ghcr.io/nimblecoorg/...`, so there was nothing to repoint. Added a callout making that path explicitly **canonical** ("what the wizard deploys, what `lib/seed.ts` defaults to,

## What

- Adds `lib/core/`: one policy record, a 35-rule catalogue, and `decide()`, the single function that says who an agent may hear and answer, which tools it may run, and when its budget is spent.
- Adds `lib/door/`: the sidecar that owns chat in, chat out and model traffic. Fake connector only. Receipts for every decision, outbound redaction that fails closed, one reply per turn, a model route that swaps a placeholder for the real key, meters tokens and keeps spend in a ledger by month.
- Adds `lib/runtimes/pi/`: the Pi shim (one `pi --mode rpc` process per session), a prompt preamble a sender cannot forge, and a tool gate extension that blocks on anything but an explicit allow.
- Adds `conformance/`: 38 scenario pairs, fake-proof guards with negative controls, a scripted model, a fake Pi for CI, fourteen shim checks, eight deliberately broken shims, and a matrix file generated from a real Pi 1.5.2 run.
- Adds `conformance/docker/`: a sealed Docker cell for Pi and the rig around it (the sidecar's side, a sink that stands in for the internet, a control that proves the sink can be hit), a probe that tries each way out, a runner that starts one rig per check and removes only what it made, and a second matrix file generated from that run.
- Adds the spec, the plan and a report under `docs/lab/`.

Nothing is wired into the app, the UI, the Hermes path or any running agent. No dependency was added.

## Why

Every harness enforces chat rules differently, so each new harness has meant re-rendering the same rules and hoping they hold. This slice tries the other shape on Pi: rules are decided once, outside the harness, and the per-harness code shrinks to "start it, send text, read text, veto a tool".

## Verification

- `npx vitest run`, after merging main (which now has #337): 211 files, 4149 passed, 1 skipped (pre-existing).
- `npx tsc --noEmit`: clean.
- Sanitization gate, deterministic layer, on the PR diff: clean. The semantic layer runs in CI only.
- `SWARMLAB_PI_BIN=... npm run conformance` against a real Pi 1.5.2 install: 23 of 23. All fourteen checks pass, and each of the eight broken shims turned its named checks red. `conformance/matrix/pi-1.5.2.process.json` was written by that run, and a CI test now fails if that file no longer matches the suite.
- `npm run conformance:docker` with real Pi 1.5.2 in a sealed cell, on Docker Desktop 4.76 for Mac (engine 29.5.2): 29 of 29. S0-S3, C8, C9 and C10 pass, and so do the thirteen process-level checks run again in the cell. Ten rigs broken on purpose (a route to the sink, an ordinary network, the key in the cell's environment, the key in a file, a writable cell, a host folder mounted, a file where a Docker socket would be, a door with a route out, a sink nobody can prove works, C10 with the gate left in) each turned its named checks red for the reason it names. A rig handed a real-looking key is refused before Docker is asked for anything, and again by the cell itself. `conformance/matrix/pi-1.5.2.docker.json` was written by that run, and a CI test fails if it no longer matches the suite.
- The Docker checks were then broken by hand twice (the sink's log ignored; the probe's answers ignored) and the must-fail tests went red both times.
- An audit of the Docker cell then tried, by hand in a live cell, ways out the probe does not: every TCP port on Docker's side of the cell network, a port another lab container published, DNS watched with a packet capture (with a control that was seen leaving), IPv6 without the cell's own setting, and the model route and the door's port poked from inside. Nothing got out and no key came back. It found the run went red on a network that answers no IPv6 DNS question (fixed), three checks with no broken rig (added), and that S1-S3 did not read what Docker actually gave the container (they now do; a cell given a shared process namespace, a published port and loosened seccomp turned S1 and S2 red when tried). These by-hand trials are not standing checks; the report says which.
- Not run: C13 (no tool verdict depends on who asked yet, so it could not fail for the reason it names), C7, C12b. The Docker run is not in CI.
- Mutation checks, run by hand and not committed: listed in `docs/lab/pi-slice.md`, "What this does not show", item 11.
- Not verified: the Docker run on any other machine, Docker version or engine, or on Linux.

## Risk

- **The wall is shown on one machine, for the ways out that were tried.** With Pi in the lab's Docker cell, a tool it ran reached nothing but the door and read no secret, also with the tool gate removed. That is Docker Desktop for Mac, one version, and a list of probes, not a proof: a way out that is not on the list was not tried. `docs/lab/pi-slice.md` lists the limits (DNS judged by its answer, no IPv6 control, wall-check lines with no broken cell behind them, the cell token readable inside the cell, no limits tested, and more). Do not read this PR as "Pi is safe to deploy".
- **These are lab images and a lab rig.** Nothing in Swarm Map starts a cell like this, and no running agent is in one. In the rig the door has no route out either; a door that talks to a real model and a real chat platform needs one, and that side is not tested.
- **The Docker run needs an internet connection for its controls.** A one-off container asks DNS for three names before a run (and, if this machine's resolver answers no IPv6 question, asks a public resolver itself), and one cell that is broken on purpose is put on an ordinary network and opens one connection from there. No public address is written in the repo.
- **At process level, "nothing left this machine" is shown for Pi's own Node runtime only.** The tripwire there does not see a program Pi starts that is not Node. The Docker cell is what covers that.
- **The key swap and the budget cap exist for one wire format** (OpenAI chat-completions). A harness that speaks another has neither; the route refuses its calls.
- **Pi is given no direct messages**, because its sessions share one folder on disk.
- **The bot loop limit is not enforced.** With bots allowed, two bots can answer each other without end.
- **The credential preflight is a list of names and shapes.** A credential it has not been taught goes through; Pi's environment is listed by hand for that reason.
- **Several check lines have no broken shim behind them** (C2, C4a, C12, C15 and parts of C1, C5v, C8p). The report lists them.
- A scripted model tests plumbing only.
- The fake Pi was wrong once already (real Pi never asks the gate about an undeclared tool). The real-Pi run caught it. The fake can drift again when Pi changes; the pin is 1.5.2.
- `tsconfig.json` gains `allowImportingTsExtensions`, and `vitest.config.ts` excludes `conformance/suites/*.real.test.ts`. Both are small, but they touch shared config.
- This is one branch rather than the four stacked PRs the plan described. It is large (about 16,100 lines, 1,600 of them a lock file, mostly tests and scenario files). The commits can be read one at a time.
- An earlier commit on this branch held a longer copy of the spec. The tip does not, but the branch history still does. Squash on merge if that matters.

## Links

- `docs/lab/pi-slice.md`: what exists, how to run it, what it does not show.
- `docs/lab/primitives.md`: the spec. `docs/lab/plan-pi.md`: the plan as written.

**Question from Juniper (2026-07-24):** can a user recover HSM dashboard access if they lose their decryption key? People WILL lose keys; losing everything with it is not acceptable.

**Reality check:** if the encryption is doing its job, lost key = the ciphertext is gone — there is no honest "recover the plaintext" path, and building a backdoor would defeat the vault. But HSM's contents are almost entirely **API keys and tokens**, which are *rotatable*. So the right recovery story is probably not decryption recovery but a **reset-and-rotate flow**:

1. Operator proves identity out-of-band (org admin action, not a self-serve password reset)
2. HSM issues a fresh keypair / operator token
3. Dashboard walks through every stored provider entry as a **rotation checklist** — old values marked unrecoverable, operator re-mints each upstream (GitHub App key, OpenRouter, Telegram, …) and pastes the new ones
4. Assigned agents' `.env`s regenerate + containers recreate, same as a normal key update

Optional hardening for org installs: Shamir-split a recovery key across 2–3 org members, or an org-admin escrow key — decide deliberately, it's a real trust tradeoff.

Also worth: a **"break-glass inventory" export** — a plaintext-free list of what providers/keys exist and where they're used, so a reset never turns into archaeology.

Flagging for the gardener lane per Juniper.

## What
- Model the cascade the way hermes-agent consumes it: **primary = `model:` section, fallbacks = `fallback_providers` rows**. New `readCascade()` / `cascadeChain()` in `lib/services/harness.ts`; the writer, scheduler, API routes, cascade library and editor all work on that chain.
- Remove the PR #243 `primary-mismatch` 409 and its banner, plus `allowPrimaryChange`: with chain semantics the "mismatch" cannot occur.
- Preserve each file's convention on write: a file that repeats its primary as `fallback_providers[0]` (HSM-saved: cryptids/nimbleco/osint, blackhouse) keeps that duplicate row, in sync with `model.default` across rotations; a file that does not (cyborg, matilde, iris) never gains one. `model.fallback` (unread by the runtime) is rewritten only where it already exists.
- Primary rows are now trackable: the scheduler/report list the primary first with `role: 'primary'`, rotation of the primary rewrites `model.default` (and the duplicate row when present), and `PUT /models/tracking` validates against the chain. A file with rows but **no primary** reports every entry as a fallback and a rotation on it is refused (`blocked: no-primary-in-file`, manual apply 409) instead of inventing a `model.default`.
- API: `GET /models` adds `chain`, `primaryEntry`, `primaryDuplicatedAsRow0` (old fields kept); `PUT` accepts `{ chain, expected_chain }` and `{ cascade }`. The pre-chain `{ fallback_providers }` body is now **fallback-only**: it rewrites the rows and never touches the primary (GET → PUT of the raw `fallbackProviders` is a byte-identical no-op on all five fleet shapes; on a duplicate-row-0 file the primary's row stays the writer's; a file with no primary gets 409 pointing at `{ chain }`). Cascade library records store `chain` (`entries` migrated on read, accepted as an input alias).
- The primary is read the way hermes loads it (`cli.py:487-498`): `model.default`, else `model.model`, else a scalar `model: <id>`. The writer keeps whichever form the file uses (no `default:` added beside `model.model`; the scalar form stays scalar until the primary needs a provider/base_url). README / AGENTS.md updated.

## Why
PR #243 assumed `fallback_providers[0]` is the primary. On the real fleet both conventions coexist: cyborg's primary (`z-ai/glm-5.3`) is only in `model:` and its rows start with `claude-sonnet-4-6`, so the editor showed "the primary is not the first row… Saving is refused" for a perfectly valid file. Verified against the runtime (`hermes-agent-mt`): the primary is `model.default` (`cli.py:528-539`, `gateway/run.py:2571`), the chain is `fallback_providers` in order (`hermes_cli/fallback_config.py:71-97`, `agent/agent_init.py:1187-1199`), and `try_activate_fallback` walks it one row per failure, skipping a row equal to the current (provider, model) (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:1453-1490`), so a duplicate row 0 is harmless and `model.fallback` is never read. The review round on this PR found the old `{ fallback_providers }` body still took row 0 as the primary (so a raw-rows round trip demoted the primary on 3 of 5 agents), the reader missed hermes' scalar / `model.model` forms, and a no-primary file got a rotated fallback written as a brand-new primary; all three are fixed here with a failing test first.

## Verification
- `pnpm vitest run` → 131 files, 1718 tests passed (was 129 / 1620 on main; 130 / 1665 before review round 1; 131 / 1690 before review round 2). New coverage: `lib/services/__tests__/read-cascade.test.ts` (15), chain-semantics + new-format blocks in `cascade-writer.test.ts` (+16, incl. a byte-identical no-op save over each of the five real fleet shapes in `__tests__/fleet-shapes.ts` and over the scalar / `model.model` forms), `model-update-scheduler.test.ts` (+10, incl. the no-primary file), and a new `app/api/harnesses/[id]/models/route.fleet-shapes.test.ts` (11: the route over the real fixtures on disk with the real readers — GET → PUT round trip is a no-op on every shape, reorder keeps the primary, no-primary → 409). Route/library/UI tests updated rather than deleted.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` → clean.
- `npx eslint` on every touched file → 0 errors; 5 warnings in `page.tsx` are pre-existing on `main` (unused imports), untouched.
- Not run against a live agent (no SSH/browser in this task).

## Risk
- Cascade library records change shape on disk (`entries` → `chain`) on the next write; readers of `GET /api/cascades` that expected `entries` must read `chain` (input still accepts `entries`).
- `{ fallback_providers }` can no longer change the primary (it never should have been able to without saying so). A caller that relied on "row 0 becomes the primary" must send `{ chain }`; on a duplicate-row-0 file a body that omits the primary's row still gets it back at row 0.
- A file with rows but no primary is now refused by the scheduler and by `{ fallback_providers }` rather than gaining a `model.default`. None of the five fleet agents is in that state.
- Pre-chain reports persisted in `model-updates.json` lack `role`; the type marks it optional.

## Review round 2
Fixed (each with a failing test first; the two MAJORs are reproduced on the real fixtures in `route.fleet-shapes.test.ts`):
- **MAJOR 1 — silent promotion on a no-primary file.** `PUT { chain }` on a file with rows but no `model.default` is refused with 409 `no-primary-in-file: …` unless the body carries `set_primary: true` — the same refusal the scheduler / manual apply already make. The editor shows row 1 with a "no primary on disk — save will make this the primary" note instead of the PRIMARY badge when `primaryEntry` is null, and sends `set_primary: true` only from that state. A fresh file with no rows at all still takes a `{ chain }` without the flag (nothing to promote).
- **MAJOR 2 — root `provider:` / `base_url:` siblings.** `readModelBlock` (and so `readCascade` / `readModelProvider`) reads root-level `provider:` / `base_url:` / `api_base:` onto the primary when the `model:` section lacks the key, as hermes' `_normalize_root_model_keys` does (fallback-only, block wins). The writer leaves the root lines alone while the primary's provider and base_url are unchanged (no-op save byte-identical; a model-only rotation keeps the scalar form) and, when `chain[0]` changes either, moves provider/default/base_url into the `model:` block and deletes the root lines. New `P2` fleet shape (`model: qwen3:30b` + root ollama + root base_url + one anthropic fallback) is in `FLEET_SHAPES`, so every no-op suite covers it; GET `chain[0]` = `{ollama, qwen3:30b, base_url}`; promoting anthropic leaves no root `base_url`, the block gets `provider: anthropic` + `default:`, and the ollama row is written as a fallback exactly when the chain carries it.
- **(a)** `{ fallback_providers }` drops a row equal to the primary on every file — a non-duplicate file is never flipped to the duplicate convention.
- **(b)** `checkModelUpdates` sets `blocked: no-primary-in-file` on every entry with a successor on such a file in notify mode too; that refusal no longer appends the per-run `cascade:auto-update:blocked` audit row (manual apply still returns 409 `Blocked: no-primary-in-file`); the editor disables the Update button (title = the reason) on a blocked row.
- **(c)** `parseExistingModelBlock` treats an empty `default:` as absent (mirrors the reader): `model.model` is the primary's key, the duplicate row 0 is detected and its `key_env` survives an edit.
- **(d)** Passthrough keys keep their on-disk place among the managed keys, so a block with both `model.model` and `model.default` (and e.g. `api_mode:` before `provider:`) round-trips byte-identical; a managed key the file lacked is inserted in canonical position.

Skipped: nothing. Verification: `pnpm vitest run` 131 files / 1718 tests green (+28); `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; eslint 0 errors on touched files (same 5 pre-existing `page.tsx` warnings).

## Root cause (#113)

`nextAvailablePort()` in `lib/services/harness.ts` derived the next free host port **only from observable sources** — scanning `compose/*/docker-compose.yml` `published:` lines plus `docker ps`. Neither reflects a port that has been *allocated but not yet written* (compose file not created / container not yet started). The three call sites — `createOverlay`, `duplicateOverlay`, `importFromDir` — each allocate-then-write **non-atomically**, so two near-concurrent creates (or a create racing a duplicate/import) both derive the same `BASE_PORT` (8642). The second container then binds an already-claimed host port and hangs in `Created` with no network.

Compounding it: the `Harness` type had **no port field** (only a `channel: ":${port}"` display string), so `harnesses.json` couldn't be consulted as an authoritative source and there was no post-hoc duplicate detection.

## The fix

1. **`lib/types.ts`** — add `apiPort?: number` to `Harness`: an authoritative, persisted record of the published host port (the display `channel` string is not machine-usable, and live Docker state is absent for not-yet-started agents).
2. **`nextAvailablePort(composeBaseDir, reservedPorts = [])`** — union caller-supplied reserved ports into the used-set, so allocated-but-not-yet-observable ports are honored.
3. **All three call sites** (`createOverlay`, `duplicateOverlay`, `importFromDir`) now seed reserved ports from the persisted overlays (`overlays.map(h => h.apiPort).filter(...)`) and persist `apiPort` on the written overlay. `importFromDir` pins the authoritative compose port onto the overlay (and aligns `channel`), overriding the throwaway port `createOverlay` allocates internally.
4. **Fail-loud guard** — `assertPortAvailable(overlays, port, selfId)` runs immediately before each compose write and throws if another persisted overlay already owns that port. This catches the one path that bypasses allocation: `importFromDir` honoring a port hard-coded in an imported agent's `.env` (`API_SERVER_PORT`).

## Test evidence

New `lib/services/__tests__/harness-port-alloc.test.ts` (red → green): (a) `createOverlay` twice → distinct persisted `apiPort`s; (b) a persisted `apiPort` is treated as reserved so the next create skips it; (c) a colliding import (`.env` declares an already-owned port) fails loud instead of producing a stuck container.

```
 RUN  v4.1.6 /private/tmp/hsm113

 ✓ lib/services/__tests__/harness-port-alloc.test.ts (3 tests)
   ✓ (a) createOverlay twice persists distinct apiPorts
   ✓ (b) a persisted apiPort is treated as reserved — next create skips it
   ✓ (c) a colliding allocation fails loud rather than producing a stuck container

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
```

Existing lifecycle tests (`harness-create`, `harness-duplicate`, `harness`) still pass (18/18), and `tsc --noEmit` is clean.

Closes #113

---

**Autonomous gardener PR — DRAFT, Tier-2** (touches harness create/duplicate/import lifecycle on a live fleet); needs human review before merge.

Note: adds `apiPort` to `lib/types.ts` — may conflict with the #114 PR which also edits `types.ts` (resolve on second merge).

## The confirmed hole

HSM has **no transport auth**. A compromised agent container can reach every mutating route via `host.docker.internal:3000` (agents already get `SWARM_MAP_POLICY_URL=http://host.docker.internal:${PORT}` injected into their `.env`). There is no login today, and the dashboard mutates purely via browser `fetch('/api', {method})` — no server actions.

**Why source-IP / binding fixes are impossible:** a live measurement proved that agent-container requests and dashboard requests **both arrive at HSM as source `127.0.0.1`** — Docker Desktop SNATs container egress to loopback. There is no packet-level attribute that separates the agent from the operator. The only viable separator is a **credential the agent cannot obtain**.

## The design (minimal, reversible, kill-switched)

- **Server-only secret** `HSM_OPERATOR_TOKEN`, read from `process.env` only. Never referenced in any agent `.env`, never `NEXT_PUBLIC_`, never in the client bundle, never logged.
- **Stateless session cookie** `hsm_session` = `HMAC-SHA256(key = HSM_OPERATOR_TOKEN, msg = "hsm-operator-v1")`, hex. No session store — the middleware recomputes and constant-time compares. `httpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Secure` only when served over https (HSM is http on the trusted plane, so unconditional `Secure` would make the browser silently drop the cookie).
- **Root `middleware.ts`** matching `/api/:path*`:
  - **GET / HEAD (and OPTIONS etc.) → always pass.** Agents' policy/is-admin reads are GETs; all dashboard reads are GETs. Unaffected.
  - **POST / PUT / PATCH / DELETE → require a valid `hsm_session` cookie** (recompute HMAC, constant-time compare). Missing/invalid → `401 {error:"auth required"}`.
  - Excludes `/api/auth/login` and `/api/auth/logout`.
- **`POST /api/auth/login`** — `{token}`, constant-time verified, sets the cookie. **`POST /api/auth/logout`** clears it.
- **Dashboard UX:** `/login` token form; a `window.fetch` wrapper mounted in the dashboard layout redirects to `/login` on any `/api` 401. (The shared `useApi` hook is GET-only and mutations are scattered inline `fetch` calls, so a single global guard covers every call site without editing them. It is UX only — the middleware is the enforcement.)

### Crypto discipline
- Web Crypto (`crypto.subtle`) HMAC so the **same module runs on both the middleware (edge) and Node route runtimes** — verified by a green `next build` (registers as `ƒ Proxy (Middleware)`).
- Constant-time compare for both the token check and the cookie verify (length-guarded XOR accumulate; operands are fixed-length 64-char hex, and the login path compares HMACs so raw-token length never leaks).

## Fail-open kill-switch + rollout

**If `HSM_OPERATOR_TOKEN` is unset/empty, the middleware passes everything through — identical to today.** Protection activates only when the token is set.

Rollout sequence:
1. **Deploy this code** — no-op while the token is unset.
2. **Set `HSM_OPERATOR_TOKEN`** in HSM's server env (e.g. `openssl rand -hex 32`) and restart. Gate goes live.
3. **Verify** from inside an agent container: `curl -X POST http://host.docker.internal:3000/api/harnesses/x/stop` → expect `401 {"error":"auth required"}`; a dashboard GET still works.
4. **Kill-switch:** unset the token and restart to instantly disable the gate.

## Excluded routes

- `POST /api/auth/login`, `POST /api/auth/logout` — establish/clear the session; gating them would lock everyone out.

**No external/webhook/platform-callback routes exist.** I grepped `app/api` for inbound-signature verification (`x-signature-ed25519`, `x-slack-signature`, `verifyKey`, `X-Hub-Signature`, any `request.headers.get('x-...')`) — **zero matches**. The `surfaces/*/verify` routes are **browser-initiated** operator credential checks (e.g. discord/verify calls Discord's API server-side to dodge CORS), not inbound webhooks — so they are correctly gated, not excluded.

## Agent-legitimate mutations: none

The only agent→HSM caller is the `swarm_map_policy` plugin (`infra/templates/plugins/swarm_map_policy`), which makes **GET-only** calls (`.../surfaces/{platform}/groups/{id}`, `.../admins/{id}`). GETs always pass. No agent performs a POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE, so gating all mutations breaks no legitimate agent path.

## For human review

- **Setup routes** `POST /api/setup/{complete,deploy}` and `POST /api/harnesses/import` run during first-time setup. They are browser-driven and correctly gated; with the token set, the operator logs in first. With the token unset (fresh install), fail-open lets setup proceed. Flagging in case first-boot ordering matters to you.
- **Next 16 deprecation:** the build warns that the `middleware` file convention is being renamed to `proxy`. It still works on the pinned `next@16.2.6` (build is green). Renaming `middleware.ts` → `proxy.ts` is a trivial future follow-up.

## Test evidence

`pnpm exec vitest run` — **69 files, 603 tests passed** (includes 19 new: `lib/auth/session.test.ts`, `app/api/auth/login/route.test.ts`, `middleware.test.ts`). Covers: valid token → cookie set; wrong token → 401 + no cookie; mutating w/ no or tampered cookie → 401; mutating w/ valid cookie → pass; GET w/ no cookie → pass; token-unset → everything passes (fail-open); tampered-cookie reject; `Secure` gated on https.

`pnpm exec tsc --noEmit` — **exit 0**. `pnpm exec eslint` (new files) — **0 errors**. `pnpm exec next build` — **exit 0**, middleware compiled.

## What
- New setting `discordApproverRoles` (Discord role IDs only). Swarm-map writes it into every Discord agent's `config.yaml` at `platforms.discord.extra.approver_roles`, the key the adapter already checks live at click time (hermes-agent-mt#175, merged). Only that one line changes.
- Sync runs once per server start (`instrumentation.ts`) and on `POST /api/fleet/discord-approver-roles`. `GET` on the same route reports each agent's roles, whether `require_admin_for_exec_approval` is on, and drift. It writes nothing.
- `allow_admin_from` and `require_admin_for_exec_approval` are never touched. `[]` writes `approver_roles: ''` (nobody approves by role). `null` or unset means swarm-map leaves the key alone.

## Why
Juniper wants one Discord role, not a hand-kept ID list, to decide who can approve dangerous commands. Role membership is checked live by the adapter, so adding or removing someone from the role needs no config write or restart. Only changing *which* role does, and that is this setting.

## Verification
- Red first: the new module, setting and route tests failed on `main` (module missing / unknown settings key).
- `pnpm vitest run`: 141 files, 1900 tests passed. `npx tsc --noEmit` clean. `eslint` on touched files clean.
- Mutation check: removing the `shadowed` guard fails its test; so do a no-op write, the wrong `extra` block, and dropping the duplicate top-level `discord:` guard.
- Review fix: role IDs are rechecked at write time. `settings.json` is read back without the PUT check, so a hand-edited value with a newline could have written `require_admin_for_exec_approval: false` into every agent. Now refused, nothing written.
- Dry run against read-only copies of all 9 live Discord agent configs (nested `display.platforms` block, top-level `discord:` block, real `extra`): each one `updated`, exactly one line changed (the `approver_roles` line), line count unchanged. Copies deleted afterwards.

## Risk
- Once the setting is set, every HSM start rewrites `approver_roles` on every Discord agent, including cyborg-public. A hand edit to that key on one agent will be overwritten. There is no per-agent opt-out.
- The adapter only lets role holders click if they also pass basic access (`DISCORD_ALLOWED_USERS` / `DISCORD_ALLOWED_ROLES`). Most agents gate on the user list, so an `approver` holder who is not on it still cannot click.
- Roles never apply in DMs (no guild). DM approvals still need `allow_admin_from`.
- Agents read `config.yaml` at start, so a change needs a restart of each agent.
- Writes are in place (`writeFileSync`, same inode and mode), matching the `.env` heal. A crash mid-write could truncate a `config.yaml`.

## Links
- hermes-agent-mt#175 (adapter `approver_roles`), #173 (admin gate keys). Both are merged, so this PR does not stack on anything.

## Summary

Swarm Map's generated agent composes never set `HERMES_UID`/`HERMES_GID` (and deliberately set no `user:` directive), while hermes-agent-mt's image bakes `useradd -u 10000 hermes` and only remaps the uid when `HERMES_UID` is provided. On a native Linux bind mount, any agent whose data dir is not owned by uid 10000 crash-loops with `RuntimeError: SessionStore SQLite handle unavailable` while the container still reports `Up`. Invisible on macOS (VirtioFS squashes bind-mount ownership) — so this has shipped and gone unnoticed.

## Evidence

- **swarm-map:** zero `HERMES_UID`/`HERMES_GID` references anywhere (`grep` across `lib/`, `app/`, `infra/`, `docs/`). The no-`user:` stance is explicit — `lib/services/harness-compose.ts:5` ("s6-overlay handles privilege dropping internally — never set `user:` in compose").
- **hermes-agent-mt:** the image bakes the uid — `Dockerfile:191` `RUN useradd -u 10000 -m -d /opt/data hermes`. The stage2 hook only remaps when told — `docker/stage2-hook.sh:104-107` (`HERMES_UID="${HERMES_UID:-${PUID:-}}"`; if empty, no remap → gateway runs as 10000). Upstream's own compose documents the contract — `docker-compose.yml:5-10` ("HERMES_UID=$(id -u) HERMES_GID=$(id -g)", "Set ... to the host user that owns ~/.hermes so files created inside the container stay readable/writable on the host") and `:39-40`/`:73-74` (`HERMES_UID=${HERMES_UID:-10000}`).
- **Failure path on Linux:** host data dir owned by e.g. 1000 → gateway (uid 10000) cannot open/write `state.db` → `SessionStore SQLite handle unavailable` restart loop; container healthcheck never runs so nothing reports it.

## Compounding issue

Swarm Map's `state-init` service chowns the named state volume to **the data dir's owner** *before* the s6 stage2 hook chowns `/opt/data` to the runtime uid (`STATE_INIT_SCRIPT` in `lib/services/harness-compose.ts`: `chown "$(stat -c '%u:%g' "$DATA" ...)" "$STATE"`). The stage2 hook never revisits `/state`, so the volume keeps the stale owner and the symlinked DBs become unwritable even for the correct uid — a mismatch that (with a non-10000 host owner) produces `state.db` files owned by nobody-in-the-container.

## Suggested fixes

1. **swarm-map:** populate `HERMES_UID`/`HERMES_GID` in the generated compose's `environment:` from the Swarm Map process uid (`process.getuid()`), mirroring upstream's own recommended invocation `HERMES_UID=$(id -u) HERMES_GID=$(id -g)`.
2. **hermes-agent-mt (complementary):** re-chown `$STATE` after the stage2 remap, so the volume ownership follows the runtime uid rather than the pre-remap data-dir owner.

## Impact

Any Linux deployment where the Swarm Map process (or the agent data dirs) is not owned by uid 10000 ships agents that cannot boot. We currently work around it in our deploy role by pinning the service uid/gid to 10000 so the host owner matches the image — an accident of layout, not a guarantee.

Fixes #273.

The named-volume + state-init layout (#204 PR2) exists to escape macOS VirtioFS torn writes, but it is applied **unconditionally** in all three compose generators. On native Linux it breaks every agent from birth: hermes-agent-mt's profile check (`gateway/run_runtime.py`) resolves the symlinked DBs to `/state` and refuses a session DB outside the reserved profile `/opt/data`, so the gateway crash-loops (see #273 for the repro on a native ext4 box).

This gates the layout behind `ComposeOptions.useStateVolume` (default **off**) in:
- `generatePlainCompose` / `generateVpnCompose` (`lib/services/harness-compose.ts`)
- `generateAgentCompose` (`lib/services/agent-deploy-templates.ts`, the deploy path — also unconditional before, with the same effect)

threading from `Settings` (`lib/types.ts`, `lib/services/config.ts` default `false`) through the four `ComposeOptions` call sites (harness create/duplicate/import + settings regenerate) and the deploy route. With the layout off, `depends_on` is omitted entirely when there is no sidecar to gate (an empty `depends_on:` key is invalid compose), and no top-level `volumes:` trailer is emitted.

The explicit per-harness **migrate-db transformer is untouched** — it remains the deliberate way to opt a harness into the migrated layout (and now also correctly migrates a default, state-volume-off fresh compose; covered by a new test).

Hosts that genuinely need the VirtioFS escape can enable the setting; the migration runbook flow is unchanged. A complementary hermes-side fix is proposed in cyborg-garden/hermes-agent-mt#187.

Tests: full suite `pnpm vitest run` green (2036); the existing migration-wiring tests now opt in explicitly, and new tests lock in both states for plain/VPN/deploy (off: no init service, no `hermes-state-*:/state`, no `depends_on`, no trailer; on: all present) plus ollama-without-state-volume keeping a sidecar-only gate.

## Two things, one root

### 1. The manifest bug (silent, live in prod today)
`person_memory/plugin.yaml` ships `name: person-memory` (dash), but every agent's `config.yaml` enables it as `person_memory` (underscore). The loader matches the enabled-list entry against `manifest.key or manifest.name` (hermes-agent-mt `hermes_cli/plugins.py:1454-1457`), so **dash ≠ underscore → the plugin is discovered but never enabled.** Verified 2026-08-06: on primo chur-bot/im7-bot the log showed `person_memory: registered` = **0** and discovery "N found, M enabled" never counted it. **person_memory had NEVER actually loaded on any agent.** Fix: set `name: person_memory` (underscore, matching the dir + every config). After the fix, all 12 agents (9 garden + chur-bot/im7-bot/pmf) now log `person_memory: registered` and enabled count +1. Whatever ships person_memory as an artifact must carry the underscore name.

### 2. Make it a default (HSM is the right layer)
Enabling a `standalone` hook plugin needs BOTH the files in the agent dir AND the name in `config.yaml → plugins.enabled` (`plugins.py:243-268`, `:1450-1469` — standalone plugins are opt-in). The image can't own enablement; per-template defaults drift across N templates. HSM already writes `plugins.enabled` (`lib/templates/config-yaml.ts generateDefaultConfig`, `app/api/setup/deploy/route.ts`) and installs plugin files — single choke point. Add `person_memory` to the base `enabledPlugins`.

### Boundary/privacy review — clears (SAFE-WITH-CONDITIONS)
- Egregore `boundary-check.sh` is unrelated (governs Claude Code cross-instance file access, not the Hermes runtime).
- Hermes SECURITY.md §2.3/§2.5: in-process plugins may read what the agent reads; person_memory reads only its own `memory_dir/people/*.md`, ephemeral, turn-scoped, never persisted, never into the system prompt (cache-safe).
- `credential_redactor` is already a de-facto default and *modifies* turns; person_memory is read-only + fail-open — a weaker ask.
- **Condition (shared group sessions):** HSM default is `group_sessions_per_user: false`. Confirm the injected directive is behavioral, NOT raw PII — a directive echoing raw phone/Slack IDs would surface sender A's identifiers to B in a shared session. Gate to per-user/DM or strip identifiers if so. (Relevant now that we seed `people/*.md` with phone numbers + Slack IDs on both fleets.)

## Acceptance
- person_memory manifest name is `person_memory`; HSM-provisioned agents load it with no manual config; existing agents pick it up on next artifact sync; the shared-session PII condition is verified before flipping default.

Context: 2026-08-06 fleet rollout — org memory `knowledge/decisions/2026-08-06-identity-ledger-design.md`, board `[identity-ledger-directory]`.

Fixes #274.

hermes-agent-mt's image bakes `useradd -u 10000 hermes` and only remaps that uid when `HERMES_UID`/`HERMES_GID` are set (s6 stage2 hook, `docker/stage2-hook.sh`); upstream's own compose documents `HERMES_UID=$(id -u) HERMES_GID=$(id -g)`. - Deploy path (`generateEnvContent`): same pair into the generated `.env` — `env_file` entries reach the container environment, so stage2 reads them there too (this generator deliberately has no compose `environment:` block).

Once this lands, the compounding `STATE_INIT_SCRIPT` issue in #274 also resolves: state-init chowns the named volume to the data dir's owner, which now equals the remapped runtime uid.

## What

Add an **Analytics** tab within each harness (per-agent view) plus a **fleet-wide analytics view**, showing regularly-updating operational metrics.

## Per-harness analytics tab

### Per-surface breakdown (who's messaging, which surfaces are busiest)
- Which surfaces are being used most (Signal / Telegram / Discord / Slack / Mattermost)
- Who is messaging the bot the most per surface (top users by message count in time window)
- Message volume per surface per day/week

### Not per-surface (agent-level metrics)
- **Cost tracking:** estimated spend per agent per day/week/month (model usage × per-model pricing)
- **Tool calls:** which tools the agent is calling, frequency, success/failure rates
- **Model usage breakdown:** which models in the cascade are being used, input/output tokens per model, escalation frequency (cheap → premium)

## Fleet-wide analytics view

- Total token spend across all agents, broken down by model
- Cost breakdown by agent (which agents are expensive vs cheap)
- Surface distribution across the fleet
- Model cascade efficiency (how often cheap tier handles requests vs escalating)

## Cost-calculation correctness requirement (critical)

Cost estimation **must not be independently re-implemented in every place cost is mentioned** across the codebase. Instead:

- There should be a **single source of truth** for per-model pricing (one config table / module, not scattered constants)
- The analytics tab should consume that shared variable, not compute its own estimate
- Add a **check/audit** that cost values displayed across Swarm Map (analytics tab, any existing cost displays, budget alerts, etc.) are all derived from the same source — flag any place that hardcodes or re-computes pricing independently

This prevents the maintenance trap where pricing updates in one place silently diverge from another.

## Context

- Connects to the gardener analytics handoff (`handoffs/2026-07/23-juniper-hsm-analytics-tab-harness-fleet-tools-model-tokens.md` in nimbleco-memory) — that has the full Phase 1-3 breakdown
- digicryptids already has per-request `req.llmUsage.totalTokens` tracking and a `usage_logs` table — that's the existing pattern to generalize fleet-wide
- The `[token-spend-audit]` thread (Anthropic spend is not sustainable) is the financial pressure driving this

## Open questions (for design, not blocking the issue)

- Data collection model: push (agents emit metrics to HSM) vs pull (HSM reads agent logs/DB)?
- Storage: time-series in Postgres, SQLite per-agent, or central analytics DB?
- Time granularity: real-time, hourly, daily?

## What

Add a per-agent setting for Hermes's `agent.max_turns` (how many model and tool steps an agent may take in one turn), editable in Swarm Map like the per-harness memory and CPU limits from #114.

## Why

Today new agents get a fixed `max_turns: 60` from `lib/templates/config-yaml.ts`, and changing it afterwards means hand-editing each agent's `config.yaml` on the host. Agents doing long research or ops work need a higher ceiling; cheap chat-only agents may want a lower one to cap spend. Hand edits are easy to lose and invisible in the UI.

## Suggested shape

- A number field per agent (and a fleet default), written to `agent.max_turns` in that agent's config.
- Show the current value read from the config, so hand edits are visible.
- Sensible bounds and a note on cost: a higher limit means longer, pricier turns.
- Optional: the same for the delegation/background limits (`max_iterations`, nested `max_turns`) if Hermes exposes them.

Takes effect on the agent's next restart, or live if Hermes reloads config.

## Summary

`person_memory` 0.3.0 (#219) made person cards **self-seeding**: every sender is
auto-recorded on first contact. That was the right fix for the problem it solved
— cards previously had to be hand-written, so in practice the adaptation layer
adapted to nobody — but it turns a hand-curated handful of cards into an
auto-accumulating record of everyone an agent has ever spoken to, across every
surface it runs on.

Three related gaps follow from that. None of them is urgent for a deployment
where every participant is trusted. All of them are load-bearing the moment an
agent sits in a room with someone who isn't. Filing this as hardening work for
that era rather than as a live incident.

## Gap 1 — person cards have no context scoping

Cards are scoped to the **agent** and keyed by `platform:id`. There is no
channel, group, or surface dimension. A card learned in a DM applies in a group
and vice versa.

The adaptation directive is appended to the user message, so in a shared session
its contents are visible to everyone present. Today that is bounded by the
writable-field allowlist and the identifier rejection added in #219, but the
structural point stands: what the agent learned about someone in one context is
applied, and shown, in another.

## Gap 2 — the person store is enumerable through general-purpose tools

Cards are files under the agent's home directory, and **the filenames are raw
platform identifiers**. Agents configured with a local (unsandboxed) terminal
backend can read that directory with ordinary file tools.

A directory listing is therefore sufficient to enumerate every person an agent
has a card for, without opening a single file. Self-seeding did not create this
property — it raises the value of the target, because the directory now fills
itself.

Worth noting explicitly: this is derivable from the public source in about a
minute, which is part of why it's being filed openly rather than quietly.

Possible directions:
- move the person store outside the agent's tool-reachable home
- mediate access through a plugin accessor that only ever returns the current
  sender, so there is no listable directory
- hash or opaque-ify filenames so a listing is not itself a contact list

## Gap 3 — no requester-tier gating on tools

`remember_person` is offered to every sender. `enabled_toolsets` /
`disabled_toolsets` are per **agent**, not per **requester**, so there is no way
to express "this tool is available to an operator but not to an arbitrary group
participant."

This generalizes well past this plugin — it is the tier question for the whole
tool registry, and it is the piece most worth designing before it is needed.

## Prior art in our own design

Earlier design work already sketched the axes this needs: a habitat/trust tier
concept (`HabitatTier`), per-tool `allowedTiers` and `risk` metadata, and a
memory-scope notion with siloed vs tag-gated strategies. The vocabulary exists;
what is missing is **enforcement keyed to the requester**. A useful reframe:
person memory is a memory scope with no tier, sitting inside an agent whose
tools also have no tier — the enumeration surface is what those two facts
produce together.

## Levers that exist today

- `PERSON_MEMORY_READONLY=1` — keeps adaptation, stops all accumulation, per agent
- `PERSON_MEMORY_DISABLED=1` — disables the plugin entirely

## Scope of this issue

Design and hardening, not a patch. Reasonable first slices, in rough order of
value:

1. Requester-tier metadata on tools + enforcement at registry exposure time
2. Non-enumerable person store (accessor-mediated or opaque filenames)
3. A scoping dimension on cards (surface, then channel/trust-context)
4. Consent/disclosure and retention: people are not told a durable card is being
   written about them, and nothing ages out

## Overview

In a multi-agent deployment where multiple Hermes agent containers share a single inference backend — whether a local Ollama instance or a cloud provider API with a shared org-level key — KV cache is not isolated between agents. This is a latent privacy and security concern worth documenting and mitigating.

## How it arises

HSM deploys multiple agent containers that each make independent inference calls to the same upstream endpoint:

- **Local models (Ollama):** All agents point to the same host Ollama instance (`host.docker.internal:11434`). Ollama has no tenant isolation — it is designed for single-user local use.
- **Cloud APIs (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.):** These providers scope prompt cache to the API key / organization. HSM deployments typically share one org-level API key across all agents, meaning all agents share the same cache namespace at the provider.

## What leaks and how

**Prefix cache sharing (passive):**
LLM inference servers implement KV cache reuse for common prompt prefixes as a performance optimization. When two agents share an identical prefix — which is likely if they use the same base system prompt — the inference server reuses the same cached KV state for both. The model's internal attention state for the shared prefix is the same physical computation for all agents sharing that prefix.

This does not cause spontaneous content bleed (Agent B's output won't contain Agent A's private tokens), but it means the attention state is not isolated between agents.

**Stale slot memory (passive):**
In Ollama and vLLM, KV memory slots are not zeroed on release. When a slot is freed by one agent and reassigned to another, the new agent's prefill overwrites it — but there is a window where physically non-cleared prior state exists. This is a design assumption in both systems (single-user or trusted multi-tenant use).

**Timing side-channel (active/adversarial):**
Peer-reviewed research (PROMPTPEEK, NDSS 2025; Cache Me Catch You, NDSS 2026) demonstrates that an adversarial client sharing the same inference backend can reconstruct other users' recent prompts with >95% accuracy using timing oracles derived from KV cache hit/miss latency differences. This requires intentional probing (~500-1000 requests per token) but only needs API access — no elevated privileges.

The same attack class applies to shared Ollama instances and to shared-key cloud API deployments.

**Published CVEs:**
- CVE-2025-25183 / GHSA-rm76-4mrf-v9r8: vLLM prefix cache hash collision enabling cache poisoning (patched v0.7.2)
- CVE-2025-1953: vLLM/SGLang KV cache hash collision via meet-in-the-middle (NDSS 2026)
- Azure OpenAI Nov 2025: cross-tenant training data contamination via fine-tuning cache race condition (MSRC advisory)

## Risk levels

| Scenario | Passive risk | Active/adversarial risk |
|----------|-------------|------------------------|
| Shared Ollama, all first-party trusted agents | Low | Medium (if any agent ever compromised) |
| Shared cloud API key, same org | Low | Medium (same) |
| Shared Ollama with any untrusted or third-party agent | Medium | High |
| Separate API keys per agent (different orgs) | None | None |

## Mitigations

**Short term — break shared prefix matching:**
Insert a unique non-guessable token (e.g. a per-agent UUID or HMAC) in the first few tokens of each agent's system prompt. Since KV cache reuse is keyed on exact token sequence, this ensures no two agents ever share a cache block, regardless of how similar the rest of their prompts are. Low cost, no infrastructure change required.

**Medium term — per-agent key provisioning:**
Where the provider supports it, provision separate API keys per agent so caching is scoped per-key rather than per-org. Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI currently offer a sub-key/per-user key provisioning API, so this is not available today for those providers. Worth tracking as providers evolve their multi-tenant offerings.

**Longer term — inference isolation:**
For deployments with strict privacy requirements between agents, run separate inference backend instances per agent or per trust boundary. This provides full KV isolation at the cost of additional resource overhead.

## References

- arXiv:2502.07776 — Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs (Stanford/CRFM, 2025)
- PROMPTPEEK — I Know What You Asked (NDSS 2025)
- Cache Me, Catch You (NDSS 2026)
- NVIDIA Security Blog — Structuring Applications to Secure the KV Cache (Apr 2025)
- Ollama issue tracker: no documented per-caller KV isolation
