Implements the two features promised on the [agent observability page](https://www.chiranjeevthomas.com/projects/agent-observability): per-step tracing of every agent run, and a golden-set eval that runs on every prompt or model change.

## Tracing
- Every run (chat, escalation, decision, client reply, CLI) records its steps: model calls (the prompt, tools offered, tokens, latency), tool calls, refused tools, approval cards, the human decision (an edited approval is labelled `approved_with_edits`) and the email send.
- Runs go to new `agent_runs` and `agent_trace_steps` tables.
- Text is redacted and capped. Traces are kept for 30 days (`pg_cron` purge), with RLS on.
- Tracing is fail-open: a trace write times out after 3 s, and dropped traces are counted in `/api/health`.
- Responses carry `X-Trace-Id`. `GET /api/invoices/{id}/traces` serves the invoice's owner, and a new **Trace** tab in the invoice page shows the runs.

## Golden-set eval
- 18 disputes across levels 0–3, including prompt injection through client replies.
- Cases run through the real API and graph, offline, and are graded from their traces: tool choice, no send or approval-gated action without an approval, tone rules, and an LLM judge.
- Tier 1 replays scripted runs inside `pytest`. Tier 2 (`python -m evals.run`) runs the live model, and `.github/workflows/evals.yml` posts its scorecard on PRs that touch the agent.
- `python -m evals.promote` turns a bad trace into a case.
- Baseline: 94% tool choice, approval rule 100% (18/18), judge 4.33/5.

## Bugs it found and fixed
- **Escalation gating was advisory.** Above-level tools still ran, and above-level drafts reached the approval card. `enforce_tool_gate` now refuses them.
- **Injected client replies could escalate or rewrite the client's email**, using tools with no approval step. Runs started by a reply can no longer use those tools.
- **Opening a chat erased a waiting approval card** proposed by a client reply. The cause: `None` vs `''` in the state sync, plus `/history` writing state while a card was waiting.
- **The CLI crashed after approving**, because it resumed without the freelancer context.
- **Two leaks in the new redaction**, both caught by review (bounded regexes, merged overlapping spans).

## Not in scope
Deferred items are in `TODOS.md`. The P1s: putting `escalate_dispute` behind an approval card, and the empty reply to small-claims questions that the eval flags.

## Test plan
- [x] `pytest`: 400 passed
- [x] `npx vitest run`: 133 passed; `tsc -b` and `npm run build` pass
- [x] Live `python -m evals.run` passes its gates
- [x] Schema validated on a local Postgres 16 (idempotent re-run, retention, cascades)
- [ ] Production smoke test after deploy

## Summary

Makes the app safe for multiple freelancers to use in parallel and ships the in-flight invoice-upload / balance-chasing work.

### Multi-tenant hardening (`aeaee5d`)
- **Per-user Telegram routing** — `send_telegram_notification(user_id, msg)` looks up `users.telegram_chat_id`; soft-fails when unconnected. New `/api/telegram/{connect,webhook,status,disconnect}` endpoints implement a deep-link handshake (`t.me/<bot>?start=<token>`). Dashboard now has a Connect Telegram card.
- **Per-session guest IDs** — anonymous visitors get a unique `guest-<hex>` identity in an HTTP-only cookie (`ic_guest_session`, 30 days). Replaces the shared `"guest"` namespace where every anonymous invoice collided. On Google sign-in, guest invoices + communications migrate to the real account and the cookie is cleared.
- **Invoice ownership enforced** — `authorize_invoice_access()` guards `/api/chat`, `/api/invoices/{id}/{history,details,sender,resume}`. Returns 404 (not 403) so existence isn't leaked across tenants.
- **`communication_history.user_id`** — direct column instead of join-only. Backfilled from `invoices.user_id`.
- **`FreelancerContext.user_id`** — carries identity so downstream tools can route side-effects per-user. Default values changed from `Alex Rivera` demo data to placeholders.
- **CORS with credentials** — explicit `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` env (defaults to localhost:5173) so the guest cookie flows in cross-origin dev.
- **Env cleanup** — drops `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID`; adds `TELEGRAM_BOT_USERNAME`, `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS`.

### Invoice upload + balance-based chasing (`260428e`)
- PDF/DOCX upload UI in the New Invoice modal. Backend extracts fields with `pypdf`/`python-docx` + a Groq structured-output pass with a regex/heuristic fallback for missing fields. Form prefills and surfaces warnings before submit.
- Agent state, drafting tools, late-fee + status tools all read `balance_due` / `amount_paid` instead of the invoice total. New `record_partial_payment` HITL tool reduces balance and flips status to `paid` on full settlement.
- Escalation prompts (1/2/3) instruct the model to route partial-payment replies to `record_partial_payment` and stop chasing once `status=paid`. `/api/chat` short-circuits paid invoices with an explicit "will not continue chasing" reply.
- Frontend stats/table/chat panel show `Original` / `Paid` / `Balance` / `Status`. DraftApproval renders the partial-payment confirmation with amount + date args.
- Deps: `pypdf`, `python-docx`, `python-multipart`; langchain/langgraph bumped to 1.x.

### Fixes
- `c2a77d4` Persist payment state from agent response, not interrupt task — `sync_agent_state_from_invoice` clears pending interrupts before the resume handler can read `approved_tool_name`, so DB writes silently skipped. Driving the persist off `response["amount_paid"] / response["status"]` instead. Caught during the smoke walk.
- `9d123cf` Fix vite proxy target — was 8001, uvicorn runs on 8000 (CLAUDE.md).

## Deployed and verified

- **Supabase migration applied** — `supabase/schema.sql` ran against project `fdsglieendnihbfozbag` (project was paused; restored first). All Plan A/B columns + `invoice-files` storage bucket present.
- **Vercel prod deployed** — https://invoice-chaser-chi.vercel.app. Health endpoint OK.
- **Vercel env vars set/cleaned**:
  - Added `SUPABASE_INVOICE_FILE_BUCKET=invoice-files`
  - Added `TELEGRAM_BOT_USERNAME=freelance_invoices_bot` (discovered via `getMe`)
  - Added `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (64-char URL-safe random; same value mirrored to local `.env`)
  - Removed legacy `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID`
- **Telegram webhook registered** — `https://invoice-chaser-chi.vercel.app/api/telegram/webhook` with `secret_token` and `allowed_updates=["message"]`. Verified via `getWebhookInfo` (0 pending, no errors). `/api/telegram/webhook` now rejects requests missing the matching `x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token` header.
- **End-to-end smoke against prod Supabase** — upload DOCX → parse → create invoice + store file → chat draft (balance-aware) → record_partial_payment → DB persists → mark_invoice_paid → DB status=paid → followup chat short-circuits.
- **Bot profile sanitized** — the bot was previously named "Tips Best" with spam description/short-description referring users to an unrelated NSFW bot. Replaced via Bot API: name → "InvoiceChaser"; description + short_description rewritten with neutral InvoiceChaser-appropriate text; commands list emptied. The bot's profile photo cannot be changed via Bot API — if a sketchy photo is still attached, replace it via BotFather (`/setuserpic`).

## Known gaps (non-blocking, follow-up work)

- **`DATABASE_URL` is stale** — the LangGraph Postgres checkpointer can't reach `aws-0-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com:5432` (`Tenant or user not found`), likely because the password rotated when the project was paused/restored. App falls back to `InMemorySaver` so this only affects in-flight LangGraph chat history across cold starts (invoice/agent state itself is re-synced from Supabase REST per request, so the user-visible behavior is fine). Re-pull the pooler URI from Supabase → `vercel env add DATABASE_URL production --force` → redeploy. **Skipped here because completing this autonomously would require either the DB password or a destructive password reset — neither of which I have explicit authorization for.**
- **Supabase RLS** is disabled on all 3 public tables. Plan explicitly defers this (backend uses service role; anon key isn't exposed). Advisory captured.
- **Groq llama-3.3-70b** occasionally emits malformed tool-call syntax causing the first agent invocation on `/api/invoices/upload` to return `initialization_error`. Invoice + file are still saved; the user just needs to send one chat message to get the first draft. Long-term fix: pin a model with more reliable tool calling, or add a "tool_use_failed → chat-mode draft" fallback middleware.

## Test plan (still useful for review)

- [ ] Sign in with two Google accounts and confirm each dashboard only shows that user's invoices
- [ ] Open two incognito windows; create an invoice in each as a guest; confirm isolation
- [ ] Sign in via Google in one guest window; confirm guest invoices migrate to the real account
- [ ] Connect Telegram from the dashboard; trigger an escalation; only the connected user's chat receives it
- [ ] Trigger an inbound client reply; only the invoice owner's Telegram gets pinged
- [ ] Confirm `gmail_refresh_token` and `telegram_link_token` are never returned by any API response
- [ ] Forge a `/api/telegram/webhook` POST without the secret token — should 403

## Summary

Adds an **Invoice Generator** module: freelancers fill a form, pick one of three templates (Modern · Classic · Minimal), embed a payment URL (Stripe / LemonSqueezy / any https), see a live PDF preview, and either download locally or **Save & Download** — which uploads the rendered blob to Supabase Storage, creates an `invoices` row at `escalation_level=0`, and routes to the chase view so the AI agent takes over if the client doesn't pay.

All PDF rendering happens client-side with `@react-pdf/renderer` — no new server-side rendering dependency.

## Spec & Plan

- Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-05-23-invoice-pdf-generator-design.md`
- Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-05-23-invoice-pdf-generator.md`

## What's included

**Frontend (`frontend/src/components/invoice-generator/`)**
- 3 PDF templates with snapshot tests (Modern · Classic · Minimal)
- `useInvoiceGeneratorForm` hook (16 validation tests)
- `useSenderProfile` hook + per-user sender profile (business name, your name/email, address, logo URL, tax ID) persisted across invoices
- `TemplatePicker` (radiogroup with full keyboard nav · 6 tests)
- `LineItemsEditor` (add/remove/edit · integer-cent math · 8 tests)
- Live PDF preview with **double-buffered iframes** — no flicker as you type
- Landing page: new "Create polished invoices" feature card; Dashboard split CTA ("Generate Invoice" / "Chase Existing")

**Backend (`api/index.py` + `src/db.py`)**
- `GET/PATCH /api/users/me/sender-profile`
- `POST /api/invoices/generated/upload` (multipart PDF → Supabase Storage)
- `POST /api/invoices/generated` (creates the invoices row, links to the uploaded file)
- Both write endpoints rate-limited

**Database**
- Migration: `users.sender_profile JSONB` (already applied to production Supabase via MCP)

**Tests**
- 64 frontend unit/snapshot tests passing
- 15 backend pytest tests passing (sender profile + generated invoice + security regressions)
- 6 frontend page-flow tests skipped (`@react-pdf/renderer`'s PDFViewer is incompatible with jsdom — covered manually)

## Code review fixes (applied before merge)

The superpowers `requesting-code-review` agent surfaced one Critical and two Important issues. All fixed in commit `957ef69`:

- **Critical · path traversal** — `POST /api/invoices/generated` previously accepted `generated/{user_id}/../victim/foo.pdf` via raw `startswith`. Now normalized with `posixpath.normpath()` + `..` segment check. Regression test added.
- **Important · `logo_url` SSRF** — `PATCH /sender-profile` accepted any string; `<Image src>` could fetch `file://`, IMDS, etc. Now validated to http(s) only. Two tests added.
- **Minor · rate limits** — Both write endpoints now go through `enforce_rate_limit()`.

## Money math

All totals are integer cents end-to-end (`computeTotals.ts`). The only float-touching boundary is the user-input "flat" dollar discount, which is rounded to cents immediately.

## Payment link

Any `http(s)` URL. The form validates with `new URL()` + protocol check (`javascript:` and others rejected). Empty is valid (the block is omitted entirely from the PDF). Renders differently per template: filled button (Modern) / labeled hyperlink (Classic) / underlined link (Minimal).

## Test plan

- [x] `cd frontend && npm run build` — clean
- [x] `cd frontend && npm test` — 64 passed
- [x] `pytest tests/` — 15 passed
- [x] Manual smoke: download a real PDF in each template; payment link clickable in Preview + Chrome
- [x] Manual smoke: Save & Download creates an invoice row + navigates to /invoice/:id
- [x] Manual smoke: PDF preview no longer flickers while typing (double-buffered iframe swap)

## Vercel notes

- No new env vars required.
- The Supabase migration is **already applied to production** — no migration step needed during deploy.
- Bundle increased by ~600 KB minified due to `@react-pdf/renderer`. The Vite build warns about chunk size; consider code-splitting `/generate-invoice` behind `React.lazy()` in a follow-up if first-paint regresses.

## Summary

Capture runtime failures in dedicated Sentry projects and post Sentry links to Slack using the free Web API.

```text
FastAPI / React / handled API failures → Sentry issues → grouped email alerts
                                      ↘ Slack bot → #invoicechaser-alerts
```

- Capture all error events and sample production traces at 10%. Scrub request data, invoice IDs, arbitrary exception messages, locals and user identity.
- Report caught summary failures without changing their responses. Drain telemetry at the end of Vercel invocations.
- Upload hidden frontend source maps and remove them before publication.

## Why
The golden-set eval failed on almost every run, each time on different cases. I measured it: most failures weren't agent mistakes.

1. **Throttling graded as wrong answers.** Groq's free tier allows 8,000 tokens/min per model per key, and one agent turn uses ~4–6k. When a *client-reply* case was rate-limited, `handle_client_reply` logged and swallowed the error (correct for a webhook), so the eval saw "the agent didn't call the tool". `l3-client-pays` scored 0/3 under load, then passed on its own.
2. **Placeholders.** The agent wrote `[date]` / `[Client Name]` (tone-rule failures). It had no date to work with, since the product stores only `days_overdue`, and no person's name for a company client.

## Changes
- **Agent context:** adds `Today's date: YYYY-MM-DD` to the current-invoice block.
- **Prompts (all levels):** "If you don't know a contact person's name, greet the company by its name. Write real dates, counted from today's date in the invoice details, or leave the date out." Deliberately no bracketed example, per the existing `test_no_prompt_shows_a_placeholder_to_copy`.
- **Harness:** after a client reply, a failed `inbound_reply` trace raises `client reply failed: …`, so the runner retries a 429 as "provider busy" instead of grading it.
- **CI:** `--pace 20` between cases, timeout 30 min. The judge can use its own key (`EVAL_JUDGE_GROQ_API_KEY`, now set as a repo secret).
- No thresholds or baseline changed.

## Tried and dropped
An extra prompt line forbidding `update_invoice_details` / `escalate_dispute` on client replies: an A/B on the affected cases showed no difference (the recipient-change case was 3/3 either way), and the tool gate already refuses those calls.

## Why

When a client says "I'll pay on the 15th", the agent proposes `mark_invoice_pending` and you approve it. Until now that approval **saved nothing**: the promise and its date were lost, the dashboard never showed them, and the agent forgot them on the next turn.

Fixing that showed that invoice data was written from several routes in `api/index.py`. The escalation level had three writers, one of which rewrote it after every approval. Payment changes were reconciled inside `/resume`. So invoice writes now go through a single module.

We also considered giving the agent an open-source CRM to work through, and decided against it. The README explains why (AGPL licences; no invoice model; the wrong tool shape for an agent).

## What changed

- **`src/services/invoice_service.py`**: the only writer of invoice data (status, payments, promise to pay, escalation level, settling, client details). Routes call it, and tools still only propose changes in agent state. Approving a tool commits only that tool's allowed fields (`COMMITTABLE_BY_TOOL`).
- **Promise to pay:** `mark_invoice_pending` validates the date and proposes `status=pending` + `follow_up_date`. Approval saves both; the agent sees the date in its context.
- **Dashboard:** "Promised to pay by Nov 15, 2026" / "Promise missed (…)" status, a Promised filter, and the date in the chat side panel.
- **README:** reasons, an animated flow (`docs/promise-to-pay.svg`), and 3 sequence diagrams.
- Removed the unused mock MCP server and a dead DB helper; exposed `build_agent()` for tests.

## Fixed by adversarial testing (including against the real LangGraph graph)

| Attack | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Approve an email draft while agent state says `paid` | Invoice marked paid, chasing stopped | Email approvals commit no invoice changes |
| Model records a payment of `inf` | Invoice marked paid | Rejected by the tool and the service |
| `inf`/`NaN` in any tool call | Chat and history 500 on every load | Responses replace them with `null` |
| Late approval racing a settle | Could reopen the invoice | Writes carry `status != paid` |
| `/details` with a recipient list or a 5,000-char name | Saved | 422 |
| Ungated tool resets the level to 1 | Written back on the next approval | The level only goes up |

## Migration

`ALTER TABLE invoices ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS follow_up_date TEXT;` is **already applied** to the production Supabase project, and is also in `supabase/schema.sql`.

## Tests

- `pytest`: 220 passed. New files: `test_invoice_service.py`, `test_promise_to_pay.py`, `test_pentest_invoice_writes.py`, `test_real_graph_payments.py`.
- `npm test`: 116 passed. `tsc -b` is clean and the build passes.

## Summary

**Bugs fixed**
- **Approved emails were never sent.** `/resume` synced invoice details into the agent *before* reading the pending draft, and LangGraph's `update_state()` empties a pending interrupt. Approve now reads the draft first, and the sync writes only changed fields, so opening an invoice no longer wipes a waiting draft. Only email drafts send email, and the recipient comes from the invoice row.
- **"Escalate" didn't escalate.** The button sent a chat message and hoped the model would call its tool. New `POST /api/invoices/{id}/escalate` raises the level directly, then asks the agent for a draft in the new tone.
- **AI chat didn't respond.**
  - The keyword guard blocked normal requests like "make it firmer" or "yes".
  - Groq retired `llama-3.3-70b-versatile`. The model is now configurable with `GROQ_MODEL`, defaulting to `openai/gpt-oss-120b`.
- **PDF fallback parser:** it cut the client name short ("Bill To: Client Co." became "Co.") and picked the sender's email instead of the client's.

**Email: no warning screen, no restricted Google scopes**
- Sign-in asks for basic profile access only. **Connect Gmail** asks for `gmail.send` only. `gmail.readonly`/`modify`, the Gmail watch and the Pub/Sub webhook are removed, so Google verification is free and needs no security assessment.
- Replies come back through **Resend Inbound** (free plan). Each email carries `Reply-To: you, inv-<token>@<id>.resend.app`. `POST /api/email/inbound` verifies the Svix signature and stores the reply on exactly one invoice.

**Product UI**
- **Landing page:**
  - Two-column hero with a live, browser-framed agent run and a presenter.
  - Interactive situation selector, three-step band, with/without table, real testimonials and FAQ.
  - Copy matches how the app works today, with unverified claims removed.
  - SEO: meta description, Open Graph tags, JSON-LD, noscript summary, robots.txt and sitemap.
- **Dashboard:** a "Waiting for you" approval queue, a filterable invoice list with plain-language status, and a Connect Gmail banner. The app shell uses the landing page's theme.
- **README:** rewritten, with an animated flow diagram (`docs/how-it-works.svg`) and Mermaid diagrams.

**Removed for now:** late-fee calculation and the unused Telegram service.

## Before merging / deploying

Implements the two features promised on the [agent observability page](https://www.chiranjeevthomas.com/projects/agent-observability): per-step tracing of every agent run, and a golden-set eval that runs on every prompt or model change.

## Tracing
- Every run (chat, escalation, decision, client reply, CLI) records its steps: model calls (the prompt, tools offered, tokens, latency), tool calls, refused tools, approval cards, the human decision (an edited approval is labelled `approved_with_edits`) and the email send.
- Runs go to new `agent_runs` and `agent_trace_steps` tables.
- Text is redacted and capped. Traces are kept for 30 days (`pg_cron` purge), with RLS on.
- Tracing is fail-open: a trace write times out after 3 s, and dropped traces are counted in `/api/health`.
- Responses carry `X-Trace-Id`. `GET /api/invoices/{id}/traces` serves the invoice's owner, and a new **Trace** tab in the invoice page shows the runs.

## Golden-set eval
- 18 disputes across levels 0–3, including prompt injection through client replies.
- Cases run through the real API and graph, offline, and are graded from their traces: tool choice, no send or approval-gated action without an approval, tone rules, and an LLM judge.
- Tier 1 replays scripted runs inside `pytest`. Tier 2 (`python -m evals.run`) runs the live model, and `.github/workflows/evals.yml` posts its scorecard on PRs that touch the agent.
- `python -m evals.promote` turns a bad trace into a case.
- Baseline: 94% tool choice, approval rule 100% (18/18), judge 4.33/5.

## Bugs it found and fixed
- **Escalation gating was advisory.** Above-level tools still ran, and above-level drafts reached the approval card. `enforce_tool_gate` now refuses them.
- **Injected client replies could escalate or rewrite the client's email**, using tools with no approval step. Runs started by a reply can no longer use those tools.
- **Opening a chat erased a waiting approval card** proposed by a client reply. The cause: `None` vs `''` in the state sync, plus `/history` writing state while a card was waiting.
- **The CLI crashed after approving**, because it resumed without the freelancer context.
- **Two leaks in the new redaction**, both caught by review (bounded regexes, merged overlapping spans).

## Not in scope
Deferred items are in `TODOS.md`. The P1s: putting `escalate_dispute` behind an approval card, and the empty reply to small-claims questions that the eval flags.

## Test plan
- [x] `pytest`: 400 passed
- [x] `npx vitest run`: 133 passed; `tsc -b` and `npm run build` pass
- [x] Live `python -m evals.run` passes its gates
- [x] Schema validated on a local Postgres 16 (idempotent re-run, retention, cascades)
- [ ] Production smoke test after deploy

## Summary

Makes the app safe for multiple freelancers to use in parallel and ships the in-flight invoice-upload / balance-chasing work.

### Multi-tenant hardening (`aeaee5d`)
- **Per-user Telegram routing** — `send_telegram_notification(user_id, msg)` looks up `users.telegram_chat_id`; soft-fails when unconnected. New `/api/telegram/{connect,webhook,status,disconnect}` endpoints implement a deep-link handshake (`t.me/<bot>?start=<token>`). Dashboard now has a Connect Telegram card.
- **Per-session guest IDs** — anonymous visitors get a unique `guest-<hex>` identity in an HTTP-only cookie (`ic_guest_session`, 30 days). Replaces the shared `"guest"` namespace where every anonymous invoice collided. On Google sign-in, guest invoices + communications migrate to the real account and the cookie is cleared.
- **Invoice ownership enforced** — `authorize_invoice_access()` guards `/api/chat`, `/api/invoices/{id}/{history,details,sender,resume}`. Returns 404 (not 403) so existence isn't leaked across tenants.
- **`communication_history.user_id`** — direct column instead of join-only. Backfilled from `invoices.user_id`.
- **`FreelancerContext.user_id`** — carries identity so downstream tools can route side-effects per-user. Default values changed from `Alex Rivera` demo data to placeholders.
- **CORS with credentials** — explicit `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` env (defaults to localhost:5173) so the guest cookie flows in cross-origin dev.
- **Env cleanup** — drops `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID`; adds `TELEGRAM_BOT_USERNAME`, `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS`.

### Invoice upload + balance-based chasing (`260428e`)
- PDF/DOCX upload UI in the New Invoice modal. Backend extracts fields with `pypdf`/`python-docx` + a Groq structured-output pass with a regex/heuristic fallback for missing fields. Form prefills and surfaces warnings before submit.
- Agent state, drafting tools, late-fee + status tools all read `balance_due` / `amount_paid` instead of the invoice total. New `record_partial_payment` HITL tool reduces balance and flips status to `paid` on full settlement.
- Escalation prompts (1/2/3) instruct the model to route partial-payment replies to `record_partial_payment` and stop chasing once `status=paid`. `/api/chat` short-circuits paid invoices with an explicit "will not continue chasing" reply.
- Frontend stats/table/chat panel show `Original` / `Paid` / `Balance` / `Status`. DraftApproval renders the partial-payment confirmation with amount + date args.
- Deps: `pypdf`, `python-docx`, `python-multipart`; langchain/langgraph bumped to 1.x.

### Fixes
- `c2a77d4` Persist payment state from agent response, not interrupt task — `sync_agent_state_from_invoice` clears pending interrupts before the resume handler can read `approved_tool_name`, so DB writes silently skipped. Driving the persist off `response["amount_paid"] / response["status"]` instead. Caught during the smoke walk.
- `9d123cf` Fix vite proxy target — was 8001, uvicorn runs on 8000 (CLAUDE.md).

## Deployed and verified

- **Supabase migration applied** — `supabase/schema.sql` ran against project `fdsglieendnihbfozbag` (project was paused; restored first). All Plan A/B columns + `invoice-files` storage bucket present.
- **Vercel prod deployed** — https://invoice-chaser-chi.vercel.app. Health endpoint OK.
- **Vercel env vars set/cleaned**:
  - Added `SUPABASE_INVOICE_FILE_BUCKET=invoice-files`
  - Added `TELEGRAM_BOT_USERNAME=freelance_invoices_bot` (discovered via `getMe`)
  - Added `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (64-char URL-safe random; same value mirrored to local `.env`)
  - Removed legacy `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID`
- **Telegram webhook registered** — `https://invoice-chaser-chi.vercel.app/api/telegram/webhook` with `secret_token` and `allowed_updates=["message"]`. Verified via `getWebhookInfo` (0 pending, no errors). `/api/telegram/webhook` now rejects requests missing the matching `x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token` header.
- **End-to-end smoke against prod Supabase** — upload DOCX → parse → create invoice + store file → chat draft (balance-aware) → record_partial_payment → DB persists → mark_invoice_paid → DB status=paid → followup chat short-circuits.
- **Bot profile sanitized** — the bot was previously named "Tips Best" with spam description/short-description referring users to an unrelated NSFW bot. Replaced via Bot API: name → "InvoiceChaser"; description + short_description rewritten with neutral InvoiceChaser-appropriate text; commands list emptied. The bot's profile photo cannot be changed via Bot API — if a sketchy photo is still attached, replace it via BotFather (`/setuserpic`).

## Known gaps (non-blocking, follow-up work)

- **`DATABASE_URL` is stale** — the LangGraph Postgres checkpointer can't reach `aws-0-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com:5432` (`Tenant or user not found`), likely because the password rotated when the project was paused/restored. App falls back to `InMemorySaver` so this only affects in-flight LangGraph chat history across cold starts (invoice/agent state itself is re-synced from Supabase REST per request, so the user-visible behavior is fine). Re-pull the pooler URI from Supabase → `vercel env add DATABASE_URL production --force` → redeploy. **Skipped here because completing this autonomously would require either the DB password or a destructive password reset — neither of which I have explicit authorization for.**
- **Supabase RLS** is disabled on all 3 public tables. Plan explicitly defers this (backend uses service role; anon key isn't exposed). Advisory captured.
- **Groq llama-3.3-70b** occasionally emits malformed tool-call syntax causing the first agent invocation on `/api/invoices/upload` to return `initialization_error`. Invoice + file are still saved; the user just needs to send one chat message to get the first draft. Long-term fix: pin a model with more reliable tool calling, or add a "tool_use_failed → chat-mode draft" fallback middleware.

## Test plan (still useful for review)

- [ ] Sign in with two Google accounts and confirm each dashboard only shows that user's invoices
- [ ] Open two incognito windows; create an invoice in each as a guest; confirm isolation
- [ ] Sign in via Google in one guest window; confirm guest invoices migrate to the real account
- [ ] Connect Telegram from the dashboard; trigger an escalation; only the connected user's chat receives it
- [ ] Trigger an inbound client reply; only the invoice owner's Telegram gets pinged
- [ ] Confirm `gmail_refresh_token` and `telegram_link_token` are never returned by any API response
- [ ] Forge a `/api/telegram/webhook` POST without the secret token — should 403

## Why
The golden-set eval failed on almost every run, each time on different cases. I measured it: most failures weren't agent mistakes.

1. **Throttling graded as wrong answers.** Groq's free tier allows 8,000 tokens/min per model per key, and one agent turn uses ~4–6k. When a *client-reply* case was rate-limited, `handle_client_reply` logged and swallowed the error (correct for a webhook), so the eval saw "the agent didn't call the tool". `l3-client-pays` scored 0/3 under load, then passed on its own.
2. **Placeholders.** The agent wrote `[date]` / `[Client Name]` (tone-rule failures). It had no date to work with, since the product stores only `days_overdue`, and no person's name for a company client.

## Changes
- **Agent context:** adds `Today's date: YYYY-MM-DD` to the current-invoice block.
- **Prompts (all levels):** "If you don't know a contact person's name, greet the company by its name. Write real dates, counted from today's date in the invoice details, or leave the date out." Deliberately no bracketed example, per the existing `test_no_prompt_shows_a_placeholder_to_copy`.
- **Harness:** after a client reply, a failed `inbound_reply` trace raises `client reply failed: …`, so the runner retries a 429 as "provider busy" instead of grading it.
- **CI:** `--pace 20` between cases, timeout 30 min. The judge can use its own key (`EVAL_JUDGE_GROQ_API_KEY`, now set as a repo secret).
- No thresholds or baseline changed.

## Tried and dropped
An extra prompt line forbidding `update_invoice_details` / `escalate_dispute` on client replies: an A/B on the affected cases showed no difference (the recipient-change case was 3/3 either way), and the tool gate already refuses those calls.

## Testing
- `pytest`: 430 passed (new: today's date in the context, judge key, and a rate-limited client reply surfaced as a retryable error).
- The live eval runs on this PR (it touches `src/prompts/` and `evals/`).

Implements the two features promised on the [agent observability page](https://www.chiranjeevthomas.com/projects/agent-observability): per-step tracing of every agent run, and a golden-set eval that runs on every prompt or model change.

## Tracing
- Every run (chat, escalation, decision, client reply, CLI) records its steps: model calls (the prompt, tools offered, tokens, latency), tool calls, refused tools, approval cards, the human decision (an edited approval is labelled `approved_with_edits`) and the email send.
- Runs go to new `agent_runs` and `agent_trace_steps` tables.
- Text is redacted and capped. Traces are kept for 30 days (`pg_cron` purge), with RLS on.
- Tracing is fail-open: a trace write times out after 3 s, and dropped traces are counted in `/api/health`.
- Responses carry `X-Trace-Id`. `GET /api/invoices/{id}/traces` serves the invoice's owner, and a new **Trace** tab in the invoice page shows the runs.

## Golden-set eval
- 18 disputes across levels 0–3, including prompt injection through client replies.
- Cases run through the real API and graph, offline, and are graded from their traces: tool choice, no send or approval-gated action without an approval, tone rules, and an LLM judge.
- Tier 1 replays scripted runs inside `pytest`. Tier 2 (`python -m evals.run`) runs the live model, and `.github/workflows/evals.yml` posts its scorecard on PRs that touch the agent.
- `python -m evals.promote` turns a bad trace into a case.
- Baseline: 94% tool choice, approval rule 100% (18/18), judge 4.33/5.

## Bugs it found and fixed
- **Escalation gating was advisory.** Above-level tools still ran, and above-level drafts reached the approval card. `enforce_tool_gate` now refuses them.
- **Injected client replies could escalate or rewrite the client's email**, using tools with no approval step. Runs started by a reply can no longer use those tools.
- **Opening a chat erased a waiting approval card** proposed by a client reply. The cause: `None` vs `''` in the state sync, plus `/history` writing state while a card was waiting.
- **The CLI crashed after approving**, because it resumed without the freelancer context.
- **Two leaks in the new redaction**, both caught by review (bounded regexes, merged overlapping spans).

## Not in scope
Deferred items are in `TODOS.md`. The P1s: putting `escalate_dispute` behind an approval card, and the empty reply to small-claims questions that the eval flags.

## Test plan
- [x] `pytest`: 400 passed
- [x] `npx vitest run`: 133 passed; `tsc -b` and `npm run build` pass
- [x] Live `python -m evals.run` passes its gates
- [x] Schema validated on a local Postgres 16 (idempotent re-run, retention, cascades)
- [ ] Production smoke test after deploy

## Problem
At level 3 the prompt tells the agent to answer small-claims questions *"using the jurisdiction in the invoice details"*, and final notices must name it. But `build_user_invoice_context`, which builds the "Current invoice" block the model sees, **never included the jurisdiction**. So the agent asked the freelancer for something the invoice already stored:

> "To give you accurate instructions, I need to know the jurisdiction… Could you let me know the applicable jurisdiction for Acme Corp's invoice INV-EVAL-3?"

That's what the golden case `l3-small-claims-help` caught. It failed **5/5** on the live model, and it was already failing in the committed baseline. It also explains final notices that leave out the jurisdiction (a `l3-final-notice` tone failure on the first CI eval run).

## Change
- `api/index.py`: add `Jurisdiction: <value or "not set">` to the current-invoice block.
- Two tests: the context shows the jurisdiction, and a missing one shows as "not set".

## Evidence (live `openai/gpt-oss-120b`, level 3, 5 runs per case)
| Case | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `l3-small-claims-help` (tool choice) | 0/5 | **5/5 call the research tools** |
| `l3-final-notice` | 5/5 | 5/5 |
| `l3-client-pays` | 4/5 | 5/5 |
| `l3-injected-reply` | 3/5 | 5/5 |

`l3-small-claims-help` still leaves a `[date]` placeholder in 2/5 answers (a tone rule): the product stores no due or issue date, only `days_overdue`. I've left that alone here.

## Summary

Makes the app safe for multiple freelancers to use in parallel and ships the in-flight invoice-upload / balance-chasing work.

### Multi-tenant hardening (`aeaee5d`)
- **Per-user Telegram routing** — `send_telegram_notification(user_id, msg)` looks up `users.telegram_chat_id`; soft-fails when unconnected. New `/api/telegram/{connect,webhook,status,disconnect}` endpoints implement a deep-link handshake (`t.me/<bot>?start=<token>`). Dashboard now has a Connect Telegram card.
- **Per-session guest IDs** — anonymous visitors get a unique `guest-<hex>` identity in an HTTP-only cookie (`ic_guest_session`, 30 days). Replaces the shared `"guest"` namespace where every anonymous invoice collided. On Google sign-in, guest invoices + communications migrate to the real account and the cookie is cleared.
- **Invoice ownership enforced** — `authorize_invoice_access()` guards `/api/chat`, `/api/invoices/{id}/{history,details,sender,resume}`. Returns 404 (not 403) so existence isn't leaked across tenants.
- **`communication_history.user_id`** — direct column instead of join-only. Backfilled from `invoices.user_id`.
- **`FreelancerContext.user_id`** — carries identity so downstream tools can route side-effects per-user. Default values changed from `Alex Rivera` demo data to placeholders.
- **CORS with credentials** — explicit `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` env (defaults to localhost:5173) so the guest cookie flows in cross-origin dev.
- **Env cleanup** — drops `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID`; adds `TELEGRAM_BOT_USERNAME`, `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS`.

### Invoice upload + balance-based chasing (`260428e`)
- PDF/DOCX upload UI in the New Invoice modal. Backend extracts fields with `pypdf`/`python-docx` + a Groq structured-output pass with a regex/heuristic fallback for missing fields. Form prefills and surfaces warnings before submit.
- Agent state, drafting tools, late-fee + status tools all read `balance_due` / `amount_paid` instead of the invoice total. New `record_partial_payment` HITL tool reduces balance and flips status to `paid` on full settlement.
- Escalation prompts (1/2/3) instruct the model to route partial-payment replies to `record_partial_payment` and stop chasing once `status=paid`. `/api/chat` short-circuits paid invoices with an explicit "will not continue chasing" reply.
- Frontend stats/table/chat panel show `Original` / `Paid` / `Balance` / `Status`. DraftApproval renders the partial-payment confirmation with amount + date args.
- Deps: `pypdf`, `python-docx`, `python-multipart`; langchain/langgraph bumped to 1.x.

### Fixes
- `c2a77d4` Persist payment state from agent response, not interrupt task — `sync_agent_state_from_invoice` clears pending interrupts before the resume handler can read `approved_tool_name`, so DB writes silently skipped. Driving the persist off `response["amount_paid"] / response["status"]` instead. Caught during the smoke walk.
- `9d123cf` Fix vite proxy target — was 8001, uvicorn runs on 8000 (CLAUDE.md).

## Deployed and verified

- **Supabase migration applied** — `supabase/schema.sql` ran against project `fdsglieendnihbfozbag` (project was paused; restored first). All Plan A/B columns + `invoice-files` storage bucket present.
- **Vercel prod deployed** — https://invoice-chaser-chi.vercel.app. Health endpoint OK.
- **Vercel env vars set/cleaned**:
  - Added `SUPABASE_INVOICE_FILE_BUCKET=invoice-files`
  - Added `TELEGRAM_BOT_USERNAME=freelance_invoices_bot` (discovered via `getMe`)
  - Added `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (64-char URL-safe random; same value mirrored to local `.env`)
  - Removed legacy `TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID`
- **Telegram webhook registered** — `https://invoice-chaser-chi.vercel.app/api/telegram/webhook` with `secret_token` and `allowed_updates=["message"]`. Verified via `getWebhookInfo` (0 pending, no errors). `/api/telegram/webhook` now rejects requests missing the matching `x-telegram-bot-api-secret-token` header.
- **End-to-end smoke against prod Supabase** — upload DOCX → parse → create invoice + store file → chat draft (balance-aware) → record_partial_payment → DB persists → mark_invoice_paid → DB status=paid → followup chat short-circuits.
- **Bot profile sanitized** — the bot was previously named "Tips Best" with spam description/short-description referring users to an unrelated NSFW bot. Replaced via Bot API: name → "InvoiceChaser"; description + short_description rewritten with neutral InvoiceChaser-appropriate text; commands list emptied. The bot's profile photo cannot be changed via Bot API — if a sketchy photo is still attached, replace it via BotFather (`/setuserpic`).

## Known gaps (non-blocking, follow-up work)

- **`DATABASE_URL` is stale** — the LangGraph Postgres checkpointer can't reach `aws-0-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com:5432` (`Tenant or user not found`), likely because the password rotated when the project was paused/restored. App falls back to `InMemorySaver` so this only affects in-flight LangGraph chat history across cold starts (invoice/agent state itself is re-synced from Supabase REST per request, so the user-visible behavior is fine). Re-pull the pooler URI from Supabase → `vercel env add DATABASE_URL production --force` → redeploy. **Skipped here because completing this autonomously would require either the DB password or a destructive password reset — neither of which I have explicit authorization for.**
- **Supabase RLS** is disabled on all 3 public tables. Plan explicitly defers this (backend uses service role; anon key isn't exposed). Advisory captured.
- **Groq llama-3.3-70b** occasionally emits malformed tool-call syntax causing the first agent invocation on `/api/invoices/upload` to return `initialization_error`. Invoice + file are still saved; the user just needs to send one chat message to get the first draft. Long-term fix: pin a model with more reliable tool calling, or add a "tool_use_failed → chat-mode draft" fallback middleware.

## Test plan (still useful for review)

- [ ] Sign in with two Google accounts and confirm each dashboard only shows that user's invoices
- [ ] Open two incognito windows; create an invoice in each as a guest; confirm isolation
- [ ] Sign in via Google in one guest window; confirm guest invoices migrate to the real account
- [ ] Connect Telegram from the dashboard; trigger an escalation; only the connected user's chat receives it
- [ ] Trigger an inbound client reply; only the invoice owner's Telegram gets pinged
- [ ] Confirm `gmail_refresh_token` and `telegram_link_token` are never returned by any API response
- [ ] Forge a `/api/telegram/webhook` POST without the secret token — should 403

  (HITL-approved, wired through middleware + agent.py) reduces balance and

* Persist payment state from agent response, not interrupt task

The resume endpoint was reading the approved tool name out of
snapshot.tasks before invoking the agent. But sync_agent_state_from_invoice
(added a few changes back to merge DB state into LangGraph) clears pending
interrupt tasks as a side-effect, so approved_tool_name was always None for
real approvals — the DB persist block silently skipped, leaving
amount_paid/status stale even though the agent's in-memory state updated
correctly via the tool's Command(update={...}).

Drive the DB persist off the post-invoke response state instead. Whatever
the tool wrote (record_partial_payment / mark_invoice_paid /
mark_invoice_pending all emit Command(update=...) for amount_paid + status)

places (one rewrote it on every resume), payment reconciliation inside
resume, settling in its route. They now all go through
src/services/invoice_service.py, which the routes call. Tools still only
propose changes in agent state; approving one commits it.

mark_invoice_pending used to return a message and nothing else, so a
client's promise to pay and its date were lost. It now proposes status
"pending" plus follow_up_date, saved on approval and shown to the agent.
Needs: ALTER TABLE invoices ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS follow_up_date TEXT;
(in supabase/schema.sql) before deploying.

Fixes found by adversarial testing, including against the real graph:
- Approving an email draft could commit a "paid" status left in agent
  state, which stopped the chasing. Each payment tool may now commit only
  its own fields and statuses.
- An inf amount marked the invoice paid; inf/NaN tool args made chat and
  history return 500 on every load. Payment amounts must be finite and
  positive, and responses replace inf/NaN with null.
- A late approval racing a settle could reopen the invoice: the write now
  carries status=neq.paid.
- /details accepted recipient lists and unbounded names; a non-string
  status crashed the service.
- The escalation level can no longer go down.

Also removes the unused get_invoices_by_client_email and exposes
build_agent() so tests can run the production graph with a scripted model.

* Persist payment state from agent response, not interrupt task

The resume endpoint was reading the approved tool name out of
snapshot.tasks before invoking the agent. But sync_agent_state_from_invoice
(added a few changes back to merge DB state into LangGraph) clears pending
interrupt tasks as a side-effect, so approved_tool_name was always None for
real approvals — the DB persist block silently skipped, leaving
amount_paid/status stale even though the agent's in-memory state updated
correctly via the tool's Command(update={...}).

Drive the DB persist off the post-invoke response state instead. Whatever
the tool wrote (record_partial_payment / mark_invoice_paid /
mark_invoice_pending all emit Command(update=...) for amount_paid + status)
shows up in response and is the authoritative source. Diff against the
current DB row and write only when something actually changed.

DB. DB stayed at amount_paid=0 even though /api/chat reported
balance_due=1500.

hits.message:
Write invoice facts in one place, and save promises to pay

Invoice writes were spread across the routes: escalation level in three
places (one rewrote it on every resume), payment reconciliation inside
resume, settling in its route. They now all go through
src/services/invoice_service.py, which the routes call. Tools still only
propose changes in agent state; approving one commits it.

mark_invoice_pending used to return a message and nothing else, so a
client's promise to pay and its date were lost. It now proposes status
"pending" plus follow_up_date, saved on approval and shown to the agent.
Needs: ALTER TABLE invoices ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS follow_up_date TEXT;
(in supabase/schema.sql) before deploying.

Fixes found by adversarial testing, including against the real graph:
- Approving an email draft could commit a "paid" status left in agent
  state, which stopped the chasing. Each payment tool may now commit only
  its own fields and statuses.
- An inf amount marked the invoice paid; inf/NaN tool args made chat and
  history return 500 on every load. Payment amounts must be finite and
  positive, and responses replace inf/NaN with null.
- A late approval racing a settle could reopen the invoice: the write now
  carries status=neq.paid.
- /details accepted recipient lists and unbounded names; a non-string
  status crashed the service.
- The escalation level can no longer go down.

build_agent() so tests can run the production graph with a scripted model.

hits.body:
Hi — been reading through SwarmLLM (impressive work, especially the NAT traversal and the cross-node prefix-KV sharing numbers).

I noticed distributed speculative decoding is in there as a flag-gated speedup. I've been thinking about it from a different angle and wanted to share it in case it's useful.

Framed as a **trust** mechanism rather than a performance one, it has a property I haven't seen discussed: the verifier already recomputes every drafted token, so a drafter that lies is caught by the protocol's normal operation. No attestation, no activation hashing, no extra cost. Output stays bit-identical to the target model's, so a bad drafter can waste its own effort but cannot degrade quality.

That changes the node economics. Instead of every peer needing to be trusted and hold part of the model, you get many cheap drafters (a 1B q4 draft model is ~0.6 GB — it runs on a phone) plus a smaller set of verifiers holding the whole model.

**Edited 2026-09-07 after @enapt's review below.** Two corrections, both his:

- This paragraph originally said "untrusted drafters". That is overstated. A verifier holds the whole model and sees the plaintext prompt and the sampled tokens, so trust does not disappear — it **relocates**. The defensible claim is *fewer trusted parties*, not *untrusted*. The drafter is also the party that is local in SwarmLLM today; the untrusted counterparty here is the verifier.
- The original arithmetic assumed 80% acceptance with K=8 (~4.3 tokens per round-trip, ~10k concurrent users on tens of verifiers). I have no evidence for 80%, and the measurements discussed below argue against it. **Consider that capacity number withdrawn** until it is measured — and the binding resource looks like verifier KV cache rather than compute regardless.

Two things I'm unsure about and would value your read on:

1. Does your current speculative path treat the drafter as trusted, or is rejection already doing the policing implicitly?
2. What acceptance rates are you seeing in practice over WAN? My estimates assume 70–90% and the economics collapse below ~50%.

Happy to run nodes and report back if that's useful — I have a Linux box I can point at it.

hits.body:
Hi — been reading through SwarmLLM (impressive work, especially the NAT traversal and the cross-node prefix-KV sharing numbers).

I noticed distributed speculative decoding is in there as a flag-gated speedup. I've been thinking about it from a different angle and wanted to share it in case it's useful.

Framed as a **trust** mechanism rather than a performance one, it has a property I haven't seen discussed: the verifier already recomputes every drafted token, so a drafter that lies is caught by the protocol's normal operation. No attestation, no activation hashing, no extra cost. Output stays bit-identical to the target model's, so a bad drafter can waste its own effort but cannot degrade quality.

That changes the node economics. Instead of every peer needing to be trusted and hold part of the model, you get many cheap drafters (a 1B q4 draft model is ~0.6 GB — it runs on a phone) plus a smaller set of verifiers holding the whole model.

**Edited 2026-09-07 after @enapt's review below.** Two corrections, both his:

- This paragraph originally said "untrusted drafters". That is overstated. A verifier holds the whole model and sees the plaintext prompt and the sampled tokens, so trust does not disappear — it **relocates**. The defensible claim is *fewer trusted parties*, not *untrusted*. The drafter is also the party that is local in SwarmLLM today; the untrusted counterparty here is the verifier.
- The original arithmetic assumed 80% acceptance with K=8 (~4.3 tokens per round-trip, ~10k concurrent users on tens of verifiers). I have no evidence for 80%, and the measurements discussed below argue against it. **Consider that capacity number withdrawn** until it is measured — and the binding resource looks like verifier KV cache rather than compute regardless.

Two things I'm unsure about and would value your read on:

1. Does your current speculative path treat the drafter as trusted, or is rejection already doing the policing implicitly?
2. What acceptance rates are you seeing in practice over WAN? My estimates assume 70–90% and the economics collapse below ~50%.

Happy to run nodes and report back if that's useful — I have a Linux box I can point at it.

Phase 2 of the GPU-coverage work (Phase 1 — the candle sm_75 floor + llama.cpp arch pin — is already on main and green).

**What this does**
- Linux CUDA toolkit **12.4 → 12.8** (first nvcc that knows sm_120) + adds native **`120-real;120-virtual`** to the local-model (llama.cpp) arch list, so RTX 50-series gets the native fastest path instead of the ~5×-slower PTX-JIT/cuBLAS path.
- **Windows stays on 12.4** deliberately: Windows CUDA is candle-only (PTX → driver-JIT, so Blackwell already works) and llama.cpp there is Vulkan; also avoids the `Jimver@v0.2.19` version-list risk.
- Cache key bumped `gpuarch2 → gpuarch3` so the toolkit+arch change actually takes effect.

**Why a PR:** CI's Linux `Feature compile-check (candle-cuda)` compiles candle against the 12.8 toolkit here, *before* this reaches main. If green, merge; then the `cache-warm` workflow on main is the first thing to exercise the full native-sm_120 llama.cpp build (watched closely — revert the `120` addition if the old bundled llama.cpp rejects the arch).

**Known validation gaps** (can't be tested without hardware / a tag): whether the bundled `llama-cpp-2 0.1` accepts arch `120` (cache-warm covers this post-merge), and runtime correctness on real RTX 50 hardware (Discord testers before any *stable* tag).

## First real user report 🎉

Hey ! Just installed and ran SwarmLLM on 2 machines (Arch Linux GPU + Debian server). Here is some feedback from a first-time user:

### ✅ It works
- Smooth install (CUDA binary on Arch, source build on Debian)
- Private pool working between 2 machines (mDNS auto-discovery)
- 5 models installed and synced through the pool
- Clean dashboard UI

### 🚧 What is missing for the network to take off

1. **Bootstrap peers** — currently `bootstrap_peers = []` by default. No way to join a global network without knowing at least one peer address. Maybe add a few public relay nodes or a discovery mechanism?

2. **Community space** — No Discord, no GitHub Discussions. For an emerging P2P network, a place where early adopters can share node addresses and coordinate is crucial.

3. **Network documentation** — How does one join the "mainnet"? Any plan for bootstrapping the public network?

### Suggestion
If you open a Discord or any channel, I am happy to point my nodes there and help bootstrap the network.

Great tech, keep it up!

---

*Setup:*
- raw-pc (Arch Linux, RTX 4050 6GB, CUDA)
- raw-proxamd5 (Debian 12, Ryzen 5700U, CPU-only)
- Pool: raw-swarm (2 nodes, LAN-connected)

hits.body:
Hi — been reading through SwarmLLM (impressive work, especially the NAT traversal and the cross-node prefix-KV sharing numbers).

I noticed distributed speculative decoding is in there as a flag-gated speedup. I've been thinking about it from a different angle and wanted to share it in case it's useful.

Framed as a **trust** mechanism rather than a performance one, it has a property I haven't seen discussed: the verifier already recomputes every drafted token, so a drafter that lies is caught by the protocol's normal operation. No attestation, no activation hashing, no extra cost. Output stays bit-identical to the target model's, so a bad drafter can waste its own effort but cannot degrade quality.

That changes the node economics. Instead of every peer needing to be trusted and hold part of the model, you get many cheap drafters (a 1B q4 draft model is ~0.6 GB — it runs on a phone) plus a smaller set of verifiers holding the whole model.

**Edited 2026-09-07 after @enapt's review below.** Two corrections, both his:

- This paragraph originally said "untrusted drafters". That is overstated. A verifier holds the whole model and sees the plaintext prompt and the sampled tokens, so trust does not disappear — it **relocates**. The defensible claim is *fewer trusted parties*, not *untrusted*. The drafter is also the party that is local in SwarmLLM today; the untrusted counterparty here is the verifier.
- The original arithmetic assumed 80% acceptance with K=8 (~4.3 tokens per round-trip, ~10k concurrent users on tens of verifiers). I have no evidence for 80%, and the measurements discussed below argue against it. **Consider that capacity number withdrawn** until it is measured — and the binding resource looks like verifier KV cache rather than compute regardless.

Two things I'm unsure about and would value your read on:

1. Does your current speculative path treat the drafter as trusted, or is rejection already doing the policing implicitly?
2. What acceptance rates are you seeing in practice over WAN? My estimates assume 70–90% and the economics collapse below ~50%.

Happy to run nodes and report back if that's useful — I have a Linux box I can point at it.

hits.message:
fix(download): a retried download no longer discards the parts it had already fetched

Reported from the field: a shard download failed with "expected 523493376 bytes
... wrote 0 bytes" after logging that one of its byte ranges had come back
incomplete and was being retried.

When a range arrives short the loop rewinds the file to the length it recorded
before that range started, so the retry does not append a second copy of bytes
it already wrote. That length was read without flushing first, and a file's
reported length covers what has reached the operating system, not what is still
sitting in its write buffer — so the recorded value can be smaller than what had
actually been written. Rewinding to it then truncates away ranges that had
already succeeded, and the finished file fails its size check having genuinely
received the bytes.

Whether the two agree is a race on the background writer, which is why this is
intermittent and why the same probe on this machine reported 8192 one run and
the full 65536 the next. The retry path already flushed before its own rewind
for exactly this reason; capturing the checkpoint without the same flush was the
half that was missed.

The test pins the property the fix relies on — after a flush the recorded length
is the whole file — rather than the race itself, which cannot be asserted
without flakiness.

hits.message:
a long question no longer locks up the next one for ten minutes

Ask this node a long question, and for the next ten minutes it would refuse
every other long question with "not enough free memory on this node" — even
the exact same question, and even though the memory was already free. The
advice it gave ("close other programs") could not have helped, because
nothing else was using that memory.

A conversation reserves memory before it starts, and hands it back when it
finishes. The handing-back freed the memory but forgot to cancel the
reservation, so the node kept the full amount marked as taken until a
ten-minute timer cleared it. On a node with a smaller graphics card this made
it look broken: one long request, then nothing but refusals.

It affects every request on a node that serves a model it holds, which is the
ordinary case. Larger requests hit it soonest, because they reserve the most.

The two records are now released together in one place, so a future path
cannot release the memory and leave the reservation behind. Measured on a live
node: a 5101-token question left 1848 MB reserved out of 3042 MB available.

This also explains a release-gate check that has reported "could not run" for
two releases and was put down to flakiness. It was not flaky — its second
request was one of the refused ones, so it never had the numbers it needed to
compare. The check was reporting this bug the whole time.

docs: the manifest-hash fault came and went rather than sticking

A listener placed on the live network showed the shape more precisely than the
unit tests could. Announcements that fail their own integrity check really are
circulating — one was refused within ninety seconds — but a node does not stay
in that state: the stale stamp is written only on the announcement where a
correction fires, and the next one that needs no correction is written correctly
again.

So the fault intermittently poisons a node's announcements rather than
permanently disabling a model, which matches a log where one model is refused
over and over while others from the same senders pass. Recorded where the fix
is, and the changelog softened to match. No behaviour change.

hits.message:
fix(inference): a reply no longer stops at its first "#" on Qwen models

A coding answer that began with a Rust attribute, a Python comment, a markdown
heading or an #include could come back as a single character, with no error and
nothing in the response to say what happened — the caller saw a normal, finished
reply that was one token long.

The node kept a single fallback end-of-turn token for models whose own value it
could not read. That fallback was Llama-2's, and in Qwen2.5's vocabulary the same
number is an ordinary "#". Any model whose end-of-turn token could not be
resolved therefore ended its turn the first time it wrote one.

Reported three times over the past few days by a team running a coding agent
against qwen2.5-coder-7b: one completion token, no error, and intermittent —
roughly three attempts in four. The intermittency was the sampler deciding, run
by run, whether the answer happened to start with "#".

The fallback no longer guesses. Every family wraps its end-of-turn markers in
angle brackets while ordinary tokens are bare, so a candidate is now checked
against the model's own vocabulary before being believed: a real Llama-2 model
still ends on that token, and Qwen no longer ends on a "#". Byte tokens are
bracketed too and are excluded, which is the one case a plain bracket check gets
wrong.

Where there is no vocabulary to check against at all, the node now reports that
it does not know rather than substituting a wrong answer, and says so in its log.
A wrong end-of-turn token truncates a good reply in silence; an unknown one at
worst lets the reply run to the length the caller asked for. Those are not close
in severity, and the old behaviour chose the silent one.

The same bad default was in four places, including the architecture-aware helper
that looked like the correct alternative to the other three.

Whether this is the cause of that team's reports is not yet confirmed — the
fallback is only reached when a node holds neither the loaded model nor its
header, and theirs holds the model. A grep has been sent to them to settle it.

hits.message:
perf(swarm): peer-served replies can draft ahead too, and now honour sampling

Speculation across peers was switched off for every request that did not
ask for temperature 0 — which is no client by default, since the OpenAI
surface defaults to 0.7 and the Anthropic one to 1.0. So the path built
for the network case never ran in the network case.

Unlike the local path, the gate there was correct for what the code did:
it compared a draft against the target's raw argmax, and an argmax
verifies nothing once sampling is on. It now samples each position
through the same sampler every other decode step uses and keeps a draft
only when it matches, which is the speculative-sampling rejection rule
for a draft that proposes one token and no distribution behind it.

At temperature 0 with no penalties this reproduces the argmax decision
exactly, so nothing already using the path changes — pinned by a test
that runs both against the same logits across accept, partial-accept and
first-token-mismatch cases.

It also closes a difference that depended on routing rather than on the
request: repetition penalties have always applied on the local worker and
never across peers, because the raw argmax could not express them. The
same prompt could get a different answer depending on which machine
served it.

The guard against non-finite logits from a peer is carried over
deliberately. These numbers arrive from another node, NaN comparisons are
non-deterministic, and without it a malicious segment could steer which
drafts get accepted. A test asserts both helpers reach the same verdict
on that so they cannot drift apart.

Draft-model speculation stays greedy-only on purpose: a draft model has a
real distribution, so doing this properly there needs the accept ratio
and a residual built from both sides. That is a different algorithm, and
this one works only because an n-gram draft is a point mass.

hits.message:
key_rotation: stagger eviction and rotation timers by half a period

Both timers used Duration::from_secs(600) starting near t=600 and
relied on tokio::time::interval(period). Even with MissedTickBehavior::
Skip, they hit the same wall-clock instant every cycle, and the
select! arms picked non-deterministically. If eviction won, sessions
that were exactly at MAX_SESSION_AGE got purged before rotation read
active_peers(); rotation then skipped re-keying the just-evicted
peers and traffic stalled until a fresh handshake.

Switch both to tokio::time::interval_at with explicit start instants:
eviction first tick at +600s, rotation first tick at +900s (300s
offset). Net cadence eviction t=600,1200,...; rotation t=900,1500,...
— never on the same iteration, and rotation always runs at peer-age
~300s (well clear of the 600s eviction boundary).

needs interval offset or per-peer cooldown.'

hits.message:
perf: top-p nucleus sampling partial sort (match doc comment claim)

The doc comment claimed partial-sort but the code was a full
sort_unstable_by over the full vocabulary (32K–151K indices). For
typical p=0.9 the nucleus is 10–500 tokens, so sorting the whole vocab
is ~1000× more work than needed.

New implementation:
- select_nth_unstable_by to partial-sort top-K (K=4096, O(vocab))
- sort_unstable_by over just that K prefix (O(K log K))
- Walk prefix accumulating probability mass until ≥ p
- Fallback: if top-K didn't contain the full nucleus (pathologically
  flat distribution or p→1), sort the tail and keep walking. O(vocab
  log vocab) in that rare path — net no worse than before.

Correctness guaranteed by the existing top_p_with_ctx_matches_allocating_
version property test. Runs per-token on any temperature > 0 request.

hits.message:
Inference path: tensor shape + NaN/Inf validation (C2, H6)

A malicious peer in a multi-segment pipeline could otherwise crash honest
workers on demand or steer accepted tokens.

- distributed.rs: validate intermediate-segment activation byte length
  matches the input we forwarded. Transformer layers preserve shape, so
  any mismatch indicates a malicious or buggy peer; trigger failover
  instead of forwarding garbage to the next worker (which would crash
  candle, evict the worker per gotcha #20, and DoS the node).
- dsd.rs: same shape check on intermediate DSD segments.
- speculative.rs greedy_accept_reject: reject NaN/Inf rows from a peer.
  IEEE 754 NaN comparisons make argmax non-deterministic, letting a
  malicious target segment steer accepted tokens. Treat non-finite rows
  as all-rejected with bonus=0 so the caller falls back safely.
- allreduce.rs ring path: reject NaN/Inf in received chunks before
  accumulating. Star-topology TpAllReduceCollector::reduce_sum already
  has this check.
- tensor_parallel.rs: reject NaN/Inf in attn/ffn AllReduce result before
  feeding it into the residual + next layer.

hits.message:
fix(inference): say why a prompt was not cached for sharing

Sharing a processed prompt with other machines is one of the larger
speedups available — measured here at 16.5x on a real pair of machines,
182s down to 11s for a 709-word prompt the peer had already processed.

But it is intermittent, and it was impossible to see why. The step that
saves a prompt for sharing gives up under five different conditions and
said nothing under any of them, so a machine that quietly stopped sharing
looked identical to one where the feature was working. A measurement that
showed no speedup at all could not be told apart from one where the peer
simply had nothing to offer.

Each of the five now records what stopped it and the values behind the
decision. No behaviour change; the next time a machine stops sharing, the
log will name the reason.

fix(prompt): a reply that stops after one word now explains itself

When the prompt handed to a model ends by closing a conversation instead of
opening the model's turn, the model correctly says nothing. That arrives as a

symptom comes and goes while the cause is deterministic.

token is generated — and names the model and the marker it ended on. There is
nothing to enable and no experiment for anyone to run.

rendered prompt ended where the model expects to answer. The node has the
rendered prompt; it was asking a person to determine something it could
establish itself.

hits.message:
fix: a reply from another machine could come back empty and still be charged

Reported as intermittent blank answers on a node that sends work to peers —
about half of calls, each taking 35 to 40 seconds to return nothing, with no
error raised and nothing refunded.

Words of a reply travel separately and can arrive out of order, so they are
put back in order before being shown. The check for "did anything come back"
asked whether a word had arrived rather than whether any had been shown.
Those became different questions when reordering was introduced two releases
ago: if the first word is lost and later ones arrive, there is something in
hand but nothing showable, and the request was treated as a normal, complete,
empty answer.

It now fails, so the request can be retried elsewhere rather than quietly
costing money for nothing. A reply that loses a word in the middle still
returns the part before the gap, which beats an error; only a reply with
nothing at all to show is treated as failed.

Two tests cover the distinction, including the case that must NOT error. The
first version of one of them asserted the wrong thing — the count of
unshown words is not the count of lost ones — which the test caught.

hits.message:
feat(net): prefer the inference relay over a flaky relay-circuit connection

Completes the NETWORKING_PLAN Phase 1 core. Two nodes that can't connect
directly are still "connected" to each other through a libp2p relay *circuit*,
so a request looked deliverable and went over the circuit — which is exactly the
path that can't reliably round-trip a reply (the observed "peer never
acknowledged" for two NAT'd nodes). We now track which connections are direct
(non-circuit) per peer, and when a peer is reachable only over a circuit, an
inference message takes the application-level relay instead — a solid hop to the
relay, then a solid hop to the target — rather than the fragile circuit.

If no relay path exists it falls through to a best-effort circuit send, so
behaviour is never worse than before. A genuinely direct connection is always
used as-is.

hits.message:
fix(routing): stop throwing away a route already known to be cheaper

When a machine cannot work out its own speed, the planner says so and stops
comparing. It was then handing the request to whichever single peer an earlier
check had accepted, and discarding the multi-machine route it had just costed —
even when that route was the cheaper of the two.

Not being able to price this machine says nothing about the two remote options.
Both are costed by the same function and are directly comparable to each other,
so they are now compared. Where the single peer really is cheaper it still wins,
which is the whole reason that path exists; where it is not, the cheaper route
stands.

A note on how often this happens, because the first description of it was wrong
and is corrected in the deferred-work file. It is not a brief window while a
fresh machine works itself out: the speed measurement is taken the first time it
is asked for, so it is available from the very first request. Reaching this
branch means the measurement itself failed — a machine too short of memory to
set aside the buffer it needs. Rarer than described, and a more interesting
population, since those are exactly the machines that most need the work sent
elsewhere.

Also records a null result on the one intermittent test: it did not reproduce in
forty-eight runs, including eight full-suite runs under heavier load than the
original failure, and the explanation the note offered is disproved — the send
it blamed is awaited before the check that was supposed to race it. Deliberately
not "fixed", since editing a passing test with no established cause would hide
nothing and slow every run.

hits.message:
test(scheduler): stop the tensor-parallel tests depending on the machine they run on

Two tests asserting that a tensor-parallel group forms were passing on both
machines here and failing on CI. Not flakiness: the local node is now priced from
its measured memory speed, so which computer wins the first slice of the model
depends on the hardware running the test. Yesterday's attempt at this pinned the
peer's speed but left the local side reading the real machine, which moved the
threshold rather than removing it — the break-even sat at 3 GB/s and a shared CI
runner, on an unoptimised build, fell under it.

The peer fixture is now slow enough that the outcome is not a threshold at all.
The memory measurement refuses to report below 1 GB/s and falls back to a fixed
estimate when it cannot measure, so both arms are covered and the local node
cannot lose on any machine in any build profile. The reasoning is written at the
fixture so the number is not re-tuned by guesswork.

The tests also now assert the thing they were silently assuming — that the local
node holds the first slice, since a group can only form around a slice assigned
to us. When that premise broke, the failure read "left: 0, right: 1", which is
true and tells you nothing about what actually went wrong.

hits.message:
fix(tools): recover a tool call whose array is closed with the wrong bracket

Local models emit near-miss JSON constantly, and one near miss was costing the
entire call. Observed live on llama-3.2-3b at default temperature, 1 run in 3:

    {"tool_calls": [{"id": …, "function": {"name": "get_weather",
                     "arguments": {"city": "Paris"}}}}
                                                    ^ should be ]}

`parse_embedded_json` scans for a brace-balanced object and deliberately ignores
`[`/`]`, so this yields a slice that looks complete to the scanner and is then
rejected by serde. The parse fails, and a perfectly good tool call is handed to
the caller as the assistant's reply — raw JSON where a tool result belongs. On
the Anthropic endpoint that is what Claude Code sees, so the tool simply does
not work, intermittently, with no error to explain it.

`repair_unbalanced_close` tracks the real delimiter stack and emits the closer an
open delimiter actually requires. It is purely structural: it inserts `]` or `}`
and nothing else, so it cannot invent a name or alter an argument — the
plausible-but-wrong call this file's argument renderer already warns about.
Everything it produces must still satisfy `try_generic`'s string-`name`
requirement, capped at 4 corrections because a long run of mismatches is not a
near miss and guessing at it is worse than showing the text. Truncated
generations stay text, as before.

The regression test is the exact string the model produced, and asserts the
arguments survive unchanged rather than merely that something parsed.

feat(net): distributed inference across NAT — tensor relay send + return path

  peer bytes so the result is addressed home.

hits.message:
feat(net): inference relay transport — route sealed requests through a reachable peer

NETWORKING_PLAN Phase 1 (foundation). Adds the mechanism for two nodes that
cannot connect directly (both behind NAT, no hole-punch) to complete an
inference request by routing it through a mutually-reachable relay peer —
typically the anchor, but any node that opts in with `network.relay_forwarding`
(auto-on in `--anchor` mode) can serve.

The relay is a dumb pipe: it routes on a cleartext header but the inner message
is sealed end-to-end for the final recipient's key (derived from its node id, no
prior session needed), so a middle relay never sees the prompt or the streamed
tokens — same privacy boundary as a direct connection. Forwarding is bounded to
a single hop (a relay only forwards an envelope whose sender is its own origin),
which blocks loops and amplification, and per-origin rate-limited.

Mechanics: a new `RelayedEnvelope` message, a learned reverse-route table so
replies and later turns flow back the same way, and relay fallback wired into
the directed-send path — so the remote-generate fast path transparently falls
back to a relay when a peer isn't directly reachable, with no change to the
inference code. Strictly additive and backward-compatible: the new message and
capability flag default off, and a sender only wraps traffic for a peer whose
advertised version understands it, so older nodes are never handed something
they can't decode.

Follow-ups in this phase: prefer the relay over a flaky relay-*circuit*
connection, and let the scheduler select a relay-reachable holder. +25 tests.

hits.message:
fix(net): let NAT'd nodes actually reach each other

A networking audit found that our relay transport was sound but three of
its consumers never used it, and one unrelated setting had quietly turned
off hole punching altogether. Each was invisible on its own; together
they are why inference between two home machines degraded the longer a
node stayed up.

Hole punching could never succeed. Upgrading a relayed connection to a
direct one requires briefly holding both at once, but we capped
connections per peer at one, so the direct connection was refused before
it could form. Nothing ever moved off a relay circuit, circuits were
never released, and the relay eventually ran out — at which point peers
vanished from scheduling entirely rather than falling back. The cap was
added to stop a stale-connection bug that the deterministic dialer now
handles properly, and it was making that bug worse regardless.

Requests also spread themselves blindly across every connection to a
peer, so even after a direct path existed half the traffic kept going
over the slower, flakier relay. They now prefer a direct connection
whenever one is available.

A holder we could only reach through a relay was never offered to the
scheduler at all, so the relay could rescue a stalled connection but
never make an unreachable machine usable — the case it exists for. Such
holders are now selectable, ranked behind directly-connected ones.

Relay capacity was whichever machines ran with --anchor, because the
opt-in setting for everyone else was one nothing ever switched on. A node
that is confirmed reachable from the internet now donates relay capacity
automatically, so capacity grows with the swarm instead of resting on one
machine. Set network.relay_forwarding_auto = false to decline.

Finally, the relay accepted 128 waiting peers but only 16 live circuits —
a ratio inherited from libp2p, whose circuits last two minutes to our
hour. Raised so a peer that gets a slot can actually use it.

Docs corrected: the plan claimed to be fully implemented and was not.
