hits.message:
feat(hedge): tell the losing holder to stop, and re-scope KV quantization

**Remote cancellation.** The local cancel from the previous commit closed
the remote-generate path for free: the inbound handler already aborted
its `gen_fut` on `CancelInference`, and aborting that task now drops
`generate`'s future, drops the armed `ResponseGuard`, and messages the
worker. Before, `abort()` stopped the daemon-side task while the worker
generated the full token budget anyway.

Hedge losers needed the explicit send. `hedge_dispatch` fires a duplicate
forward to a second holder by design and discards whichever loses — the
comment there said so plainly ("the worker on the loser's holder will
compute the response and find no receiver"). That waste is the main cost
of hedging, and it is why `hedge_enabled` can't be turned on casually. The
race now dispatches `CancelInference` to the loser.

The inbound handler gained a `ModelProcessPool::cancel_request(request_id)`
fan-out alongside the abort-handle lookup: an in-flight `LayerForward` has
no abort handle, because the coordinator just stopped waiting. Fan-out
across workers rather than keyed by model, since the wire message carries
only a request id — workers are few and an unknown id is a worker-side
no-op. Handles are collected before awaiting so no DashMap ref is held
across an await.

**KV cache quantization (Tier 2F) re-scoped after research, not
implemented.** The entry specced KIVI 2-bit. Two findings say don't:
KIVI's numbers depend on fusing dequant into the attention matmul plus a
Triton kernel for group-wise quantisation — the authors note dequant "can
be computationally expensive" without them, and SwarmLLM runs on candle
with no custom kernels, so we would take the memory win and pay full
dequant cost on every attention call. Separately, production (vLLM,
TensorRT-LLM) converged on FP8 KV via FlashAttention-3, not 2-bit.

Revised recommendation recorded in FUTURE_WORK: if KV ever becomes the
binding constraint, use Q8_0 through the existing `inference/quant.rs`
(already has a quality gate, already on the wire) for ~2x rather than
2.6x, with no new dependency — and measure that KV actually dominates
first. For the contexts this project's users run, weights dominate and
shard windows / `gpu_layers = 0` are the cheaper lever.

hits.message:
perf(card): three small steps before every attention layer are now one, with identical replies

Before attention, each layer adds the model's bias to its queries, keys
and values, turns them by their position in the text (RoPE), and
rearranges them the way attention reads them. On a graphics card those
were eight small jobs a layer for a model with biases; they are now three,
one per projection, producing exactly the same numbers. The replies of
nine model families were byte-identical with it on and off, on the card.

The small guessing model's call is 8-11% faster (12.7-12.8 ms against
14.3-14.4, 600 tokens in), and a 7B's check of 24 guesses about 4%.

- kernels/fused_decode.cu: heads_first_f32 (bias + NEOX/interleaved/
  partial RoPE + [b,seq,h,d] -> [b,h,seq,d] in one pass), the shape
  TensorRT-LLM's addFusedQKVBiasTranspose takes
- inference::heads_first: the op, and when it applies. A projection
  with no bias and no rotation (V in Llama, Mistral) is left alone: there
  it is only the copy, which a single-token decode skips for free, and
  fusing it added a launch a layer (caught by examples/kernel_count_ab.sh)
- layers::LayerWeights::heads_first: the one preparation of Q, K and V
  for attention. Models that normalise each head before RoPE (Qwen 3,
  Gemma 3/4) keep the old steps.

Off switch: SWARMLLM_HEADS_FIRST=compose. Evidence:
docs/invariants/inference.md, "Q, K and V reach attention heads-first
in one launch". docs/plans/large_model_splits.md records what was built
since the flow and that the real link is next.

hits.message:
fix(routing): a conversation's next turn on the same peer is priced for what that peer already read

When this node hands a whole model to a peer, the peer keeps the prompt in its
prompt cache, so the conversation's next turn there only reads what is new.
The router still priced every turn as a full read of the prompt. On the live
swarm, a repeated 505-token prompt was priced at 20.2 s and the whole request
took 7.1 s. A price that wrong can send the next turn somewhere else, where it
really has to read the whole prompt again.

This node now remembers what it handed each peer, and credits the matching
opening of the next prompt on a whole-model run there. This is how SGLang's
cache-aware router and llm-d's approximate prefix scorer work.

What is remembered: the prompt's 64-token block chain. It is keyed with this
process's secret and never sent anywhere.

The credit is limited:
- A record lasts 300 s, the idle-unload time, and is dropped when a hand-off
  to that peer fails.
- It applies only to a request the hand-off will take. That check is now
  shared with the hand-off itself, so the price and the path cannot disagree.
- It applies only while the peer still holds the whole model.
- It is a price, never a pin: a faster or less loaded route still wins.

On the new split_rig.sh handoffcache rig, turn 2 of a 2,744-token agent
conversation is credited 2,688 tokens, and the peer's worker reports a cache
hit of 2,713. The turn is priced 7.8 s and takes 15.1 s, where v0.3.243 priced
it at 148.8 s for 14.8 s.

The old reason for crediting no peer, that the n-gram path ran before the
hand-off, had been out of date since 2026-09-27.

FUTURE_WORK #3 (c), moved to Closed.

hits.message:
perf(qwen3.5): a flowing tree's kept rows are written once, and fewer memory refusals cut a split reply's guessing short

What changes for users of Qwen 3.5/3.6/3.8 models split across computers, which guess ahead in a flowing tree:

- The rows each recurrent layer keeps for the tree are now written once into a buffer for each kind, rather than
  joined again on every forward. Only when the buffer is full are the kept rows gathered into a larger one, half
  again as large. A level of the 0.8B guessing model dropped from 705 to 644 card launches. On the
  Thailand-Australia link (Qwen3.5-9B, 0.8B guessing) the guessing model's call took 38-39 ms a forward against
  38-41 before. Replies were within the runs' spread: prose 14.04 and 12.56 tok/s against 13.13 and 13.37, code
  22.04 and 25.94 against 26.24 and 19.65. A/B: SWARMLLM_FLOW_ROWS=joined.
- A full buffer now asks only for the memory it grows by. Before, it counted a whole new buffer on top of the old
  one, which was already counted as in use. That over-count refused the growth on the guessing model (268 + 65 MB
  of a 308 MB budget) and on the 9B's first layers (308 + 184 of 491). The reply then lost its guessing model or
  its flow and ran at 7.5-8 tok/s. None of the four uncaptured arms on this build met a refusal.
- A card worker's idle recording of its step graphs is marked done when a message arrives just after its last
  graph. Before, nothing was left to record, so the recording was never marked done, and every tree shape left to
  it ran without a graph for the worker's life. Whether a sitting captured anything came down to message timing.
  Test a_recording_whose_last_graph_is_made_is_finished_though_a_message_came, red without the fix.

Built and left OFF (SWARMLLM_FLOW_GRAPH=1): a flowing level captured as one CUDA graph. Everything it would make
outside a kernel is made before the capture: the walk's replay, its row tables, a scratch pair, room in the
buffer, and its memory claim. The claim reads the card's free memory after a synchronize, and a synchronize
inside a capture silently invalidates it. On the card alone a captured guessing-model level reads bit for bit as
the ordinary one, at 9.6-9.8 ms against 13.1-13.2. On the real link most captures were refused inside the capture
(q35_deltanet: CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE), and the captured arms met memory refusals: 4.8-8.4 tok/s. It stays off
until that is understood (docs/FUTURE_WORK.md #228).

New DIAG lines say why a step or flowing level runs uncaptured. A memory refusal now reports the card memory CUDA
graphs hold.

Prior art: vLLM and SGLang set every captured input in buffers before the capture; llama.cpp fills a graph's
inputs once (llm_graph_input_*::set_input). Growth claims count the delta, as an allocator's reserved memory rises
by a reallocation's growth (PyTorch's caching allocator returns the old block to its pool). A cancellable loop
checks completion before cancellation; vLLM and SGLang record graphs at start-up in one pass, uninterruptible.

hits.message:
R136 research: SWARM-SPEC proposal — layered cascade inference acceleration

Second-pass research after R135's initial inference performance
backlog. User asked for a state-of-the-art design — better than
existing options, with constraints (non-technical UX, low overhead,
no new dependencies).

The proposal is a 4-layer cascade purpose-built for P2P inference:

- Layer 0: wire-level Q8_0 with one-shot quality gate per model
  (already implemented, just needs default flip + gate)
- Layer 1: token-level cascaded speculation — n-gram prompt lookup,
  generated-output n-gram, SWIFT layer-skip, DSD chain spec; each
  failure falls through to the next, cheapest-method-wins
- Layer 2: pipeline-level adaptive hedging (EWMA latency + duplicate
  forward to second-best holder when above 1.5× p99, cancel loser
  via existing cross-wire cancel infra)
- Layer 3 (novel): conversation-level predictive prefetch using
  peer idle time between user turns — activation seeding, prefix-
  cache warming, pipeline placement prediction
- Layer 4 (research): activation-delta streaming for 2-4× further
  bandwidth reduction on top of Q8_0

Key insight: data-centre frameworks (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM)
each ship ONE speculation method and assume zero-latency
interconnect. SwarmLLM's bottleneck is network, not compute, and
peers are cheap to use concurrently. Cascade + hedging + idle-time
prediction are P2P-native wins production frameworks don't bother
with.

Expected speedup matrix per workload (Claude Code, RAG, code
completion, free-form, long-context) and decision matrix with five
options (Conservative pilot → Maximalist) for the user to authorise.

Zero new dependencies — every layer uses existing tree crates
(candle, blake3, dashmap, tracing, serde). Total new LOC ~1500
for layers 0-3, ~500 more for research layer 4.

Recommendation: Option B (Layer 0 + n-gram lookup, 2-3 weeks) as
the v0.1 — biggest practical speedup for the actual workload
(Claude Code subscriptions, MCP tool use, RAG), validates cascade
pattern at low risk. Option C (full cascade) as v1.0 target;
Option D as 1-year vision.

R136 — autonomous research session.

hits.message:
fix: Claude clients could not read an error from this server

A failure on /v1/messages came back in the OpenAI envelope with an OpenAI error
type. Anthropic's clients expect neither.

Measured against the live node: a prompt-privacy refusal returned
{"error": {"type": "prompt_privacy_error", ...}} — no top-level "type": "error"
for an SDK to branch on, and an inner type Anthropic does not define. Anthropic
returns {"type": "error", "error": {"type": ..., "message": ...}} with the type
drawn from its own set.

The translation already existed. anthropic_error_type has mapped our canonical
types onto Anthropic's since the streaming error frame was added, and its own
comment says an unknown type deserialises no better than the made-up "error"
stop_reason did — but only the streaming path called it. This is the codebase's
recurring shape: one invariant, several paths, and the fix applied to the path
in the bug report.

It is now a layer on the route rather than an error type in the handler,
deliberately: JsonBody's rejection for a missing max_tokens is produced by the
extractor before any handler runs, so a handler-side type could never have
reached it. Verified live — that rejection is reshaped too.

Success responses are returned untouched and never buffered; reading the body
there would defeat streaming. Verified end to end: a real streaming completion
still produces the full message_start / content_block_delta / message_stop
sequence with token deltas, and /v1/chat/completions still answers in the OpenAI
envelope as a control.

Anything that is not our envelope passes through unchanged, so a failure that
never went through classify_error is never reshaped into a claim about its own
type. The actionable hint and its translation key are kept — Anthropic clients
ignore fields they do not know, and dropping them would cost the caller the part
of the message that says what to do next.

hits.message:
fix(vision): pictures reach the model where you put them; Gemma 3 can read images

A picture sent with a message used to go in front of the whole prompt — ahead
of the chat template's opening — whatever the message said around it. No API
surface marked where the picture belonged (the OpenAI surface dropped its
place, the Anthropic surface dropped image blocks altogether, the fallback
wrote the word `<image>` as text), and the code that puts a picture into the
prompt silently prepended it when it found no mark. LLaVA still answered
plausibly, which is why it went unnoticed.

Now:
- Every surface writes llama.cpp's image marker where the picture was, and
  the picture's rows are put exactly there (`vision::splice_image_rows`, the
  one place, which refuses a prompt with no mark instead of guessing).
- The prompt's length counts each picture's rows, from the picture data
  itself, so the conversation memory is sized right.
- A picture that cannot be read is the request's error, with advice in all
  21 languages — never a reply written as if no picture was sent.
- Gemma 3's image reader is supported (letterboxed to 896 px, SigLIP, pooled

hits.message:
fix(observability): locally-streamed requests were invisible to every metric

`split_stream_response` and its Anthropic sibling bypass the router, and unlike
`split_non_stream_response` they built no `RequestTrace` at all. So a request
served by the local model over SSE was counted nowhere. Measured live before the
fix:

    swarmllm_inference_requests_total          11  ->  11   (after a stream)
    gen_ai_server_time_to_first_token_seconds_count      0

Streaming is the path every interactive client uses — the dashboard chat, Claude
Code, most OpenAI-compatible apps — so on a single-node install the counters and
the shipped Grafana panels could read near-zero while the machine served
continuously. The non-streaming sibling being traced is what made this look fine
in diagnostics.

Both paths now build a trace, register it as in-flight so worker progress lands
on it, and publish before the terminal SSE frames — a client that has walked
away must not cost us the record of work actually done.

`spawn_split_stream` takes the trace as a REQUIRED parameter rather than
defaulting to none, so a future streaming path cannot silently repeat this. The
sender it already returns is `StreamingTokenTx`, which exists to stamp TTFT
without every emit site remembering to; it simply had never been told which
trace it belonged to.

Verified live: requests_total 0 -> 2 across one OpenAI and one Anthropic stream,
ttft samples 0 -> 2, and diagnostics now reports e.g. `total=26455ms
ttft=24950ms` — 25s before the first token and 1.5s producing the rest, which is
the distinction the total alone cannot show.

Found by reading the live metrics, not the code. Note the near-miss in the same
investigation: an earlier grep for `mark_first_token` truncated by `head -8` led
me to claim no production caller existed at all. There is one, in the
`StreamingTokenTx` wrapper. Reading a truncated grep as a complete source is the
error `.claude/rules/diagnosis.md` rule 2 is about.

hits.message:
fix(api): a client that hangs up on a split model's reply now stops the work

When a request for a model split across computers was sent without streaming
and the client gave up (a timeout, a closed tab, a killed script), every
machine in the split kept generating the reply to its end. Nothing read it,
and the next request waited behind it. The stop signal was wired into two of
the paths a non-streamed request can take, not the one a split request takes
first.

The signal now lives in the one helper every non-streamed request waits on
(api::submit_to_router), so no surface can skip it: OpenAI chat and the
Responses API through it, Anthropic, and MCP (an MCP call that hits its own
timeout is cancelled the same way). Measured with the new
`split_rig.sh disconnect` (tinyllama, two processor nodes, client hangs up
after 8 s): the previous build kept going for 113 more steps; this one logs
the disconnect and stops 77 ms later.

Found while running FUTURE_WORK #220's graphics-card fault rig under NVIDIA's
memory checker. That run's results are recorded in #220: the checker works on
this machine with one registry value, and found no bad memory access in 15
minutes of the 10-04 shape. This commit does not fix #220.

hits.message:
Agent programs no longer hang up while a slow computer reads a long prompt

Agent tools such as nanobot send a prompt of several thousand words on every
turn. On a computer without a graphics card, reading it can take minutes, and
during that time the reply stream carried only progress comments. The OpenAI
Python library these tools are built on discards comments before the tool sees
anything, so after 90 seconds of apparent silence nanobot gave up (field report
on v0.3.206).

A stream that has carried no data for fifteen seconds now sends an empty
opening piece of the reply, the same shape every OpenAI-style stream begins
with; the Anthropic-style endpoint sends its own "ping". A reply that is
already producing words is byte-for-byte unchanged.

Checked with the OpenAI library itself and a 20-second per-chunk timeout, the
way nanobot waits: on v0.3.207 the client hung up at 20 s; with this change a
199-second prompt read completed, one keep-alive every 15 s, reply intact.

hits.message:
feat(api): one request can be kept on this computer, whatever the model's setting

A caller can now ask for a single request to run only on this computer:
the header `X-SwarmLLM-Keep-On-This-Computer: true`, or
`"swarmllm": {"keep_on_this_computer": true}` in the body of
/v1/chat/completions, /v1/messages or /v1/responses, or, for an MCP tool
call, `"_meta": {"com.swarmllm/keep_on_this_computer": true}`. Such a
request is treated like one for a model kept here from its ⚙ panel: no
other computer, in the swarm or a pool, and no cloud provider is handed
anything of it. If this computer cannot run it alone, it is refused with
`kept_on_this_computer_error` (503) and a hint, in all 21 languages, that
names the instruction. The strictest instruction wins, so `false` never
undoes the model's own setting or private mode. An instruction the node
cannot read (another header value, a misspelt field, an MCP `_meta` that is
not an object) is refused with a 400 rather than ignored. The `swarmllm`
field is never passed on to a provider.

The instruction travels with the request as a required value
(`InferenceRequest.keep`) into every scope question
(`pool::scope::request_scope`), and never crosses the wire. The worker's
prompt cache marks the entries it stores for a kept request, so they are
never announced to peers or handed to one. A new guard,
`a_requests_keep_instruction_is_never_replaced_by_none`, fails the build
when a request path writes "no instruction" where the request's own
belongs. 11 tests are new or extended, 7 mechanisms were each turned off and
shown to fail their test, and `examples/split_rig.sh keep` checks every
form live against a second computer, which was handed nothing while a
request asked to stay. A security review of the change found no leak.
Closes FUTURE_WORK #251 (2b).

Also removed: the router's "reuse the conversation's previous route"
branch, which skipped the scope check but could never run (every
conversation is recorded with an empty route). FUTURE_WORK #301 covers
the rest of that table, which decides nothing.

And the repo-consistency scanners matched braces byte by byte, so one
`"{"` string in `api/openai/mod.rs`'s tests hid that file's whole test
module from the helper that tells test code from production code. They now
share one matcher that skips strings, character literals and comments,
pinned by `a_brace_inside_a_literal_does_not_end_a_span`.

fix(api): a tool call wrapped in a tag no longer leaves the tag in the reply text

When a model wrapped its tool call in a tag, like Qwen2.5-Coder-7B's
<tools>...</tools>, the call was read correctly but the client also got
"<tools>" back as reply text, on the OpenAI and Anthropic endpoints,
streamed or not. A streamed reply could also send a "```json" line ahead
of a call. Found by a smoke test of v0.3.226: at temperature 0 the stray
tag came back on every request.

- The tag before a call, like a code fence, is now treated as part of the
  call. llama.cpp does the same.
- While a reply streams, a tag or fence at its very end waits for the next
  token. Released at once, it could not be taken back when the call followed.
  Ordinary answers with markup or code blocks still stream; a fence waits
  one token.
- A call written with a doubled opening brace and closed only once,
  {{"name": ...}, is read as a call. It used to come back as text.

Checked on the live node with a development build. At temperature 0,
v0.3.226 returned the stray tag on 4 of 4 requests (OpenAI and Anthropic,
streamed and not) and the fix on 0 of 4. At the default temperature the
fix returned the call with no stray text on 4 of 4. Three new tests fail
with the change switched off.

hits.message:
docs: prefix-affinity routing is a bigger change than its notes said

Investigated the open item about a conversation's later turns not going
back to the machines that already hold its context — the largest
remaining speed win between machines — and the notes understated what it
takes. Writing that down rather than starting it, so the next attempt
does not find out halfway.

The plan on file was to work out a key for each conversation and look it
up. The router does not work that way: one identifier per request serves
both the lookup and the recording, and a successful lookup deliberately
skips recording. So the identifier has to be one thing that stays the
same for a whole conversation — and the only part of a conversation that
never changes is how it opens, which is precisely the approach the notes
already rule out as worse than doing nothing. Two chats that begin the
same way would then wipe out each other's context on every turn.

Doing it properly means separating the lookup from the recording and
teaching the cache to rename an entry as a conversation grows, which is a
change to how a session is identified rather than a helper function.

Two useful things came out of it. The safety worry about a derived key
turns out to be provable away: two conversations can only collide when
their histories are genuinely identical, in which case sharing is
correct. And the scope is narrower than assumed — only the OpenAI-shaped
path can reach this at all today; the Anthropic one does not carry what
it would need, through four handlers.

No behaviour change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01FetzKRPeiMQCtHQz2cmYjG

Implement all 7 deferred fixes from bug audit

1. SSE client disconnect cancellation (pipeline.rs + openai.rs)
   - Pipeline checks token_tx.send() result and stops generating on error

   - Prevents zombie receiver when push_task exits first

   - Replace guessable x-swarm-forwarded header with per-process OsRng token
   - Checked via x-swarm-internal-token header on loopback only
   - Prevents localhost auth bypass by arbitrary local processes

   - Add RouterCommand::UpdateCacheTokens variant

hits.message:
fix(api): a conversation's earlier tool calls and their answers now reach the model

Agents that call tools send the whole conversation back on every turn: the
question, the model's own earlier tool call, and what the tool returned. Until
now those calls never reached the model as calls. The OpenAI surface dropped
them, and the Anthropic surface rewrote them as made-up text. Gemma 4's chat
template only shows a tool's answer next to the call it answers, so a Gemma 4
agent never saw what its tools returned. Gemma 2 refused the tool turn
outright, and the two surfaces built different prompts for the same
conversation.

Each message now carries its tool calls, and which call a tool's answer
belongs to, in HuggingFace's chat format. Arguments are passed as an object, as
vLLM does. One place, at the step that builds every prompt, decides how the
model's own template sees them:

- If a test render shows the template can display calls and answers, it gets
  them unchanged. This is the check llama.cpp's minja runs.
- If not, it gets them in a form it accepts: the call as JSON in the
  assistant's turn, the answer as a user turn. These are minja's polyfills.

Measured on a processor-only test node, OpenAI / Anthropic prompt tokens for
one weather-tool conversation:

- Llama 3.2 3B: 235 / 250 before, 258 / 258 now. 258 is jinja2's render of
  the model's own template under llama.cpp's tokenizer.
- Gemma 2 2B: 201 / 214 before, 234 / 234 now. Its template no longer fails.

For Gemma 4, the prompt now matches jinja2's byte for byte. Given that prompt,
llama.cpp's Gemma 4 12B answers "The current weather in Paris is 17.3°C with
light rain…".

The new fields are optional on the wire, so older peers are unaffected.
Closes FUTURE_WORK #283.

Fix three scalability bugs surfaced by sweep

1. anthropic.rs streaming: on client disconnect, drop token_rx +
   skip result_rx to cancel pipeline + release handler. Mirrors
   the OpenAI disconnect pattern — previously the Anthropic path
   kept the pipeline generating wasted tokens and blocked the
   handler task on result_rx.await.

2. dispatch.rs peer_shard_downloads: cap Vec at 64 entries per
   shard. Popular shards with many racing downloaders could grow
   the Vec unboundedly, turning every gossip update into an O(n)
   scan. Evicts the lowest-progress entry when full.

3. websocket.rs RecvError::Lagged: escalate debug → warn. Slow
   WebSocket clients silently dropped activity events at default
   log level with no operational signal.

Three OpenAI/Anthropic-compatibility fixes found by external testing of
v0.3.16-alpha:

- Claude Code backend: its built-in tools carry long safety/protocol text

  under the 64 KB schema cap, and Anthropic itself bounds tool descriptions
  by the context window, not a small per-tool limit.

- OpenAI /v1/chat/completions now echoes the model id the client requested
  in the response `model` field, instead of the manifest's display name
  (the two can diverge, e.g. `...-fp16` vs `...`). Keeps model-routing
  clients (litellm, LangChain) working and matches the Anthropic endpoint.
  Covers both the local-complete fast path and the direct-executor stream.

- The local-complete streaming fast path (both OpenAI and Anthropic) now
  stops the instant the client disconnects, rather than running the whole
  generation (~55 s) to its natural end with nobody listening. v0.3.16
  fixed the router path; these two sibling functions were missed.

Sweep R109: complete the 3 R108-deferred items (MoE/stop_sequence/usage)

MoE routing — false positive resolved (clarification only):
- The R108 finding claimed topk_cpu's softmax-over-topk diverges from
  DeepSeek-V2/Mixtral by up to 10x in weight magnitude. Re-derived: the
  current code is mathematically EQUIVALENT to the canonical
  softmax-all→topk→renorm pattern (Mixtral, Qwen3-with-norm, DeepSeek-V3
  post-normalization). The global softmax denominator Z cancels:
  softmax(raw[topk])[i] == p[i]/sum_{j∈topk}(p[j]) where p = softmax(all).
  Documented the algebraic identity and the reference impls covered.
  Arch-specific config for DeepSeek-V2-strict (no renorm) and V3-sigmoid
  is deferred — those need a per-arch routing-mode flag plumbed from
  GGUF metadata, not exercised by today's models.

Anthropic stop_sequence — full plumbing landed:
- Sampling: find_stop_sequence() callers in model_worker.rs (3 sites:
  forward_streaming non-swift, swift_decode_loop emit_token, slot-driven
  batch decode at line 2434) capture the matched string instead of just
  detecting a hit.
- Worker IPC: WorkerMsg::GenerateDone carries matched_stop_sequence
  (#[serde(default, skip_serializing_if)] keeps wire-compat with older
  workers).
- EmitOutcome enum split into ::Stop (EOS) and ::StopMatch(String) so
  swift_decode_loop's return signature carries the matched string back
  out to the caller.
- Slot.matched_stop_sequence field + finish_stop_with_match() helper.
- executor::GenerationResult.matched_stop_sequence (llama-feature path)
  populated at the find_stop_sequence call site.
- StreamingTokenEvent.matched_stop_sequence on the final event so SSE
  consumers can read it.
- InferenceOutput.matched_stop_sequence end-to-end through
  pipeline/local.rs and process_pool.rs (worker → daemon → router).
  Distributed path leaves None — matching across LayerResult would need
  a new optional field on NetworkFinishReason::Stop; deferred since the
  local-worker path is the common Anthropic case.
- AnthropicSseEvent::MessageDelta carries stop_sequence; new
  send_sse_epilogue_with_stop helper; existing send_sse_epilogue stays
  for callers that don't have the matched string.
- map_finish_reason_with_match() returns 'stop_sequence' (not 'end_turn')

hits.message:
Implement OpenAI frequency_penalty / presence_penalty (closes R89 deferred #1)

Per OpenAI spec: logits[j] -= count[j] * frequency_penalty + 1[count[j]>0] * presence_penalty
applied BEFORE temperature scaling, where count[j] is the number of
occurrences of token j in the completion-so-far (NOT prompt). Both
penalties documented in the [-2.0, 2.0] range; we don't clamp.

Previously the SamplingParams.frequency_penalty and presence_penalty
fields were deserialized but silently ignored — clients passing
frequency_penalty=1.0 to discourage repetition got zero effect. This
was a real OpenAI API contract violation.

Implementation:

- inference/sampling.rs: new apply_repetition_penalties(logits, ids,
  freq, pres, ctx) helper, called inside sample_token_with_ctx BEFORE
  apply_temperature so the penalty isn't scaled by temperature
  (otherwise frequency_penalty=1.0 + temperature=2.0 silently inverts
  user intent). New scratch buffer SamplingContext.penalty_counts so
  the histogram doesn't allocate per-token in the hot path.
- inference/sampling.rs: new sample_token_with_history() and
  sample_token_with_logprobs_history() entry points. The non-_history
  variants stay as zero-history wrappers (backward compatible — tests
  and one-shot validation paths get no behavior change).
- inference/tensor_util.rs: matching sample_token_with_logprob_history
  and sample_token_with_params_history wrappers for tensor inputs.
- inference/split/mod.rs: re-export sample_token_with_params_history.

Wiring through the worker decode paths:

- Standard worker decode loop (model_worker.rs handle_generate around
  line 1603): now passes &generated to sample_token_with_logprob_history.
  generated already tracked at line 1524.
- BatchGenerate path (model_worker.rs around line 2499): added
  generated_ids: Vec<u32> field on slot_table::Slot (separate from the
  Decoding state variant so other state machinery is unchanged); seeded
  with [first_token] in promote_to_decoding; appended after each sample.
- Distributed forward serving on the LAST segment (model_worker.rs
  lines 789, 1197): now uses sample_token_with_params_history with
  IpcForward.generated_ids.
- crates/swarmllm-types/src/inference.rs: LayerForward gains
  generated_ids: Vec<u32> with skip_serializing_if = Vec::is_empty so
  zero-penalty requests stay on the existing wire shape.
- worker_ipc.rs: matching IpcForward.generated_ids field with the same
  serde gate.
- pipeline/distributed.rs forward_through_segments + process_local_segment
  now thread generated_ids through; only the LAST segment gets a
  populated slice (intermediate segments don't sample). Empty slice
  means no wire bloat.
- execute_distributed already tracks generated_tokens at line 80; passed
  through on every forward_through_segments call.
- pipeline/dsd.rs prefill call passes &[] (no tokens generated yet).

7 new unit tests verify the OpenAI formula (frequency scales with count,
presence is boolean, combine, negative encourages repetition, out-of-range
token id is harmless, no-op on empty history / zero penalties, end-to-end
with history applied to greedy sampling).

897 lib tests pass.

Two low-severity follow-ups from the HTTP API audit:

# MCP method reflection cap (mcp/mod.rs)

`POST /mcp`'s method-not-found arm reflected the full `req.method`

# x-swarm-forwarded comment (openai/mod.rs)

The previous comment claimed "middleware already validates that
x-swarm-forwarded only passes from known peer IPs or loopback with
valid internal token" — that's not actually what middleware does.
Middleware lets x-swarm-forwarded fall through to normal Bearer auth
on non-loopback. Updated the comment to accurately describe the threat
model: any Bearer-authed caller can set the header, but the only
effect is forcing this node to skip peer-forwarding (a routing-only

hits.message:
fix(privacy): local_embedding_privacy works, and refuses rather than send token ids

The config-file setting inference.local_embedding_privacy makes this computer
turn the prompt into the model's first-layer input itself whenever another
computer may run the model's first part, so that computer is sent those
numbers instead of token ids. It had never worked on a real node:

- The embedder opened shard_000.bin as a whole GGUF file. A part is raw
  tensor data (the header is gguf_header.bin), so every load failed with
  "unknown magic", the setting did nothing, and the prompt went out as
  token ids.
- Had it loaded, the prompt pass was sent at the prompt's length instead of
  position 0, which would have garbled every reply (and dropped a Gemma 3
  picture's attention spans).
- The speculative split paths (DSD, draft, n-gram) never checked it.

Now the embedder is the first segment's own loader asked for no layers
(load_model_range, shared with the model worker), loaded when a request
first needs it; its rows equal the first segment's bit for bit. The pass
starts at 0. It is used only where the first layers, or a stand-in for
layer 0, may run on another computer; a first part run here reads token ids
as before, since an embedded one skipped the LoRA adapter, tensor-parallel
and split prompt-cache paths. Where this computer cannot embed, such a
request is refused with EmbeddingPrivacyUnavailable, a new error whose
message and hint (in all 21 languages) name this setting rather than "Start
and finish on this computer". The fast paths stand aside for such a plan,
and no tensor-parallel group takes an embedded first part.

The HTTP forward to a computer in your pool, for a model this computer does
not know, hands the request over whole and asked neither privacy setting,
while the libp2p hand-off and the led split asked both. All three now ask
one question (SharedState::privacy_refuses_a_whole_hand_off); the forward is
refused with the setting's own message.

Rig (Llama 3.2 3B split across two nodes, n-gram off): replies with the
setting on are byte-identical to replies with it off, in both topologies,
and score 116/120 and 119/120 rank-1 against llama.cpp. Each new test fails
with its fix turned off.

The docs claimed the setting makes the prompt "harder to invert". It does
not: what is sent is one row of the model's own embedding table per token,
which the receiving computer maps back exactly. The docs, config comment and
book now say it keeps token ids off the wire and does not hide the prompt.

Also in the 0.3.245 notes: a picture sent through the Anthropic API to a
model that cannot read pictures is now refused with a message, as on the
OpenAI API, where it used to be dropped silently.

FUTURE_WORK #316.

hits.message:
fix(api): a reply streams as it is written, even when the request offers tools

Any request that lists tools — which is every coding agent, every time — got
its whole reply in one piece at the end instead of word by word. Measured on
the live node, same model and prompt, only `tools` differing: 120 content
chunks became 1. On a fast machine that is a curiosity; on a slow one, or a
long prompt, it is minutes of a completely silent connection that looks exactly
like a crash, and it is what makes a client give up and report a timeout. That
is the "OpenClaw takes ages and times out" report.

The reason was real. A local model can only write a tool call as ordinary text,
so the whole reply had to be read before a call could be told from an answer,
and the obvious shortcut is wrong: a call can appear after prose, and the
non-streaming path discarded that prose, so streaming it first would have made
the two ways of asking disagree about the same reply.

vLLM answers this in its own source. It streams the text before a tool-call
marker as ordinary content, holds back only a tail that could be half a marker,
and its non-streaming path keeps that prose too. So content alongside tool calls
is not a divergence to weigh up — it is the shape both the OpenAI and Anthropic
formats already expect, and matching it is what makes the two ways of asking
agree.

SwarmLLM now sends everything up to the first thing that could begin a tool
call and holds back only the rest. An ordinary answer streams in full, a real
tool call is still recognised whole, and text written before a call is kept
rather than thrown away. One boundary rule and one buffer, shared by all four
paths — OpenAI streaming and not, Anthropic streaming and not — so none of them
can drift from the others.

Verified end to end against the released binary as the control, same model and
prompt: 1 chunk became 99 on the OpenAI surface and 1 became 55 on the
Anthropic one, with tool-calling replies still emitting their calls and not one
character of a marker leaking. 2306 lib tests, 54 repo-consistency, 79
integration; the new tests go red with the old behaviour restored.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01Lepyz2hnD2ZqXemenZtv5K

hits.message:
fix(tools): honour a request that says the model must not call a tool

A request can supply tools and separately say that the model must not call one
this turn — the usual way to ask for a plain answer once a tool has already
run. Neither the OpenAI nor the Anthropic path read that setting for a locally
served model. Measured on llama-3.2-3b, it called a tool every time.

A cloud provider enforces this itself. A local model only knows its tools exist
because they are described in its prompt, so the only way to hold it to the
setting is to not describe them — which is what now happens.

Both surfaces shared the defect and now share one predicate, which accepts both
spellings: the plain string OpenAI sends and the object Anthropic sends. Every
other value, including "required", deliberately leaves the tools described: a
local model cannot be compelled to call one, and refusing the request outright
would be worse than letting it answer.

Verified on both surfaces: with the setting, a plain text answer; without it,
the tool call as before.

hits.message:
api: forward anthropic-beta header + max_completion_tokens alias + model aliases + cache usage

Four research-driven API currency fixes:

1. **Forward anthropic-beta header in proxy** (providers.rs + anthropic/mod.rs)
   Claude Code + the Anthropic SDK send features like
   advanced-tool-use-2025-11-20, context-1m-2024-08-07,
   token-efficient-tools-2025-02-19, code-execution-2025-08-25 via this
   header. Our proxy was pinning `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` and
   dropping `anthropic-beta` entirely, silently downgrading users to
   vanilla behaviour. Now captured from the incoming HeaderMap on
   /v1/messages and threaded through to `proxy_to_anthropic`.
   Caller's `anthropic-version` is also honored when provided.

2. **max_completion_tokens alias** (openai/types.rs)
   One-line serde alias so reasoning-model callers (o-series, gpt-5) that
   default to `max_completion_tokens` don't silently fall into our
   default of 2048 — at which point reasoning tokens eat the whole
   budget and content comes back empty.

3. **Anthropic model aliases** (anthropic/convert.rs resolve_model)
   Bare aliases `opus` / `sonnet` / `haiku` now expand to
   `claude-opus-4-7` / `claude-sonnet-4-6` / `claude-haiku-4-5`.
   Without this, the `.starts_with("claude")` router at mod.rs:241
   bounced them to the non-Claude path and 404'd.

4. **AnthropicUsage cache fields** (anthropic/types.rs)
   Added `cache_creation_input_tokens` + `cache_read_input_tokens`
   as optional fields (skipped when zero, so existing snapshot tests
   pass). Local-inference path can now populate them when our prefix
   cache hits; matches the shape the Anthropic SDK expects.

All four gaps surfaced by the overnight research pass against
docs.anthropic.com + platform.openai.com current reference (2026-04-24).
712 lib tests + clippy clean.

hits.message:
fix(inference): Llama 3 models get the prompt format they were trained on

Their chat template was failing to load, so a fallback format from a
different model family was used instead. The model would follow that
format and answer in it — which is where the stray control-token markers
in replies came from, and why an answer was sometimes cut short or empty.
Three earlier releases removed those markers from the reply text; this
fixes the reason they were there. Affects every official Llama 3.x
Instruct model file.

The template binds the message list to a name before looping over it,
and the loop detector matched the literal text " in messages", which the
bound name is not. The loop was skipped, the template produced nothing,
and the caller fell back to a format meant for models that ship no
template at all. Iterating a bound name now works, and a slice or filter
on the list still behaves as before.

Three more fixes in the same shape as v0.3.27 — a rule applied to one
path and not its sibling:

- Naming a provider explicitly now works on the Anthropic API too.
  v0.3.27 removed the prefix on the OpenAI-compatible endpoint only, so
  /v1/messages still passed it upstream and the provider rejected it.
  The same gap stopped anthropic:<model> from being recognised as an
  Anthropic request, and stopped the short model aliases from being
  expanded on any cloud path.
- Quantization is now actually reported correctly. v0.3.27 fixed how the
  tag is read but read it from the display name, which never carries one,
  so every model still reported Q4KM. It reads the model id now.
- Models no longer all report as unserveable. The flag was never filled
  in and always read false, including for models this node hosts itself.

1238 lib tests.

hits.message:
feat(api): SwarmLLM works as an OpenClaw model provider — /v1/models now advertises context_length

OpenClaw (a personal AI agent with a very large user base) can point at any
OpenAI-compatible server, and SwarmLLM already answered its requests
correctly: tools, tool_choice, content parts, streamed usage — verified on a
live node. What was missing was one field. OpenClaw's model discovery reads a
model's context window from `/v1/models` under `context_length`, and when it
finds nothing it assumes 128,000 tokens — so it would send prompts a node
serving 8192 had to refuse, on every turn.

`GET /v1/models` now reports `context_length` beside `max_model_len`, the
same figure under the name each client family reads. `ModelInfo::new` sets
both from one value so they cannot drift, and both are omitted (never
guessed) when a model's declared context is unreadable. Pinned by
`a_model_entry_advertises_its_context_under_both_names_or_neither`.

Docs: the README's "Use it as an API" section now speaks to people who run
an agent, coding assistant or chat UI and want a free backend for it, with
the one setting an agent needs (a context window above the 8192 default —
an agent's system prompt alone is larger) and a ready-to-paste OpenClaw
config; the book's OpenAI page gains the same plus the corrected embeddings
status (501, not 503); ARCHITECTURE.md's endpoint note no longer says 4096.
The plan for a proper OpenClaw provider plugin, researched against
OpenClaw's own source, is recorded in docs/FUTURE_WORK.md. Test count
2217 → 2218.

hits.message:
fix(api): a model that starts its reply inside its thinking answers with the answer

Qwen3.5-4B, the copy the network holds, thinks before every answer unless
asked not to, and its chat template ends the prompt with `<think>`: the reply
begins inside the thinking block without opening it. Both places that split a
reply from its thinking recognised only a block the reply opened, so the
model's whole reasoning ("Thinking Process: ...") came back as the answer on
every API, streamed or not. Seen on v0.3.266 and main.

The prompt's ending is now read once, where the prompt is rendered
(`inference::PromptOpened`), and the opener is put back in front of the reply
before it is split, as llama.cpp does (`common/chat.cpp` parses the generation
prompt plus the output). It is a required argument of `finalize_reply_text`
and of both generate calls, and reaches a stream through the token channel.
Only the first pass over raw text uses it. Nothing changes between computers:
the computer leading a request splits the raw reply itself.

Verified on a probe node off the network, Qwen3.5-4B on the processor:
OpenAI and Anthropic, streamed and not, answer "51" with the reasoning kept
apart, and a reply cut short while thinking returns the thinking as
reasoning; v0.3.266 on the same data, same requests, returned the reasoning
as the answer on all six.

Closes FUTURE_WORK #392.

hits.message:
feat(chat): say what is actually happening while a reply is being prepared

The chat showed a fixed "Thinking…" from pressing send until the first
word arrived. That window is model loading and reading your prompt —
prefill is linear in prompt length and most of a long request — so on a
modest machine one unchanging label covered minutes of very different
work, and it was shown for models that do no reasoning at all. It was
also indistinguishable from a hang.

The node had already worked all of this out. `progress_ticker` has been
interleaving a progress snapshot — phase, percent, tokens done, and an
ETA measured from that request's own rate — into every streamed reply for
weeks. It reached the browser and `readSseStream` dropped it on its first
line, which skipped everything that was not a `data:` frame.

So the chat now shows it: loading the model, reading your message with a
percentage and a countdown, and the phases that used to have no report at
all — waiting for a turn, working out where to run this, contacting the
other computers. Those come from `RequestTrace::live_status`, which reads
the marks the trace already carries. Nothing cycles on a timer: a label
that advances whether or not anything is happening looks like information
and cannot be told apart from the hang it would be hiding.

It travels as an SSE comment, because this rides an OpenAI-compatible
stream: every conforming reader drops a `:` line, so nothing else on
/v1/chat/completions is affected. Two lines per keep-alive — prose for
someone watching in a terminal, JSON for a client that can draw it.

A new setting, off by default, additionally lists the computers working on
a reply and which part of the model each is running. The plain line
answers "is it working and how long", which is what someone asking a
question wants; which node holds which layers is a node operator's
question and does not belong in everyone's chat bubble. It is a browser
preference rather than node config, so it neither needs the daemon nor
rides the Settings panel's config save.

Translated across all 21 languages. Verified in a browser end to end
against a live dev node — every phase, both toggle states, the fallback,
the hand-off to real tokens, and a late status correctly declining to
paint over an answer already on screen.

fix(api): Qwen2.5-Coder tool calls are read as tool calls, not returned as text

Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (Qwen's official upload, the copy the swarm uses since
v0.3.221) answers a tool request in the shape its own chat template shows
as an example, braces doubled: <{{"name": "get_time", "arguments": ...}}}}.
That came back to the client as reply text with no tool call, so agent
clients executed nothing. llama.cpp gives the identical reply on the
identical prompt, so it is the model's habit, not our prompt.

optional "<" or <tool_call> before it, one call object, only closing
braces after), and the stray "<" is not returned as text. Prose that
merely contains doubled braces, or an echoed tool definition, is still
text.

endpoints, streamed and not, all return the call; v0.3.224 returned the
text on all four. The new test fails without the change. FUTURE_WORK #214.

Anthropic→OpenAI proxy: faithful tool-block translation

Replaces the lossy `ChatMessage` flattening in `anthropic_to_openai_proxy`
with a direct Anthropic→OpenAI Chat Completions translation. Multi-turn
function calling on non-Claude cloud providers now actually works:

- Tools translate from Anthropic flat `{name, description, input_schema}`
  to OpenAI nested `{type:"function", function:{name, description, parameters}}`.
- Assistant `tool_use` blocks become `tool_calls` on the assistant message,
  with `content: null` when no text accompanies them.
- User `tool_result` blocks expand to one `role:"tool"` message per
  tool_call_id (each carries a flattened-string `content`).
- System messages hoist to a leading `role:"system"` message; the
  full block-array form (`SystemContent::Blocks`) is supported.
- Image blocks (base64 / url) translate to OpenAI `image_url` content
  parts on the user message.
- `tool_choice` translates: auto → "auto", any → "required",
  none → "none", \{type:"tool", name\} → \{type:"function", function:\{name\}\}.

Non-streaming response: OpenAI `tool_calls` come back as
`ResponseContentBlock::ToolUse` blocks alongside text content;
`finish_reason:"tool_calls"` maps to `stop_reason:"tool_use"`.

and `ContentBlockInputJsonDelta` variants. The translator opens an
Anthropic content block per upstream tool_call `index`, streams
`function.arguments` fragments as `input_json_delta`, and emits
`stop_reason:"tool_use"` on `finish_reason:"tool_calls"`.

modes, response `tool_calls` translation, edge cases). Test count

hits.message:
fix(network): a tensor forward is never sent unsealed while encryption is on

With encryption on (the default), a split's tensor forward to a peer
this node could not find in its id map — a reconnect before the peer
identified itself, or a pruned entry — went out without its session
seal. The connection itself is always encrypted (Noise or TLS, relay
circuits too), so no third party could read it; what was lost was the
per-session seal and the binding of the forward's header to it.

The peer's node is now derived from its id, which carries the same
Ed25519 key, so it is never missing. A forward with no session yet
fails and the request is re-planned. The failure now comes back to the
network loop, so a machine in the middle of a chain reports it to the
machine that started the request instead of leaving it to wait out its
deadline (found by the security review of this change).

Verified: split rig at debug level, 63 forwards sealed and 0 plain;
fail-over rig with one machine killed mid-reply, 382 sealed, 0 plain,
answered. FUTURE_WORK #285 closed.

Also: an empty reply after clean-up stays an HTTP 200, as OpenAI, vLLM
and llama.cpp answer it (#186, moved to "Decided — not doing").

hits.message:
fix(api): a Qwen model's tool call reaches the client as a tool call, its arguments typed by the tool's schema

Qwen 3.5 and the Qwen models after it, and Qwen3-Coder, call a tool in an
XML form their own templates ask for:

  <tool_call>
  <function=get_weather>
  <parameter=city>
  Paris
  </parameter>
  </function>
  </tool_call>

The reply reader knew only JSON call bodies, so every such call came back
to the client as plain text with finish_reason "stop": an agent saw a
model that never used its tools.

The reader now reads that form as llama.cpp does
(common/parsers/qwen3-coder.cpp): each argument is typed by the tool's
schema (a number arrives as a number, text as text), and a bare
<function=NAME> counts only for a tool the request defined. To make that
possible, one value built from the definitions the prompt carried
(RequestTools) replaces the tools-requested flag on all four reply paths,
so no path can read a reply knowing tools were asked for but not what
they take. The OpenAI paths build it from the same list the prompt is
built from, so tool_choice "none" now reads the reply as text.

Checked on a real request, Qwen3.5-4B on the processor: v0.3.266 returned
the call as text; main returns tool_calls get_weather {"city":"Paris"}
with thinking off and on (reasoning kept separate), finish_reason
tool_calls when streamed, and a tool_use block on the Anthropic API.

hits.message:
api: a request can turn a model's thinking on or off — chat_template_kwargs, reasoning_effort and Anthropic's thinking (#391)

Models such as Qwen 3, Qwen 3.5 and Gemma 4 switch their reasoning in the
chat template (`enable_thinking`), and nothing set it for a model run on the
network: a request's `chat_template_kwargs` and `reasoning_effort` reached
cloud providers only. Asked with `enable_thinking: false`, Qwen3.5-4B still
began its reply "Thinking Process:".

Now, the way vLLM and llama.cpp take it:
- OpenAI chat: each `chat_template_kwargs` entry is a template variable;
  `reasoning_effort: "none"` sets `enable_thinking` false and any other
  effort true, an explicit `enable_thinking` winning. The Responses API's
  `reasoning.effort` and Anthropic's `thinking.type` (disabled / enabled /
  adaptive) do the same. A request that asks nothing gets the template's
  default, as before. Both fields are still forwarded to cloud providers.
- Settled once at the door (`chat_template::vars`) into
  `InferenceRequest::template_vars`; every prompt render takes it as a
  required argument, the planner's warm-prompt pricing included.
- Rendered under the renderer's own names: a variable never replaces the
  conversation, its tools, the special tokens or a function a template calls
  (`namespace`, `range`, ...).
- A split another computer leads carries them (`DelegatedSplit::
  template_vars`), handed only to a head advertising the new feature bit 37;
  an older head is not asked to lead such a request. A whole-model hand-off
  already sends the rendered prompt.

Verified on a probe node off the network, Qwen3.5-4B on the processor:
`enable_thinking: false` answered "51" (26 prompt tokens), where v0.3.266 on
the same data dir began "Thinking Process:" (24). A security review of the
wire change found nothing above low; its one hardening (the template's own
functions) is in.

Correction: v0.3.229's notes said Qwen3.5-4B's publisher's template asks it
to answer without reasoning. That is the 0.8B's template; the 4B's own asks
it to think unless told not to. With nothing asked, that template opens the
reasoning block in the prompt itself, and the reasoning then reaches the
reader as the reply — filed as #392, next.

hits.message:
fix: stop swallowing the reasons requests fail

Four fixes from an external checklist report, plus the diagnostic gap
underneath three of them.

A failed local generation closed its stream without saying anything, so
the dashboard received an empty-but-successful response and had to guess
a cause — it displayed 'the model might still be loading', which was a
guess, not a diagnosis. The reason now travels to the client on both the
OpenAI and Anthropic streaming paths.

More seriously, a machine that agreed to serve a request and then failed
was careful to send a reason back, but the send result was discarded. If
that reply was lost, the requester saw only a timeout while the server's
own log showed a completed request. That asymmetry is why an external
tester's serving-side failures stayed undiagnosable across several
rounds: from the outside it looked like a routing bug on the requesting
side. Both reply paths now report a lost reply loudly, and say which side
actually failed.

Also fixed: chat-template markers such as <|im_end|> could appear as
visible text, because the local fast path was the one route that didn't
apply the stop strings implied by a model's own template (the other two
already did). And 'get-model' on a model already fully downloaded
re-fetched every shard — around 353MB of identical bytes in the reported
case — with no check for what was already on disk.

Two of the five reported issues did not reproduce here across cold
non-streaming, cold Anthropic streaming, and cold OpenAI streaming
requests, so the fixes address the mechanisms rather than an observed
failure. Local tool calling is still unfinished and tracked separately.

hits.message:
feat(api): a reply asked for JSON is JSON — response_format is enforced token by token on a model this computer runs whole (#336)

Until now `response_format` (and the Responses API's `text.format`) was only passed to the model as a
request in its prompt, and a small model would often answer in prose, wrap the JSON in markdown, or
add keys the schema forbids. Where this computer runs the whole model, every token of the reply is
now held to the format: the reply is valid JSON, and with `json_schema` it matches the schema.

- How: the JSON schema is compiled with llguidance 1.9.1 (MIT; the engine vLLM and SGLang offer),
  once at the API door. `strict: true` with a schema the engine cannot enforce is refused with a
  400 that says why; without `strict`, unsupported keywords are not enforced and an unreadable
  schema holds the reply to JSON of any shape. Each draw in the model process masks the tokens
  the JSON cannot take next, before penalties, top-k/top-p and logprobs see the scores, and the
  end-of-reply token is allowed only once the JSON is whole.
- Every draw site must pass the grammar, and a draw for a held reply handed none is an error, so
  a new path cannot quietly let a reply off its JSON. Speculative guessing is switched off for a
  held reply (a guess is drawn without the mask); batching stays on.
- Not yet held: a model split across computers or answered by a peer — there the format is still
  only asked for (docs/FUTURE_WORK.md #336 keeps the rest, tool calls included).

Checked on four real models from four tokenizer families (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B, Gemma-2-2B,
TinyLlama-1.1B) asked "Tell me about Paris.": prose without a format; with a strict schema every
reply parsed and matched — streamed, non-streamed, through /v1/responses, and beside a second
request held to a different schema. As with OpenAI, ask for JSON in the prompt too: with
`json_object` and no mention of JSON, two of the four wrote their answer into one string value
until max_tokens ran out.

fix: a thinking model's reasoning now streams as it is written instead of arriving in one block at the end

With stream: true, a reasoning model (Qwen3 and similar) sent nothing while it
thought, and a reply cut off inside its thinking (a small max_tokens) arrived as

the field llama.cpp's server and DeepSeek's API use, a chunk per token. A reply
that ends inside its thinking is reasoning, never the answer: streamed and
non-streamed alike, content is empty and reasoning_content holds it. Checked on

reasoning chunks then 79 answer chunks. The Anthropic surface is unchanged (its
thinking blocks exist only when a request enables thinking).

- With tools requested, a brace inside the model's thinking held the whole
  answer back to the end of the stream — the tool-call search ran over the
  thinking too. Agentic clients always send tools.
- JSON a model sketched while thinking could come back as a tool call when

hits.message:
fix: a wrong API key was reported to Claude clients in the wrong format

The error envelope added for /v1/messages was layered on the route, which put it
INSIDE the auth and rate-limit layers — so the single most likely failure a new
user meets, a wrong or missing API key, still came back in the OpenAI envelope.
Anthropic reports authentication failures in its ordinary error shape, so that is
the shape they have to arrive in. The layer now sits outside both, checks the
path first, and returns everything else untouched before reading a byte.

Verified live with controls: /v1/chat/completions still answers in the OpenAI
envelope, /mcp is untouched, successful responses and SSE streams are unchanged.
The existing auth test now asserts the envelope on both surfaces and fails if the
layer is moved back inside auth.

/mcp is deliberately NOT given the same treatment. Its authorization spec puts
auth failures at the transport level — an HTTP status plus WWW-Authenticate —
and says nothing about the body, so an HTTP 401 is already the conformant answer
there. Checking that before refactoring is what kept this from becoming a much
riskier change to the auth layering.

Four JSON-RPC conformance fixes on /mcp, all verified against a running node:

- Valid JSON of the wrong shape was reported as a parse error. It is an Invalid
  Request (-32600), which this file's own comment already said — but only the
  wrong-version case implemented it, because serde returns the same error type
  for "not JSON" and "not this shape". A JSON-RPC batch array, which MCP removed
  in revision 2025-06-18, is the case that made it visible.
- A response omitted `id` entirely when it was unknown. The spec makes the member
  required and says it MUST be null; the test even accepted either.
- A notification was acknowledged with a four-byte `null` body where the
  transport spec requires 202 with no body — axum serializes an Option
  unconditionally, so Json(None) does not mean "no body".
- resources/read answered -32602 for a URI that is well formed but names nothing
  here. The resources spec names -32002 for that, and it is a different thing
  from a malformed argument.

Also: delegate hardcoded INTERNAL_ERROR for a failed model call while chat's
identical failure went through tool_error_code, so the same underlying problem
told the client "the tool is broken" through one tool and "fix your call"
through the other.

hits.message:
fix(api): refuse OpenAI options we cannot honour instead of ignoring them

`n` and `logit_bias` arrive in `extras` and nothing reads either. A client
asking for three completions got one; a client suppressing a token got it
anyway. Both requests returned 200, so the caller had no way to tell the setting
had not applied — they get a wrong result to debug instead of one clear error.

Both now return 400 naming the option. Deliberately narrow so nothing that works
today stops working: `n: 1` is what every SDK sends by default and still passes,
as does an absent `n` and an empty `logit_bias` object. Only a request for MORE
than one completion, or a logit_bias with entries, is refused.

Checked the neighbours rather than assuming: `response_format`, `seed`,
`presence_penalty` and `frequency_penalty` ARE implemented, so they are left
alone.

Verified against the running API — n=3 and a non-empty logit_bias give 400 with
a readable message; n=1, no n, and an empty logit_bias all give 200.

hits.message:
fix: compute logprobs from raw logits (pre-sampling) per OpenAI spec

Previously sample_token_with_logprobs computed logprobs from the
post-temperature/top-k/top-p distribution. OpenAI spec requires
logprobs to reflect the model's raw (pre-sampling) distribution.

Fix: save raw logits to a new buffer in SamplingContext before
sampling mutates them, then compute log-softmax from the saved
raw logits. This correctly reports what the model predicted, not
what the sampling filter selected.

Also fixes greedy mode (temperature=0) to produce logprobs, which
was previously broken because the softmax probs buffer wasn't
populated correctly for the logprob computation.

hits.message:
fix(tools): stop letting the model name its own tool calls

A tool call carries an identifier the client uses to match a result back to the
request, so it has to be unique across a conversation. It was whatever the
model wrote. Measured on llama-3.2-3b at temperature 0, four runs of four: it
emits call_1, call_2, call_3 for every tool-using reply, so three such turns
leave three different calls all claiming to be call_1. Nothing prevented a
model reusing one identifier twice within a single reply either, which breaks
matching outright.

Identifiers are now assigned when the call is parsed out of the model's text.
That is the one point every tool call crosses — all four callers, streaming and
not, on both the OpenAI and Anthropic surfaces, go through it — so a new caller
inherits this rather than having to remember it.

Verified against the running node; test fails without the fix.

Also probed and found correct on that surface: the system parameter in both
forms, content-block messages, stop_sequences reporting stop_reason and
stop_sequence, max_tokens reporting max_tokens, and the streaming event order.

hits.message:
fix(api): a client that goes away no longer locks the model for everyone else

Sending a long request and then closing the connection left that request
running to completion. It kept hold of the model for the whole generation, so
every later request for the same model queued behind work whose answer nobody
was waiting for. On a long prompt this looked like the node had frozen, with no
error anywhere and no way back short of killing the process.

Cancellation existed but was only ever wired to an explicit header that one
internal caller sets, so an ordinary client simply disappearing signalled
nothing. Requests now carry a cancel flag whether or not the caller supplied
one, and it is set if the connection drops before the answer is ready.

Applied to both the OpenAI and Anthropic non-streaming paths. Streaming is
deliberately excluded: those handlers return as soon as the stream is
established and generation continues afterwards, so treating their return as a
disconnect would cut every stream short.

Reported by a user whose next trivial request stayed blocked after abandoning
an 8000-word prompt.

hits.message:
fix: a reply from another machine could run past its ending

Models mark the end of their turn with a short piece of text rather than
only a token id. When the work ran on another machine, that marker was
not sent with the request, so nothing stopped the reply there — the model
carried on and wrote the next question itself, which arrived looking like
part of the answer. Seen with TinyLlama over the network.

The path that sends work to a single peer built the chat-formatted prompt
and then forwarded the caller's sampling settings untouched, so the
markers implied by that format never left this machine. The serving side
cannot make up for it: it only trims the list it is given.

The prompt and its markers are now produced together as one value, from a
single read of the model's header, so a caller cannot take one and forget
the other. The shared helper also moved out of the OpenAI module into the
inference layer — the paths most likely to need it were the ones that
could not reach it, which is why they went without.

Pinned two ways, because the leak only shows when the model happens to
emit a marker: a unit test on the parameters, and a source-level check
that this path cannot go back to forwarding them untouched.

hits.message:
fix(api): three findings from provider and model-metadata testing

Explicit provider:model syntax reached the provider with the prefix still
attached. The prefix picks which provider to use — the provider itself has
never heard of it — so DeepSeek rejected deepseek:deepseek-v4-flash as an
unknown model name. The Anthropic path already stripped it; the
OpenAI-compatible path forwarded the request body untouched. Stripped at
the proxy boundary now, so it applies wherever the request came from.

Updating provider keys could silently do nothing. The fields are named
<provider>_key, and anything unrecognised is discarded during parsing — so
a request naming the field 'mistral' rather than 'mistral_key' changed
nothing and still returned success. A request that would change nothing
now explains what the fields are called instead of reporting ok.

Quantization was misreported for any model whose id carries a multi-part
tag. Ids use hyphens where filenames use underscores, so q8_0 becomes
q8-0, and the parser both stripped only underscores and looked at just the
final segment — reading '0' rather than 'q8-0', failing, and falling back
to a Q4KM placeholder. A Q8_0 model was reported as Q4KM.

hits.message:
fix(api): stop generating when a client stops reading, not just when it disconnects

Closes the last gap in the disconnect-cancel work. Earlier fixes cancel the
moment a client CLOSES the connection; this covers a client that holds the
connection open but stops reading the response — a crash, a client-side
timeout-and-retry, or a closed laptop. In that case the streamed-token buffer
fills and the next send blocks on backpressure instead of failing, so the old
code kept the worker generating a reply nobody was draining (an external tester
measured a processor pegged at ~1200% for 13+ minutes after the client had
moved on).

A send that stalls for 60s with a full buffer now counts as a departed consumer:
the stream stops and the worker is cancelled, bounding wasted compute to that
window instead of the whole token budget. The threshold is generous enough never
to cut off a live client — a send unblocks the instant the client accepts a
single token, so only a fully-stopped reader trips it. Applied to every SSE path
(OpenAI + Anthropic, local-complete fast path + router). +2 tests.

hits.message:
V4: GET /v1/responses/:id/input_items pagination

OpenAI SDKs hit this endpoint in retried-tool-call flows — v1 had no
route for it, so the SDK call errored out. V4 wires it.

Shape: standard OpenAI list object
  { object: 'list', data: [...], first_id, last_id, has_more }

Semantics:
- Text input produces a single synthetic message item with content =
  [{type: 'input_text', text: ...}]. The id 'item_0' is stable.
- Array input produces one item per entry; synthetic ids are 'item_N'
  where N is the zero-based position in the original request. The
  original InputItem fields round-trip through a serde_json::to_value,
  with a new 'id' key spliced in.
- 'after={cursor}' matches by synthetic id and returns items strictly
  after that position (empty if cursor is the last item).

hits.message:
fix(diagnostics): say when a caller's stop sequence ended a reply early

A reply that comes back with one token and `finish_reason: "stop"` looks
exactly like a model with nothing to say. The OpenAI schema has no field
for which stop sequence fired, so the client cannot tell the difference —
and the node, which knew, said nothing either.

An external tester hit exactly that shape against a coding agent and
spent a testing session narrowing it, with plain curl unable to
reproduce. Reproduced here in one request: a `stop` value matching the
model's second token gives `completion_tokens: 1, finish_reason: "stop"`,
silently. Nodes now warn, naming the stop sequence and the token count,
when a stop match leaves the caller with two tokens or fewer. An ordinary
stop trimming the tail of a real answer stays at debug — warning about
that would train operators to ignore the warning.

Whether this is what the tester hit is NOT established; their client's
`stop` array is the missing piece, and the reproduction attempts left it
out. What is established is that the product could not have told them.

Wired at the three places a generation finishes carrying a matched stop:
the local worker, the whole-model remote path, and the coordinator that
assembles from remote segments.

It deliberately does NOT live in `finalize_reply_text`, which looks like
the right choke point — all four reply sources funnel through it — and is
not. Every generator applies the caller's stop sequences during
generation and breaks before keeping the matching text, so by
finalisation the text no longer contains the stop and there is nothing
left to notice. That version was written, and silently never fired; the
end-to-end check caught it, the diff would not have.

hits.message:
docs(routing): the scheduler cannot tell a short prompt from a long one

vertex_cost prices a candidate from its per-layer decode latency times a
fixed 64 forward passes. Nothing in the scheduler ever sees prompt_tokens,
so a ten-token request and a ten-thousand-token one are routed the same
way, while prefill cost is linear in prompt length.

The hardware gap is also much wider on prefill than on decode: measured
here, 36 against ~2000 tokens a second for prompt processing (55x) versus
8 against 47 for generation (6x). A five-thousand-token agentic system
prompt is about 140 seconds on the processor node and 2.5 on the graphics
one, a difference nine times larger than the ratio the cost model prices.

It does not always bite — routing already prefers a faster node, so an
idle GPU wins anyway. It bites when the costs are close: a loaded GPU
against an idle CPU is the right answer for a short prompt and the wrong
one for a long prompt, and today those two requests look identical.

Recorded with what a fix would need, including that it has to be validated
on a real pair of nodes rather than argued — changing a routing cost model
without that is how an earlier delegation penalty priced out every good
split.

hits.message:
diag(prompt-cache): name a long saved prompt the cache lets go, and why (#470)

A saved prompt lets a long conversation or agent prompt skip re-reading
its opening on the next turn. When the cache needs room it lets an old one
go, and each save's log line counted those but never said how long they
were - so nobody could tell whether long prompts (minutes to read again on
a processor or across computers) were being dropped and re-read. That is
the condition for keeping saved prompts on disk as well (FUTURE_WORK #470).

A prompt of 8,192 tokens or more that the cache lets go now gets one line:
for which model, why (the cache's caps, room planned for a new save, or
memory asked for), how many and the longest. Shorter ones stay silent.
Logging only; nothing about what is kept changes.

hits.message:
perf(inference): a graphics card holds three times the conversation in the same memory

A conversation's memory on a graphics card now takes a third of the space.
It is kept in half precision, as llama.cpp keeps it, instead of in full
precision with a half-precision copy beside it. On an 8 GB card beside
Qwen2.5-Coder-7B that is room for about 38,000 tokens of conversation where
there was room for about 12,700, so an agent's long instructions fit beside
the model instead of being refused. Computers that run models on the
processor are unaffected.

Also fixed: a node with inference.max_seq_len_override set, which is how agent
users make room for a long prompt, kept no limit at all on its card's
conversation memory. A long prompt could fill the card and the reply then
crawled. Measured on v0.3.231 with a 15,648-token prompt: 307 s, the card at
7885 of 8192 MiB. With this change it answers in 51.5 s. A prompt that truly
does not fit is turned away at once, and a swarm sends it to another computer.
The limit was skipped by a condition left over from July, when this step still
shortened the context to fit the card.

How: layers::kv_storage is the one rule for how a layer keeps its cache. It
is asked by the cache as it is built (layers::append_to_cache, every forward
path) and by every estimate of its cost: the loader's budget, the
card/processor split planner, admission, and the bound a coordinator holds a
peer to. A peer is priced by the new features::KV_HALF_ON_CARD bit, so older
peers are priced as before. Flash attention reads the half cache in place,
the one-token decode kernel reads f16 (kernels/decode_attn.cu), and a step's
K/V is written into it in one launch (kernels/kv_append.cu). DeepSeek-2's MLA
cache stays f32, and the rule requires the attention kind so no estimate can
forget it.

Why the full-precision copy existed: it was kept on a reading of arXiv
2604.15409 as "an f16 cache diverges". That paper compares decoding with and
without a cache, both in f16. llama.cpp, the reference replies are judged
against, stores f16 by default.

Measured on an RTX 3070 Laptop, A/B in one binary (SWARMLLM_KV_F16=0 is the
old layout):
- Memory: the 7B's cache is 59 MB against 176 MB at 896 positions, 352 MB
  against 1057 MB at 6000.
- Speed: decode is level at 23.3 ms a token with 6016 positions cached.
  Prompt reading is level; with stage timers synchronised, attention took
  528 ms against 533 ms.
- Replies: 400-token greedy replies scored against llama.cpp come out the same
  on six models; Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B are word-for-word
  identical. Phi-3.5's logits, teacher-forced on the card, sit marginally
  closer to llama.cpp: median cosine 0.999828 against 0.999821.

Closes FUTURE_WORK #194; #237 re-ranked to P3. Evidence:
docs/invariants/inference.md "A card keeps its KV cache as f16" and
docs/invariants/memory.md "A card's KV budget is kept whatever the context
setting".

hits.message:
fix(routing): the scheduler can finally tell a short prompt from a long one

Routing priced every request as if it were the same size. A ten-token question
and a ten-thousand-token agentic prompt were sent to exactly the same node,
because the cost model charged a fixed number of decode passes and nothing in
the scheduler had ever seen how long the prompt was.

That matters because reading a prompt and writing a reply are bounded by
different things. Decode is limited by memory bandwidth, where the machines in a
swarm differ by around six times. Prefill is limited by arithmetic, where they
differ by around fifty-five: a 5000-token system prompt is about 140 seconds of
reading on a processor-only node against about 2.5 on a graphics card. The model
priced the six and ignored the fifty-five.

Prefill is now its own term, linear in prompt length. Where this node has
actually prefilled through a peer it uses that measurement — peer_speed has
tracked prefill separately from decode since August — and otherwise falls back
to a device-class prior taken from real numbers on real hardware, which the
first real measurement then replaces.

Two things keep the change from destabilising what already worked. An unknown
prompt length prices a request exactly as before, so the offline allocator and
every non-request path are untouched. And at a short prompt the new term is a
few percent of the decode term, so short-prompt routing cannot move; the choice
only shifts once the prompt is long enough that reading it is the dominant cost,
which is the case this exists for.
