hits.message:
docs: a plan to make split inference fast without anyone holding the whole model

Nobody in the network should need to hold a whole model, not even a
compressed copy: the models worth splitting are the ones nobody can hold. So
the plan is to parallelize the REPLY rather than the token. One token must
still pass through every machine in turn, but each trip around the machines
can carry many rows at almost no extra cost, and today it carries one.

- More tokens per trip from guessing that lives on one machine: draft heads
  built into newer models (Qwen 3.5/3.6, GLM, DeepSeek) sit on the last
  machine and give about 3 tokens a trip in llama.cpp's measurements; a small
  same-family model gave 3.5 a trip here (10 on code).
- More streams per reply in the same trip: several workers writing one answer
  while reading each other (Hogwild!, which splits its cache by layers exactly
  as our machines already do), outline-then-expand for list-shaped answers,
  and an agent's parallel calls.
- Prompt reading is parallel already, and bandwidth-bound rather than
  latency-bound across a WAN.
- Shorter trips: keep the requester out of the loop (FUTURE_WORK #143) and
  build rings of nearby machines.

Measured and ruled out: repairing a drafted reply all at once (1.07 tokens a
trip) and streaming weights to the requester. The earlier "same model at fewer
bits on your own card" design is kept only as a possible opt-in.
Plan: docs/plans/wan_parallel.md, FUTURE_WORK #145.

hits.message:
fix(memory): asking your own model again right away moves it back onto the graphics card

When one of your requests had to run partly on the processor (another
computer's model held the card at that moment), your next requests kept it
there as long as they came less than 5 seconds apart. An agent's loop or a
nightly check never leaves that gap, so the model stayed slow for all of them
(#483 (a)). Your own requests now move it back to the card as soon as it
has room. Other computers' requests still wait for a pause in the traffic,
so a peer's request is not charged a cold load.

The 5 s wait stood in for a race: a request handed the model's process a
moment before it is retired, registering its reply just after the retirement
looked for work in flight. That race is now closed for every retirement:
each hand-out is stamped under the pool's lock, and a retirement waits 250 ms
past the last one before it drains. A new guard fails the build if a way to
take a model process out of the pool skips the stamp. After a refusal, the
graphics card is read at most once every 5 seconds per model.

The guard that keeps "is this process in use?" in one place scanned only the
first thousand lines of the 25,000-line pool. It stopped at the first test
attribute, which sits on a field. It now scans the whole file and finds
nothing.

Prior art: HikariCP's connection pool makes a borrow and an idle eviction
compete on one atomic, so it never closes a connection that was just handed
out.

hits.message:
docs(gpu): re-check the half-precision KV copy against its new purpose

Moving grouped-query decode onto the standard kernel retired the reason
the f16 KV mirror was kept: it existed so flash DECODE would not convert
the whole history every token, and decode no longer calls flash on either
head layout.

The mirror stays, because re-measuring found it is still worth its cost
for a different reason — it is now read by prompt chunks after the first,
which go to flash, and without it each chunk re-converts the whole
history. That is O(history) per chunk and so quadratic over a prompt, and
the measurements show exactly that shape: one 128-token chunk on a warm
prefix costs 4% more without it at ~960 tokens of context, 9% at ~2048
and 20% at ~4096. Long prompts are where agentic clients live.

Decode showed no resolvable difference either way, so the 50% of extra
KV memory it costs now buys prompt processing rather than generation.
That memory is a hard limit — admission charges and refuses on it — so
the note says plainly that if the chunked-prefill reader ever goes away
too, this should be switched off rather than left standing.

No behaviour change: same predicate, corrected reasoning, and
SWARMLLM_KV_MIRROR to A/B it inside one binary. A right answer resting on
a stale reason is what let the decode routing go a week out of date in
the first place.

hits.message:
fix(diagnostics): also say when the model itself ended the turn at once

Completes the previous change. A reply that comes back with nothing has
two possible causes and a client cannot see either: a stop sequence in
the request matched immediately, or the model emitted end-of-turn
straight away. Both look identical from outside — `finish_reason: "stop"`,
HTTP 200, a blank or one-word answer — and the difference is precisely
what tells someone whether to look at their client's `stop` values or at
the prompt.

The second case is now reported too, and says what it points at: the chat
template for that model, and whether the rendered prompt ends where the
model expects to answer.

A caller who asks for one token and gets one is not a fault, so the token
budget is part of the condition — otherwise this would fire on every
deliberate single-token request, which is how a useful warning becomes
noise. Verified against that control, and against a stop sequence
trimming the tail of a real answer, which also stays quiet.

Also records two prefill hypotheses that were measured and did not
survive, so they are not re-derived:

- Prefill chunking was NOT costing 2-3x on a GPU. Raising the chunk from
  128 to 512 or 2048 changes nothing (1983 / 1803 / 1896 tok/s at ~2370
  tokens), and all three match the benchmark's own throughput. The gap
  that suggested otherwise came from comparing the live node — connected
  to the swarm, several models resident, serving — against an idle
  benchmark. The arms differed by machine state, not by chunk size.
- The prefix cache IS working for the agentic pattern, which was the
  bigger worry: a ~4200-token system prompt costs 11.94s cold, 0.12s
  repeated, and 0.25s with a new user turn on the same system prompt.

be read from scratch, even when this computer had just read nearly all of it
and kept it. A later turn of an agent conversation could then be sent
through other machines and take longer than the first: 847 seconds in one
report, against a few seconds to read only what was new. The router now
reads the prompt the way the model will, counts how much of it this
computer already holds, and prices a local run on the rest. It is a price,
not a rule: a much faster route still wins.

Also in this change:
- Long prompts are kept for reuse. A prompt over 8,192 tokens was never
  stored, and agent tools send 4,000 to 14,000 a turn. The store is now
  sized by the memory set aside for it, and a longer prompt keeps its
  opening, the instructions and tool list every turn repeats.
- A computer told not to use its graphics card is priced as the processor
  it runs on. It was priced as reading prompts about nine times faster than
  it can.
- A prompt's estimated length now counts its tool definitions.

Checked with a new two-computer test (examples/split_rig.sh cache): the
second turn of an agent-shaped conversation stayed on its computer and read
2,713 of its 2,744 tokens from what it had kept. Only this computer's own
store is counted so far; why other computers' are not yet is written up in
docs/FUTURE_WORK.md item 10.

hits.message:
Dev tooling: never block context compaction, and let helper agents edit files they read

No effect on the app — this is the tooling the project is developed with.

A hook refused to compact a development session's context while any file
was uncommitted. When the context then filled, compaction was refused and the
very next request failed outright ("Prompt is too long"), with no room left to
make the commit the hook was asking for — the whole session was lost. Claude
Code documents that outcome for a blocked compaction at the context limit.

Compaction never touches files on disk, so the block protected nothing. It is
replaced by a hook that runs AFTER compaction and lists what is still
uncommitted, so the resumed session knows the work is pending. It cannot block.

Separately, the read-before-edit gate looked only at the main session's
transcript, so every helper agent was refused permission to edit a file it
had itself just read. The gate now also reads the helper's own transcript,
which Claude Code identifies by `agent_id`. Verified with a planted pair (the
helper that read the file is allowed; a caller that never read it is still
refused) and the gate's own probe script.

fix(prompt-cache): a computer sharing long saved prompts is no longer ignored by its peers

A computer that shares its saved prompts with peers (off by default) tells
them which prompt openings it holds, so a peer can send it a request whose
opening it has already read. Peers refuse that list whole past 1,024 blocks
of 64 tokens, but the sender listed every block of every saved prompt for
the model: one 70,000-token agent prompt, or sixteen of 4,000, and peers
kept an older list instead.

The list now carries at most 1,024 blocks, the earliest of each saved
prompt first, so every saved prompt's opening can still be matched; a match
only reaches less far into a very long one. Found by checking every limit a
receiver applies against the computer that sends that message.

hits.message:
docs: require looking a problem up before working on it

Adds researching the problem as the first diagnosis rule, and as the first step
the root-cause agent takes, rather than something remembered when convenient.

Most of what this project runs into — renewing keys, deciding what fits in
memory, detecting replayed messages, planning a pipeline, getting through home
routers — is solved in systems with far more scars than ours. Their answer
usually names the failure and carries the one detail that would otherwise be
missed.

Both times it was done in one recent session it changed what was built. Reading
how WireGuard renews keys is what made the kept key carry its own duplicate
detection — without that the fix would have let the same message be accepted
twice and weakened the very thing it was protecting. Reading how a serving
system admits work under memory pressure named the pattern and drew out the
distinction that mattered: it has nowhere else to send work, and a swarm does.
Where it was skipped the same day, the work went worse. Minutes, both times.

The rule is explicit that this does not replace measuring: something that is
correct in the literature and never runs here is still not the cause. And it
asks for the source to be cited where the decision lives, so the next person can
check the reasoning rather than rebuild it.

hits.message:
Agent programs no longer hang up while a slow computer reads a long prompt

Agent tools such as nanobot send a prompt of several thousand words on every
turn. On a computer without a graphics card, reading it can take minutes, and
during that time the reply stream carried only progress comments. The OpenAI
Python library these tools are built on discards comments before the tool sees
anything, so after 90 seconds of apparent silence nanobot gave up (field report
on v0.3.206).

A stream that has carried no data for fifteen seconds now sends an empty
opening piece of the reply, the same shape every OpenAI-style stream begins
with; the Anthropic-style endpoint sends its own "ping". A reply that is
already producing words is byte-for-byte unchanged.

Checked with the OpenAI library itself and a 20-second per-chunk timeout, the
way nanobot waits: on v0.3.207 the client hung up at 20 s; with this change a
199-second prompt read completed, one keep-alive every 15 s, reply intact.

feat(api): SwarmLLM works as an OpenClaw model provider — /v1/models now advertises context_length

OpenClaw (a personal AI agent with a very large user base) can point at any
OpenAI-compatible server, and SwarmLLM already answered its requests
correctly: tools, tool_choice, content parts, streamed usage — verified on a
live node. What was missing was one field. OpenClaw's model discovery reads a
model's context window from `/v1/models` under `context_length`, and when it

serving 8192 had to refuse, on every turn.

same figure under the name each client family reads. `ModelInfo::new` sets

guessed) when a model's declared context is unreadable. Pinned by
`a_model_entry_advertises_its_context_under_both_names_or_neither`.

an agent, coding assistant or chat UI and want a free backend for it, with
the one setting an agent needs (a context window above the 8192 default —
an agent's system prompt alone is larger) and a ready-to-paste OpenClaw
config; the book's OpenAI page gains the same plus the corrected embeddings

hits.message:
fix(inference): a client that gives up during a long prompt now stops the work, on this node and on its peers

v0.3.150 taught a worker to check for cancellation between layers, but on
the pipeline path nothing told it to. The request's cancel flag was read in
one place — the top of the per-token loop — and the two streaming surfaces
never set it at all: they dropped the token receiver, which the pipeline
notices when it next has a token to send, i.e. after the prompt pass. On a
card that gap is seconds. On a processor-only node running an agent's
14,000-token prompt through a 14B it is longer than any client waits: a
tester found the worker at 400% CPU with 81 minutes of accumulated time and
a thermal warning after three abandoned attempts, each queued behind the
last — even though, on v0.3.151, that node was only computing the two
one-layer local ends of a privacy pipeline while a peer ran the middle.

Every wait that can run for minutes now watches the request's cancel flag
(`inference::cancel::unless_cancelled`, polled every 250 ms):

- the wait for a local worker's answer (`ModelProcessPool::forward_for_request`)
  — the wait only, never the send, since a half-written frame would corrupt
  the worker's stream; dropping the wait sends `CancelRequest`, and the
  worker skips a forward it has not started and stops one between layers;
- the wait for a remote segment's result — the peer is told to stop and the
  request ends, instead of failing over to a fresh peer for nobody;
- both SSE surfaces give the request a flag and flip it the instant the
  connection closes; the router never retries a cancelled request.

What this cannot yet stop is a single layer already computing: the
between-layer check has nowhere to fire on a one-layer segment, so on a
processor the current layer still finishes. Recorded in FUTURE_WORK with the
worker-side chunking that would close it. Gotcha #445.

hits.message:
fix(api): a conversation's earlier tool calls and their answers now reach the model

Agents that call tools send the whole conversation back on every turn: the
question, the model's own earlier tool call, and what the tool returned. Until
now those calls never reached the model as calls. The OpenAI surface dropped
them, and the Anthropic surface rewrote them as made-up text. Gemma 4's chat
template only shows a tool's answer next to the call it answers, so a Gemma 4
agent never saw what its tools returned. Gemma 2 refused the tool turn
outright, and the two surfaces built different prompts for the same
conversation.

Each message now carries its tool calls, and which call a tool's answer
belongs to, in HuggingFace's chat format. Arguments are passed as an object, as
vLLM does. One place, at the step that builds every prompt, decides how the
model's own template sees them:

- If a test render shows the template can display calls and answers, it gets
  them unchanged. This is the check llama.cpp's minja runs.
- If not, it gets them in a form it accepts: the call as JSON in the
  assistant's turn, the answer as a user turn. These are minja's polyfills.

Measured on a processor-only test node, OpenAI / Anthropic prompt tokens for
one weather-tool conversation:

- Llama 3.2 3B: 235 / 250 before, 258 / 258 now. 258 is jinja2's render of
  the model's own template under llama.cpp's tokenizer.
- Gemma 2 2B: 201 / 214 before, 234 / 234 now. Its template no longer fails.

For Gemma 4, the prompt now matches jinja2's byte for byte. Given that prompt,
llama.cpp's Gemma 4 12B answers "The current weather in Paris is 17.3°C with
light rain…".

The new fields are optional on the wire, so older peers are unaffected.
Closes FUTURE_WORK #283.

hits.message:
perf(split): a model split across computers no longer re-reads the whole conversation every turn

Coding agents send the entire conversation again with each message. When the
model was split across computers, every computer in the split read all of it
again, every turn: on a 14B that is ~79 MB of hidden states per hop and about
50 s of network time per turn at 25 Mbps before any computing.

Now each computer keeps its part of the conversation's opening for the next
turn. The coordinator names the prompt's blocks with a keyed hash chain
(vLLM's prefix-caching rule) and asks every computer in the split to resume
where it is believed to hold them; each keeps its part in the same prefix
cache, under the same memory budget, as its own conversations. A computer
that no longer holds it (restarted, or needed the room) says so, and the
prompt is read from the start once more - never a penalty, never a wrong
reply. The keys cannot be turned back into text by the computers that hold
them.

Measured on a 3B model split across two computers, one binary with an env
switch (SWARMLLM_SPLIT_PROMPT_CACHE=0 is the old path): the second turn of an
agent conversation took 7.1 s and 8.2 s instead of 65.2 s; with the far
computer restarted between turns it re-read and answered in 70.2 s. Replies
were scored against llama.cpp and agree as closely as before.

Additive on the wire: a new feature bit (20) and two trailers, sent only to
computers that advertise it. Every computer in a split must run this version
for it to apply. FUTURE_WORK #10 keeps its other half: routing a turn to the
computers that already hold its opening.

hits.message:
fix(routing): a long prompt read in pieces now teaches the split its prompt speed

A split reads any prompt past about 1,000 words in pieces of 512, every
computer working at once (#171). No piece was ever timed, so a computer's
prompt speed was learned only from prompts short enough to read whole. One
that only ever saw long prompts, such as a coding agent's, stayed on the
unmeasured guess however often it served.

Each piece is now timed for its computer:
- a piece on this computer around its own forward;
- a piece on another computer from when it was sent, or from the answer to
  the piece before it if it waited behind that one, to its own answer
  (that computer runs its pieces in order).
The word count is the piece this computer cut, never a number another
computer reported.

On a two-computer TinyLlama split with three ~1,220-word prompts, each read
in three pieces: before, neither computer had a prompt speed after any
request; after, both did from the second request on (4.1 and 5.8 ms a layer
and word). That matches the 72 s each pass took on that one-processor rig.

Also records why the heat guard's two-minute clock still restarts when a
card dips under its line with full clocks (FUTURE_WORK #440).

hits.message:
perf(card): replies on a graphics card no longer stall to make CUDA graphs

About a third of a 7B's replies on the card decoded 3-8x slower than the rest
(10-24 tok/s against 67-70) whenever questions came back to back, as an agent
or a script asks them, and the first reply after a load was slow too. Each
slow reply was making one of the card's CUDA graphs mid-reply, which under
WSL2 took 4.9-9.8 s; the idle recording that makes them ahead only runs when
the worker has nothing to do, and back to back it never had.

A reply now makes no graph before that recording has run: a step whose graph
is not made yet runs the ordinary way (about 8% slower than a graph, never
3-8x), and every reply after the first idle moment replays the graphs the
recording made. A graph a shape already has is updated in replies as before.
Measured on v0.3.299 against itself with graphs off (6 replies an arm):
graphs on 9.9-70.4 tok/s, off 54.6-65.4 with none slow.

Prior art: vLLM captures every batch size before it serves and pads to a
captured size rather than capture mid-serving; SGLang records its graphs at
start-up. A/B SWARMLLM_CUDA_GRAPH_MADE=in-replies; card test
a_reply_before_the_idle_recording_makes_no_graph fails under it. FUTURE_WORK
#357 (d).

hits.message:
perf(cache): a saved prompt makes room before it is copied, so the copy reuses memory instead of faulting in fresh pages

A long prompt's snapshot (a 14B's 1,800 tokens: 569 MB) was copied first and only
then were the entries it replaces — a growing conversation's previous turn — and the
least recently used ones over the cache's caps dropped. The save held both, and the
copy landed in fresh memory: under WSL2 569 MB took 43 ms into memory already held,
255 ms into fresh memory with memory free and 0.6-0.8 s with the page cache full, as
after a build (the kernel's huge-page compactions failing). Both inserts now make room
first, in llama.cpp's server prompt cache order; the cache ends up holding exactly the
same entries. In a turn-by-turn model of an agent conversation a save went from
171-274 ms to 81-125 ms; the real worker's gain is measured next.
A/B SWARMLLM_SNAPSHOT_ROOM=after-copy. FUTURE_WORK #367 narrowed.

hits.message:
docs(openclaw): what to do when an agent turn takes ages and times out

Three causes, told apart from the node's own log: a model split across
machines on v0.3.153 or older refusing any prompt past about 8,000 tokens
(fixed in the next release); a reply that might be a tool call arriving in
one piece at the end, which is expected for now; and a long prompt simply
being slow to read on a processor. The suggested provider timeout goes from
300 s to 1800 s, with the reason next to it — an agent turn sends thousands
of tokens of tool schema and OpenClaw can legitimately see nothing for
minutes.

Also notes that the plugin's own test suite needs Node 22.5+: OpenClaw
imports `node:sqlite`, so on Node 20 the suite fails to load before any test
runs.

hits.message:
perf(inference): a model on your own computer copies from your earlier replies too

An agent's requests repeat much of what its earlier requests got back. A
split across computers already guessed ahead from the owner's earlier
replies; a model running whole on this computer looked only in the
conversation in front of it. Its model process now keeps the owner's
earlier replies in its own memory and guesses from them where the
conversation offers nothing; both decode paths keep a finished reply.

Only the owner's own requests read or add to it: one predicate,
owner_replies::the_owner_asked, decides it for the daemon's store and the
model process's alike, and the model process is told through
IpcGenerate::reads_owner_replies. requested_by is now a required argument
of the pool's generate, threaded from both chat APIs, so a request passed
on by a pool member is told apart from the owner's own. Nothing is saved
to disk or shown to another computer.

TinyLlama on the processor, the same question asked twice: 74 of the
second reply's 96 tokens came from guesses instead of 45, in 24 checks
instead of 53, and the reply was identical. The test fails with the
lookup taken out. (#337)

docs(plans): a drafter that learns within a session is ruled out; copying from earlier sessions works best where they agree (#337, #338)

Offline measurements for the split-speed track (faster_than_local.md § 7.5-7.6):

- Training the guessing model on the session as it goes (Online Speculative

  a code session and -1.3 on chat, with no session reaching the +2-point stop
  rule, so the every-layer form was not run. Both forms tried are ruled out.
- Copying from the owner's earlier sessions (#337): llama.cpp's lookup
  decoding drafts from its cross-run cache only where earlier runs agree. Its
  lax thresholds keep the store's gain (-0.2 of 9.3 points on 400 agent
  sessions) and cut the store's copied rows by 24%; #337 will use them. A
  correction: the store does add rows (+27%), contrary to what § 7.6 said.
- Ending a copied run where its earlier matches disagree (as SuffixDecoding
  stops a draft): 20% fewer copied rows at the same coverage. Filed as #338.

hits.message:
perf(split): stop a copied guess where earlier copies of the text disagree

When a model is split across computers, a reply that repeats earlier text
now sends about a quarter fewer wasted guesses, with the same number of
right ones. Replies are unchanged: a guess changes only what is checked.

The n-gram lookup copied the most recent occurrence's continuation whatever
the other occurrences did. `ngram_lookup::copied_run` now walks the matched
n-gram's last 32 occurrences together and ends the run once the leading
next token holds under 67% of those still following (`agreed_run`, the rule
SuffixDecoding stops a draft by). Offline on 400 SWE-agent sessions, capped
as the flow caps a run: 64.6% of reply tokens covered either way, copied
rows 3.29 -> 2.36 a reply token (-28%). Replayed through the Rust function
over 100 of them, the script's figures match to the digit on both rules.

One lookup serves the flow's copied runs, the rounds' n-gram guesses and a
single computer's own; the owner's earlier-reply store keeps its own vote,
where the cut saved nothing. A/B SWARMLLM_COPY_AGREEMENT=0. Closes #338.

hits.message:
fix(memory): a long Gemma conversation is kept for the next turn again

The prefix cache sized a saved prompt by its memory budget over what a
position weighs on every layer, but a sliding-window layer that has moved
on is saved only from where it now starts - and a saved prompt can never
stop short of where that window still answers. For a long Gemma prompt
the old figure fell short of that point and nothing was kept: Gemma 4 12B
on a processor kept no prompt past about 3,000 positions at the default
2 GiB, so every turn of an agent conversation re-read the whole prompt.

Each windowed layer is now charged the positions it really holds, which
is exactly what the copy takes. Measured on Gemma 2 2B with a 1,200 MB
budget: a 6,943-token prompt is kept whole (1,153 MB) and the next turn
answers in 36.8 s instead of 357.9 s, with the same reply as a cold run.

Closes FUTURE_WORK #281.

hits.message:
fix(api): a Qwen model's tool call reaches the client as a tool call, its arguments typed by the tool's schema

Qwen 3.5 and the Qwen models after it, and Qwen3-Coder, call a tool in an
XML form their own templates ask for:

  <tool_call>
  <function=get_weather>
  <parameter=city>
  Paris
  </parameter>
  </function>
  </tool_call>

The reply reader knew only JSON call bodies, so every such call came back
to the client as plain text with finish_reason "stop": an agent saw a
model that never used its tools.

The reader now reads that form as llama.cpp does
(common/parsers/qwen3-coder.cpp): each argument is typed by the tool's
schema (a number arrives as a number, text as text), and a bare
<function=NAME> counts only for a tool the request defined. To make that
possible, one value built from the definitions the prompt carried
(RequestTools) replaces the tools-requested flag on all four reply paths,
so no path can read a reply knowing tools were asked for but not what
they take. The OpenAI paths build it from the same list the prompt is
built from, so tool_choice "none" now reads the reply as text.

Checked on a real request, Qwen3.5-4B on the processor: v0.3.266 returned
the call as text; main returns tool_calls get_weather {"city":"Paris"}
with thinking off and on (reasoning kept separate), finish_reason
tool_calls when streamed, and a tool_use block on the Anthropic API.
With the new reader removed, nine of the new tests fail.

FUTURE_WORK #395.

hits.message:
fix: a model split between graphics card and processor no longer fails concurrent requests

When a model does not fit the card whole, its first layers go on the card
and the rest on the processor. A single request worked, but any burst of
requests arriving together - several chats, or an agent's parallel calls -
went down the batched path, which never brought the last layers' output
back to the card before the final norm: every request in the burst failed
with 'final_norm: device mismatch' (HTTP 500). Present in v0.3.209 and
earlier; found by the v0.3.210 gate, reproduced on v0.3.209 with the same
4-of-4 failure.

Both forward paths now go through one helper,
SplitModel::output_on_primary_device, and a repo-consistency guard fails the
build if either stops calling it (red with the batched call removed).

hits.message:
fix(api): Qwen2.5-Coder tool calls are read as tool calls, not returned as text

Qwen2.5-Coder-7B (Qwen's official upload, the copy the swarm uses since
v0.3.221) answers a tool request in the shape its own chat template shows
as an example, braces doubled: <{{"name": "get_time", "arguments": ...}}}}.
That came back to the client as reply text with no tool call, so agent
clients executed nothing. llama.cpp gives the identical reply on the
identical prompt, so it is the model's habit, not our prompt.

The parser now reads that one shape when it is the whole reply (an
optional "<" or <tool_call> before it, one call object, only closing
braces after), and the stray "<" is not returned as text. Prose that
merely contains doubled braces, or an echoed tool definition, is still
text.

Verified on the live node with a development build: OpenAI and Anthropic
endpoints, streamed and not, all return the call; v0.3.224 returned the
text on all four. The new test fails without the change. FUTURE_WORK #214.

hits.message:
fix(auto-manage): a model in constant use was unloaded as idle minutes after loading

Seen on the live node while an agent framework was using it: `Idle unload —
freed model … idle_secs=150432 threshold_secs=300`, logged five seconds after
a request completed, for a worker that had existed for 215 seconds. Every
request after that paid a cold model reload and lost the worker's prefix
cache — for an agent that means re-reading a 14k-token system prompt every
turn.

The idle check trusted `model_trust.last_request_at`. Nothing in the current
code writes that field — the comment saying the distributed executor does was
stale — so its value is whatever an older build persisted, here about two
days old, and the 2026-07-31 residency fallback only applied when there was
no history at all. The local split path, the common one, has never written
either history, so a model answering every few seconds looked idle after
`idle_unload_secs` of residency regardless.

The check now also reads the worker's own last-use time
(`ModelProcessPool::model_idle_secs`, from the `last_used` that
`register_response` stamps on every execution path), and residency is a hard
upper bound on the answer rather than a fallback: a model cannot have been
idle longer than it has been loaded. Two tests pin it; the stale-history one
fails against the old semantics. Lib test count 2218 → 2220. Gotcha #437.

hits.message:
docs(plan): what distance allows a split, and how the swarm gets as fast as local

A deep dive into whether a model split across the internet can decode as
fast as one machine. It cannot, without prediction: each token must reach
the far machine and come back before the next can start, which Petals
measured to the millisecond, and splitting beats one device only over
microsecond links (Groq, Cerebras). So the plan works per situation: run
MoE models with their experts in system RAM (30-45 tok/s on 8 GB cards),
make our card+processor path read memory at full speed, route agent
requests to peers already holding their prompt, hand CPU users' long
prompts to GPU peers, remove a protocol round trip we add to every split
token, and keep speculation for splits that cannot be avoided.

docs/plans/faster_than_local.md; FUTURE_WORK #135-#139. Test counts:
3025 lib, 182 repo-consistency (dev,claude-subscription).

hits.message:
perf(split): a split reply can copy from your own earlier replies, never showing a computer text it did not help write (#337)

When a model is split across computers and its guesses flow as a tree, a copied
run (text that appeared before) gives the guesses depth the small guessing model
does not pay for. It looked only in the current conversation. Where the
conversation has no match, it now also looks in the owner's earlier replies to
the same model (`inference::owner_replies`).

- Only the owner's: a request that presented this node's key directly
  (`InferenceRequest::requested_by`, required in `::local`, never read off the
  wire) and that this node runs for itself. A store's matches show in a reply's
  speed (REST's datastore leaked through it, arXiv 2411.01076), so nobody
  else's reply reads it or is kept in it.
- A computer in the split is never sent a copy of a reply it did not serve, and
  is sent token ids only from a reply it was sent as ids.
- Memory only, bounded (256K tokens and 4,096 replies a model, 4 models); never
  saved, shared or announced.
- llama.cpp's lax vote over the last 32 matches decides whether the earlier
  replies agree.

Offline, on 400 recorded SWE-agent sessions: a copy predicted 60% of the tokens
of a session's first three replies, against 28%, and 73.3% over whole sessions,
against 64.6%. A/B SWARMLLM_FLOW_COPY_STORE=0. Eight tests, each safeguard's
test red with that safeguard switched off. Security-reviewed.

hits.message:
fix(api): /v1/models lists the context this computer can actually hold

A model's listed context (max_model_len / context_length) came from its file
alone. On a 12 GB card Qwen3-14B was listed at 8,192 tokens while the card held
about 5,100, so a chat app or an agent sizing its conversations found the real
limit only from refused requests (field report #035, FUTURE_WORK #252).

While a model is loaded on this computer whole and no other connected computer
that may take part in its requests holds any of it (the model is kept on this
computer, private mode leaves nobody, or nobody else has it), the list now gives
the longest prompt plus reply this computer's memory accepts, never more than
the model declares. Where another computer could take the rest of a longer
prompt, or nothing is loaded yet, the declared figure stands.

The model process measures the figure from the same budget its admission check
uses and reports it in a new message, sent only to a daemon that reads it.

hits.message:
Long prompts read 20% faster on a computer without a graphics card

Once a conversation passed about 5,400 tokens, reading each further part of
a prompt on the processor took twice as long. Past that length the model's
attention step outgrew a memory budget, and the path it then fell back to
copied the model's memory of the conversation three times over on every
step. That copy was only needed to split the work up, and splitting it by
position instead needs no copy at all, with the same memory ceiling.

Measured on a Ryzen 7 5800H with Llama 3.2 3B, same program both ways: a
6,900-token prompt went from 33.2 to 39.8 tokens a second, and the time
spent in attention from 86 to 54 seconds. Agent programs send prompts of
4,000 to 14,000 tokens, so most of their prompt reading happens past this
point. The result is checked against the previous computation in a new
test, which also confirms the copy no longer happens.

Function-calling models that write their calls as a JSON array (xLAM, and

runs on this computer"): it said this computer answers the Mistral-7B

hits.message:
Your own prompts are read with all of your processor's cores

The contribution level decides how much of your computer SwarmLLM may use
to answer other people's requests, but it was also limiting your own: at the
default level, a prompt you sent to your own node was read on half of your
processor's cores, where tools like llama.cpp use all of them. That was most
of a reported "three times slower than llama.cpp" for agent programs, which
send prompts of several thousand words on every turn.

Your own prompts are now read on every physical core. Work your node does
for other people still stays within your contribution level, writing a
reply keeps the thread count measured to suit it, and a thread limit you
set yourself (max_cpu_threads) still applies to everything.

Measured on a Ryzen 7 5800H with Llama 3.2 3B, same program both ways:
a 2,400-token prompt went from 35.5 to 49.5 tokens a second (+39%), a
6,900-token one from 28.8 to 32.4. Long prompts gain less because of how
attention reads memory there, which is the next thing to improve
(docs/FUTURE_WORK.md item 119).

hits.message:
fix(routing): a conversation's next turn on the same peer is priced for what that peer already read

When this node hands a whole model to a peer, the peer keeps the prompt in its
prompt cache, so the conversation's next turn there only reads what is new.
The router still priced every turn as a full read of the prompt. On the live
swarm, a repeated 505-token prompt was priced at 20.2 s and the whole request
took 7.1 s. A price that wrong can send the next turn somewhere else, where it
really has to read the whole prompt again.

This node now remembers what it handed each peer, and credits the matching
opening of the next prompt on a whole-model run there. This is how SGLang's
cache-aware router and llm-d's approximate prefix scorer work.

What is remembered: the prompt's 64-token block chain. It is keyed with this
process's secret and never sent anywhere.

The credit is limited:
- A record lasts 300 s, the idle-unload time, and is dropped when a hand-off
  to that peer fails.
- It applies only to a request the hand-off will take. That check is now
  shared with the hand-off itself, so the price and the path cannot disagree.
- It applies only while the peer still holds the whole model.
- It is a price, never a pin: a faster or less loaded route still wins.

On the new split_rig.sh handoffcache rig, turn 2 of a 2,744-token agent
conversation is credited 2,688 tokens, and the peer's worker reports a cache
hit of 2,713. The turn is priced 7.8 s and takes 15.1 s, where v0.3.243 priced
it at 148.8 s for 14.8 s.

The old reason for crediting no peer, that the n-gram path ran before the
hand-off, had been out of date since 2026-09-27.

feat(integrations): an OpenClaw provider plugin — SwarmLLM in OpenClaw's setup wizard, every served model discovered

integrations/openclaw is a provider plugin for OpenClaw, built on the same
SDK helper as OpenClaw's bundled vLLM and SGLang providers, so it inherits
their onboarding wizard entry, non-interactive setup flags and live model
discovery. What a user gets over the config-only path documented earlier:
"SwarmLLM" in `openclaw onboard`, `openclaw models list --provider swarmllm`
listing every model the node can serve with its real context window (from
the `context_length` the node now reports), and a hint that names the key
and the model list when a `swarmllm/<model>` ref cannot be resolved.

Verified against the live node with OpenClaw 2026.8.2: install, onboard,
discovery of all nine models the node served, and an agent turn that reached
the node and streamed. Five vitest tests cover registration and wizard
wiring, and discovery against a real node's `/v1/models` body — including
that a model without `context_length` is assumed to have 128k, which is the
trap the field exists to close, and that OpenClaw's non-secret local markers
send no Authorization header at all, so a node's real key is required.

The same run measured what an agent framework asks of a node, recorded
honestly in the READMEs and docs/FUTURE_WORK.md: a fresh OpenClaw workspace's
first turn is 14,633 prompt tokens plus an 8192-token reply reservation (so
the 8192 default context refuses it, and 32768 is the documented override);
the KV cache for that prompt is 5 GB on a 3B model and fills an 8 GB card;
and a 30-tool streamed request decoded at 1.2-1.35 tok/s against ~8 tok/s
for the same prompt without tools, with nothing delivered until the model
stopped — two node-side items now written up for the next round.

Publishing to ClawHub (`clawhub package publish`) needs the project's
credentials and is the open step; until then the README shows the local
install. A path-filtered workflow runs the plugin's build, typecheck and
tests when it changes.

docs: how inference between nodes gets dramatically faster — ranked, with the physics

An ideation worker's survey, checked against the tree by hand: pipeline
chaining is already the default (and silently off for repetition penalties
and for boomerang); a stateless agent client re-ships its whole 14,633-token

full-vocabulary logits, which makes speculation net negative over a home
uplink until accept/reject moves to the tail; then ring decode, prefill
microbatching across segments, and feeding the ACK-RTT estimator into
routing. Physics table, citations and what was ruled out are in the entry.

fix: a thinking model's reasoning now streams as it is written instead of arriving in one block at the end

With stream: true, a reasoning model (Qwen3 and similar) sent nothing while it
thought, and a reply cut off inside its thinking (a small max_tokens) arrived as
one chunk of scratchpad when the stream ended. Field report: qwen3-1.7b sent 1
content chunk thinking against 50 with /no_think.

The OpenAI chat surface now streams the scratchpad as delta.reasoning_content,
the field llama.cpp's server and DeepSeek's API use, a chunk per token. A reply
that ends inside its thinking is reasoning, never the answer: streamed and
non-streamed alike, content is empty and reasoning_content holds it. Checked on
qwen3-1.7b: 55 reasoning chunks and no content at max_tokens 60; with room, 141
reasoning chunks then 79 answer chunks. The Anthropic surface is unchanged (its
thinking blocks exist only when a request enables thinking).

Two older defects in the same stream buffer, fixed with it:
- With tools requested, a brace inside the model's thinking held the whole
  answer back to the end of the stream — the tool-call search ran over the
  thinking too. Agentic clients always send tools.
- JSON a model sketched while thinking could come back as a tool call when
  streamed, and as plain text when not.

swarmllm bench --stream now counts reasoning deltas, so time-to-first-token is
measurable on a reasoning model.

chore(release): v0.3.154-alpha

Three fixes for problems the current testers are hitting, all found and
verified this week:

- A prompt longer than about 8,000 tokens could not be answered by more than
  one machine at all. The receiving machine refused the hidden state outright,
  on every model, silently, since March.
- A machine holding a whole model could not serve part of one it could not
  hold — the case splitting a model across machines exists for. Its own memory
  was the one thing the planner did not check, and the loader priced a whole
  model however little of it was being loaded.
- A reply arrived in one piece at the end whenever the request offered the
  model tools, which is every coding agent, every time. Measured: 1 chunk
  where there should have been 99.

Plus the storage-budget accounting fix and six smaller closures already on
main. Full detail in CHANGELOG.md.

hits.message:
docs: name the foreign peers correctly — openhydra, not IPFS

The nodes that were being wrongly adopted as swarm peers were described
as IPFS. They are not: they identify as openhydra/0.1.0 on rust-libp2p
0.45. That was inferred from their port (4001) and written down as fact.
4001 is the libp2p convention — every project that keeps the example
config lands there — so it identifies nobody.

Nothing in the fix depended on it: the check keys on whether a peer
advertises a SwarmLLM protocol, not on who the peer turns out to be, and
the test still uses an IPFS-shaped protocol list because the rule must
reject any foreign namespace rather than one particular project.

The rejection log line reports the peer's agent string, which is how the
real identity became known, and means the next one need not be guessed at.

hits.message:
docs: add a diagnosis discipline and an agent that enforces it

Three wrong claims about what caused what reached commits in a single session,
each corrected afterwards, and a fourth was caught on the edge. None were
careless — each had a plausible mechanism and supporting evidence, which is
exactly why a habit is not enough.

The shape was the same every time: a symptom attributed to the most recent
change, or the most obvious part, before establishing it does not happen without
that change.

Adds .claude/rules/diagnosis.md, drawn from what actually went wrong: get a
baseline before blaming, treat an absence as evidence only from a source that
would have shown it (ring buffers drop entries, debug lines are invisible at the
normal level), check a measurement is not taken while the system is still
settling after a restart, confirm the mechanism ran rather than only that the
outcome changed, and prove a test fails without its fix. Also records that
blaming a single cause is itself a known error when several factors contribute.

Adds .claude/agents/root-cause.md, which answers only whether a suspected cause
causes a symptom, and is forbidden from proposing fixes. It may not report
"caused" without having watched the symptom disappear when the suspect is
removed, and "undetermined" is an acceptable answer.

Verified rather than assumed: given one of the session's wrong claims with the
answer withheld, the method reached the correct verdict from its own reading of
the logs — and found a detail the original investigation missed, that the check
in question exited at its first condition and never influenced the request at
all.

hits.message:
docs: eighteen setup and troubleshooting instructions in the guide now match what the program does

Instructions that would have failed or misled:
- Claude Code: the command on the Anthropic API page had no access token,
  so every request was refused (the README version already had it).
- Config reference: leaving `max_seq_len_override` unset does not "use the
  GGUF value" — it serves the model's declared length capped at 8192. The
  row now says how to raise it for long agent prompts.
- Cross-node prefix sharing is OFF by default, but the performance page
  listed it with the default-on features and the benchmark recipe never
  turned it on, so its fetch could not fire. Both say so now.
- Logging: the default level is info (which already prints the
  `DIAG: request complete` line); `-v` is debug, not info.
- Tailscale page: the dashboard has no "Join Network" field (it is
  Computers → Connect a computer), and for a changed IP it told people to
  delete their database, which resets the access token and unlinks the
  device. A stale cached address only fails to dial and is replaced.
- Joining page: `private_mode_allow_lan` applies without a restart.
- Claude subscription: the build command was the contributor build (it
  serves the dashboard from the source folder); the release build needs
  `--features claude-subscription`, which official downloads leave out.
- README: the LAN test is under about 2.5 ms, not 5 ms; CONTRIBUTING lists
  the build per release variant, not every feature flag.

Descriptions corrected against the code: MCP protocol version 2025-11-25
(and the two resources the page left out), the update checker (it runs
unless started with --no-update-check, and re-reads the mode each time),
connection limits (3 per peer, total by contribution level), config
priority (seven named variables, not any SWARMLLM_ prefix), the first-token
deadline (120 s plus 0.5 s per prompt token, at most 600 s), activation
compression (on by default), and the "Find models" label.

hits.message:
build: pre-commit and pre-push checks finish in about half the time — one build setup instead of three, and the slowest check made 35x faster

No change to the program itself. This is how changes are checked before
they are published.

- One feature set for local checks. `cargo lint`, `cargo dev-test`,
  `cargo dev-build` and `cargo dev-run` (aliases in .cargo/config.toml)
  all use `--no-default-features --features dev,claude-subscription`.
  Measured on one edit followed by a commit and a push: ~140 s of
  compiling across three feature sets before, ~78 s now. The pre-push
  hook still lints default features, but only when the push touches code
  that only default features compile (the frontend crate's `embedded`
  paths, `cfg(not(feature = "claude-subscription"))` arms, Cargo.toml).
  CI lints both sets on every push, as before.
- `every_config_setting_is_read_somewhere` re-split every source file
  for every config field: 26 s of the suite's 27 s. Each file's words are
  now split once. 0.73 s, and it still fails on a planted dead setting.
  The whole repo-consistency suite runs in 2 s, at commit, at push and
  in CI.
- The per-edit `cargo check` hook is removed (~13 s and 1.8 GB after
  every Rust edit, on a feature set nothing else used). So is a hook that
  protected two specification files which no longer exist, and a Stop
  hook whose log nobody read. Its two checks are now real guards:
  `no_shared_state_path_names_a_sub_struct_twice` (wrapped chains
  included) and `the_frontend_leaves_no_debug_output_in_the_console`,
  each shown to fail on a planted violation.
- Agent teams are switched off (roughly 7x the tokens of a normal session).
- CLAUDE.md is back under its 200-line target. Per-release status moved
  to the notes that already carried it, and rules repeated across the
  always-loaded files are stated once. Test counts are now refreshed at
  release instead of in a separate commit after each change.

hits.message:
fix(providers): long cloud answers no longer stop after five minutes

A reply proxied from a cloud provider was cut off once the whole exchange
passed five minutes, even while it was still streaming normally — reachable
by a long agentic turn, or any model doing extended thinking.

The limit was written for how long a provider may take to START replying but
applied to the whole exchange. It now measures silence instead: a provider
that has stopped responding is given up on just as quickly, while one still
sending is left to finish.

hits.message:
R125: ease-of-use copy refresh for non-technical users

Audit by 3 parallel agents (first-run, day-to-day UX, error/recovery)
mapped where engineering jargon was leaking through to end users —
"shards", "VRAM", "manifest generation", "NetworkPopular", "Worker
started", "Fragile", "auth_error", percentage-of-CPU descriptions,
etc. Target audience is explicitly non-technical (MEMORY.md notes
"UX, copy, defaults, error messages must assume zero engineering
background"); the audit found ~40 user-facing strings that violated
this. R125 applies the bulk of the copy fixes plus two functional
gaps the agents surfaced.

# Functional fixes

* `frontend/js/core/utils.js::extractErrorMessage` — backend errors
  carry an `error.hint` field built by `src/error.rs::error_hint`,
  designed specifically to tell non-technical users what to do when
  something goes wrong. The frontend was extracting only
  `error.message` and silently discarding the hint, making the
  carefully-written recovery directions invisible. Now appends
  ` — <hint>` to the displayed message when present.
* `frontend/js/components/notifications.js` — provider health badge
  tooltips were rendering raw backend status strings ("auth_error",
  "rate_limited") instead of the i18n labels already used elsewhere.
  Added `_statusLabel(status)` helper; bar item + card badge titles
  now go through it. Also adds `provider.up: "Healthy"` for the
  always-OK case (was unmapped before, leaked the literal `up`).

# Copy fixes — i18n/en.json (39 keys)

Replace "shards" with "model parts" / "parts" everywhere user-facing:
* `setup.auto_download_label`, `setup.auto_download_desc`,
  `settings.auto_on`, `dashboard.info_shards`, `dl.shards_progress`,
  `pool.stats_shards`, `pool.disk_usage`,
  `settings.contribution_mode_hint_auto`

Drop cryptic abbreviations:
* `dashboard.info_arch` "Arch" → "AI type"
* `dashboard.info_quant` "Quant" → "Quality"
* `dl.source_hf` "HF" → "HuggingFace"
* `dashboard.tick_mod` "Mod" → "Moderate"
* `dashboard.health_fragile` "Fragile" → "At risk"
* `dashboard.cb_fragile{,_tip}` rewritten with what-to-do context

Activity feed jargon → plain English (high-visibility — these toast
on every event):
* `activity.model_promoted` drops literal Rust variant "NetworkPopular"
* `activity.vram_soft_unload` drops "VRAM pressure" + "shards"
* `activity.shard_verification_failed` adds auto-recovery context
* `activity.shard_finalize_failed` drops "finalize"
* `activity.shard_p2p_exhausted` drops "peers served shard"
* `activity.manifest_gen_failed` drops "Manifest generation"
* `activity.worker_spawned/unloaded` drop "Worker started/stopped"
* `activity.rebalance_peer_left` drops "Rebalancing"
* `activity.none{,_network}` empty states now reassure rather than
  look broken

Setup wizard plain-language pass:
* `setup.step2_title` "Get Online" → "Connect to Other Users"
* `setup.contrib_{minimal,moderate,maximum}_desc` drop %CPU/%storage
  numbers in favour of observable consequences ("barely noticeable" /
  "still feel fast during normal use" / "ideal if running overnight")
* `setup.hw_limited_vram` drops "VRAM" → "No dedicated GPU"

Settings panel:
* `settings.swarm_compute_memory{,_tip}` drops "GPU VRAM" jargon
* `settings.contribution_mode_hint_auto` plain-language rewrite
* `dashboard.credits_header_tip` drops the self-defeating "credits
  are an internal accounting signal — not enforced for inference
  yet" — replaced with a forward-looking framing

Wishlist + capacity:
* `swarm.tab_capacity` "Capacity plan" → "What we could run"
* `swarm.wishlist_intro` rewritten as user-centric explanation
* `wishlist.status.aspirational` "In progress" → "Being downloaded"
* `wishlist.status.blocked` "Held back" → "Needs review"
* `wishlist.status.unreachable` "Out of reach" → "Too large for this
  swarm"

Empty / failure states:
* `dl.state_failed` adds where-to-look-for-details guidance
* `browse.trending_empty` redirects to search instead of "check back"

# i18n propagation — 20 locales × 41 keys

Two translator-agent passes covered the value updates across all
non-English locales (es, fr, de, pt, it, nl, ru, zh, ja, ko, ar,
tr, pl, sv, th, hi, vi, id, uk, cs). Idiomatic translations per
locale, matching the new plain-language tone (not literal). All 21
locales end at 1133 entries (1131 keys + `_lang` + `_dir`); files
re-sorted; native scripts preserved. `_statusLabel` lookup uses
existing per-locale `provider.*` keys; `provider.up` translated
in each locale (Operativo / Opérationnel / 正常稼働中 / 正常 / etc.).

# README

* "Who it's for" now leads with "Anyone who wants to chat with AI
  without paying subscription fees or sharing data with a cloud
  service" before the developer / researcher / pool-operator
  personas. The agent flagged this as the entry-point persona for
  the stated target audience.

# Build / tests

913 lib tests pass; clippy clean default + dev features. No
behaviour changes on the inference path — frontend copy refresh
plus two frontend-side recovery-affordance fixes.

# Bigger UX items NOT addressed here (surfaced for decision)

The agents also flagged structural changes that need explicit
direction:
* README architecture-section reorganization (collapse subsystem
  table + "12 Tokio tasks" sentence behind `<details>` so the lay
  user doesn't have to skip past it)
* Header overload (12+ icons unexplained on first load — would
  benefit from a first-run guided tour or `?` tooltips)
* `worker_spawned` / `worker_unloaded` duplicate `model_loaded` /
  `model_unloaded` — pick one path for the activity feed
* `models.hf_score_breakdown` exposes fit/quality/demand/size
  decomposition — should be a single human verdict
* `models.encrypted_pipeline` / `models.meta_*` GGUF metadata —
  belongs under an "Advanced" sub-section
* `dashboard.api_log_link` — link text stayed English in 20 locales
  by convention; intentional or oversight?

These are tracked in `docs/FUTURE_WORK.md` for the next pass.

hits.message:
fix(tools): a model that wraps its tool call in a list is no longer ignored

An agentic client asked a distributed model to write a file and run it. The
model produced two correct tool calls and the client executed neither: they came
back as ordinary message text with a normal stop reason, so nothing ran and
nothing reported an error — the silent failure this parser exists to prevent.

The cause is on our side, not the model's. We tell models to answer with
{"tool_calls": [...]}, and this one answered with exactly that inside a
one-element list. The parser accepted the object and the bare entry but not the
list, so a model that did what it was asked was ignored.

Also accepts a bare list of entries with the wrapper dropped, for the same
reason the single-entry case was already accepted. Nothing else is swept up: an
entry only counts if it carries a name, so an array of ordinary JSON still
parses as ordinary text, which is pinned by its own test.

Reported from the field and reproduced here on qwen2.5-14b-instruct. The same
client and chat template work with qwen2.5-coder-7b, so it is a per-model habit
rather than anything about how we prompt.

hits.message:
fix(streaming): streamed replies no longer stop dead at 65 tokens

A streamed reply from a GPU build running a whole model file (`-m`) stopped
after about 65 tokens and reported `finish_reason: "stop"`, as though the model
had finished its answer. It was cut mid-sentence. The same request without
streaming ran to completion, so anything driving the daemon the normal way — a
chat client, an agent — got a truncated answer with nothing in the response to
say so.

Two faults in series. The in-process generation loop runs to the end without
pausing, and it was started on a thread the async runtime needed in order to
deliver tokens to the client — so nothing was delivered at all until generation
had finished. The buffer it fills holds 64 tokens; once full, the code that
hands over each token could not tell "the reader is a little behind" from "the
reader has gone away", and stopped generating. Hence 65, every time, whatever
the model or the hardware.

Generation now runs where blocking is expected, so tokens reach the client as
they are produced, and a full buffer waits for room instead of ending the reply.
The same applies to the event that carries `finish_reason`: dropping it made the
encoder repeat the entire answer as one chunk.

Measured on a 0.5B model, one node, same prompt: 65 tokens in 121 s before, 390
tokens arriving about 20 ms apart after — matching what the non-streaming path
produces for the same request. Distributed inference across peers was never
affected and is unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

hits.message:
test(release): the pre-release check now catches what it was written for

The long-prompt cold check passed throughout v0.3.128 while a cold request with
a long prompt was answering with a single token. Two reasons, both fixed here.

Its prompt was about 1400 tokens. The fault it was meant to catch scaled with
prompt length — a short prompt still read correctly — so the check was below
the threshold at which anything goes wrong. It is now the size an agentic
client actually sends, and sized deliberately: large enough to break, small
enough to stay inside the shipped context default, because a refused request
would fail the check for the wrong reason.

And it asserted only that the reply was longer than three tokens. The same
fault also produces one token repeated to the limit, which passes that
comfortably — confirmed by running it: on the release carrying the bug the
reply-length check passes and the new one fails. The number of tokens in a
prompt is a property of the prompt, so the node must report the same figure
whether or not the model happened to be loaded. It reported 6159 cold against
5101 warm, and that disagreement is the fault itself rather than a symptom.

Verified in both directions on real nodes: fails on the release that has the
bug, passes on a build that does not.

hits.message:
chore(release): v0.3.173-alpha

Streamed replies no longer stop dead after about 65 tokens. On a graphics build
running a whole model file, every streamed answer was cut off mid-sentence and
reported as though the model had finished normally, so a chat client or an agent
received a truncated answer with nothing in it to say anything was missing. The
same question asked without streaming answered in full, which is why it went
unnoticed: most testing is done that way and most real clients stream. Generation
was running on a thread the program needed in order to send tokens out, and the
queue it filled in the meantime holds 64 items, after which the code handing
tokens over could not tell a reader that was slightly behind from one that had
gone away. Measured on one machine with the same question: 65 words in two
minutes before, the full answer in two and a half seconds after. Inference spread
across several machines was never affected.

Phi-4-mini can be served at all. Every request to it failed before producing a
single word, as did every request to any other model that rotates only part of
each attention head — GLM-4 and Qwen 3.5 are in that group and were equally
unusable, which nobody had noticed because no such model had been run here. The
cause recorded when this was first reported was wrong and is corrected in the
notes.

Gemma models are told about their tools in their own prompt format. A Gemma-2
request carrying tools was never rendered with the format that ships inside the
model; it quietly fell back to a generic one, and so did any Gemma or Mistral
request carrying a system message. Those models reject a system message outright
rather than ignoring it, and a tool description is delivered as one.

hits.message:
fix(network): a large prompt forwarded to a distant machine is not abandoned before it can have arrived

The receipt deadline for a tensor forward was derived from round-trip time
alone. An acknowledgement is sent when the whole message has arrived, so a
20 MB prompt-pass forward to a peer 625 ms away got the same ten-second floor
as a two-kilobyte decode step, and the coordinator gave up on it with the
transfer still in flight. Measured on the live swarm today on an 8,111-token
prompt: the request failed with "failover exhausted" after the standby was
abandoned that way. At agent-sized prompts a hop is tens of megabytes, so
every such forward over a home uplink was failed by construction.

The deadline now adds the time the payload takes at a slow home uplink
(1 MiB/s, rounded down so decode steps add nothing), capped at the protocol's
own timeout. And forwards larger than 256 KiB no longer feed the per-peer
acknowledgement-latency estimator, which routing reads: a transfer-dominated
sample measures the payload, not the peer, and would have priced the machine
as slow for every decode step after one prompt.

The first half of the same failure — a single QUIC stream carrying a
multi-megabyte forward being closed by the receiver's QUIC stack after too
many out-of-order fragments — is recorded in FUTURE_WORK with the evidence
and the two mitigations (chunked forwards behind a feature bit, or ranking
TCP above QUIC for large payloads). Gotcha #446.

Also documents seeing and retiring a stuck worker in the troubleshooting
guide.

hits.message:
docs: a request carrying tools gets no streaming, and what the single-token hunt ruled out

Two findings from chasing an external report, neither of which is the
reported bug.

A request that sends `tools` receives one content delta at the end
instead of a stream. Measured on llama-3.2-3b with an identical prompt:
40 deltas without tools, 1 with. Every token is buffered because a local
model can only express a tool call as text and the parser needs the whole
reply to recognise one. So every agentic client gets a working request
that does not stream, which is the one thing it asked for.

Deliberately not patched here, because the obvious guard is wrong: the
parser supports a tool call embedded after prose, and the non-streaming
path discards that prose when it finds one. Streaming it first would make
the two surfaces disagree about the same reply. The options and their
costs are written down; the honest one changes what a tool-calling reply
looks like, which deserves a decision rather than a patch.

Also records the single-token investigation. Five hypotheses were
falsified by measurement, including by downloading the reporter's exact
model onto an isolated node and driving it with their exact request shape
eight times without a failure.

What could not be replicated is their topology: their node is one of two,
and an earlier report says the scheduler routes work to the second. Every
reproduction here ran on one isolated node, so the remote-serving path was
never exercised. Model, request body and version were all asked for and
none discriminated; one response header would have.

network/manager/mod.rs subnet anti-gaming RFC check:
  Identify handler had a hand-rolled inline RFC 1918/loopback check

  is_non_public_ipv4_bytes(&[u8; 4]) helper (byte-array sibling to

  swap(0) → flush → fetch_add(pending) on failure had a race: a
  concurrent earn_inference between swap and fetch_add caused
  double-counting (the earn lands on the now-zeroed field, then
  fetch_add adds the original  on top). Switched to
  compare_exchange so the clean-restore path only fires when no
  concurrent earn happened; on contention we fall back to fetch_add
  with a logged warning. Trade-off: rare overcount under contention
  beats losing user credits to the floor.

hits.message:
fix(diagnostics): say when a caller's stop sequence ended a reply early

A reply that comes back with one token and `finish_reason: "stop"` looks
exactly like a model with nothing to say. The OpenAI schema has no field
for which stop sequence fired, so the client cannot tell the difference —
and the node, which knew, said nothing either.

An external tester hit exactly that shape against a coding agent and
spent a testing session narrowing it, with plain curl unable to
reproduce. Reproduced here in one request: a `stop` value matching the
model's second token gives `completion_tokens: 1, finish_reason: "stop"`,
silently. Nodes now warn, naming the stop sequence and the token count,
when a stop match leaves the caller with two tokens or fewer. An ordinary
stop trimming the tail of a real answer stays at debug — warning about
that would train operators to ignore the warning.

Whether this is what the tester hit is NOT established; their client's
`stop` array is the missing piece, and the reproduction attempts left it
out. What is established is that the product could not have told them.

Wired at the three places a generation finishes carrying a matched stop:
the local worker, the whole-model remote path, and the coordinator that
assembles from remote segments.

It deliberately does NOT live in `finalize_reply_text`, which looks like
the right choke point — all four reply sources funnel through it — and is
not. Every generator applies the caller's stop sequences during
generation and breaks before keeping the matching text, so by
finalisation the text no longer contains the stop and there is nothing
left to notice. That version was written, and silently never fired; the
end-to-end check caught it, the diff would not have.

hits.message:
R121: auto-manage scale-back at swarm saturation

Auto-manage learned to scale a node's contribution DOWN, not just up.
At swarm scale (1000s of nodes) a popular model is held by far more
peers than the geo-aware target needs — an idle node's shards become
redundant and just waste VRAM. This change lets auto-manage shed those
shards voluntarily, without waiting for VRAM/disk pressure to build.

Driven by audit synthesis from four parallel exploration agents:

  1. scoring/prune (model/auto_manage/scoring.rs + prune.rs) only
     scales target replicas UP with demand (1.0×–3.0×); no abundance
     factor; prune gate requires local resource pressure to fire.
  2. SwarmCapacity (state.events.swarm_capacity) is collected on peer
     connect/disconnect but never consumed by auto-manage.
  3. ContributionMode is startup-frozen — PUT /api/admin/config writes
     disk but does not hot-reload into the auto-manage loop.
  4. max_gpu_vram_mb exists in [resources] config but is not exposed
     via ConfigUpdate — users must edit TOML + restart.

# Backend

* `NodeConfig.contribution_auto: bool` (default `true`). Auto mode
  lets auto-manage scale contribution up AND down within the user-set
  `[node].contribution` cap and `[resources]` caps. Manual mode pins
  contribution at the user-set level — pre-R121 behaviour.
* `model/auto_manage/prune.rs::effective_prune_target(target, pressure,
  holder_count, contribution_auto, min_replicas)` — pure helper. When
  `contribution_auto` AND `holder_count >= 1.5×target`, returns
  `target.max(min_replicas)` (bypasses the RELAXED-state +1 nudge from
  `pressure_adjusted_target`). Otherwise falls through. 4 unit tests
  cover boundary + extreme-saturation + min-replicas-floor cases.
* `prune.rs::evaluate_and_prune` loop body uses `effective_prune_target`
  per shard; adds +1.0 prune-score bonus when `holder_count >= 2×target`
  (severe saturation) to break selection ties. All existing guards
  intact: active-pipeline, pinned/locked, configured-range, would-
  eliminate-region, can-reacquire, recently-acquired, encrypted-pipeline.
* `state.models.contribution_auto: AtomicBool` — runtime mirror so PUT
  takes effect on the next prune tick without a daemon restart.
  `state.config` is startup-frozen, so the atomic is the only runtime
  source of truth for the toggle; documented as a SharedState invariant
  in `.claude/rules/architecture.md`.
* `OperationalParams` gains `contribution`, `contribution_auto`,
  `max_gpu_vram_mb` (broadcast on hot-reload for completeness).
* `ContributionMode` now derives `PartialEq + Eq` so `OperationalParams`
  can hot-compare across reloads.

# API

* `ConfigUpdate` and `GET /api/admin/config` gain `contribution_auto:
  bool` and `max_gpu_vram_mb: u64`. PUT clamps VRAM at 1 TiB so a UI
  typo can't disable VRAM accounting entirely.
* PUT also mirrors `contribution_auto` to the atomic.

# Frontend

* Auto/Manual segmented toggle in Settings panel above the existing
  contribution control. In Auto mode the "Contribution Level" label
  flips to "Upper Cap" and the hint explains the scale-back semantics.
  Wired via `App.settings._applyContributionMode(modeAuto)`. Save
  payload extended with `contribution_auto`.
* New i18n keys: `settings.contribution_label_cap`, `settings.
  contribution_mode_{auto,manual,auto_sub,manual_sub,label,hint_auto,
  hint_manual}` (8 keys total) — idiomatic translations in all 21
  locales via translator-agent pass. 1130 keys / 1132 entries per
  locale.

# Browser-verified

Manual smoke through the dev frontend: GET returns both new fields,
PUT round-trips, toggle relabels correctly between Auto/Manual,
backend atomic updates on save.

# Tests / lint

913 lib tests passing (+4 for the new effective_prune_target tests).
Clippy clean default + `--features dev,claude-subscription`.

# Deferred

* Setup wizard toggle exposure (additive; backend default is Auto).
* True global holder count for `redundancy_ratio` — at realistic
  targets (<25 replicas) the 50-cap on `shard_holders` doesn't break
  the gate, only underestimates the displayed ratio. Both items
  captured in `docs/FUTURE_WORK.md`.

hits.message:
perf(chat): do not price a model to answer a question that cannot depend on it

The chat privacy banner asks whether a request would actually be answered by
this machine. Answering that involves working out whether the model fits the
graphics card, which reads the model's header off disk — fine once per
request, not fine once per model in a list.

The rule it feeds only consults that figure when this node has other machines
to hand work to and is not already shedding load. Those two are cheap to
check, so they are now checked first and the expensive one is skipped when it
cannot change the answer. A truth table over all eight combinations pins that
the short form and the full form agree.

hits.message:
perf: generating after a long prompt was ~10x slower per token than after a short one

On a GQA model, decode attention used the standard path below a 2048-token
crossover. That path expands the key/value cache to the full head count on every
token of every layer, so its cost grows with the conversation. Profiled on
llama-3.2-3b Q4_K_M it reached 91% of decode time at ~1150 tokens of context.

Measured, milliseconds per generated token, standard -> fused:
  kv ~82     141.2 -> 129.2   (attention   16.8 ->  14.7)
  kv ~1150  1368.1 -> 249.2   (attention 1242   -> 136 )   5.5x

Fused wins at both ends, so grouped-query decode now always takes it. The old
crossover came from models with higher expansion ratios than this one, and the
expansion is exactly what makes the standard path expensive, so they should
benefit at least as much -- 24/8 is the least favourable grouped-query shape and
it already wins at 82 tokens.

Multi-head models are unaffected and keep the standard path, where the expansion
is a no-op and the transposes would be pure overhead.

hits.message:
fix(models): automatic downloads pause on a metered connection

A new computer left on a phone's USB tether downloaded 1.4 GB of model
parts in five minutes, and 9 GB in its first 44 minutes, with nothing
asked of it but the default "help the network" (field report
2026-10-15). Nothing asked what the connection cost.

Downloads the computer starts on its own now wait while the system says
the connection is metered, and resume when it no longer is:

- Linux: NetworkManager's own answer (a phone's hotspot is guessed
  metered, and counts).
- Windows, and Linux under WSL2: the internet connection's cost
  (charged, roaming or over its data limit).
- macOS cannot tell yet; Settings offers "Always pause" for it.

It is asked just before such a download starts, by both places that
start one: the regular download pass and the replacement of copies when
another computer leaves. A guard in the repository's consistency checks
keeps a new one from skipping it. Models you download yourself, the
repair of parts already held, and transfers already running are not
paused. The dashboard says so once when downloads pause and once when
they resume, and the diagnostics report shows what the system said.

Settings → "On a metered connection": follow the system (default),
always pause, or never pause (`auto_manage.on_metered_connection`).
Seven new strings in all 21 languages. Checked on native Windows.

hits.message:
perf(routing): a small piece of work on a slow machine is no longer priced as small

When a model is split across machines, the router decides who gets which layers
by estimating what each one costs. That estimate assumed a machine given half as
many layers costs half as much — so the cheapest way to include a slow machine
looked like giving it a couple of layers.

Measured on the live swarm, that is badly wrong. One machine given 2 layers of
32 took the whole reply from 152 milliseconds a word to 3768: the other 30
layers together cost less than those 2. Most of what a visit to a machine costs
is paid before any layer is computed, and the old estimate had nowhere to put it.

Each machine's cost is now learned as two numbers — what a visit costs, and what
each layer adds — fitted from the timings already being collected. A narrow
segment on an expensive machine is priced at what it really costs, so the router
stops reaching for it.

This also fixes a second problem with the same root: the deadline for a segment
was sized the same way, so a small piece of work on a slow machine was given a
correspondingly small budget and abandoned before it could have answered.

Two things it deliberately does not do. It never guesses the fixed cost from
network round-trip time — on this swarm a machine a second away is five times
faster than one two-thirds of a second away, so ping says nothing about it. And
where a machine has only ever been given one size of work the two numbers cannot
be told apart, so it is priced exactly as before; that is most machines today.

Not yet confirmed on a live multi-node run. The figure is on the peer list and
in the routing log so the first real occurrence can be read rather than assumed.

Each node times its own model loads and the planner charges a computer
that must first load a model at that measured speed. The figure lived
only in memory, so after every restart, and so on every node after each
release's automatic update, the first request was priced as if this
node loaded at 10 s per GiB. On this project's own split traffic

stored and restored at startup, and the next timed load updates it as

perf(split): a chain that starts and finishes here guesses past the other computer's layers

With "Start and finish on this computer" on, a split model runs its first
and last layers here and its middle on another computer, so every word cost
a round trip. This node now guesses the next few words on its own: it runs
its two ends with the other computer's layers skipped, bridging the gap
with a small stand-in its model worker learns from the hidden states that
already pass through it (what it sends out and what comes back, at every
position the reply kept). The other computer then checks the guesses in
one trip. Nothing more is downloaded, no far-layer weights are needed, and
nothing new goes over the wire.

ends (layers 0-12 and 35-48) on an 8 GB laptop card, the middle (12-35) on
a processor-only node, one binary, alternating arms. Decode 1.34-1.48x with
50 ms added to the other node's sends, 1.08-1.20x with none; 33-55% of the
guesses kept. Replies part from writing one word at a time only at
near-ties, checked against llama.cpp (worst rank 2-3, gap under half a
logit, as the control's own reply).

The guess runs on the request's own caches and cuts both back; a request
that learns one is never batched (batching would skip the capture); its
reply joins the model's stand-in prior. The rig's prompt-file mode now
