hits.message:
feat(privacy): tell people what keeping their prompt private is costing them

Someone measured a reply taking 74 seconds with prompt privacy on and 12
with it off. The two steps kept on their own machine are a thirty-sixth of
the model and were 55 of those 74 seconds: reading a long prompt is slow on
a processor, and those two steps are where it happens.

Privacy is on by default for a machine that holds both ends, so nobody
chose that trade and nothing on screen explained the wait. The node now says
so, in plain words, when it is material — how many seconds it is adding,
why the ends stay home, and where to turn it off for that model. Once every
ten minutes per model, since the same decision is taken on every request.

We considered simply dropping the guarantee automatically when it gets
expensive, and rejected it. Every comparable system that has faced this
either refuses to downgrade silently or is criticised for doing so: the TLS
standard added a whole mechanism because browsers downgraded on a failed
handshake and a passing network glitch could trigger it; Chrome warns before
falling back to an insecure connection; Apple tells you when a network has
switched Private Relay off. The one that falls back quietly is faulted
precisely for the quiet.

The deciding argument is sharper than any of those, though. The trigger
would be "this is slow", and the prize for triggering it is the user's
prompt in the clear — which is the exact thing being protected. A machine
that wanted to read people's prompts would only have to answer slowly.

So the figure is shown and nothing acts on it.

hits.message:
fix(routing): stop handing a long prompt to a machine that is slow at reading it

A node deciding whether to hand a whole model to a peer compared machines on
how fast they write words. Reading the prompt is a different kind of work —
it is limited by raw computation rather than memory speed, and the spread
between machines on it is roughly nine times wider. On a long prompt that
reading is nearly all of the wait, so the comparison was made on the wrong
thing entirely.

Measured by someone running two nodes: an Apple M4 advertising the best
speed on their network was handed two prompts of about eleven thousand words
and took five to six minutes before the first word came back, twice. The
routing search had already priced that same machine as far and away the
worst choice for reading a prompt, and had avoided it — but the hand-off
decision never looked at a price at all. Their own guess, that the two paths
were not sharing a cost model, was exactly right.

They now share one: the hand-off asks the same pricing function the search
uses, over the prompt in hand, and declines a machine that comes out worse
than doing the work here. Not knowing still never excludes — a machine
nobody has measured is still tried, since refusing on missing information
would leave a node grinding away beside one that may well be faster. The
first request is what produces the measurement that stops the second, which
is why the same machine was picked twice.

The decision also logs both prices now, so the choice can be checked rather
than guessed at.

Separately recorded, and needing a decision rather than a fix: the same
report shows privacy-by-default costing six times the total time on a long
prompt, because the two layers kept at home are the expensive ones to read.
That trade is real and is not ours to make silently.

hits.message:
fix(scheduler): price a whole model on one peer as the delegation it is

A peer that runs every layer is handed the request in one message and streams
tokens back. A peer that runs half the layers is re-entered by the coordinator
after every token. Those cost wildly different things, and the router was
pricing both from the same measurement.

The consequence ran one way: delegating to a single peer looked far more
expensive than it is, so the router kept preferring to split. A figure measured
on a six-layer mid-chain segment carries the coordinator's round trip amortised
over six layers; reusing it for a sixteen-layer delegation charges that round
trip about 2.7 times over for a trip the delegation never makes. Measured
earlier at 11.2s delegated against 17.8s split, with the router choosing the
17.8s route.

The delegated coefficient to price it with has existed since 2026-08-18 and had
no reader at all — one production writer, and nothing that could consult it. So
a node could time a peer running a whole model, store the result, and never let
it affect a decision. It is consulted now.

Where no delegated sample exists yet the mid-chain figure still stands in, and
that is deliberate. It is an honest upper bound: it contains everything the
delegated cost contains plus a round trip, so a peer it calls slow really is
slow. Discarding it was tried and is worse — a peer measured at 107 ms/layer got
re-priced at the unknown-candidate prior of 25, so a node we had measured and
found slow outranked one we knew nothing about. That is the failure the prior
was raised from zero to prevent, arriving through a different door, and four
existing tests caught it. The overcharge is bounded and self-correcting: one
delegated request replaces it with the right-shaped number.

Reading the predicate turned up a second mis-pricing. A segment was charged
per-token network only when it did not start at layer zero, which let a remote
first segment of a split pay its network once. The coordinator drives every hop,
so after sampling a token it hands that token back to segment zero — a remote
first segment pays the round trip exactly as a mid-chain one does. Splitting was
being quietly subsidised, with the model unable to see most of the cost of the
boundary it was choosing.

Three tests, each verified red without the fix. One existing test asserted the
old first-segment behaviour; its subject was the delegated-versus-mid-chain
asymmetry, which is unchanged, so it now makes that comparison against an actual
delegation.

hits.message:
perf(inference): 15-30% faster text generation on NVIDIA GPUs

Generating a reply on a GPU node now runs 15-30% faster, with identical
output. Smaller models gain most: a 1.1B model went 55.7 -> 72.5 tok/s and a
3B went 49.6 -> 57.1, measured A/B/A/B inside one binary at temperature 0,
with byte-identical replies in every arm and against the v0.3.197 release.

The cause was not the graphics card. A decoded token was spending most of its
time asking the driver to do things rather than waiting for them to be done:
1,085 separate GPU submissions per token, 17.6 of 23.0 ms inside the driver
API on a single saturated CPU thread, while the card itself sat idle about
half the time. Cost per layer was flat across a 3.3x span of model size --
which a bandwidth-bound decode cannot be -- so layer count, not model size,
was predicting how long a token took.

A third of those submissions were zero-filling buffers that the very next
operation overwrote in full. Those fills are now skipped, removing 321 of
them per token (992 -> 672 submissions, with launches, allocations and event
counts unchanged between arms). The kernels that fill each buffer were read
first to confirm every element it owns is assigned rather than accumulated
into; the one buffer whose kernel was not verified is deliberately still
zeroed, as are the padded weight buffers whose padding no kernel writes.

SWARMLLM_ZERO_QMATMUL_BUFFERS=1 restores the old behaviour, so the change can
be A/B'd inside a single binary rather than across two builds.

Measured on one machine (WSL2), where a GPU submission costs roughly 2-3x
what it does on native Linux: the direction holds anywhere, the magnitude is
that box's. Expect the gain to shrink as models grow, since bandwidth is a
larger share of a bigger model's token.

Also adds the two probes that found this -- examples/decode_bound_by.py (is
decode bound by the GPU or by one CPU thread) and examples/decode_submissions.sh
(GPU submissions per token) -- and corrects docs/plans/regional_pipelines.md,
whose cost model had treated that per-token time as arithmetic that a split
merely relocates.

hits.message:
perf: guessing ahead across computers now works at the temperatures chats actually use

When a split reply guesses several tokens ahead and the far computer checks
them, a guess used to be accepted only when the far computer's own random
draw happened to land on it - so at temperature 0.7 or 1.0, where most chat
clients sit, guessing paid off much less than at 0. Both computers now draw
from the same shared random stream for that request (a new capability,
offered only to computers that understand it), so a guesser close to the
real model reproduces the real model's draw. Each computer still draws an
exact sample of its own model's choices, so replies are exactly as random as
before.

Measured on a two-computer test rig with a 3-bit copy of the far layers as
the guesser, temperature 0.7: 80.6% of guesses kept against 70.0%, 4.11
tokens per network round trip against 3.71 (one token per trip without
guessing). Guessing from repeated phrases is skipped while the shared
stream is in use - it cannot reproduce a random draw, and trying it first
cost the rig 16%.

The test rig can now ask at a chosen temperature (RIG_TEMPERATURE).

hits.message:
perf: a model split across computers answers 15-20% faster — its guesses are checked as a stream

When a model is split across computers and the first one guesses ahead with a
small model, each batch of guesses used to wait a full round trip for the far
computer's verdict before the next batch could even be guessed. Now the next
batch is guessed, run through the first computer's layers and sent while the
last one is still being checked. Each batch carries one guess past what it
checks; when the far computer agrees with everything, the batch already on its
way was built on the right text. When it disagrees, the batches built on the
refused guess are dropped, and the far computer skips any it has not started.

Measured on one machine with the far half on the processor and a 24 ms round
trip between the halves (7B model, 0.5B guesser): 14.5-17.4 tokens/s against
13.6-14.3 for the old round-by-round checks. Replies score against llama.cpp
exactly as the round-by-round ones and plain local decoding do.

Used only between two computers that both run this version; anything else
keeps the old rounds. SWARMLLM_SPEC_STREAM=0 turns it off. A test setup that
runs both halves on the SAME graphics card reads it about 15% slower, because
the two halves then compete for one card - that setup measures its cost, not
the gain a split across machines gets.

A retried request can no longer confuse its answers with the failed attempt's:
each attempt's stream is numbered apart from the last one's.

hits.message:
perf(split): the card clock hold pauses while another of our model processes works on the card (#489)

The clock hold keeps a split's card from slowing down between forwards. It
helped the 27B split, but cost about 10% on the 14B split, where the drafter
model runs as a second process on the same card. The card time-slices
between processes, so filler work in one delayed the other's real steps.
That is why the hold has been off by default.

whether another of its card workers has work in flight, and the hold
pauses while it does. A drafter model never holds; its target holds the
card for both. The hold is still off unless SWARMLLM_CARD_CLOCK_HOLD=1,
and is measured on both split shapes before it can be turned on by default.

hits.message:
perf(gpu): switching between two models that don't both fit is 3.4x faster

The daemon waited a full minute before letting a model take the graphics card
from another, on the reasoning that two models would otherwise keep evicting
each other. Measured, that wait cost far more than it saved: two models
alternating in conversation on one card took 299 seconds with it and 82 without,
because the model left on the processor was slower at every turn than the reload
it was being spared. What actually happened in practice was that one model kept
the card for the whole conversation and the other never got it at all.

The wait is now five seconds, which is what an idle-time rule can honestly claim
— don't take the card from a model someone is still actively using. A model
asked something every few seconds keeps it; one that has gone quiet for the
length of a turn gives it up.

Two things the measurement contradicted, both of them our own prior reasoning.
That discarding a model's cached prompt prefixes on eviction would make swapping
lose in conversation: it does not, because a reload plus re-prefill on the card
is cheaper than any turn on the processor. And that this kind of wait prevents
thrashing: under alternation the model holding the card has always just been
used, so the rule is either never in force or always in force, and never
anything in between.

Costing the swap properly — the load against what the processor would cost for
that model, which removes the constant entirely — is written up with the
numbers. An attempt at it in the same sitting is written up too, along with why
it was reverted.

The harness ships as examples/swap_patience.sh so the next change to that value
has to argue with a measurement. Found by a tester timing it on their own
hardware; we ran the experiment we had argued would show the opposite.

fix(mcp): asking for the fastest model stopped choosing one that must be loaded

SwarmLLM can be asked to pick a model itself, preferring speed, cost or
capability. The speed option took whichever model came first in the registry,
ignoring the thing that dominates how long a caller waits: whether the model is
already in memory. Observed live picking a cold 3.8B model and taking 57
seconds while a 3B sat loaded and would have answered in under one.

smallest. The comment above the old code claimed "smallest = fastest", which it
never implemented — the cost tier is the one that sorts by size.

hits.message:
fix(models): stop the model registry flip-flopping when two peers disagree about one file

Two peers that gossip different checksums for the same model file used to
overwrite each other for ever — neither won, and the node's record of that model
changed ten to twelve times a minute, indefinitely. On the node this was found
on, three models did exactly that and accounted for 67% of everything it
logged, right after a separate flood had been fixed.

It was not only noise. The checksum a node holds for a piece of a model is what
it uses to decide which peers are serving the same file it is, so the list of
peers considered able to serve those layers flipped with it, and a request got
whichever list happened to be current when it arrived. Each flip also cost a
database write.

A checksum already held is now kept when the newcomer describes the same file,
which is judged on the file's shape — its size and the size of every piece —
never on the checksums themselves. A genuine re-publish is different bytes, so
its shape moves and it is still adopted. The disagreement is reported once
rather than continuously, and an origin download remains what settles it.

Pieces the node holds on disk are deliberately exempt: there the claim can be
tested by hashing the file, and adopting it is the only way a node ever learns
from the swarm that what it is serving is corrupt.

The three models were exactly the three this node held least of — none, none,
and one piece of sixteen — which is the mechanism rather than a coincidence: a
piece the node downloaded itself carries provenance that settles the question
already.

Tests: lib 2772 -> 2775. The oscillation is reproduced as a unit test (it read
[1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 3, 1, 3] before), and verified by disabling the fix and watching
it go red while the re-publish, blank-fill and origin-precedence controls stayed
green. Evidence: docs/invariants/network.md, gotcha #649.

Two defects found while deciding whether to turn speculation across computers
(DSD) on by default, both measured on two nodes sharing one machine:

- The check that decides whether a model fits on the graphics card used the
  card's free memory as it stood when the node STARTED. Memory another program
  took later was invisible, so a model could be put on a card with no room left;
  here the node's workers then refused every prompt. It now reads the card at
  the moment it decides (released v0.3.212 behaves the same way).
- With the small guessing model slow relative to a fast link, speculation made
  replies six times slower (6.8 vs 38-42 tokens/s), because it could never stop
  guessing. It can now choose not to guess where guessing does not pay, remembers
  that for the next request, and no longer counts the guessing model's first,
  cold call as the cost of a guess. Over long links, where guessing pays, nothing
  changes.

The earlier worry that speculation cost a split its standby machines (FUTURE_WORK
#140) was the test rig: with the guessing model on the card, standbys and

hits.message:
fix(routing): try a machine we have never measured when staying home would take minutes

A node that would run a model on its own processor could refuse a faster route
across peers for a single reason: one of those peers had never been measured.
The rule read "a route this node can price is never given up for one it
cannot", and it was applied whatever the local alternative cost — including
when running the model here would take twelve minutes.

Three things were wrong with it.

It claimed to hold peers to the same standard as the single-peer hand-off
path. It did not. Both ask the same question — do we know anything real about
this machine — and they answered it in opposite directions: the hand-off path
lets an unmeasured peer take the whole model, on the grounds that the only way
to learn a machine's speed is to send it work once. The pipeline path refused
outright. The multi-hop route was stricter than the single-hop one and nothing
explained why.

It also doubled a caution the cost model already applies. An unmeasured
machine is deliberately charged a pessimistic rate so it cannot outrank one we
have measured; refusing the result afterwards means that rate can never do its
job.

And the arithmetic says what the rule actually blocked. An unmeasured peer is
priced above an ordinary processor at every reasonable speed — it only wins
once the local machine drops under about 1.25 tokens a second, or half that
for a peer on the far side of the world. So it was refusing the route in
exactly the situation where trying an unknown machine is the sensible thing to
do, and nowhere else.

The rule is now about the baseline instead: giving up "run it here" needs a
price for running it here, and without one the request stays. A peer that
turns out to be slow is abandoned by machinery that already exists — the
acknowledgement deadline, and this node being first in the standby list — so
one request is the whole cost of finding out, and that request is what stops
the next one making the same guess.

No threshold was invented for "how slow is too slow": it falls out of the cost
model's own constants.

perf(speculation): a block drafter checks only three guesses on a reply's first round, speeding code on processors

A block drafter (Qwen 3.5/3.6 and Gemma 4) used to check its
whole block of 15 guesses on a reply's first round, before it had any idea what
a check costs. On a processor that check costs about ten ordinary steps. A
reply that kept none of the guesses paid for all of them, and on code one wide
check that kept little made the drafter look so poor that it sat out most of
the reply.

The first check of a reply now guesses three tokens, as many as the model's own
guess head starts with. After it, the measured cost prices every round, up to
the whole block where checks are cheap (a graphics card). Both paths share the
rule: one computer and a split's first computer (#428 (b)).

Measured on this laptop's processor, in one build with the old behaviour
behind SWARMLLM_BLOCK_FIRST=whole (Gemma 4 12B Q4_K_M, debug build, greedy, 96
tokens, one run each, identical replies):
- code: 3.8 tok/s against 3.2 (plain decoding 3.4 / 3.5 in the same runs)
- a story: 3.2 against 2.8 (plain 3.5 / 3.3) — still ~9% under plain, left open
On a split of the same model over two processors 130 ms apart (the split rig,
three arms in one build, one run each, identical replies; seconds for 96
tokens, against no drafter): a palindrome function 1.15x faster (the whole
first block: 0.91x), a search-tree class 1.13x (1.18x), the story 0.93x (0.89x).
On a card the cost line widens the block after the first round; not measured
there yet.

Prior art: DFlash (arXiv 2602.06036, section 5.5.4) finds a drafter trained on
blocks of 16 keeps its quality on smaller blocks, and that wide blocks cost
where the check is compute-bound; llama.cpp's DFlash path cuts a block at its
first unsure guess; Hugging Face's assistant schedule starts narrow.

hits.message:
fix(routing): stop sending a model's middle abroad one token at a time

A node that holds a model and would run it on its own processor could hand
the middle of that model to a peer on another continent, and price the
hand-off as though the peer were running the whole thing. Those are very
different costs: a peer given the WHOLE model is entered once for the entire
request and decodes remotely, while a middle segment is entered again for
every token generated. The cost model has always known that and said so; the
delegation gate was asking it about the wrong shape.

Measured on the release pair: a processor-only node holding llama-3.2-1b
whole, asked for a 16-token prompt and one token of output, shipped the
model's middle to a machine 496 ms away and took 9.1 seconds. Its own
processor decodes that model at 4.28 tokens a second.

Prompt privacy is on by default whenever a node holds both ends of a model,
and that is exactly the shape it produces — so this was reachable on ordinary
settings, on small models, with nothing in the log to suggest anything was
wrong. The request completed and returned the right answer, slowly.

The gate now prices the shape it is about to assign, through one helper the
gate, the line that logs its verdict, and the privacy-cost estimate all
share. The same peer offered the whole model is still taken; that is the
point of the feature and there is a test holding it.

SWARMLLM_DELEGATE_SHAPE_PRICE=0 restores the old pricing for anyone who needs
to compare the two behaviours in the field.

hits.message:
feat(privacy): recommend prompt privacy, and say plainly what it costs

Prompt privacy is the only setting that stops the machine answering you
from reading your prompt, but nothing said so. The control read as a
neutral toggle among others, and the trade-offs were spread across two
sentences that mentioned latency and disk but not the part that matters
most: the cost grows with the length of the answer.

It is now marked Recommended wherever it can be turned on — in the chat
bar and on the model card — and the full cost is stated on the control
itself and in the setup guide: you need the first and last piece of the
model on disk, your machine does more of the work, data is exchanged with
helpers once per word so longer answers cost proportionally more time, and
the setting is per model so it can be on where it matters.

The setup guide also now says why it is off by default — it cannot route
unless you hold both ends of the model — rather than leaving that to be
inferred.

Two new strings, translated into all 21 languages. Verified in a browser
that they resolve natively rather than falling back to English.

hits.message:
docs(routing): the scheduler cannot tell a short prompt from a long one

vertex_cost prices a candidate from its per-layer decode latency times a
fixed 64 forward passes. Nothing in the scheduler ever sees prompt_tokens,
so a ten-token request and a ten-thousand-token one are routed the same
way, while prefill cost is linear in prompt length.

The hardware gap is also much wider on prefill than on decode: measured
here, 36 against ~2000 tokens a second for prompt processing (55x) versus
8 against 47 for generation (6x). A five-thousand-token agentic system
prompt is about 140 seconds on the processor node and 2.5 on the graphics
one, a difference nine times larger than the ratio the cost model prices.

It does not always bite — routing already prefers a faster node, so an
idle GPU wins anyway. It bites when the costs are close: a loaded GPU
against an idle CPU is the right answer for a short prompt and the wrong
one for a long prompt, and today those two requests look identical.

Recorded with what a fix would need, including that it has to be validated
on a real pair of nodes rather than argued — changing a routing cost model
without that is how an earlier delegation penalty priced out every good
split.

A computer that keeps failing a model is left out of it for a while

Field report: one computer holding part of a large model answered the start of
every question and then went silent at the first word — 5 of 6 requests that
included it failed, 3 of 3 without it worked. A failed request already stopped
using it for its own retry, but the next request picked it again, and each pick
cost a 30-second wait before failing. The only lasting penalty was a price
increase it could survive by being fast.

Now a computer that fails the same model on two requests in a row (it went
silent or its link dropped — not a polite refusal) is left out of that model's
plans for 2 minutes, doubling each time it happens again, up to 30 minutes. A
request it completes clears it. It is still used for a part no other computer
holds, so this can make a model slower to reach but never unreachable — the
same "panic threshold" Envoy's outlier detection uses.

feat(split): a computer holding none of a model can guess ahead for the one that leads it

When your computer holds none of a large model, it hands your request to
the computer holding the model's first part, which writes the reply. That
computer usually has no small model to guess the next words with, so every
word cost a full trip through the split.

If your computer holds a small model of the same family, it now follows the
reply as it arrives, guesses the next few words and sends the guesses on.
The leading computer checks them as it goes and never waits for them. A
guess never changes the reply: only a word the model would have written
itself is kept.

On a real link between Thailand and Australia (about 0.4 s apart), a 7B
model split over two computers wrote 2.5 tokens a second this way, against
2.27-2.38 with the requester driving the split itself. That is a first
step, not the goal; docs/FUTURE_WORK.md #318 lists what comes next.

The new message is sent only to a computer that advertises it takes
guesses (features bit 28), and a computer only advertises that while its
owner leaves speculative decoding on. Older nodes never see the message.
Guesses are accepted only from the computer that handed the reply over,
and only for a reply that is open. Unreleased.

A split that checks a tree of guessed words grows the next tree while the
current one is being checked. When the reply went somewhere that tree did not
cover, the next check waited for eight fresh guessing steps — most of a round

processor, the rest on an RTX 3070, QUIC with a delayed link, 160-token

  the log shows 3.0-3.2 steps a regrow
- 300 ms link: 5.54 / 5.40 against 5.12 / 5.34
- the stream of guess chains, today's default for this shape, ran 15.84 /
  16.24 and 6.00 / 6.03 — so it stays the default here.

guessing model run on a graphics card AND the farthest machine is at least

stream on a short link and level with it on a long one. The distance is the

hits.message:
docs: measure what a split across computers really costs, and why the setting that allows it stays off

There is a setting that lets a computer holding a whole model be asked to run
only part of it. It is off by default, and its own note says why: the planner
prices the network cost of a hand-off once per piece, when in truth that cost is
paid again for every single word produced. Nobody had measured the difference.

Measured now, on the live network. A reply split across four pieces ran at 0.35
words per second where the same model on one computer ran at 4 to 7. The time
per word matched the round-trip time to the computer doing the work almost
exactly, which is what "paid per word" looks like.

Turning the setting on made a real request worse, not better, exactly as its
note predicted. With it off the work went to two computers and finished in about
a minute and a half. With it on the planner found more ways to divide the work,
gave a third computer a four-layer sliver, and the reply had not arrived ten
minutes later. More freedom to split, while splitting is under-priced, is worse
than less.

Two things a future attempt to fix the pricing will need, neither of which was
written down before:

A computer's speed has little to do with how far away it is. Measured on one
model, the nearest computer was the fastest, the furthest was second, and one in
between was eleven times slower than the nearest. Distance is not throughput.

A divided reply moves at the speed of its slowest participant, and giving that
participant less to do does not help. Two layers out of thirty-two on a slow
computer cost more than the other thirty put together.

Privacy mode already routes under the permissive rule this entry calls
mispriced, since it cannot work without it. No behaviour is changed here.

hits.message:
fix: a peer is no longer ranked by a number this node never measured

A request went to a 1.26 tok/s processor node while a 20.45 tok/s RTX 4050
holding the same model sat idle, five times out of five. It came back at 0.23
tok/s; the same machine serves a larger model locally at 36.

The cost model was not at fault — replaying the three real candidates through
route_shortest_path picks the GPU, and that is now a regression test. The inputs
were. The GPU carried an observed per-layer latency of 1063 ms against the
processor node's 83 ms, and vertex_cost prefers an observation over the peer's
advertised speed and drops the network term when it has one. That priced the GPU
at 17,008 ms against 1,328 for hardware 25x slower, and its advertised figure was
never consulted.

Two things made that possible, and both are fixed.

An inherited figure could rank a peer. merge_ranking_sample seeds the decode
coefficient from gossip without touching the sample count, so decode_samples == 0
already distinguished a stranger's number from one we earned; ranking now
requires our own. The value is still stored for anything that wants the hint. The
probe that produced the capture had never sent that peer a single segment, so
what ranked it was somebody else's measurement of somebody else's network path —
one node's bad sample becoming every node's opinion, because observations travel
in NodeCapability.observed_latencies.

This is the rule the prefill coefficient has always followed: gossip deliberately
cannot seed it, because a figure we did not measure ourselves must not shorten
how long we are willing to wait for a peer. Ranking had the same exposure and no
guard, and the consequence is worse — a bad timeout costs one request, a bad
ranking costs every future one.

A cold segment could set the ranking figure. record_peer_segment_latency recorded
the sample and then marked the peer's model warm, so the first segment — the one
that paid to load the model — always looked like a warm measurement. It now reads
the warm state first and passes it to observe, which skips the decode coefficient
when cold. Prefill still takes cold samples, because that sizes how long we wait
and being pessimistic there is safe.

Verified live: the peer that a fresh probe previously ranked with a gossiped
83 ms/layer now reports no observation at all, so the scheduler falls back to the
advertised speed plus our own round trip. Six existing tests asserted the old
behaviour through the ranking accessor; their subjects — the trust gate, the
prefill isolation, the EMA arithmetic — are unchanged and now assert on the
seeded field or mark the peer warm first.

Blending or decaying inherited figures was considered and not done: both need a
tuning constant nobody can justify yet, and the narrower rule removes the harm
without one.

hits.message:
docs: first field measurements of the routing cost model, and how they were taken

The cost model has never been checked against a real outcome. It now has been,
fifteen times.

Verified without waiting for a release: a build carrying this morning's fix, run
as an ordinary node with its own data directory and no local models, joined to
the real swarm. Holding nothing, every request it made had to route to a peer,
which is exactly the case the instrument was blind to.

What the numbers say. The prediction is nearly flat in reply length while the
reality is not — replies of 2 and 192 tokens were priced 1.6x apart and took
5.3x apart. That is the shape this entry has always been about: the model
assumes a fixed number of forward passes, so it prices a two-word answer and a
long one almost alike.

What they do not say. The largest errors track the peer rather than the reply
length, so anything tuned from this without separating the two would be fitting
peer variance. Fifteen samples, two models, three peers, other people's machines
under unknown load, one short session. The open question — whether the error is
the forward-pass count or the per-token network term — is still open, and the
entry says so.

Recorded as data with its own caveats rather than as a conclusion, and the entry
keeps its instruction not to tune from a single session.

Also notes that the released binary still records nothing, so ordinary traffic
is not accumulating samples; everything here came from a node run for the
purpose.

hits.message:
docs: the warning about what prompt privacy costs has never actually reached anyone

Keeping your prompt private means the first and last steps of the model stay on
your own computer, and only the middle is sent away. That is a real guarantee
and it is not being changed here. But it costs one extra network round trip for
every word generated, so the further away the computer doing the middle is, the
slower the reply — and on a measurement today a reply that takes 5 seconds
without it took 54 seconds with it.

A decision was taken in September to leave that cost in place and tell people
about it, so anyone seeing a slow reply would know why and could switch it off
for that model. The telling was written and shipped. It has never once run.

The notice is only produced on a planning path the node stops using as soon as
a model has more than one other computer able to serve it — which is the
ordinary case, and the only case where any of this happens at all. Four days of
this machine's records contain not one occurrence.

Nothing is broken in the privacy itself, and no routing changes here. What
changed is the written record: the entry claiming this was "communicated" now
says plainly that it was not, carries today's measurements, and names what is
actually missing — a cost figure for the route finally chosen, rather than the
one that was only considered.

Re-measured at 9 to 14 times slower rather than the 6 originally recorded, and
the underlying quantity is not a multiplier at all: it tracks the round-trip
time to whichever computer holds the middle, so nothing bounds it.

Worth knowing: this only affects models your computer has finished downloading
in full. A machine holding none of a model never sees it.

hits.message:
fix(models): a machine can now be told by the network that a part it shares is damaged

Until now the only re-check of a part already in use ran a couple of seconds
after startup, against whatever that machine already believed. The periodic
rescan skips parts already in use, and the check on the download path only looks
at parts being considered for download. So a machine holding a damaged part could
not learn the fact from anyone else: by the time the network supplied the correct
fingerprint, the only check that would have used it had already run. It took a
further restart to notice.

Now, when the network reports a different fingerprint for a part your machine
holds, that part is re-checked straight away — and if it does not match, your
machine stops offering it and fetches a replacement.

Only parts actually held are re-checked; re-reading one the machine does not have
would cost hundreds of megabytes of disk for no answer. A part with a download in
flight is left alone, since re-reading a half-written file only raises a false
alarm.

hits.message:
fix(placement): a large model split across far computers can take in a third graphics card (#318)

Where no nearby computers can run a model between them, every computer plans
the same chain over all of them and fetches its own part. Three things kept the
Llama 3.3 70B's chain off a US RTX 3080 Ti with room for 22 of its layers:

- Every far link cost a flat 300 ms, and a computer running the model alone
  paid one too. Links are now priced as the router prices them at request
  time: half the round trip between the two computers' network coordinates,
  the last machine's link back to the first included, none for a computer
  running it alone (scheduler::hop_one_way_ms, now shared by both).
- The search allowed one segment more than the fewest the memory ceilings
  allow, so with one computer able to hold the whole model a third card was
  never tried. Where the cards cannot carry the model between them, every card
  may now join (up to three).
- A complete chain moved only for a quarter off its total time. It now moves
  for a lower total AND a slowest machine at most 3/4 as slow: the bottleneck,
  which is what Petals compares and what a stream of checks runs at.

By the speeds each computer states, the 70B goes from ~1018 ms a token (this
computer + Australia) to ~786 ms with the US card taking 22 layers; its slowest
machine from 855 to 447 ms. The US computer fetches its part once it runs a
release carrying this.

A published network coordinate this code could never produce (a negative
height, a position past the clamp) is no longer believed by the router or the
planner. Each change has a unit test that fails with it removed.

hits.message:
feat(hedge): tell the losing holder to stop, and re-scope KV quantization

**Remote cancellation.** The local cancel from the previous commit closed
the remote-generate path for free: the inbound handler already aborted
its `gen_fut` on `CancelInference`, and aborting that task now drops
`generate`'s future, drops the armed `ResponseGuard`, and messages the
worker. Before, `abort()` stopped the daemon-side task while the worker
generated the full token budget anyway.

Hedge losers needed the explicit send. `hedge_dispatch` fires a duplicate
forward to a second holder by design and discards whichever loses — the
comment there said so plainly ("the worker on the loser's holder will
compute the response and find no receiver"). That waste is the main cost
of hedging, and it is why `hedge_enabled` can't be turned on casually. The
race now dispatches `CancelInference` to the loser.

The inbound handler gained a `ModelProcessPool::cancel_request(request_id)`
fan-out alongside the abort-handle lookup: an in-flight `LayerForward` has
no abort handle, because the coordinator just stopped waiting. Fan-out
across workers rather than keyed by model, since the wire message carries
only a request id — workers are few and an unknown id is a worker-side
no-op. Handles are collected before awaiting so no DashMap ref is held
across an await.

**KV cache quantization (Tier 2F) re-scoped after research, not
implemented.** The entry specced KIVI 2-bit. Two findings say don't:
KIVI's numbers depend on fusing dequant into the attention matmul plus a
Triton kernel for group-wise quantisation — the authors note dequant "can
be computationally expensive" without them, and SwarmLLM runs on candle
with no custom kernels, so we would take the memory win and pay full
dequant cost on every attention call. Separately, production (vLLM,
TensorRT-LLM) converged on FP8 KV via FlashAttention-3, not 2-bit.

Revised recommendation recorded in FUTURE_WORK: if KV ever becomes the
binding constraint, use Q8_0 through the existing `inference/quant.rs`
(already has a quality gate, already on the wire) for ~2x rather than
2.6x, with no new dependency — and measure that KV actually dominates
first. For the contexts this project's users run, weights dominate and
shard windows / `gpu_layers = 0` are the cheaper lever.

hits.message:
perf(network): find out what an idle node's traffic is actually made of

The traffic figures could say which topic was expensive but not which
kind of message. One topic carries six different kinds and is most of an
idle node's upload, so the two obvious ways to reduce it targeted
different messages on that same topic, and there was no way to tell
which one mattered without guessing from message sizes and intervals.

Guessing that way has now been wrong by between ten and a hundred times
on three separate occasions in this area, so this counts it instead.
Every kind of message the node receives is tallied by name and by size,
and reported alongside the existing per-topic figures.

The answer, measured on a node holding no models over a three-and-a-half
minute window: model descriptions are 86% of everything arriving, at an
average of 32 KB each. The next largest is 6%. The capability updates
that were the other candidate are 3%.

That settles which change is worth making, and it also corrects a figure
this project has been carrying: a model description averages 32 KB, not
the 13 KB previously recorded, which was an average across all six kinds
of message on the topic rather than a measurement of one of them.

Counting only, no behaviour change.

hits.message:
fix(routing): a model is no longer sent to a computer that could never hold it

Reported by a tester on 0.3.229. The only computer holding a whole
Qwen 3.5 9B was a 6 GB machine limited to 5.2 GB, while the model
needs 6.7 GB. The request went to it anyway, from another continent, and
was turned down 8.8 seconds later. In a second request, 46 of a 30B
model's 48 layers went to one 16 GB machine.

When no plan fitted what peers said they had free right now, routing
stopped looking at their memory at all. That still matters, because a
computer may have freed memory since it last reported, or can unload an
idle model. But no amount of freeing raises its limit. Each computer
now also tells the others the most memory it could ever give one model
(a new optional field, so older computers are unaffected). Routing
weighs that limit with the receiving computer's own memory arithmetic,
for the parts it holds, and never plans past it. Where the computers
holding a model can carry it between them, it is split across them;
where they cannot, the request is answered at once with 'not enough
memory in the swarm' instead of after a wasted round trip.

Also fixed on the way: the planner's per-layer memory estimate had
counted a model's whole conversation memory as a fixed cost since
earlier in this release, so it under-counted how many layers fit here.

Checked with a new two-computer test (examples/ceiling_test.sh): with
the server's limit at 80% of what the model needs, the request is
refused in 0.1 s without the server being asked (0.3.229 asks it three
times); with the limit just above, the model is served.

hits.message:
feat(placement): nearby computers fetch complementary parts of a large model none of them can run whole

A split is only fast when its computers are close: 6.76 tok/s at 18 ms
against 0.35 across continents. Until now nothing put a large model's
parts on close computers — the download pass satisfied its replica count
with any copy anywhere, so the computers that could split a model fast
never held it.

Now computers measured within 30 ms of each other plan one chain alike
for a model somebody asks for that none of them can run whole, and each
fetches and keeps its own segment:

- The plan is exact at layer granularity over the nearby computers (at
  most 10): fewest segments, then fewest parts to fetch, ties broken the
  same way on every computer. Parts already downloading count as held, so
  a fetch landing does not move the plan, and a chain the neighbours
  already complete is never rebalanced.
- A neighbour that drops off keeps its place for 30 minutes; a part this
  computer was named for is kept a day; a computer named for parts it
  never fetches is passed over (the lease carrying a model already uses).
- Prune keeps this computer's segment below urgent disk pressure, and the
  download pass asks the same question, so nothing is fetched to be shed.
- A computer holding none of a model now learns its header when a nearby
  one holds part of it — every ceiling is weighed by the header's cost
  curve, and without it the plan naming this computer was never computed.

The policy was chosen by simulation (examples/placement_sim.py, 6c12f52f).
Pool scope and private mode apply: a computer outside the allowed set is
no part of a chain. Each rule's test was checked to fail with the rule
switched off.

diag: make the routing inputs visible, and record why a 25x faster peer lost

Benchmarking with a second GPU in the swarm for the first time showed a request
routed to a 1.26 tok/s processor node while a 20.45 tok/s RTX 4050 holding the
same model sat idle. It came back at 0.23 tok/s; the same machine serves a larger

hits.message:
perf(split): with a third of a model on the card, its guesses go through a stand-in for the layers they skip — 1.35x on code

A model split between the graphics card and the processor lets the card guess the next words by
skipping the processor's layers (#366). With only a third of a 14B on an 8 GB card, a guess skips
two thirds of the model and was kept about a third of the time, so guessing only paid for itself.

- The card's guesses now add a stand-in where the skipped layers would be (split::RunStandIn):
  a linear kernel ridge from those layers' input to their effect, fitted while the reply is
  written from the hidden states every real step and check already computes, over the last 256
  positions, kept current a row at a time (sliding-window kernel RLS, Van Vaerenbergh et al.,
  ICASSP 2006). It only changes what is guessed; the whole model still checks every token.
  Qwen2.5-14B Q4_K_M, 15 of 48 layers on an RTX 3070 Laptop, one binary, arms none/stand/stand/none:
  guesses kept 0.42-0.59 of the time against 0.28-0.36; decode 1.35x on code, 1.11x on a
  1,800-token summary, prose level. At the default placement (26 of 48 on the card) it still
  adds: 1.16x, 1.21x and 1.05x. A/B SWARMLLM_CARD_GUESS_STAND_IN=none.
- The card now guesses with a fifth of the model on it (was two fifths); at a third it decoded
  level with the old placement even before the stand-in.
- A prompt's prefix-cache snapshot is copied once the reply is done instead of before its first
  token (llama.cpp saves at slot reuse) — and, as a review of this change found, on every exit the
  worker survives, a reply cancelled mid-step included, so a retried prompt is still reused; sized
  with no reserve for a reply already written. First token on 1,800-token prompts 3.92 -> 3.80 s
  at the median. A/B SWARMLLM_PROMPT_SAVE=at-prompt-end.
- skip_agreement_probe gains `online` (the library's stand-in), `linear@λ`, PROBE_WINDOW for it,
  and `prior@λ` / `pooled@λ` (a stand-in carried from earlier conversations); stream_bench gains --gap (a back-to-back bench cannot see work moved after the reply).

Evidence: docs/invariants/inference.md (rounds 7-8, the deferred copy); FUTURE_WORK #366 (a
stand-in fitted from the whole conversation kept 2-3x the tokens on long prompts — next), #367 (a
long prompt's copy costs 0.15-2.1 s where its memory traffic is ~0.1 s); the same guess for a

hits.message:
fix(diagnostics): the route cost check could not see a hand-off

The instrumentation added in v0.3.165 records what the router expected a
request to cost, so the estimate can be checked against what it actually cost.
It was recording nothing for the most common shape there is: a request handed
whole to one machine, and the privacy arrangement where a peer runs the middle
layers while the two ends stay local.

The recording sat at the single point the multi-machine search passes through,
and route planning returns an answer from six places — four of them earlier.
That is exactly backwards for the question being asked, because the
measurement that raised the doubt in the first place was one of those shapes.

Measured on a live node before the fix: five peers, ten hours of uptime, three
deliberately remote requests across three models, and not one prediction
recorded, because every one of them was handed to a single machine.

All five routes now record through one helper. Purely additive — no routing
decision changes. Requests that run entirely on this node still record
nothing, deliberately: there is no route choice to explain.

Worth noting for anyone reading older logs: the absence of these numbers up to
now is not evidence that handing a model to one machine is rare. It is the
instrument not being able to see it.

The test for this passed at first for the wrong reason — the route it built
reached the search, not the hand-off — and a deliberately broken control
caught it. It now turns the priced search off, so the hand-off really is the
whole decision, and fails when the recording is removed.

hits.message:
fix: prompt privacy no longer strands a model on your processor

A model too big for the graphics card was handed to a nearby machine — unless
prompt privacy was on for it, in which case the request stayed put and ran
slowly. That was wrong, and it was the common case: privacy turns itself on for
any model whose first and last pieces a node holds, which is every model this
decision can apply to. So the feature shipped yesterday almost never ran.

Privacy does not rule out using another machine. It rules out that machine
seeing your prompt — and the "boomerang" this project already builds is exactly
the arrangement for that: the first and last layers run here, so the text you
typed and the words chosen in reply never leave, while everything in between
runs on the other machine as encrypted intermediate values.

Verified across two real nodes with privacy at its default: three segments
assembled — first layer here, layers 1 to 27 on the peer, last layer back here —
and the peer's log confirms it ran those 26 of 28 layers. Correct answer.

Standing aside from the local shortcut was not enough on its own. Asked to route
this, the general search answers "run all of it here", which satisfies the
privacy rule at no network cost because nothing in its costing knows this machine
is about to fall back to its processor. Rather than teach it — which is what the
reverted attempt did, and it spoiled every other route — the arrangement is built
directly, the same as the whole-model hand-off beside it.

The split is deliberately lopsided: one layer at each end and everything else
away. Those two exist only to keep the promise, and each one kept here runs on
the processor this is trying to get off.

hits.message:
fix(routing): a machine that says it lacks part of a model now loses the claim

A peer that answered "I do not have those parts" kept being picked for the same
work, over and over. Seen on the live network: one machine was the middle step of
eleven failed requests in half an hour, across three different models, refusing
each in about seven milliseconds — and its standing was untouched at the default
the whole time, because nothing recognised what it had said.

The machinery for this already existed. A peer that reports missing parts is
supposed to lose its claim to them and be skipped for the rest of the request. It
was looking for the wording our own code produces.

But a serving node deliberately rewrites those errors before sending them, so it
does not leak file paths and internals to strangers. Every parts-related failure
leaves as one short generic sentence. So the wordings being looked for were
exactly the ones that can never arrive over the network — correct on its own,
blind in company.

Both sides now share one string rather than two that had to be kept in step by
memory. The test puts a real error through the rewrite and checks the far side
still recognises it, because testing either half alone passes happily and that is
why this lasted. A second test keeps the converse true: an unrelated failure must
never cost a healthy machine its claim, since that pushes work off a good node.

This is separate from the graphics-memory work earlier. That explains why a
request is spread across machines at all; this explains why the attempt then
failed every time.

hits.message:
docs: record the open question about how patient GPU swapping should be

A tester timed the trade on a 6 GB card: a model answering from the processor
inside the protection window took 8.1 seconds, while swapping it onto the card
outside the window took 2.5 seconds end to end. On those numbers the protection
costs more than the thing it protects against.

Not changing it on that evidence. Both that measurement and ours used one-shot
prompts, and the cost the window actually guards is invisible to those: freeing
a model discards its cached prompt prefixes and live conversations along with
it, so two models alternating in conversation would re-prefill each other every
swap. Nobody has measured that case yet, and the entry says what would.

Reported alongside a confirmation that the v0.3.130 placement fixes behave as
described, on different hardware and a different pair of models than ours.

hits.message:
perf(split): a split that starts and finishes here skips more work nobody reads (+17% prose)

On a split that starts and finishes on this computer, this computer runs the
model's last layers on every answer the other computers send back. That
includes answers to guesses already proven wrong, so its copy of the
conversation stays in step with theirs. Such an answer now waits to be run
together with the next useful one, or is dropped where the guesses are cut
back anyway (`dsd_flow::dead_wait_on`, now ON; SWARMLLM_FLOW_DEAD_WAIT=0
gives the old behaviour).

It was built on 2026-10-30 and left off after one test found it no faster.
That test's own logs refute the cause written down at the time ("the freed
sends leave in a burst"):
- no forward left within 5 ms of the one before;
- 65-80% of the extra delay came after the far computer had received the
  forward;
- the far computer's slow spells hit the old arm just as hard;
- the two dead-wait runs had been back to back inside one slow spell.

Measured again with the runs interleaved (Thailand-Australia, Qwen2.5-14B,
release v0.3.266 binary, 12 runs):
- prose: 8.16 tokens a second against 6.98, ahead of the run beside it in
  every pair;
- code: level (17.81 against 18.01);
- accuracy: scored against llama.cpp, the replies are as faithful as before.

The flow's guard was measured off and on in the same sitting. It makes no
difference on a calm link and is kept, since a 5 Mbit uplink needs it. Its
one cost was a reply where the far computer was slow on its own and the
guard narrowed the tree anyway. FUTURE_WORK #369 records the next step: the
far computer reports its own time, so the guard reads only the link's delay.

hits.message:
fix(network): a computer holding more than 512 model parts is seen by the swarm again

A computer that held more than 512 parts announced them in one message, and
every other computer drops a message that long unread. From that moment the
swarm credited it with nothing new: its models read as held by nobody, chats
needing its parts failed with "No reachable node holds layers …", and other
computers gave back healthy copies to fill "holes" it already filled. One
node in the network crossed the line on 2026-11-02 (565 parts, 43 models).

The sender now cuts a long list into pieces of at most 512, each model kept
whole in one piece (a receiver treats a model's parts in one message as that
holder's full set and retracts the rest, so a model split across two pieces
would be half-retracted by each). This is done at the two places every
announcement leaves the node — gossip and the direct reply to a new peer —
so no caller can skip it. Older receivers take the pieces as they are; the
message format is unchanged.

fix(routing): a model too big for the graphics card is priced as the card/processor split it runs as

When a model does not fit the graphics card, part of it runs on the card and
the rest on the processor. When choosing where to send a request, this
computer priced its own route as if the model ran entirely on the processor
before it was loaded, and as if it ran entirely on the card once a split
worker was resident (that worker holds card memory, so it read as "on the
card"). Both now count the card's share of the layers, for the route search
and for the check that decides whether to hand a whole model to a faster
peer, through one shared figure.

graphics cards: Qwen2.5-14B with 22 of its 48 layers on an 8 GB card was
priced at 6.3-7.0 (7B-reference tokens/s) instead of 4.55 cold and 56 warm.
Run locally it delivered ~4.0 tokens a second for the 14B; the processor
figure predicted ~3.0 and the split figure ~4.6. Both versions kept the
request local here, since no peer had room for all 48 layers. FUTURE_WORK
#129: what remains is the prompt pass's prior for a split and the
per-crossing network cost.

hits.message:
fix(routing): a standby is chosen by what it costs, not by what it pings

Picking the backup for a pipeline segment ranked candidates on their health-ping
round trip, which says nothing about how fast a machine computes. On this swarm
the nodes span 0.37 to 20.45 tokens a second and nearness is unrelated to speed,
so the backup was routinely the slowest box available.

That became sharper with prompt-length routing: a long request is now correctly
steered to a machine that can read it quickly, and if that machine dropped, the
request landed on one that could not — turning seconds into minutes, with
nothing in the log saying the replacement had been chosen by a different measure
than the original.

The standby is now priced by the same cost model as the primary, prompt length
included, since it serves the same request. Local-first and region anti-affinity
still come first — a standby exists to survive a failure and those two answer
that — so this only replaces the tiebreak among equals.

Two other cost models are still prompt-blind and were before this work: the
greedy assigner used when the shortest-path search finds no route, and the
decision to hand a whole model to a nearby peer. Both are recorded in
docs/FUTURE_WORK.md rather than changed unmeasured. Also noted there and at the
call site: a pipeline reused for KV-cache affinity is not re-routed, so prompt
length is priced on the first turn of a conversation and not on later ones.

hits.message:
perf(speculation): a split sizes its chunks of guesses by the far computer's measured pace

The previous change let a model split across computers check 3 or 5 of a
small model's guesses at a time, whichever pays. It priced the two extra
guesses from whole round trips, and on a 70B split across two machines
(~430 ms apart) those varied by ~190 ms while the two guesses cost the far
machine ~82 ms - so the price it learned read anywhere from 4 to 208 ms and
the choice was close to random.

The far machine's own time per chunk is now read from the gap between two
answers when the later chunk was already queued there: the round trip
cancels out, and on the same split it read 752-767 ms for 3 guesses and
837-865 ms for 5, about twenty times steadier. Each width is priced from
that, remembered per model and set of machines, and the width not chosen is
still tried now and then so the figure stays current. Answers are also now
timed when they arrive rather than when the stream gets round to them.

On the 70B split (six runs alternating against always checking 3, one
build): 2.8% faster overall - 20% faster on one reply, 2% on another, 6%
slower on a third whose wording came out differently at the wider width.
Where the far computer keeps up (a home network), nothing changes.
examples/stream_chunk_noise.py reads the new per-chunk debug lines.

fix(models): getting a model you already hold part of no longer downloads those parts again

Every download through /api/admin/hf/download-shards (the dashboard's Get,
`swarmllm get-model`, the reference models) fetched each part it named from
HuggingFace in full, even a part already on this computer, and replaced the

it was asked for this computer already holds: the parts

whole on disk, none being downloaded), cut exactly as the file is cut now.

part of a copy waiting to be replaced, is fetched as before, since a fresh
download is how it is put right.

asked for part 1, it kept the file ("not fetched again"); v0.3.266 on the

hits.message:
fix(memory): a Gemma model is placed by the memory its cache will really use

Before loading a model, a node weighs it: whether it goes on the graphics
card, how much of it fits beside the processor, and how many layers to offer
a plan. Every one of those charged each layer the widest layer's cache at
every position. On Gemma 2, 3 and 4 most layers only look back over a window,
and since #281 (1)/(2) their caches keep only that window. So the estimates
overstated these models: Gemma 4 12B's admission was priced at 3 GiB of cache
where the worker holds 1.1. A model that fits could be sent to the processor,
split more than it needs to be, or offered to fewer plans.

Now the estimates read the same per-layer layout the loader builds its own
budget from (`kv_budget::KvLayout`, read once off the header). It covers which
layers keep a cache, each layer's own shape and storage, and a sliding-window
layer charged its window plus the widest prompt forward its worker reads
(`prefill_pacer::widest_prompt_forward`, the worker's own rule). Admission's
footprint, the segment cost curve and the card/processor split all price
through it (`VramFootprintInputs::kv`), so the estimate and the worker cannot
disagree about one model. DeepSeek-2's MLA cache is now priced as the loader
keeps it rather than at its grouped shape.

Tests: a_layout_prices_each_layer_by_its_own_shape_and_window (Gemma 4 12B's
real per-layer keys) and admission_charges_a_windowed_layer_its_window (a
header read through the pool) both fail with the window pricing turned off.

A peer's bound on a coordinator still charges every position; it stays open
as FUTURE_WORK #281.

hits.message:
fix(memory): a computer without a graphics card no longer offers the swarm memory it will then refuse to use

A processor-only node told the swarm it had room for a model when its free
memory was low, then refused every request it was sent for that model with
"0 MB available for conversations". Seen on a peer that offered all of
TinyLlama and refused even a 43-token prompt; each refusal cost the
requester a round trip and a re-plan, and since the previous commit was
reported as "busy, try again" though retrying could not help.

The offer (70% of available memory) and the node's own admission check
(available memory minus a reserve of 5% of the machine, at least 256 MB)
were two different rules. When free memory falls below about three times
that reserve the offer was larger. The offer is now never more than the
admission check allows. The same bound also refuses loading a model into
memory when what would be left could not hold a single conversation.

A new test checks the pairing across 4-64 GB machines against the admission
code itself; it caught a 1 MB rounding over-offer before release. Takes
effect on each peer as it updates. Closes FUTURE_WORK #219.

perf(qwen3.5): a split reply's guessing model grows two levels of guesses a call, not three

A Qwen 3.5 split reply's flowing tree now grows two levels of guesses per call to its guessing model, not three.
Its levels became cheaper with the CUDA graph, so the forward a level adds now costs more than the tokens it brings.

One level read a little higher in its one sitting, within two's spread. It sends half again as many forwards
across the link, so it is left for a sitting where the far end is the slower side. SWARMLLM_FLOW_LEVELS sets it
for every flow, as before. Checked with no switch set on the same link: every reply's flow
grew two levels a call, and the replies wrote prose at 15.78 and 14.43 tok/s and code at 28.26 and 24.79.

room only for the growth. The forward's rollback copy holds the old buffer until the next forward, so for that
one forward the card holds both. It stayed inside the budget's margin in every arm measured, and is listed as
open work.

Prior art: EAGLE-2 and SpecInfer size a draft tree's depth by what its levels are accepted at against what a level
costs; this is that trade-off measured on the link, where a level's cost changed under it.

hits.message:
docs: a plan to make split inference fast without anyone holding the whole model

Nobody in the network should need to hold a whole model, not even a
compressed copy: the models worth splitting are the ones nobody can hold. So
the plan is to parallelize the REPLY rather than the token. One token must
still pass through every machine in turn, but each trip around the machines
can carry many rows at almost no extra cost, and today it carries one.

- More tokens per trip from guessing that lives on one machine: draft heads
  built into newer models (Qwen 3.5/3.6, GLM, DeepSeek) sit on the last
  machine and give about 3 tokens a trip in llama.cpp's measurements; a small
  same-family model gave 3.5 a trip here (10 on code).
- More streams per reply in the same trip: several workers writing one answer
  while reading each other (Hogwild!, which splits its cache by layers exactly
  as our machines already do), outline-then-expand for list-shaped answers,
  and an agent's parallel calls.
- Prompt reading is parallel already, and bandwidth-bound rather than
  latency-bound across a WAN.
- Shorter trips: keep the requester out of the loop (FUTURE_WORK #143) and
  build rings of nearby machines.

Measured and ruled out: repairing a drafted reply all at once (1.07 tokens a
trip) and streaming weights to the requester. The earlier "same model at fewer
bits on your own card" design is kept only as a possible opt-in.
Plan: docs/plans/wan_parallel.md, FUTURE_WORK #145.

hits.message:
fix(credits): stop penalising and stop inventing balances (bug report #4)

Two separate credit-display problems, both from the same report.

**Flat penalty on framework failures.** Every failed distributed request
applied `penalty_serve_failure` unconditionally, including failures the
local node caused. Debugging the three bugs in this report drove the
reporter's own node from 0 to -470 credits without a single peer
misbehaving: an unnecessary AllReduce group, a local GPU OOM, and a
config setting that wasn't being honoured.

New `failure_is_penalty_worthy` gates the penalty on (a) the assignment
actually having had a remote segment, and (b) the error not being
locally attributable. `ServiceUnavailable` is by definition "THIS server
can't serve", `Internal` is our own bug, and the scheduling/config
variants never involved a peer — none of them cost anyone credits now.
Network faults, timeouts waiting on a peer, shard-integrity mismatches
and bad signatures still do.

Erring toward "penalise" is the expensive direction: it pushes an
honest, reachable node toward Bronze and eventually below
`MIN_BALANCE_FOR_INFERENCE`, degrading it for bugs it did not cause.
Erring the other way lets a bad peer keep its credits for one more
request, and trust scoring plus spot-checks still catch it.

**The "+2500" was fabricated.** The reporter saw a node showing itself
at -90 while its peer displayed +2500 for it, and reasonably read that
as ledger divergence. It wasn't: `api/identity.rs` fell back to
`trust_score * 5000.0` whenever no balance gossip had been received, and
DEFAULT_TRUST is 0.5 — so every unknown peer rendered a confident,
indistinguishable-from-real "+2500 credits". The endpoint now returns
`credits: null` + `balance_known: false` and the dashboard shows an em
dash with an explanatory tooltip. Unknown peers sort last rather than as
zero: not knowing a balance is not a claim that it is empty.

i18n: `leaderboard.balance_unknown` + `activity.model_cpu_fallback`
(the toast added by the previous commit) across all 21 locales,
1186 -> 1188 entries each.

1115 -> 1118 lib tests.

hits.message:
fix(tokenizer): Llama 3 prompts were costing twice the tokens they should

Every Llama-3/3.1/3.2 model file names its text-splitting rule 'llama-bpe'.
That name was not recognised, so it fell through to a plain whitespace split,
which strands each space as its own token instead of attaching it to the word
that follows — the form these models are trained on. 'The quick brown fox jumps
over the lazy dog' came to 19 tokens where the reference tokenizer gives 9.

Reading the prompt is most of the work in a long request, so this roughly
doubled the cost of the most widely used model family on the network, and fed
those models text in a shape they had never seen in training.

Verified against a reference tokenizer built from the same vocabulary and
merges, over fifteen varied samples: fourteen previously differed, 43% more
tokens overall; all fifteen now match exactly, 1.00x.

Two further defects in the same code:

- The Qwen rule actually held the Llama-3 pattern, grouping digits up to three

hits.message:
docs: research the case for chaining pipeline hops peer to peer

Records why an eight-shard model currently pays sixteen round trips per token
where it could pay two, and why that is a topology choice rather than a limit.

The prior art is decisive and it is not theoretical. Petals runs a 176B model
across fourteen volunteer machines on the open internet by having each server
forward activations to the next rather than back to the client, and its measured
latency sensitivity shows the property we lack: raising client latency by 100ms
cost about 211ms per step, which is two round trips regardless of how long the
chain was. Under our design the same change would cost that much per segment. A
second paper reaches the same architecture independently and keeps the first and
last layers on the client, which is already how our prompt privacy works.

Petals also answers the objection that looks fatal. Failover does not need the
coordinator holding every boundary: the client keeps what it sent and can rebuild
a replacement server's cache from it.

The design here is deliberately an optimisation with a fallback rather than a
replacement. A hop that cannot be made directly relays through the coordinator,
which is exactly today's cost for that hop alone, and any chain failure retries
the whole request the old way. So a swarm where only some peers can reach each
other still gets most of the benefit, and nothing is ever worse than it is now.

Names the part with real unknowns rather than glossing it: chaining makes the
latency between two PEERS the thing that matters, and we do not measure that at
all today.

Prices the two alternatives so they are not revisited from scratch. Tensor
parallelism has a 9.4 second per token floor at this distance from the speed of
light alone. Sequence parallelism is bandwidth-bound at roughly 2.2 Gbps per
extra node, so moving machines closer does not help it, and the prompt length
cancels out of that ratio entirely.

Recommends the cheaper win first: speculative verification already batches five
tokens into one round trip and is off by default, which divides the same cost by
five with no wire change.

is bit-identical to the old path (new test, red when the summation order is changed), and the
40-token reply was identical in all six arms.

the processor; before, it sat in "unattributed" at ~80% of a step. It shows what is left:
the card's experts cost ~41 ms per token (host overhead, not arithmetic), and at equal

hits.message:
fix(memory): asking your own model again right away moves it back onto the graphics card

When one of your requests had to run partly on the processor (another
computer's model held the card at that moment), your next requests kept it
there as long as they came less than 5 seconds apart. An agent's loop or a
nightly check never leaves that gap, so the model stayed slow for all of them
(#483 (a)). Your own requests now move it back to the card as soon as it
has room. Other computers' requests still wait for a pause in the traffic,
so a peer's request is not charged a cold load.

The 5 s wait stood in for a race: a request handed the model's process a
moment before it is retired, registering its reply just after the retirement
looked for work in flight. That race is now closed for every retirement:
each hand-out is stamped under the pool's lock, and a retirement waits 250 ms
past the last one before it drains. A new guard fails the build if a way to
take a model process out of the pool skips the stamp. After a refusal, the
graphics card is read at most once every 5 seconds per model.

The guard that keeps "is this process in use?" in one place scanned only the
first thousand lines of the 25,000-line pool. It stopped at the first test
attribute, which sits on a field. It now scans the whole file and finds
nothing.

Prior art: HikariCP's connection pool makes a borrow and an idle eviction
compete on one atomic, so it never closes a connection that was just handed
out.

fix(memory): a computer holding part of a large model now offers the wider share it could load

  the gate that replaces the worker already does.

  scheduler takes a request's reference on a runner only once it is loaded.

hits.message:
fix: resuming a saved conversation no longer costs speed on some models

The graphics-card speed-up added recently keeps a second copy of the
conversation cache, and only some models can use it. Which models was
decided when a conversation started — but a conversation resumed from a
saved one is rebuilt from a snapshot that does not record enough to make
that decision, so it kept the second copy regardless.

The result was the same model behaving differently depending on how the
conversation began: models that cannot use the copy paid a few percent per
token, and half again as much memory, for something nothing reads —
but only when resuming.

The decision is now made on each pass by the code that knows both numbers,
so a resumed conversation is corrected on its first token. Models that can
use the copy keep it and keep the speed-up.

Turning the copy back on midway is deliberately ignored, and now says why:
it would start empty against a cache already holding the conversation and
could never catch up, so it would be refused on every use while still
costing memory. Two tests cover both directions.

hits.message:
fix: asking for longer conversations no longer pushes a model off your GPU

Two settings worked against each other. A coding assistant sends its whole tool
list as a system prompt before you type anything — one measured at about 5000
tokens — so the shipped 4096-token limit rejected its very first message, with
an error telling the caller to send a shorter prompt. The prompt is not theirs
to shorten.

Raising the limit was the documented fix, and it had a hidden cost: the check
that decides whether a model fits on the graphics card charged for the full
conversation length up front. Raising the limit therefore made models stop
fitting, and they were loaded on the processor instead. A report on 2026-08-17
measured that as six and a half minutes to read one prompt, and the machine
reaching its temperature warning.

That charge is no longer needed. Since 2026-08-08 memory for a conversation is
taken as the conversation grows, and every step checks the free memory it is
about to claim, refusing politely and letting another machine take the request
if there is not enough. The worst case is enforced where the memory is actually
taken, so pre-paying for it when the model loads bought nothing and cost people
their graphics card.

So the fit check now prices a normal working conversation rather than the
longest one permitted, and the default conversation length rises to 8192. A user
who never changed the setting is charged exactly what they were charged before.

The processor-side check is deliberately NOT capped the same way: nothing bounds
a processor worker's memory while it runs, so that estimate stays the only place
the ceiling is priced at all. Erring high there refuses a load; erring low makes
the whole machine swap.

The "conversation too long" message now names the setting that fixes it.

perf(flow): a Qwen 3.5 split's 16-row steps go to the card as one graph

The computer holding a Qwen 3.5 split's first layers runs them on every row
its guessing model grew in one call: two levels of 8, so 16 rows. Steps of up
to 8 rows were already recorded and sent to the card as one CUDA graph; these

tiled tree kernel over the half-precision cache. A shape's first step still

inside a capture.

rows a step 37.9 -> 35.0 ms; a captured step's output matched the same step run
one launch at a time exactly (9B and 0.8B), and the test fails with the
mechanism off. On the Thailand-Australia 9B split, this computer's part of a
step took about 1.1 ms less (18.5-19.0 against 19.6-20.6 ms for prose); reply
speeds stayed within the runs' spread, since the guessing model's time varies

the drafter about what one 8-row level does: every tree shape tried reads the
same reply speed, so what moves it is the cost of a level.

hits.message:
perf: a model split across nearby computers with speculation runs 30-80% faster than a plain split

Measured on one machine with an emulated link (a new test switch,
SWARMLLM_TEST_TENSOR_DELAY_MS), Qwen 2.5 Coder 7B split over two nodes with a
0.5B guessing model, tok/s:

  round trip   plain split   speculation before   speculation now
     10 ms         31             31-33               39-41
     24 ms         21             26-28               30-33
     50 ms         12             19                  21-22

What was in the way, found from one round's timeline:
- The guessing model opened every call with a slow two-token pass; it now
  reads short catch-ups one step at a time, each sent as a CUDA graph.
- A graph needed the very next position, so every round's first step after a
  rejected guess ran the slow way; any step of a known conversation is now
  captured.
- The guessing cost was an average, so two slow calls could switch guessing off
  for ten minutes; it is now the median of recent calls.
- Checking several guesses at once was never captured: it built a mask the
  graphics card never reads, and candle uploaded each tensor layout from the
  host on every call (155 copies in one check). Layouts are now kept on the
  card after their first use, and the unread mask is not built.

Replies with speculation still score as the model's own against llama.cpp
(118/120 tokens its first choice, near-ties only), and single-machine replies
are byte-identical to the previous build. Note: a 0.5B guessing model in fp16
takes about 3 GB of graphics memory; a Q8_0 build of it fits where fp16 does not.
