hits.message:
fix(routing): stop handing a long prompt to a machine that is slow at reading it

A node deciding whether to hand a whole model to a peer compared machines on
how fast they write words. Reading the prompt is a different kind of work —
it is limited by raw computation rather than memory speed, and the spread
between machines on it is roughly nine times wider. On a long prompt that
reading is nearly all of the wait, so the comparison was made on the wrong
thing entirely.

Measured by someone running two nodes: an Apple M4 advertising the best
speed on their network was handed two prompts of about eleven thousand words
and took five to six minutes before the first word came back, twice. The
routing search had already priced that same machine as far and away the
worst choice for reading a prompt, and had avoided it — but the hand-off
decision never looked at a price at all. Their own guess, that the two paths
were not sharing a cost model, was exactly right.

They now share one: the hand-off asks the same pricing function the search
uses, over the prompt in hand, and declines a machine that comes out worse
than doing the work here. Not knowing still never excludes — a machine
nobody has measured is still tried, since refusing on missing information
would leave a node grinding away beside one that may well be faster. The
first request is what produces the measurement that stops the second, which
is why the same machine was picked twice.

The decision also logs both prices now, so the choice can be checked rather
than guessed at.

Separately recorded, and needing a decision rather than a fix: the same
report shows privacy-by-default costing six times the total time on a long
prompt, because the two layers kept at home are the expensive ones to read.
That trade is real and is not ours to make silently.

hits.message:
feat(privacy): tell people what keeping their prompt private is costing them

Someone measured a reply taking 74 seconds with prompt privacy on and 12
with it off. The two steps kept on their own machine are a thirty-sixth of
the model and were 55 of those 74 seconds: reading a long prompt is slow on
a processor, and those two steps are where it happens.

Privacy is on by default for a machine that holds both ends, so nobody
chose that trade and nothing on screen explained the wait. The node now says
so, in plain words, when it is material — how many seconds it is adding,
why the ends stay home, and where to turn it off for that model. Once every
ten minutes per model, since the same decision is taken on every request.

We considered simply dropping the guarantee automatically when it gets
expensive, and rejected it. Every comparable system that has faced this
either refuses to downgrade silently or is criticised for doing so: the TLS
standard added a whole mechanism because browsers downgraded on a failed
handshake and a passing network glitch could trigger it; Chrome warns before
falling back to an insecure connection; Apple tells you when a network has
switched Private Relay off. The one that falls back quietly is faulted
precisely for the quiet.

The deciding argument is sharper than any of those, though. The trigger
would be "this is slow", and the prize for triggering it is the user's
prompt in the clear — which is the exact thing being protected. A machine
that wanted to read people's prompts would only have to answer slowly.

So the figure is shown and nothing acts on it.

hits.message:
docs(routing): the scheduler cannot tell a short prompt from a long one

vertex_cost prices a candidate from its per-layer decode latency times a
fixed 64 forward passes. Nothing in the scheduler ever sees prompt_tokens,
so a ten-token request and a ten-thousand-token one are routed the same
way, while prefill cost is linear in prompt length.

The hardware gap is also much wider on prefill than on decode: measured
here, 36 against ~2000 tokens a second for prompt processing (55x) versus
8 against 47 for generation (6x). A five-thousand-token agentic system
prompt is about 140 seconds on the processor node and 2.5 on the graphics
one, a difference nine times larger than the ratio the cost model prices.

It does not always bite — routing already prefers a faster node, so an
idle GPU wins anyway. It bites when the costs are close: a loaded GPU
against an idle CPU is the right answer for a short prompt and the wrong
one for a long prompt, and today those two requests look identical.

Recorded with what a fix would need, including that it has to be validated
on a real pair of nodes rather than argued — changing a routing cost model
without that is how an earlier delegation penalty priced out every good
split.

hits.message:
perf: generating after a long prompt was ~10x slower per token than after a short one

On a GQA model, decode attention used the standard path below a 2048-token
crossover. That path expands the key/value cache to the full head count on every
token of every layer, so its cost grows with the conversation. Profiled on
llama-3.2-3b Q4_K_M it reached 91% of decode time at ~1150 tokens of context.

Measured, milliseconds per generated token, standard -> fused:
  kv ~82     141.2 -> 129.2   (attention   16.8 ->  14.7)
  kv ~1150  1368.1 -> 249.2   (attention 1242   -> 136 )   5.5x

Fused wins at both ends, so grouped-query decode now always takes it. The old
crossover came from models with higher expansion ratios than this one, and the
expansion is exactly what makes the standard path expensive, so they should
benefit at least as much -- 24/8 is the least favourable grouped-query shape and
it already wins at 82 tokens.

Multi-head models are unaffected and keep the standard path, where the expansion
is a no-op and the transposes would be pure overhead.

fix: streaming Anthropic replies reported zero prompt tokens

A streamed /v1/messages reply reported input_tokens: 0 where the identical
non-streaming request reported the real count (measured: 0 against 59, and 0
against 38). Anything tracking cost or remaining context from the stream was
therefore working from a wrong number, while its non-streaming sibling was
correct — the recurring shape in this codebase, one invariant and several paths.

Anthropic reports input tokens on message_start, which this server emits before
generation begins and therefore before the prompt has been tokenised, so the
value there was hardcoded to 0 and never revisited. The split streaming path
already received the true (prompt, completion) pair when generation finished and
discarded it into `_usage`. It is now reported on message_delta, which is where
the number exists and what the official SDKs accumulate.

Paths that genuinely cannot know it — the cloud-provider proxy, which relays an
upstream stream without parsing its usage chunk — omit the field rather than
sending 0, so a client summing usage is never handed a confident zero. The
parameter is required at every call site rather than defaulted, so the compiler
found all six and a new streaming path cannot quietly skip it.

Verified against the non-streaming sibling on the same request: 38 and 38.

hits.message:
fix(routing): the scheduler can finally tell a short prompt from a long one

Routing priced every request as if it were the same size. A ten-token question
and a ten-thousand-token agentic prompt were sent to exactly the same node,
because the cost model charged a fixed number of decode passes and nothing in
the scheduler had ever seen how long the prompt was.

That matters because reading a prompt and writing a reply are bounded by
different things. Decode is limited by memory bandwidth, where the machines in a
swarm differ by around six times. Prefill is limited by arithmetic, where they
differ by around fifty-five: a 5000-token system prompt is about 140 seconds of
reading on a processor-only node against about 2.5 on a graphics card. The model
priced the six and ignored the fifty-five.

Prefill is now its own term, linear in prompt length. Where this node has
actually prefilled through a peer it uses that measurement — peer_speed has
tracked prefill separately from decode since August — and otherwise falls back
to a device-class prior taken from real numbers on real hardware, which the
first real measurement then replaces.

Two things keep the change from destabilising what already worked. An unknown
prompt length prices a request exactly as before, so the offline allocator and
every non-request path are untouched. And at a short prompt the new term is a
few percent of the decode term, so short-prompt routing cannot move; the choice
only shifts once the prompt is long enough that reading it is the dominant cost,
which is the case this exists for.

were - so nobody could tell whether long prompts (minutes to read again on
a processor or across computers) were being dropped and re-read. That is
the condition for keeping saved prompts on disk as well (FUTURE_WORK #470).

A prompt of 8,192 tokens or more that the cache lets go now gets one line:
for which model, why (the cache's caps, room planned for a new save, or
memory asked for), how many and the longest. Shorter ones stay silent.
Logging only; nothing about what is kept changes.

perf(split): a chain that starts and finishes here guesses past the other computer's layers

With "Start and finish on this computer" on, a split model runs its first
and last layers here and its middle on another computer, so every word cost
a round trip. This node now guesses the next few words on its own: it runs
its two ends with the other computer's layers skipped, bridging the gap
with a small stand-in its model worker learns from the hidden states that
already pass through it (what it sends out and what comes back, at every
position the reply kept). The other computer then checks the guesses in
one trip. Nothing more is downloaded, no far-layer weights are needed, and
nothing new goes over the wire.

Measured with Qwen2.5-14B Q4_K_M on two nodes of one machine: this node's
ends (layers 0-12 and 35-48) on an 8 GB laptop card, the middle (12-35) on
a processor-only node, one binary, alternating arms. Decode 1.34-1.48x with
50 ms added to the other node's sends, 1.08-1.20x with none; 33-55% of the
guesses kept. Replies part from writing one word at a time only at
near-ties, checked against llama.cpp (worst rank 2-3, gap under half a
logit, as the control's own reply).

that learns one is never batched (batching would skip the capture); its
reply joins the model's stand-in prior. The rig's prompt-file mode now
records each ask's wall time. Off switch: SWARMLLM_FAR_RUN_GUESSES=0.

hits.message:
feat(privacy): recommend prompt privacy, and say plainly what it costs

Prompt privacy is the only setting that stops the machine answering you
from reading your prompt, but nothing said so. The control read as a
neutral toggle among others, and the trade-offs were spread across two
sentences that mentioned latency and disk but not the part that matters
most: the cost grows with the length of the answer.

It is now marked Recommended wherever it can be turned on — in the chat
bar and on the model card — and the full cost is stated on the control
itself and in the setup guide: you need the first and last piece of the
model on disk, your machine does more of the work, data is exchanged with
helpers once per word so longer answers cost proportionally more time, and
the setting is per model so it can be on where it matters.

The setup guide also now says why it is off by default — it cannot route
unless you hold both ends of the model — rather than leaving that to be
inferred.

Two new strings, translated into all 21 languages. Verified in a browser
that they resolve natively rather than falling back to English.

hits.message:
fix(routing): a standby is chosen by what it costs, not by what it pings

Picking the backup for a pipeline segment ranked candidates on their health-ping
round trip, which says nothing about how fast a machine computes. On this swarm
the nodes span 0.37 to 20.45 tokens a second and nearness is unrelated to speed,
so the backup was routinely the slowest box available.

That became sharper with prompt-length routing: a long request is now correctly
steered to a machine that can read it quickly, and if that machine dropped, the
request landed on one that could not — turning seconds into minutes, with
nothing in the log saying the replacement had been chosen by a different measure
than the original.

The standby is now priced by the same cost model as the primary, prompt length
included, since it serves the same request. Local-first and region anti-affinity
still come first — a standby exists to survive a failure and those two answer
that — so this only replaces the tiebreak among equals.

Two other cost models are still prompt-blind and were before this work: the
greedy assigner used when the shortest-path search finds no route, and the
decision to hand a whole model to a nearby peer. Both are recorded in
docs/FUTURE_WORK.md rather than changed unmeasured. Also noted there and at the
call site: a pipeline reused for KV-cache affinity is not re-routed, so prompt
length is priced on the first turn of a conversation and not on later ones.

diag(routing): log what each priced route's predicted time is made of

Each finished request that was routed across computers already logs the
time the router predicted beside the time it took (predicted_ms). It now
also logs that prediction term by term: the per-step network charge,
compute, reading the prompt, the computers' queues, moving the prompt's
data and loading the model. Nothing acts on it; it makes the routing cost
model checkable from ordinary logs.

Why now (FUTURE_WORK #3): 333 such lines from the past three weeks show
the prediction's error does not follow the reply's length, which was the
working theory. It grows with the number of computers in the route: about
right for one, 2x too slow for two, 3.35x for three. The total alone cannot
say which term causes that; the terms can.

hits.message:
fix(inference): apply the shared-projection work to prompt processing too

The change that made the attention and feed-forward projections share one
conversion of their input landed on only one of the two code paths that needed
it. Generating a token used the fixed path; processing a prompt used the other
one and kept doing the redundant work -- seven conversions per layer where four
were needed. Both paths share now.

Nothing failed and no test went red. What found it was reading the per-kernel
launch count on the path that had NOT been changed: token generation reported
four conversions per layer and prompt processing still reported seven. That is
this project's most-repeated defect, a shared rule implemented per path, and it
happened on a helper written the same hour with the rule in view. The lesson is
recorded: enumerate the paths BEFORE measuring, or the measurement confirms
exactly the half you already believed.

⚠ No speed claim for this half. Prompt processing removes 9% of its kernel
launches and shows no measurable improvement -- 13 ms against 14 as a
best-of-many over 56 chunk passes -- because processing a prompt does real
arithmetic across 128 rows at a time, so the cost of issuing work is a small
share of it. Shipped for consistency and verified by count.

Also records that time-to-first-token cannot measure prompt processing here: a
repeated prompt is served from the prefix cache, so it reads about 20 ms however
slow the work actually is, and with unique prompts it still carries tokenizing,
scheduling and HTTP and disagreed with the in-worker timer about the direction
of the change.

hits.message:
Long prompts read up to 17% faster on a computer without a graphics card

Reading a long prompt on the processor slowed down as it went, because every
128-token chunk built the full table of "how much does each new word attend to
each earlier one" in memory, then read it back twice. At 5,000 words of context
that table is 61 MB per layer per chunk, and moving it through memory cost more
than the arithmetic.

Attention for several positions at once now works through the conversation in
small tiles that stay in the processor's cache - the FlashAttention technique, as
PyTorch's CPU implementation does it, split by blocks of the conversation so each
part of the cached memory is read once. Tile sizes are fixed, so results do not
depend on how many cores a machine has. Graphics-card nodes are not affected.

Measured on one binary with the old path as the control (8 threads, prompts read
in 128-token chunks as a node reads them, best of two):

- Llama-3.2-3B, 6,144-token prompt: 43.7 -> 51.1 tokens/s (+17%)
- Llama-3.2-3B, 2,048-token prompt: 53.9 -> 56.3 tokens/s (+4%)
- Qwen2.5-7B, 2,048-token prompt: 25.2 -> 27.0 tokens/s (+7%)

For reference, llama.cpp read a 6,911-token prompt at 49.9 tokens/s on the same
threads. Correctness: checked against the old path on random shapes (breaking
the chunk merge on purpose fails that test), and on a real 1,100-token pass
scored against llama.cpp the new path agrees exactly as closely as the old one.
That pass also shows a few isolated positions where both paths differ from
llama.cpp on a synthetic prompt; recorded as FUTURE_WORK #124.

hits.message:
perf(cpu): decode attention kernel over the KV cache, vectorised exp, and row-blocked prefill matmul

Three measured changes to the CPU inference path (llama-3.2-3b Q4_K_M, 4
threads, 896-token prompt, ~900-token context; prompt processing 26.0 ->
35.1 tok/s cumulative with the previous commit, decode 7.9 -> 9.7 tok/s):

- Row blocking in the tiled quantized matmul (128 rows per pass). With the
  column as the outer loop, a whole-prompt forward streamed ~3 MB of quantized
  activations from L3 for every one of thousands of columns; blocks keep them
  in L2, the weights are re-read once per block instead (negligible). Per-row
  cost is now flat from m=128 to m=896 (0.080 -> 0.083 ms Q4_K, 0.219 -> 0.227
  Q6_K); prompt processing 28.9 -> 33.3 tok/s. The microbench is generic over
  the quant type and gains a Q6_K case and m=896; the exact-equality assert
  holds for both.
- inference::decode_attn: single-position attention straight over the KV cache
  in its stored layout, one rayon task per (batch, kv head). The two batched
  matmuls it replaces cost 1.3 ms per layer at ~920 KV for ~11 MFLOP — a quarter
  of every decoded token — in GEMM packing and dispatch. Dispatched from
  standard_attention for q_len == 1 on the CPU (MHA and GQA); returns None and
  the matmul path continues for anything outside its scope. Same binary A/B/A/B
  via SWARMLLM_DECODE_ATTN=standard: 9.77/9.68 vs 7.91/7.89 tok/s (+24%).
  Tolerance-tested against the grouped-matmul composition.
- inference::fast_math: eight-lane AVX2 expf (Cephes polynomial, ~2 ulp vs
  libm, pinned by a sweep test) for the softmax rows, a fused SiLU x up op
  (one pass, no temporaries) at the three call sites, and the decode kernel's
  softmax. Every exp on the CPU path was a scalar libm call — ~540 M in the
  softmax and ~205 M in SiLU for this prompt. Prompt processing 33.3 -> 35.1.
  Not bit-identical; the fused softmax keeps its 1e-6 bound against the
  composed reference.

chore(release): v0.3.99-alpha

Long questions no longer freeze the node for minutes on processor-only
machines. The prefix cache — the memory that lets a later question skip
re-reading a prompt it has seen before — was saving dozens of overlapping
copies of itself after every long prompt, roughly 15 GB of copying for a
question a few pages long. It now saves one. Measured: repeating a long
question answers in 4 seconds instead of two minutes or more, with memory
flat where it previously climbed to 21 GB.

Failures caused by another machine going quiet mid-request now say
"temporarily unavailable — try again" instead of reporting a bug in the
node you are talking to, and the silent machine's standing in the swarm
now reflects it.

The docker run command from the README works now: the images are public
and the latest / latest-cuda labels exist and update on every release —
they had never been published.

Debian package note: updating no longer disables the service, but this
particular update is still performed by the old version's cleanup script,
so check `systemctl is-enabled swarmllm` once after it.

fix(split): a computer that has not loaded a model checks it could load its share before saying yes (#345)

When a split asks its computers whether they have room for a prompt, one
that had not loaded the model yet always said yes - and then refused when
the first piece of the prompt reached it, after the others had loaded their
parts. On a 70B split this cost about 100 s before the request failed.

Now such a computer weighs loading its share with the same arithmetic the
load itself uses (card beside processor where it has a card), and answers
no up front with how many of the asked layers would fit, so the plan is
redone at once with that figure. It reserves and loads nothing to answer.
Only the first range asked is weighed; growth of an already loaded model is
still checked when it happens.

A/B switch: SWARMLLM_PEER_LOAD_WEIGH=0. Test:
a_peer_with_no_worker_weighs_the_load_it_is_asked_for (fails with the
check removed). Also files #346: placing a large model's parts where the
memory is, which is what the 70B still needs.

perf(cpu): quantized matmul unpacks each weight column once for eight activation rows, not once per row

Prompt processing on a CPU node spent 83% of its time in the quantized matmul,
whose per-row cost was flat from 128 to 896 rows: the tiled kernel already read
each weight column once per block, but called the single-row dot product per

row. A new GgmlType::vec_dot_rows takes all rows of a column in one call; the

feat(cache): Qwen 3.5 conversations no longer re-read their whole prompt every turn

The prompt cache skipped every model with recurrent layers, so each turn of a
Qwen 3.5 conversation read the whole conversation again. A DeltaNet layer's
state cannot be cut back to a shorter prefix the way attention memory can, so
the prompt is now saved 16 tokens before it ends (as llama.cpp's context
checkpoints do: the next turn's template re-renders the last few tokens), the
prompt read pauses at that point to copy the state, and a later turn restores
it whole or not at all.

Measured on Qwen3.5-0.8B Q8_0 on the processor: the second turn of a
2,416-token conversation took 16.7 s instead of 127.6 s, with an identical
reply, on both the batched and the sequential path. These saves stay on this
computer: they are not announced to peers or exported.

hits.message:
perf(inference): a graphics card holds three times the conversation in the same memory

A conversation's memory on a graphics card now takes a third of the space.
It is kept in half precision, as llama.cpp keeps it, instead of in full
precision with a half-precision copy beside it. On an 8 GB card beside
Qwen2.5-Coder-7B that is room for about 38,000 tokens of conversation where
there was room for about 12,700, so an agent's long instructions fit beside
the model instead of being refused. Computers that run models on the
processor are unaffected.

Also fixed: a node with inference.max_seq_len_override set, which is how agent
users make room for a long prompt, kept no limit at all on its card's
conversation memory. A long prompt could fill the card and the reply then
crawled. Measured on v0.3.231 with a 15,648-token prompt: 307 s, the card at
7885 of 8192 MiB. With this change it answers in 51.5 s. A prompt that truly
does not fit is turned away at once, and a swarm sends it to another computer.
The limit was skipped by a condition left over from July, when this step still
shortened the context to fit the card.

How: layers::kv_storage is the one rule for how a layer keeps its cache. It
is asked by the cache as it is built (layers::append_to_cache, every forward
path) and by every estimate of its cost: the loader's budget, the
card/processor split planner, admission, and the bound a coordinator holds a
peer to. A peer is priced by the new features::KV_HALF_ON_CARD bit, so older
peers are priced as before. Flash attention reads the half cache in place,
the one-token decode kernel reads f16 (kernels/decode_attn.cu), and a step's
K/V is written into it in one launch (kernels/kv_append.cu). DeepSeek-2's MLA
cache stays f32, and the rule requires the attention kind so no estimate can
forget it.

Why the full-precision copy existed: it was kept on a reading of arXiv
2604.15409 as "an f16 cache diverges". That paper compares decoding with and
without a cache, both in f16. llama.cpp, the reference replies are judged
against, stores f16 by default.

Measured on an RTX 3070 Laptop, A/B in one binary (SWARMLLM_KV_F16=0 is the
old layout):
- Memory: the 7B's cache is 59 MB against 176 MB at 896 positions, 352 MB
  against 1057 MB at 6000.
- Speed: decode is level at 23.3 ms a token with 6016 positions cached.
  Prompt reading is level; with stage timers synchronised, attention took
  528 ms against 533 ms.
- Replies: 400-token greedy replies scored against llama.cpp come out the same
  on six models; Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B are word-for-word
  identical. Phi-3.5's logits, teacher-forced on the card, sit marginally
  closer to llama.cpp: median cosine 0.999828 against 0.999821.

Closes FUTURE_WORK #194; #237 re-ranked to P3. Evidence:
docs/invariants/inference.md "A card keeps its KV cache as f16" and
docs/invariants/memory.md "A card's KV budget is kept whatever the context
setting".

hits.message:
perf(split): a flowing split copies text the conversation already holds — a file edit 23 → 45 tok/s

When a reply repeats something already in the conversation (code being edited, a
document being quoted), the requester now looks up what followed the reply's last
tokens where they occurred before — in the prompt, then the reply's last 500 tokens,
the n-gram lookup's own cascade — and pushes that run under the walk's row of the
flowing tree, before the drafter's next call. The far end still draws every row, so
the reply is unchanged; only what is checked changes.

- Run length is how far back the match goes, at least the lookup's num_pred_tokens and
  at most 32 (SuffixDecoding, arXiv 2411.04975: alpha * p with alpha = 1), so a copy the
  walk keeps following runs further ahead each time. Within the guard's live budget.
- The rows reach the drafter's worker as FlowOp::Copy, which rates each by the
  drafter's OWN log-probability of that token there (the least it listed when absent),
  so a wrong copy's followers do not crowd out the drafter's own guesses.
- Between this node and its own worker only: no wire or protocol change.
- Follows inference.ngram_lookup_enabled (read live); A/B SWARMLLM_FLOW_COPY=0.

Measured on the one-card rig (385 ms, one binary, arms alternating, 400-token warm
replies): a code edit copying a 135-line file 42.1-46.7 tok/s with copies vs
22.6-24.5 without (232-263 of 400 tokens walked through copied rows; the drafter's
time 3.4-4.4 s vs 8.9-10.2); the rig's chat prompt 8.83-9.58 vs 8.72-9.66 (copies
almost all wrong, no measurable cost). Edit replies identical either way and ranked
first by llama.cpp at all 400 tokens. The same run closes the guard's owed
alternating check: no cost with no rate limit (on 8.83-9.58, off 8.79-9.82).

Tests: a_copied_run_goes_through_the_rows_the_tree_holds_and_adds_the_rest,
a_copied_run_measures_how_far_back_its_match_goes (red with the match not measured
back), a_copied_row_is_rated_by_the_drafters_own_guess (red with a copy rated as a
push). examples/split_rig.sh repeat: prompt.txt is the RIG_BODY's own user message
when it carries one.

hits.message:
fix: asking for longer conversations no longer pushes a model off your GPU

Two settings worked against each other. A coding assistant sends its whole tool
list as a system prompt before you type anything — one measured at about 5000
tokens — so the shipped 4096-token limit rejected its very first message, with
an error telling the caller to send a shorter prompt. The prompt is not theirs
to shorten.

Raising the limit was the documented fix, and it had a hidden cost: the check
that decides whether a model fits on the graphics card charged for the full
conversation length up front. Raising the limit therefore made models stop
fitting, and they were loaded on the processor instead. A report on 2026-08-17
measured that as six and a half minutes to read one prompt, and the machine
reaching its temperature warning.

That charge is no longer needed. Since 2026-08-08 memory for a conversation is
taken as the conversation grows, and every step checks the free memory it is
about to claim, refusing politely and letting another machine take the request
if there is not enough. The worst case is enforced where the memory is actually
taken, so pre-paying for it when the model loads bought nothing and cost people
their graphics card.

So the fit check now prices a normal working conversation rather than the
longest one permitted, and the default conversation length rises to 8192. A user
who never changed the setting is charged exactly what they were charged before.

The processor-side check is deliberately NOT capped the same way: nothing bounds
a processor worker's memory while it runs, so that estimate stays the only place
the ceiling is priced at all. Erring high there refuses a load; erring low makes
the whole machine swap.

The "conversation too long" message now names the setting that fixes it.

perf(split): a reply split between two distant computers answers up to 18% faster

tokens at a time, and keeps sending while earlier checks are still on their way.

at no cost in speed. Each caller of the drafter now names its own cut.

long session, held four of 16 replies up 10-59 s on this project's test

context every machine of the chain serves.

hits.message:
fix: prompt privacy no longer strands a model on your processor

A model too big for the graphics card was handed to a nearby machine — unless
prompt privacy was on for it, in which case the request stayed put and ran
slowly. That was wrong, and it was the common case: privacy turns itself on for
any model whose first and last pieces a node holds, which is every model this
decision can apply to. So the feature shipped yesterday almost never ran.

Privacy does not rule out using another machine. It rules out that machine
seeing your prompt — and the "boomerang" this project already builds is exactly
the arrangement for that: the first and last layers run here, so the text you
typed and the words chosen in reply never leave, while everything in between
runs on the other machine as encrypted intermediate values.

Verified across two real nodes with privacy at its default: three segments
assembled — first layer here, layers 1 to 27 on the peer, last layer back here —
and the peer's log confirms it ran those 26 of 28 layers. Correct answer.

Standing aside from the local shortcut was not enough on its own. Asked to route
this, the general search answers "run all of it here", which satisfies the
privacy rule at no network cost because nothing in its costing knows this machine
is about to fall back to its processor. Rather than teach it — which is what the
reverted attempt did, and it spoiled every other route — the arrangement is built
directly, the same as the whole-model hand-off beside it.

The split is deliberately lopsided: one layer at each end and everything else
away. Those two exist only to keep the promise, and each one kept here runs on
the processor this is trying to get off.

hits.message:
docs: research the case for chaining pipeline hops peer to peer

Records why an eight-shard model currently pays sixteen round trips per token
where it could pay two, and why that is a topology choice rather than a limit.

The prior art is decisive and it is not theoretical. Petals runs a 176B model
across fourteen volunteer machines on the open internet by having each server
forward activations to the next rather than back to the client, and its measured
latency sensitivity shows the property we lack: raising client latency by 100ms
cost about 211ms per step, which is two round trips regardless of how long the
chain was. Under our design the same change would cost that much per segment. A
second paper reaches the same architecture independently and keeps the first and
last layers on the client, which is already how our prompt privacy works.

Petals also answers the objection that looks fatal. Failover does not need the
coordinator holding every boundary: the client keeps what it sent and can rebuild
a replacement server's cache from it.

The design here is deliberately an optimisation with a fallback rather than a
replacement. A hop that cannot be made directly relays through the coordinator,
which is exactly today's cost for that hop alone, and any chain failure retries
the whole request the old way. So a swarm where only some peers can reach each
other still gets most of the benefit, and nothing is ever worse than it is now.

Names the part with real unknowns rather than glossing it: chaining makes the
latency between two PEERS the thing that matters, and we do not measure that at
all today.

Prices the two alternatives so they are not revisited from scratch. Tensor
parallelism has a 9.4 second per token floor at this distance from the speed of
light alone. Sequence parallelism is bandwidth-bound at roughly 2.2 Gbps per
extra node, so moving machines closer does not help it, and the prompt length
cancels out of that ratio entirely.

Recommends the cheaper win first: speculative verification already batches five
tokens into one round trip and is off by default, which divides the same cost by
five with no wire change.

hits.message:
fix(trust): a peer that returns garbage no longer earns trust for it

A node that took part in a distributed request was credited trust the
moment the pipeline returned, and the check on what it had actually sent
ran afterwards on one result in twenty. The arithmetic that produced is
+0.01 every time against -0.1 one time in twenty, so a peer whose output
was always unusable still gained +0.005 a request on average and climbed
to the maximum trust score. Reported on issue #21, and reproduced here as
a test that reads 1.0 with the fix reverted.

That mattered because trust is not decorative: it decides which peers may
be handed a prompt in cleartext, and it orders the list of candidates a
request is routed through. A peer could ratchet itself up both by doing
its job badly.

The check now runs on every distributed result and the credit is paid
behind it. It was never expensive enough to be worth sampling — it is
three assertions over a reply already in hand, and the 5% rate had been
borrowed from credit-transaction verification, where the cost is real.

Also in this change:

- Trust is recorded once per request, not once per segment. A peer given
  three segments of one pipeline was previously paid three times for one
  piece of behaviour, so taking more of a pipeline ratcheted faster.
- A malformed result now pays nobody, and only docks a peer when it was
  the only one that served the request. Docking every participant let one
  bad node lower the trust of every honest node it shared a pipeline with,
  which — since candidates are ordered by trust — is a way to demote
  competitors rather than collateral damage.
- Removed an anti-gaming helper that ignored its argument, recorded
  nothing, and returned a constant that was only logged, next to the real
  penalty it had already applied. The log read as though two penalties
  had landed.

What this does not do: the checks are well-formedness assertions, not
verification. A peer returning fluent, confident, wrong tokens passes all
of them and still earns trust. Detecting that needs the same work computed
twice and compared, as BOINC's validator does, and there is no ground truth
to compare against here today. The limit is written up in the module and in
docs/FUTURE_WORK.md rather than implied away by the name "spot check".

Left open deliberately, in docs/FUTURE_WORK.md: the bar deciding who may
read a plaintext prompt sits at exactly the score an unknown peer starts
on, so it excludes peers with a recorded history and admits everyone else.
Raising it changes routing policy — on a small swarm it can make a model
unservable — so it needs a decision rather than a quiet patch.

hits.message:
fix(tokenizer): Llama 3 prompts were costing twice the tokens they should

Every Llama-3/3.1/3.2 model file names its text-splitting rule 'llama-bpe'.
That name was not recognised, so it fell through to a plain whitespace split,
which strands each space as its own token instead of attaching it to the word
that follows — the form these models are trained on. 'The quick brown fox jumps
over the lazy dog' came to 19 tokens where the reference tokenizer gives 9.

Reading the prompt is most of the work in a long request, so this roughly
doubled the cost of the most widely used model family on the network, and fed
those models text in a shape they had never seen in training.

Verified against a reference tokenizer built from the same vocabulary and
merges, over fifteen varied samples: fourteen previously differed, 43% more
tokens overall; all fifteen now match exactly, 1.00x.

Two further defects in the same code:

- The Qwen rule actually held the Llama-3 pattern, grouping digits up to three
  at a time where Qwen expects one.
- Text that a rule did not match was dropped rather than kept, so runs of
  spaces between words could disappear from the prompt outright.

An unrecognised rule now falls back to the general byte-level splitter rather
than a whitespace split, and warns with the name so the next unknown family is
visible instead of silent. Every name the reference implementation knows is
mapped, and rules that apply several patterns in sequence are supported.

Six tests, each checked to fail without its corresponding fix.

hits.message:
docs(cpu): the repack's 1.8x does not survive our own kernel

The prompt-processing entry named llama.cpp's Q4_K block-interleaved
repack as the next step at a reported 1.8-1.9x. That figure was measured
against their baseline, which did per-row dots. We already added multi-row
amortisation, and it took prompt processing 26 to 37 tokens a second, so
part of the win that number describes is already banked here.

Counting what is left: at four rows per pass the kernel issues about 148
operations per block for 1024 multiply-accumulates. Interleaving eight
columns shares the activation loads and nothing else — the nibble unpack
is weight data, and the multiply-accumulates are the irreducible work — so
it lands near 120 operations, about 1.23x. A two-column variant needing no
repack at all prices near 1.12x.

That is a storage-layout change, the loss of the bit-exactness assertion
that makes the current kernels safe to modify, a load-time repack cost and
fallout across gather_rows, dequantize and the GPU path, bought for
roughly 1.2x.

Records the cheap way to settle it before committing: hoist the activation
loads out of the row loop so they are reused across rows. It is
numerically wrong but it prices exactly what those loads cost, and if it
does not show about 20% then the repack cannot either.

hits.message:
fix(inference): a temperature-0 reply on the processor is the same every time, prompt cache or not

The same greedy request gave one text on its first run and another on every
repeat (Llama-3.2-3B on the processor, both rounds of a restart); with the
prompt cache off all eight replies agreed. A cache hit skips the cached
prefix, so the last prompt token runs alone as a decode step, and the decode
and prompt attention kernels summed a row differently — the prompt kernel
even split a row by the length of the forward it was in.

Both kernels now compute a row with one arithmetic (inference::attn_rows):
only the keys the row can see, in fixed 256-key chunks of absolute position,
each chunk's scores, softmax and sum in one defined order of fused
multiply-adds, the chunks folded in order by the online merge — the batch
invariance Thinking Machines describe and SGLang's fixed split-KV. Windowed
layers pass the absolute position of their first key.

Verified: eight replies one text across a restart with the cache hit on
every repeat; a row read alone and inside the prompt is bit-identical (58/58
logit rows); the reply scores against llama.cpp as before (197/200 rank 1,
worst rank 2). Speed, best of 2 in one binary: 6,144-token prompt 58.2 tok/s
(was 56.6), 2,048-token 64.2 (63.0), decode level. The direct gemm
dependency is gone. A graphics card's kernels still differ (FUTURE_WORK #313).

Closes FUTURE_WORK #179.

hits.message:
perf(cpu): a short block of tokens is no longer treated as a whole prompt

A forward pass over a handful of tokens fell into a hole between two
optimised paths. Every processor fast path was gated on the query length
being exactly one, so asking for two tokens instead of one lost the
grouped attention path, the single-position attention kernel and the
narrow thread pool simultaneously, and the work was handed to the
machinery built for whole prompts.

Measured on llama-3.2-3b at ~912 tokens of context: a 2-token forward
cost 7.8x a 1-token one, for one extra token, with attention alone going
8.5 ms to 241 ms. It is now 1.8x. Four tokens went from 9.5x to 2.5x,
eight from 11x to 3.3x — roughly 4.5x, 3.8x and 3.3x faster than before.

Two causes, both fixed here:

- Grouped-query attention read the key/value cache at its stored width
  only for a single token, and expanded it to full width otherwise. The
  regrouping works for any query length; it just needs the mask tiled to
  match. It now applies whenever the score matrix fits in one pass, which
  covers single tokens, short blocks and ordinary prompt chunks, and
  allocates no more than the path it replaces. Longer blocks still take
  the existing blocked path unchanged.

- The phase predicate asked "is this exactly one token?" when the
  question that decides the thread count is "are these matmuls bound by
  memory or by arithmetic?". A short block re-reads the same weights a
  single token does; it just carries a few more activation rows. Measured
  with examples/qmatmul_bench, the narrow pool wins at every width up to
  32 — by 1.4x to 2.2x — and draws level at 128, so the boundary is not
  sharp and 32 sits at the last width with a measured margin. Prompt
  chunks keep the wide pool they were measured on.

Who this reaches today: the last chunk of any prompt whose length is not
a multiple of the chunk size, and ordinary prompt chunks, which gained a
consistent 8% (2210 ms to 2055 ms for 128 tokens on a warm cache). It
also removes the reason speculative decoding could not pay on a
processor — a verify block had to beat a cost 8x-11x its own size, and
now needs about 2.5 of 4 tokens accepted.

Single-token decode is deliberately untouched and measured unchanged
(15.2-16.3 tok/s across both arms, no systematic difference), as is
prompt processing.

The grouping test now sweeps query lengths 1, 2, 4, 8 and 33 against a
REAL causal mask. It used to pass a permissive one, which cannot detect
the failure that matters: with nothing masked, a mask tiled in the wrong
order — repeats and positions transposed — computes the same answer.
Verified the new test catches exactly that by transposing the tiling and
watching it fail at a query length of 2.

docs: a speed-up shipped in v0.3.175 is not actually running

Requests that a node answers itself were meant to take a direct path that
reuses the work already done for a repeated prompt. Checking a full day of
logs, that path never once ran: it is switched on only for a model the node

what happens the first time anyone asks for it — never qualifies.

every time, and requests are answered one token at a time instead of in

hits.message:
fix(routing): stop sending a model's middle abroad one token at a time

A node that holds a model and would run it on its own processor could hand
the middle of that model to a peer on another continent, and price the
hand-off as though the peer were running the whole thing. Those are very
different costs: a peer given the WHOLE model is entered once for the entire
request and decodes remotely, while a middle segment is entered again for
every token generated. The cost model has always known that and said so; the
delegation gate was asking it about the wrong shape.

Measured on the release pair: a processor-only node holding llama-3.2-1b
whole, asked for a 16-token prompt and one token of output, shipped the
model's middle to a machine 496 ms away and took 9.1 seconds. Its own
processor decodes that model at 4.28 tokens a second.

Prompt privacy is on by default whenever a node holds both ends of a model,
and that is exactly the shape it produces — so this was reachable on ordinary
settings, on small models, with nothing in the log to suggest anything was
wrong. The request completed and returned the right answer, slowly.

The gate now prices the shape it is about to assign, through one helper the
gate, the line that logs its verdict, and the privacy-cost estimate all
share. The same peer offered the whole model is still taken; that is the
point of the feature and there is a test holding it.

SWARMLLM_DELEGATE_SHAPE_PRICE=0 restores the old pricing for anyone who needs
to compare the two behaviours in the field.

hits.message:
docs(gpu): re-check the half-precision KV copy against its new purpose

Moving grouped-query decode onto the standard kernel retired the reason
the f16 KV mirror was kept: it existed so flash DECODE would not convert
the whole history every token, and decode no longer calls flash on either
head layout.

The mirror stays, because re-measuring found it is still worth its cost
for a different reason — it is now read by prompt chunks after the first,
which go to flash, and without it each chunk re-converts the whole
history. That is O(history) per chunk and so quadratic over a prompt, and
the measurements show exactly that shape: one 128-token chunk on a warm
prefix costs 4% more without it at ~960 tokens of context, 9% at ~2048
and 20% at ~4096. Long prompts are where agentic clients live.

Decode showed no resolvable difference either way, so the 50% of extra
KV memory it costs now buys prompt processing rather than generation.
That memory is a hard limit — admission charges and refuses on it — so
the note says plainly that if the chunked-prefill reader ever goes away
too, this should be switched off rather than left standing.

No behaviour change: same predicate, corrected reasoning, and
SWARMLLM_KV_MIRROR to A/B it inside one binary. A right answer resting on
a stale reason is what let the decode routing go a week out of date in
the first place.

hits.message:
docs: the warning about what prompt privacy costs has never actually reached anyone

Keeping your prompt private means the first and last steps of the model stay on
your own computer, and only the middle is sent away. That is a real guarantee
and it is not being changed here. But it costs one extra network round trip for
every word generated, so the further away the computer doing the middle is, the
slower the reply — and on a measurement today a reply that takes 5 seconds
without it took 54 seconds with it.

A decision was taken in September to leave that cost in place and tell people
about it, so anyone seeing a slow reply would know why and could switch it off
for that model. The telling was written and shipped. It has never once run.

The notice is only produced on a planning path the node stops using as soon as
a model has more than one other computer able to serve it — which is the
ordinary case, and the only case where any of this happens at all. Four days of
this machine's records contain not one occurrence.

Nothing is broken in the privacy itself, and no routing changes here. What
changed is the written record: the entry claiming this was "communicated" now
says plainly that it was not, carries today's measurements, and names what is
actually missing — a cost figure for the route finally chosen, rather than the
one that was only considered.

Re-measured at 9 to 14 times slower rather than the 6 originally recorded, and
the underlying quantity is not a multiplier at all: it tracks the round-trip
time to whichever computer holds the middle, so nothing bounds it.

Worth knowing: this only affects models your computer has finished downloading
in full. A machine holding none of a model never sees it.

hits.message:
fix(routing): a split asks its peers about room for the prompt before reading it, and re-plans around one that has too little

When a split ran part of a model on a peer whose memory for conversations was
too small for the prompt, the peer found out only when its part of the prompt
arrived, after every computer before it had already read its share. The
request then failed or re-planned without that peer at all, even when most of
its layers would have fit. On the two-node rig's tight case the previous
release answered after 132.8 s, with the peer refusing two forwards. This
build answers in 1.4 s: the peer refuses one question in 3 ms, and no work is
wasted.

How it works: before the prompt pass, the coordinator sends each peer whose
segment runs after other work a PromptAdmissionAsk. It is sent only to peers
that advertise feature bit 25, so older nodes are never asked. A "no" carries
the number of layers that would fit, and the re-plan holds that peer to it
instead of barring it. A peer that does not answer within ~1-5 s is treated as
"go ahead", which is exactly the old behaviour.

The asked peer only weighs the question. It never reserves room for it (the
same split vLLM makes between can_allocate and allocate). The question goes to
the worker under a fresh id, with a required "only weigh" argument, and it
holds, frees and stamps nothing. Questions are rationed to 12 a minute per
peer and 60 a minute in all.

Two security-review passes shaped this. The first design admitted the prompt
under the asker's request id, which would have let a peer cancel a live
request or hold this node's conversation memory. The second pass fixed four
smaller issues:
- a question kept a model from ever unloading;
- a late answer could settle a re-plan's question;
- the refusal arithmetic over peer-named ranges could overflow;
- each question cost a task and a log line.
Each fix has a test that fails without it.

The coordinator also gives a peer's refusal one fixed error class, whatever
the peer wrote, and repeats its words bounded and on one line.

FUTURE_WORK #252 (b) (2), moved to Closed. Also recorded: the #91 traffic
re-read, where the Kademlia answers fell 2.3x, not the expected 12x; the next
step is to count inbound requests by kind.

hits.message:
chore(release): v0.3.78-alpha

Twelve fixes, almost all in how a question is prepared before a model ever sees
it. Llama 3 models, the most widely used family on the network, were being sent
prompts that cost about twice what they should and were shaped differently from
anything the models were trained on: the rule for splitting their text into
words was not recognised, their system prompt was included twice, and they were
told the date was 26 July 2024.

Also: telling a model not to use its tools now works, tool calls carry
identifiers that are actually unique, asking for word-by-word confidence scores
says they are unavailable instead of silently omitting them, choosing the
fastest model no longer picks one that has to be loaded first, a conversation
resumed after an update no longer restarts from the wrong place, and the network
status panel is no longer in English for the other twenty languages.

Nothing here needed a bug report. The tokeniser and the prompt builder were
checked against the reference implementations everyone else uses, from the same
model files, and made to agree with them exactly.

hits.message:
fix: a node no longer overfills its graphics card when another program starts using it, and guessing ahead steps aside where it would slow a reply

Two defects found while deciding whether to turn speculation across computers
(DSD) on by default, both measured on two nodes sharing one machine:

- The check that decides whether a model fits on the graphics card used the
  card's free memory as it stood when the node STARTED. Memory another program
  took later was invisible, so a model could be put on a card with no room left;
  here the node's workers then refused every prompt. It now reads the card at
  the moment it decides (released v0.3.212 behaves the same way).
- With the small guessing model slow relative to a fast link, speculation made
  replies six times slower (6.8 vs 38-42 tokens/s), because it could never stop
  guessing. It can now choose not to guess where guessing does not pay, remembers
  that for the next request, and no longer counts the guessing model's first,
  cold call as the cost of a guess. Over long links, where guessing pays, nothing
  changes.

The earlier worry that speculation cost a split its standby machines (FUTURE_WORK
#140) was the test rig: with the guessing model on the card, standbys and
failover behaved as without it. Speculation stays off by default for now.

hits.message:
fix(diagnostics): also say when the model itself ended the turn at once

Completes the previous change. A reply that comes back with nothing has
two possible causes and a client cannot see either: a stop sequence in
the request matched immediately, or the model emitted end-of-turn
straight away. Both look identical from outside — `finish_reason: "stop"`,
HTTP 200, a blank or one-word answer — and the difference is precisely
what tells someone whether to look at their client's `stop` values or at
the prompt.

The second case is now reported too, and says what it points at: the chat
template for that model, and whether the rendered prompt ends where the
model expects to answer.

A caller who asks for one token and gets one is not a fault, so the token
budget is part of the condition — otherwise this would fire on every
deliberate single-token request, which is how a useful warning becomes
noise. Verified against that control, and against a stop sequence
trimming the tail of a real answer, which also stays quiet.

Also records two prefill hypotheses that were measured and did not
survive, so they are not re-derived:

- Prefill chunking was NOT costing 2-3x on a GPU. Raising the chunk from
  128 to 512 or 2048 changes nothing (1983 / 1803 / 1896 tok/s at ~2370
  tokens), and all three match the benchmark's own throughput. The gap
  that suggested otherwise came from comparing the live node — connected
  to the swarm, several models resident, serving — against an idle
  benchmark. The arms differed by machine state, not by chunk size.
- The prefix cache IS working for the agentic pattern, which was the
  bigger worry: a ~4200-token system prompt costs 11.94s cold, 0.12s
  repeated, and 0.25s with a new user turn on the same system prompt.

hits.message:
docs: GPU measurement says ragged batching is not worth building

The plan was to decide this on a GPU rather than from the CPU result, since
batching only pays when generation is limited by memory bandwidth. Measured
on an RTX 3070 with a 3B model fully on the card: four times the work
returns 23% more throughput, near-flat and essentially the same as CPU.

So the feature is not worth building on this evidence. The design sketch
stays for anyone who wants it later, but nothing here justifies the work.

Also records how the number was got, because the first two attempts were
wrong in opposite directions: repeating the same prompt across trials
measured the prompt cache rather than batching and overstated the gain,
while using freshly worded prompts of differing lengths measured the
sequential fallback and understated it. A trustworthy comparison needs
fresh wording at identical length. Background load produced threefold
variance within one configuration on top of that.

Caveats are stated rather than buried: one consumer card, nearly full, so a
larger card with headroom may differ — and the measurement worth taking
before revisiting is where the time goes at batch one, since a fixed
per-request cost would cap any batching gain.

perf(qwen3.5): a Q8_0 upload's gates are one launch on the card, not five

weights (ssm_alpha, ssm_beta) in Q8_0. Up to 8 rows on a graphics card, those

each DeltaNet layer quantized the activation twice, ran two int8 products and
then the gates kernel. The new kernel is bit for bit the existing f32 one over
the dequantized weights, and no f32 copy is made at load, so no memory budget

6.3 at 2 rows. The gain is small because a captured level is limited by the

takes 8.4-9.2. SWARMLLM_SSM_GATES=matmuls restores the old path.

96 tokens each, teacher-forced on the card). The new path agrees with

hits.message:
fix(memory): a Gemma model is placed by the memory its cache will really use

Before loading a model, a node weighs it: whether it goes on the graphics
card, how much of it fits beside the processor, and how many layers to offer
a plan. Every one of those charged each layer the widest layer's cache at
every position. On Gemma 2, 3 and 4 most layers only look back over a window,
and since #281 (1)/(2) their caches keep only that window. So the estimates
overstated these models: Gemma 4 12B's admission was priced at 3 GiB of cache
where the worker holds 1.1. A model that fits could be sent to the processor,
split more than it needs to be, or offered to fewer plans.

Now the estimates read the same per-layer layout the loader builds its own
budget from (`kv_budget::KvLayout`, read once off the header). It covers which
layers keep a cache, each layer's own shape and storage, and a sliding-window
layer charged its window plus the widest prompt forward its worker reads
(`prefill_pacer::widest_prompt_forward`, the worker's own rule). Admission's
footprint, the segment cost curve and the card/processor split all price
through it (`VramFootprintInputs::kv`), so the estimate and the worker cannot
disagree about one model. DeepSeek-2's MLA cache is now priced as the loader
keeps it rather than at its grouped shape.

Tests: a_layout_prices_each_layer_by_its_own_shape_and_window (Gemma 4 12B's
real per-layer keys) and admission_charges_a_windowed_layer_its_window (a
header read through the pool) both fail with the window pricing turned off.

A peer's bound on a coordinator still charges every position; it stays open
as FUTURE_WORK #281.

hits.message:
test inference across the swarm on purpose, and stop a slow peer costing you the whole request

Two changes, both from testing inference end to end on the live node today.

A request whose first attempt waited on a peer that went silent had no
attempt left when the second one was refused. The scheduler's own log says
"a peer may refuse and the request will re-plan"; nothing kept that promise,
so a model spread across other machines could fail after two minutes quoting
a memory shortfall on the machine that was never going to run it. A peer that
refuses promptly now earns one more re-plan. A peer that goes quiet earns
nothing, so a request can never spend two deadlines waiting on silence.

The new `swarm_route` field on /v1/chat/completions plans a single request as
though the swarm's holdings were different — every layer on other computers,
or a named computer left out. It exists because replication pulls every node
towards holding whole models, which is good for reliability and hides the
split-across-machines path that most needs testing. It only ever narrows this
node's own choices, never leaves the machine, and is not a protocol change.

Verified live: the same model and prompt ran locally with no override, on a
peer in Thailand with the local parts released, and on a peer in Belgium when
that first peer was excluded as well.

hits.message:
perf(gpu): prompts and replies stop taking the slow attention kernel

Two separate places where a graphics card was handed the kernel that had
been measured as the slower one for that shape. Both are GPU-only; CPU
nodes are untouched.

**Long prompts.** A prompt is processed in chunks (128 tokens by
default), and every chunk after the first attends over the history
before it. That shape was being diverted away from flash attention on
the stated grounds that its causal mask "can't be expressed via
flash_attn's boolean causal flag". It can: the kernel we ship computes
`col_idx_limit_right = row_idx + 1 + max_seqlen_k - max_seqlen_q`
(vendor/candle-flash-attn/kernels/mask.h), which is the same predicate
`SplitExecutor::causal_mask` builds by hand. The two masks are the same
function, so the diversion bought nothing and cost the expansion of the
whole key/value history on every chunk of every GQA model.

Measured on an RTX 3070, A/B inside one binary, llama-3.2-3b:
a 128-token chunk on a ~900-token prefix falls 116 ms -> 76 ms (1.52x),
and a 4-token block 48 ms -> 21 ms (2.26x). A benchmark that processes a
prompt in a single call never sees this, which is how it survived — the
shape that regressed is one only real traffic produces.

**Replies.** Grouped-query decode was routed to flash because the
alternative rebuilt the expanded key/value cache on every token. That
work was removed in August (grouped_gqa_decode_attention, c4cc3b16) and
the routing rule outlived the reason for it by a week. Re-measured on
the same card, the alternative now wins at every context length and by
more as context grows. End to end that is ~6% at 4120 tokens of context
and too small to resolve at ~900 — the isolated call reads far larger
because production hands flash a half-precision cache that the isolated
benchmark deliberately withholds. Both numbers are recorded; the
end-to-end one is what a reply actually takes.

Multi-head decode, and prefill for every head layout, are unchanged.

Also here, because the investigation needed them:

- flash_matches_standard_on_a_warm_prefix pins the claim the first
  change rests on — flash and the explicit mask agree to ~6e-4 relative
  across five prompt/history shapes, against an F16 rounding budget of
  5e-2. A mask misalignment moves whole rows and lands orders of
  magnitude outside it.
- The kernel-pricing benchmark now reports its whole table before
  failing rather than aborting on the first bad row. It aborted at the
  smallest context and printed nothing about where the crossover had
  moved to, which is the only thing that table exists to show.
- Its flash arm runs without the half-precision cache, so its ratios are
  an upper bound on the penalty and not an estimate of it. Said at the
  measurement, since reading a production cost off it is exactly the
  mistake this round nearly repeated (#266).
- examples/prefill_bench gains SWARM_BENCH_SPEC_WIDTHS, which prices a
  K-token forward against a 1-token one at the same history depth. The
  arms are interleaved because the history grows during the sweep and a
  blocked layout measures that drift instead of the width.

hits.message:
fix: a moment of backpressure no longer discards the rest of a reply

Inbound reply tokens are handed to the waiting request over a bounded channel.
A full channel and a closed one were handled identically, and the handling was
to delete the channel — so a consumer that fell behind for an instant did not
lose one token, it lost every remaining token of that answer. Each later one
arrived, found no receiver, and was dropped without a word.

They are opposite situations. Closed means the request is over and the entry
should go. Full means the consumer is momentarily behind, which is a reason to
wait, not a reason to tear the reply down. A delayed token is now delivered out
of band instead of discarded, which is safe here precisely because the
reassembler sequences by token id — handing one to a task to deliver cannot
reorder the answer.

It logged at debug, and nodes run at info, so this was invisible in every real
log. It was also the one line that could have said whether a truncated reply
was the network losing packets or this node dropping them, which is a question
two days of measurement could not settle from the outside. It logs at warn now
and says which token and which request.

Also adds an opt-in for the structural problem underneath the routing work: a
node holding a complete model serves it locally without consulting the router
at all, so eight concurrent requests all stayed on one GPU while a peer
advertising twenty tokens a second sat idle, per-request throughput falling
from 36 to 7.5. No cost model can reach that, because nothing asks the
question.

It ships off by default and should stay off until two things are measured.
Whether shedding wins at all: aggregate throughput kept RISING with concurrency
on that GPU because batching works, so a node degrading per-request is not the
same as a node that should stop taking work, and a distant peer adds a round
trip that may cost more than it saves. And the prompt path: the local fast path
and the router build prompts through different code, the divergence behind two
earlier defects, and it cannot be checked by comparing generated text because
temperature zero with a seed does not reproduce here. Compare the rendered
prompt.

Both API surfaces ask one shared question rather than each carrying the rule,
since a rule implemented on one path and forgotten on the other is this
project's most repeated defect.

hits.message:
docs: measure how much CPU headroom is left, and close off two dead ends

Token generation is bandwidth-bound at about 69% of this machine's measured
memory roofline, with 72% of the time in the quantized matmul moving the weights.
Faster arithmetic will not move it much; fewer bytes per token or more tokens per
weight read would.

Thread count pulls the two phases in opposite directions: generation peaks at 4
and is 2.2x worse at 16, while prompt processing keeps improving to at least 6.
The shipped default lands on the generation optimum. Giving prompt processing its
own larger pool is worth about 1.18x at no cost to generation, and is written up
as open rather than attempted, since it restructures the hottest path.

Self-speculative decoding measured 1.82 tok/s against 6.01 with it off -- the
draft is essentially never accepted, so each cycle pays for a draft and a full
verify and gets one token. Recorded so it is not re-tried blind; it was worth one
re-test because the tiled matmul made its verify pass much cheaper.

hits.message:
fix(inference): long prompts no longer stall for minutes while the prefix cache snapshots them

The cross-request prefix cache captured a full KV copy at EVERY 64-token
block boundary after a long prefill — quadratic in prompt length. One
2.9k-token prompt on a 3B model copied ~15 GB of KV and held the request
for 80 s to 3.5 min between reading the prompt and answering (gotcha
#312, pre-existing since the cache shipped), ballooning worker memory to
21 GB over a handful of long requests.

Inserts now store ONE snapshot at the full prompt length; lookups narrow
a longer entry to the shared prefix at hit time — the same primitive the
cross-node export path always used — so partial-prefix reuse is intact
and now hits at ANY shared length, not just block boundaries. Repeating
an identical prompt skips the copy entirely and, new, actually HITS the
cache (an exact repeat previously missed outright).

Measured: insert at 2150 tokens 9.13 s -> 0.24 s (38x, no longer
quadratic); end to end on a real CPU node, a repeated 2k-token request
went 115.5 s -> 4.1 s with worker memory flat at 3.7 GB across three
long requests. The announce manifest and cross-node prefix serving are
unchanged.

hits.message:
fix(vision): Gemma 3 reads each picture as a whole, as llama.cpp does

Gemma 3 was trained to look at a picture all at once: every part of the
picture sees every other part. SwarmLLM read the picture in order, like
text, so each part saw only the parts before it. On a simple test image
(a red circle, a blue square and a green stripe on black) the model
described a striped tricolour flag; it now names the shapes.

How: the computer coordinating a request works out where each picture
sits in the prompt and sends those positions with the prompt to every
computer holding part of the model. Each one lets a picture's rows see
each other while the text around them stays in order (Gemma 3's
windowed layers keep their window). The positions travel in a new,
sealed field of the layer request, sent only to computers that
advertise the picture feature (bit 26, not yet in a release). Every
computer taking part must have it; an older one is skipped and the
request is planned again. A picture is never split between two pieces
of a prompt.

Verified on a real request (gemma-3-4b, processor, isolated node) by
scoring each reply through llama.cpp's own image path
(examples/score_image_reply_against_reference.cpp): 95.5% and 97.3% of
the reply's words are llama.cpp's first choice and every other one is a
near-tie, against 87.3% and 90.7% with far misses before.
SWARMLLM_IMAGE_BOTH_WAYS=0 restores the old reading for comparison.

FUTURE_WORK #115 (2b).

hits.message:
fix(privacy): local_embedding_privacy works, and refuses rather than send token ids

The config-file setting inference.local_embedding_privacy makes this computer
turn the prompt into the model's first-layer input itself whenever another
computer may run the model's first part, so that computer is sent those
numbers instead of token ids. It had never worked on a real node:

- The embedder opened shard_000.bin as a whole GGUF file. A part is raw
  tensor data (the header is gguf_header.bin), so every load failed with
  "unknown magic", the setting did nothing, and the prompt went out as
  token ids.
- Had it loaded, the prompt pass was sent at the prompt's length instead of
  position 0, which would have garbled every reply (and dropped a Gemma 3
  picture's attention spans).
- The speculative split paths (DSD, draft, n-gram) never checked it.

Now the embedder is the first segment's own loader asked for no layers
(load_model_range, shared with the model worker), loaded when a request
first needs it; its rows equal the first segment's bit for bit. The pass
starts at 0. It is used only where the first layers, or a stand-in for
layer 0, may run on another computer; a first part run here reads token ids
as before, since an embedded one skipped the LoRA adapter, tensor-parallel
and split prompt-cache paths. Where this computer cannot embed, such a
request is refused with EmbeddingPrivacyUnavailable, a new error whose
message and hint (in all 21 languages) name this setting rather than "Start
and finish on this computer". The fast paths stand aside for such a plan,
and no tensor-parallel group takes an embedded first part.

The HTTP forward to a computer in your pool, for a model this computer does
not know, hands the request over whole and asked neither privacy setting,
while the libp2p hand-off and the led split asked both. All three now ask
one question (SharedState::privacy_refuses_a_whole_hand_off); the forward is
refused with the setting's own message.

Rig (Llama 3.2 3B split across two nodes, n-gram off): replies with the
setting on are byte-identical to replies with it off, in both topologies,
and score 116/120 and 119/120 rank-1 against llama.cpp. Each new test fails
with its fix turned off.

The docs claimed the setting makes the prompt "harder to invert". It does
not: what is sent is one row of the model's own embedding table per token,
which the receiving computer maps back exactly. The docs, config comment and
book now say it keeps token ids off the wire and does not hide the prompt.

Also in the 0.3.245 notes: a picture sent through the Anthropic API to a
model that cannot read pictures is now refused with a message, as on the
OpenAI API, where it used to be dropped silently.

FUTURE_WORK #316.

hits.message:
perf(qwen35): undo a wrong guess by replaying the words that were right (#228)

Qwen 3.5 guessing ahead on one computer gets faster: a check that
rejects a guess is now taken back into, instead of thrown away whole.

Qwen 3.5's DeltaNet layers keep a running summary of the conversation,
not a list of positions, so a rejected guess cannot simply be cut off.
Until now the whole check was undone and its accepted words read again
at the head of the next one. Each check now keeps its inputs (the
convolution's inputs, q, k, v, g and beta: 64 KB a row a layer on the
4B, against 2 MB for a copy of the state), and a truncate into the
check replays the accepted rows from the state the check read, through
the same kernel a step uses — bit for bit the state the check passed
(SsmState::rewind_to, qwen35::replay_rows; the idea of Dao AI Lab's
ReplaySSM). On a card the rows live in fixed buffers made outside any
graph capture. Prompt passes keep none.

The local guess count also stopped giving up early. A cost line fitted
from checks of one width has no slope, so a two-word check was priced
like an eleven-word one and guessing was switched off for 20-40 rounds;
the old re-read had hidden this by varying the widths. Until a second
width is timed, a check is now priced through the step's known cost
(CheckCost::predict_beside_a_step), and a conversation's first check on
the card, which also makes those buffers, no longer sets the price
(DecodeGraph::note_not_ready).

Measured (release build, RTX 3070 laptop + its processor, 96-token
replies, ids identical to one word at a time on the processor):
processor 4B story 10.4 -> 15.9-17.0 tok/s (13.8-14.5 before this
change), 0.8B code 29-32 -> 33.4-33.8; card, once each check size has

hits.message:
feat(pipeline): the coordinator can hand a run of segments over in one message

Completes direct peer chaining. When enabled, the coordinator finds the longest
run of consecutive remote segments that can pass activations to each other,
sends one forward to the head carrying the rest of the run, and waits for the
tail. An eight-segment pipeline stops costing eight round trips per token and
costs one out and one back.

Off by default. With the setting off, the planned chain is always empty and
every line behaves exactly as it did before this existed.

Prompt privacy survives, and by construction rather than by care: a local
segment ends a run, so with prompt privacy on — where this node holds the first
and last segments — only the middle is ever chained, and no remote node sees the
prompt or the sampled token. That is the same shape the published designs use,
and there is a test for it.

Three things the planner refuses, each falling back to sending one segment at a
time. A peer that does not advertise the feature ignores the field and replies
to the coordinator, so chaining through it would leave us waiting on a node that
will never answer. A gap between one segment's last layer and the next one's
first is not a pipeline, and forwarding into it would produce a confident wrong
answer rather than an error. And a request carrying frequency or presence
penalties is not chained at all, because the decoded-so-far ids the sampling
segment needs travel with the coordinator's own forward, which in a chain is
built on a machine that does not have them.

Two things had to widen to match what is now being waited for. The deadline
covers the whole run, since only the tail reports back and budgeting for one
segment would time out a healthy chain. And the waiter is pinned to the tail
rather than the head, because the hops in between hand the activations along and
never report here — pinning it to the head would let an abandoned forward's late
error resolve a standby's waiter, which is the defect that cost a request 181
seconds once already.

A chained run that fails says so instead of guessing. It reveals that something
went wrong but not which hop, so replacing the head's holder would be a guess,
and a wrong guess re-sends the whole run to the same nodes that just failed. The
request fails as transient, the router retries with a fresh assembly, and
nothing is penalised because nothing here can name a culprit.

inference: a saved prompt on a card/processor split is charged to the memory each layer is in

Long prompts on a model split between the graphics card and the processor no
longer throw away every saved prompt for room the card never gets. The prompt
cache keeps a split's processor-held layers in system memory, but every memory
check counted the whole saved prompt as card memory. Admitting a long prompt
then evicted every saved prompt, and the prompt was refused a few milliseconds
later anyway: a 14B split on an 8 GB card evicted 991 MB for a card that got
408 MB back.

counts only what that memory gets back - the per-memory rule live caches have
followed since #262. A long prompt on a split sized for a typical conversation
is still refused rather than reloaded with fewer card layers (FUTURE_WORK #454).

Prior art: vLLM keeps one block pool per device; a freed CPU block is never a
free GPU block.

fix(vision): pictures reach the model where you put them; Gemma 3 can read images

A picture sent with a message used to go in front of the whole prompt — ahead
of the chat template's opening — whatever the message said around it. No API
surface marked where the picture belonged (the OpenAI surface dropped its
place, the Anthropic surface dropped image blocks altogether, the fallback
wrote the word `<image>` as text), and the code that puts a picture into the
prompt silently prepended it when it found no mark. LLaVA still answered
plausibly, which is why it went unnoticed.

Now:
- Every surface writes llama.cpp's image marker where the picture was, and
  the picture's rows are put exactly there (`vision::splice_image_rows`, the
  one place, which refuses a prompt with no mark instead of guessing).
- The prompt's length counts each picture's rows, from the picture data
  itself, so the conversation memory is sized right.
- A picture that cannot be read is the request's error, with advice in all
  21 languages — never a reply written as if no picture was sent.
- Gemma 3's image reader is supported (letterboxed to 896 px, SigLIP, pooled
  to 256 rows, its own norm and projection); an image-reader type this build
  does not have is refused by name.
- "Start and finish on this computer" carries the picture too.

Compatibility: the first computer of a split must advertise the new feature
bit 26 (`IMAGES_AT_MARKERS`) to be given a picture; an older one is skipped
and the request is planned again without it.

picture is described word for word as llama.cpp does but one verb, and a 1969
newspaper front page ("MEN WALK ON MOON") the same way, on both the OpenAI
and the Anthropic surface. Gemma 3 still reads a picture's rows one way only
(llama.cpp reads them both ways), which changes some replies — tracked as
FUTURE_WORK #115 (2b). Gotcha #901.
