Routines slice D1: the durable half of a Routine. **Nothing fires yet** — no
scheduler, no alarm hook, no cron evaluation beyond the syntax a write must
pass, no webhook route and no key store. Those are D2 and D3.

Closes part of #21 (rows 15 and 19 of the parity register move to `partial`).

## What lands

**`@frockbot/plugin-routines`** (manifest v4, contributions backend + runtime +
client, permissions `routines:read` / `routines:write`, Capability
`routine-tools` kind `tool` with an admission ceiling naming all four turn
types).

- **Records.** `RoutineRecordV1` in the Bot Durable Object — `AGENTS.md` names
  Routines as that object's authority — under keys the Package exports
  (`routine:`, `routine-run:`, `routine-receipt:`), never in `kernel-do`. It
  carries exactly one of `schedule` and `trigger`, the timezone, `enabled`, the
  writer of the creating write and of the latest one, and the timestamps. The
  XOR is enforced in the codec rather than at a call site. A webhook Routine
  records the trigger **kind** and nothing else: key minting is D3, and no key
  material can reach a record a view is projected from. Beside it, a bounded
  50-entry `RoutineRunEntryV1` log with the five statuses; it holds no
  authority, because every entry names its `runId` and the stored run carries
  `admission.origin.routineId` (PR #47's shape, reused not re-added), so
  trimming loses index rows and never facts. Every codec is strict, versioned
  and exact-field; no migrations.
- **Cron, at write time only.** `croner` (pinned `10.0.1`, zero-dependency)
  parses the five-field expression; `cron.ts` owns what it does not —
  `CRON_TZ=<zone>`, the `@hourly`/`@daily`/`@weekly`/`@monthly` aliases, and
  `@every <duration>` as a fixed interval — and `Intl.DateTimeFormat` validates
  the zone. A bad expression is a rejected command with its reason rather than a
  dead alarm.
- **One command path, two writers.** `routine/create|update|pause|resume|delete`
  carry their own idempotency keys and durable receipts, fingerprinted with the
  same canonicalization `configurationCommandFingerprintV1` uses under their own
  namespace (that helper is now factored out as
  `canonicalCommandFingerprintV1`). `routine/update` is partial; naming a
  schedule clears a trigger and the reverse. The hosted client posts to
  `/api/bots/:id/routines` and the writer is the User; the Bot calls
  `routine_manage` — mounted only inside an admitted Turn — and the writer names
  the Session and Turn that produced the write, as a Skill write does. No
  `run_now`.
- **DTOs and routes.** `GET`/`POST /api/bots/:id/routines` and
  `GET /api/bots/:id/routines/:routine/runs`, authenticated beside
  `/api/bots/:id/settings`. `RoutineViewV1` narrows a Bot writer to its `botId`,
  so no Session identifier and no key material reaches a browser.
- **UI.** `RoutinesSection.vue` mounts into a new
  `frockbot.bot-settings-sections` outlet on the Bot settings surface: list,
  create/edit form (name, prompt, cron **or** webhook, timezone), pause, resume,
  delete, and a per-Routine run log with its empty state. "Next run" is blank,
  because no authority has promised one.

## Deviations from the plan, and why

- **Routine commands are their own union, not variants of
  `ConfigurationCommandV1`.** They keep the shape and the fingerprint
  canonicalization, but carry no `expectedRevision`: a Routine is its own
  durable record rather than a field of the Bot settings view, and threading it
  through that revision would make an unrelated profile edit conflict with a
  Routine write, and the reverse. It also keeps Routine vocabulary out of
  `configuration-core`.
- **The Capability's admission ceiling is declarative today.** Ceilings are
  applied at registration only for Bot-isolate Packages
  (`BotIsolateContributionHost`); a first-party hosted Package registers without
  one. Because the Capability names all four turn types, the effective behaviour
  matches the declaration either way.
- `decodePluginCatalog` now reconstructs manifests as v4 rather than v3, so a
  Capability carrying an admission ceiling does not make the whole Package
  vanish from the Plugins surface.

## Tests

- `packages/plugin-routines/src` — 60 tests: codecs (schedule XOR trigger, bad
  cron, bad TZ, oversize prompt, unknown fields, writer provenance), cron
  normalization and rejection, store (partial update, provenance, idempotent
  replay, reused key with different bytes, bounded trimming, delete removes the
  log), the tool, the gateway routes, and the client Contribution.
- `apps/cloudflare/test/routines.workerd.ts` — create / pause / delete through
  the real Bot Durable Object with `evictDurableObject` between each step, a
  replayed command id applying once across eviction, and a bad cron writing
  nothing.
- `apps/cloudflare/test/integration/routines.integration.ts` — `POST` → `GET`
  lists, pause → `enabled:false` → resume, invalid cron → 400 with the reason
  and nothing written, schedule-and-trigger → 400, another User's Bot → 404 both
  ways with the owner's Routine untouched.

Gates: `typecheck`, `format:check`, `bun test` (1367), `test:workerd` (58),
`test:integration` (29), `lint:ui-styles`, `lint:kernel-imports`, `build`.

Add the babysitter: one owner for main, merges and production

scripts/babysit.ts reads the whole pipeline in one snapshot: main's
health, and when it is red the failed jobs, when the streak began and
every PR that landed since the last green run; the newest release's
deploy; and a next action for each open PR (merge, fix, rebase, wait,
held, skip). It changes nothing. The babysit skill acts on it every tick:
it is the only merger, squash-only and only while main is green; a red
main stops the line, a flake is rerun once and filed under `flaky`, and a
regression is attributed and fixed or its culprit reverted.

main-health.yml keeps a `main-health` commit status on every open PR from
scripts/main-health.ts: green while main is green, red while it is red,
always green on a `fix-main` PR or a revert. Once the ruleset requires it,
GitHub refuses a merge onto red main from any tool. It runs on
pull_request_target so it can write statuses, and only ever runs the base
branch's script. ci-watch reads a red main-health as held, not failed.

Add Local models: a model server on your Mac, relayed over the machine socket (#972)

* Add Local models: a model server on your Mac, relayed over the machine socket

A new keyless model provider (`provider-local`) reaches an OpenAI-compatible
server — Ollama, LM Studio, mesh-llm or another localhost port — on a paired
Mac. The cloud never dials the Mac: a `relay` frame goes down the socket the
Mac app's device host already holds, and the server's streamed answer comes
back up it.

- core/machine-protocol/relay.ts: relay frames and the one destination rule
  (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1]; no credentials, query or fragment).
- apps/device-host: the relay re-checks the address, refuses redirects,
  forwards each relay id once, caps concurrency and honours cancel; the Mac
  app's Deno --allow-net admits only the loopback hosts beside the deployment.
- User Durable Object: MachineModelRelaysV1 feeds a streamed Response from
  the Mac's frames; relayLocalModel reads the Mac and endpoint from the
  Connection. An offline Mac, or one that drops mid-answer, fails with a
  sentence the conversation shows, and never falls back to Frock AI.
- providers/local-model: Connection lifecycle with model discovery through
  the relay, and the runtime over the OpenAI-compatible transport.
- Billing records local calls as free and never refuses them for credit.
- Marketplace form: choose the Mac, choose the server, test and connect.
- Docs and a What's New entry.

Turn that owed a reconciliation writing no `turn/end`. When retrieval could
not answer — and for two of the three providers it never can — the run parked
and the Bot sat behind a "Try again" button whose only possible answer was
"give up".

Every external effect that matters already had a key. A model call's is its
`requestId`; a tool call's is its `occurrenceId`, which the tool receives as
`effectId`. So the loop stops investigating and re-issues under the key: one
`model/request` per dispatch, all carrying the same request, and an open tool
occurrence executed again with the same `effectId`. A provider that honours
the key answers once. One that does not may run the call twice, and that is
now explicit rather than reconstructed.

`admitEffect` is unchanged and is called before every dispatch, re-issues
included. Admissions are keyed by effect id, so a Stop or a supersede still
fences a call an evicted Turn had already started.

Deleted, with no compatibility shim: the session event types
`model/effect-not-started` and `model/reconciliation-required`;
`ToolEffectReconciliation`, `ToolDefinition.reconcile` and
`reconcilePrepared`; `ModelEffectReconciliationRequiredError`,
`ToolEffectReconciliationRequiredError`, `BotTurnReconciliationRequiredError`;
the `reconciliation-required` run status and phase, and with them the
`reconcileRun` RPC, the `/reconcile` route, the client's `resumeRun` and the
"Try again" button. `plugin-image`'s `generate_image` becomes idempotent by
reading its effect-keyed Workspace object before it generates, which is what
its `reconcile` did anyway.

Guarantees that are gone, deliberately:

- A dispatched model call whose response was lost is no longer retrieved from
  the provider. It is sent again, and a provider without idempotency may
  answer twice.
- A non-idempotent tool whose outcome is uncertain no longer parks the Turn.
  It is re-issued by key, or — when it threw — recorded as an error result
  that says the outcome is uncertain.
- A person can no longer resolve a parked Turn by hand, because no Turn parks.

Kept: a Turn still writes no `turn/end` when `agent/model-outcome-committed`
could not durably commit. That is the Turn's own write, not a question about
what a provider did, and a resume re-announces the same request id.

Listen to the voice session through OpenAI, not Workers AI

The continuous assistant transcribed through Workers AI Flux while dictation
had already moved to OpenAI's realtime socket. It now listens through the same
endpoint the other way round: `gpt-transcribe` with `server_vad`, which finds
turn boundaries itself — `speech_started` is barge-in, the commit is the turn
— where dictation's streaming model must refuse turn detection to stream live
text. Nothing above the transcriber changes: the cascade, the sleeping
wrapper, the ledger and both clients' wire protocol are untouched.

— moves to `app/voice/openai-realtime.ts` so both paths speak one vocabulary,
and `app/voice/pcm-resample.ts` carries the clients' 16 kHz audio up to the
24 kHz the endpoint accepts and nothing else, phase and odd byte carried
across frames.

`OPENAI_API_KEY` now gates the voice session as well as dictation, and the
transcriber's fatal path finally logs: a call that loses its ears used to look,
from every log, like a person who said nothing.

feat(provider): add an Anthropic model provider

The provider set was closed at two, and both of them spoke the same
OpenAI-shaped wire, so nothing proved the seam could take a third. This
one deliberately does not: @ai-sdk/anthropic owns the whole request —
prompt, tools, Messages-API framing and decoding — and the Package only
maps FrockBot's normalized conversation in and the stream events out.
Disabled by default, on a User's own Connection and API key, so it costs
an existing deployment nothing.

Two things had to move out of the OpenAI adapter to make that possible,
because they were never OpenAI's. The response-format degradation chain
is a promise the Agent loop makes to a Bot — a note at every step down —
and it now lives in one function both providers call. The deadline clock
likewise: the 120s-to-first-byte and 60s-idle bounds belong to the Turn,
not to a dialect, so an adapter that decodes its own wire runs under the
same clock rather than a copy of it.

hits.message:
feat(voice): dictate a message into the composer (slice A, #179)

With an empty composer the send button becomes a waveform button. Pressing
it captures the microphone and streams what is heard into the textarea as
the draft, with a level-driven wave, a bin and a send. Send commits the
audio, waits for the finished transcript, and then calls the ordinary
`sendMessage` — so a dictated message supersedes, counts and is refused
exactly like a typed one, and a rejected send gives the draft back.

The transport is a per-User `VoiceSession` Durable Object holding the
browser socket and the provider socket and no authority (voice plan D2,
the rule ADR 0017 sets for Subagent objects). The voice budget it spends
lives in `UserConfiguration` and is asked for before a microphone opens
and reported when one closes.

The upstream is selectable without a code change: with an `OPENAI_API_KEY`
Worker secret the object opens OpenAI's realtime transcription session
directly, and without one it falls back to the AI Gateway's BYOK key and
`cf-aig-authorization`. The plan's assumption that the Gateway accepts a
transcription-only session is still unverified, which is why the direct
key takes precedence.

`OPENAI_API_KEY` and `GEMINI_API_KEY` join the optional `--secrets-file`
lists in both deploy workflows: that flag replaces the Worker's whole
secret set, so a name that is not carried is deleted (ADR 0025).

hits.message:
Stream the Bot's reply as it is written. (#807)

The visible reply is a `send_to_user` call, and it used to appear only once
the model step had finished and the tool had run: the OpenAI-compatible
adapter dropped the SDK's tool-input parts, so a person watched nothing while
the model wrote.

The normalized stream gains `tool-input-delta`, a fragment of a call's
arguments while the model writes them. The OpenAI-compatible adapter (Frock AI
included) and the catalog bridge emit it; billing counts it as partial data;
the Plugin `ai` grant never sees it. The loop hands it to a per-dispatch
`watchToolInput` watcher and journals nothing. The Shell's watcher reads the
`text` of each `send_to_user` being written, alone or inside a `batch`, with a
partial JSON reader and publishes a reply draft at most every 100 ms: a
`state/draft` frame on the Bot state channel, outside the cursor, never
stored or replayed, sent only to sockets that asked with `drafts=1`. Installed
apps never ask, so their exact decoders never meet the frame; a new client on
an older server is simply never sent one.

The Flutter client draws each part as the line its message will be, under the
id that message will have, so the message fills the same bubble when it lands.

Adds the What's New entry "Replies appear as they are written".

hits.message:
fix(cloudflare): give the user application artifact a module URL so it evaluates

Since the provider catalog landed, `bun run artifact:build` emits
`var require = createRequire(import.meta.url)` as the bundle's first
top-level statement: the catalog reaches `openai`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`
and `google-auth-library`, and Bun wires their CommonJS dependencies to a
`require` it builds from the module's own URL.

A Worker Loader module has no file URL, so `import.meta.url` is
`undefined` in the isolate and that statement throws before anything
else runs. Every request then answers `Failed to start Worker: Uncaught
TypeError: The argument 'path' must be a file URL object, a file URL
string, or an absolute path string. Received 'undefined'`, which is what
the browser end-to-end job has been timing out on at `/app-manifest`,
in all four shards, before its first spec.

Name the bundle at build time instead. The `require` it builds is only
reached from the lazy CommonJS wrappers of those SDKs' Node-only code
paths, and reaching one lands on the `nodejs_compat` built-ins as any
other `require` in the Worker does. The build then reads its own output
back and refuses to ship an artifact that still mentions
`import.meta.url`, because a bundler that stopped honouring the
substitution would otherwise only be caught hours later, in the
end-to-end job, as the same unstartable Worker.

hits.message:
feat(kernel): bound every model request and every Turn in time

Nothing anywhere put a clock on a model call or on a Turn. One Turn hung for
seventeen minutes showing an animated avatar and nothing else, and would have
hung until the isolate died.

Three bounds, each at the layer that can see the thing it is bounding:

- The OpenAI-compatible provider holds a request to a first-byte deadline and
  then to an idle deadline between stream events, rearming on every event and
  always disarming in a finally. A caller's own Stop still reports as a Stop.
- The Agent loop gives each Turn a fifteen-minute wall clock on the same
  controller Stop uses, and classifies that abort ahead of the cancellation
  branch so a Turn the clock ended is never reported as one the person stopped.
- One automatic retry, and only for a failure the provider itself classified as
  never having started. Every other failure stays uncertain and is never
  retried, which is the whole of ADR 0024's durability contract; the durable
  evidence of a retry is the log it already writes.

Also: the supersede intent stays part of a Turn command's fingerprint, but the
run id it names does not. That id is whichever run the composer had observed —
a fact about its polling — and hashing it turned an ordinary retried send into
"this idempotency key was reused for a different command".

hits.message:
Retry external effects by idempotency key, not by forensics

The loop used to work out, after a crash, whether a dispatched model call had
actually happened: retrieve the response from the provider, verify it against
the durable chunk prefix, and park the Turn for a person when it could not be
retrieved. That machinery was most of the complexity in the loop and most of
the recent bug fixes.

Now every external effect that matters carries an idempotency key and is
re-issued under that key. Resumption replays the event log to the cursor and
re-sends what is not recorded complete. No Turn parks; none needs a person.

`admitEffect` and supersede fencing survive and are strengthened: admission now
runs before every dispatch, re-issues included, so a Stop still fences a call
an evicted Turn had started.

Two guarantees are gone with no replacement, both describing the shape of a
reconciliation outcome that no longer exists: `plugin-tools` normalizing an
unavailable outcome to a bounded reason, and returning unavailable when a
non-idempotent definition has no retrieval seam.

I held this back once on the belief that writing `model/usage` per dispatch
over-accounts a retry. It does not. `provider-openai-compatible` asserts that
no idempotency key reaches the provider, so a re-issued request is a genuinely
new and genuinely billed call, and counting each dispatch is correct.

The Anthropic provider, written in parallel and unknown to this work, still
declared the old three-argument `agent/model-outcome-committed`; it now matches
the two-argument event the loop emits. That single fix cleared all five
packages that failed to typecheck on the merge.

browser end-to-end tests pass.

hits.message:
fix(chat): a refused send says why, and a hung model request fails visibly

Five findings from the v3 verification wave, all of them things a person sees.

A send the server refuses is now a refusal, not a mystery. The client treated
every non-2xx from `POST /turns` as an uncertain admission, so a 120 KB message
was rendered optimistically — a full screen of it — and then answered with
"Checking whether your message went through…" over a run lookup that 500'd. Any
4xx is the server having read the request and said no: the composer keeps the
draft, shows the server's own sentence, and starts no reconciliation. The
composer also counts down to the same limit and stops before it.

A backend this tab cannot reach now says so. The placeholder sorted above the
message it reported on, and `reconcileUncertainAdmission` retried for ever. It
is ordered after its message, bounded to six attempts with backoff, and then
settles to a line that says the app could not reach the Bot, with a Retry and
the draft kept.

A hung model request fails within the minute rather than the quarter-hour. The
first-byte and idle deadlines only ever applied to the OpenAI-compatible
transport; Flock AI — the default — bypassed them entirely and was bounded only
by the 15-minute Turn deadline, which is the empty bubble the tester watched.
Both transports now go through one seam that owns the clock, with an injectable
timer so the deadlines are testable without waiting.

Also: a debug `limit` outside 1..20 is a 400 that names the range instead of a
500 and an uncaught error; the sidebar preview falls back to the transcript for
a Bot with no stored preview record, instead of "No messages yet" over six
messages; and a transcript read degrades an orphaned tool call to "no result
recorded" rather than throwing, because a read must never fail on data that is
already durable.

fix(kernel): one failed persist no longer silences the durable log

Two failures on the same seam.

The Session chained every durable write with `.then`, so the first rejection
made every later write skip its callback: no event was ever persisted again
while the Agent loop carried on in memory, every `flush` rejected with the
original error, and the rejection sat unhandled between an append and the
next flush. Writes now chain past a rejection, the first failure is
remembered, and `flush` throws it — the Turn fails loudly, once.

And a Turn whose *first* flush failed handed its input straight back: the
inbox was shifted after the flush and outside the try, so `#wake` started
another Turn, appended another `turn/start`, and failed again immediately,
forever, with nobody awaiting the rejection. The input is claimed before the
flush, and a `#drive` that rejects stops the waking.

hits.message:
One Plugin worker per User

Every Plugin a generation names now mounts into one Dynamic Worker per
User behind a generated index (frock-compose/plugin-worker-wrapper.ts),
replacing the per-member isolate host and wrapper. The host orders
providers before consumers, refuses per Plugin at resolve, fails the
worker at mount when a module does not parse, fails one Plugin at health
when its report differs from its descriptor, and registers each verified
Plugin's tools under its namespace and one loop hook per event any of
them declared. A hook call carries the enabled list; the index runs the
enabled Plugins in mount order, each seeing the value the one before it
left, and names any it skipped, which the Durable Object records.

Contract version 4: the agent/request hook, services a Plugin provides
and consumes (ctx.services), and triggers. The isolate probe gains a
two-Plugin worker that proves mount order, services and the hook chain
in a real isolate.

The binding digest still carries the Turn's authority snapshot, so the
worker reloads when that changes; holding it across Turns arrives with
the loopback rework (ADR 0026 step 5).

chore(typecheck): route the 15 vue-tsc surfaces through typescript-native-bridge

The Vue tier was the last holdout from the TypeScript 7 migration (ADR 0029):
vue-tsc embeds the TS compiler JS API via Volar, and TS 7 ships none. It was
also the heaviest part of `bun run typecheck` and the main cause of machine
thrash when several agents typecheck at once.

Alias `typescript` to typescript-native-bridge@6.0.3-bridge.16.tsgo.7.0.2 in
the 14 vue-tsc packages plus apps/cloudflare. The bridge, from the Vue Language
Tools maintainer, is a drop-in `typescript` that keeps the TS 6 JS API Volar
needs while running the checker in-process on tsgo. vue-tsc is unchanged.

Measured: plugin-shell 22.4s -> 2.8s, plugin-settings 7.9s -> 2.2s,
client-ui 7.8s -> 1.4s. Full suite: 73/73 in 14.6s.

Diagnostics verified byte-identical to stock vue-tsc for injected template-only
errors in three packages -- a checker that silently skips .vue files also goes
green.

tsconfig fixes: the bridge is TS 6, which removed baseUrl and resolves paths
relative to the tsconfig, so plugin-shell, plugin-computer and
apps/cloudflare/tsconfig.client.json move to relative paths. apps/cloudflare
also runs three plain tsc passes under the same alias; its test/tsconfig.json
replaces `types` wholesale and needed vite/client for the CSS side-effect
imports (TS2882, a diagnostic TS 5.9 does not emit).

Temporary. TS 7.1 with content mappers lets tsc check .vue directly and
deprecates vue-tsc; revisit around October 2026.

hits.message:
feat(channels): bot-to-bot group channels with durable fan-out

Parity register rows 35 and 57f: a Bot can now say something to a teammate or
to a group and be answered, because the recipient gets a Turn of its own.

The authority is split the way the constitution splits it. Channel records,
membership and the canonical message log are User-scoped, so they live in the
User Durable Object as `plugin-channels`' `ChannelStore`; a Bot's participation
is a `channel` Turn its own Durable Object admits, and nothing else may admit
one. `channel/post` appends the message with the `seq` it assigns *inside the
transaction that writes one `ChannelDeliveryV1` per recipient*, then
acknowledges; the fan-out to `BOT_STATES.deliverChannelInput` is a second,
retryable step, safe to repeat because the debt is already written down. The
recipient writes the input to its own storage, arms its one alarm, and returns
— nothing runs inside the delivery RPC, so a sender's Turn is not held open for
whatever the recipient decides to do, and a reply cannot re-enter the User
Durable Object that is still waiting. The run id is derived from the message id
and the origin names the message, so a redelivery is refused by the kernel's own
Turn idempotency rather than by a check anyone remembered to write.

Four bounds, and every refusal is a durable receipt rather than an exception:
the sender is never a recipient of its own post; `hop` increments per message
and a post past `CHANNEL_HOP_MAX` (3) is refused; a per-Channel token bucket
(20/minute) refuses beyond its rate and reopens in the next window; and
`react_to_message` writes no delivery at all, so a tapback cannot cascade.

A `channel` Turn replays no personal transcript. `plugin-channels` supplies the
Channel's own last messages as the Turn's history through the Agent runtime's
new fresh-history mode — a handler prepended to `agent/request`, so it has the
last word over every Package narrowing and depends on none of them. The messages
are never written to the Bot's durable log, and the Bot's visible transcript
hides a `channel` Turn exactly as it hides an automation one.

Three tools — `send_to_agent`, `react_to_message`, `channel_manage` — admitted
on `["chat", "channel"]` and nowhere else, which is `:419`/`:444` for chat and
the extension that makes a group conversation closed for channel. A bare
`botId` resolves to the implicit 1:1 pair Channel, whose id is derived from the
pair, so both Bots name the same room and the create is idempotent on it. The
teammate directory and the channels list are prompt sections, not tools
(`:463-464`), skipped on automation and subagent Turns.

Manifest v5 adds the `channel` Capability kind: `decodeV5` extends `decodeV4`
exactly as `decodeV4` extends `decodeV3`, and the v1–v4 branches decode
unchanged — a v4 body that declares `channel` is refused, because the version a
manifest states is the version it is read at. `StoredRunOriginV1` gains a
`channel` variant beside `routine`; each is decoded exactly, so a Routine origin
written before this is byte-for-byte the same record.

Register rows 35 and 57f move; row 36 stays "not started" — the `external`
Channel kind and `channel_manage disconnect` exist, but no connector does yet,
and the UI is N3.

Tests: `ChannelStore` receipts, membership, hop, quota and reaction idempotence
over a Map; the three tools on a real `ToolRegistry`, including that an
automation Turn is offered none of them; `ChannelStoreProbe` in workerd, where a
post's message and both its deliveries survive eviction and a redelivered
message admits one Turn; and `channels-group.integration.ts`, where two Bots of
one User meet through `SELF.fetch` — Bot A posts from a chat Turn, Bot B answers
on a `channel` Turn that is absent from its transcript, and the cascade stops at
the hop bound with a refusal that replays.

hits.message:
Deliver a Routine's hand-off, and stop a batch bricking its Session

Three defects found while working out why a Bot "could not access email".
It could: the 2026-09-16 firing read the inbox and built the triage. What
failed was everything after.

**A `batch` sub-call's result broke the Session permanently.**
`deriveMessages` skips a result whose occurrence has a `parentOccurrenceId`
— a call inside a batch answers no tool call the assistant sent — but
`messageTurnsV1` counted every `tool/result`, so the length invariant in
`turnScopedMessagesV1` failed. The events are durable, so this was not one
Turn's failure: every later Turn in that Session died the same way, before
the model was called. Bob's morning triage has failed every day since.
Both readers now take the one list, `messageEventsV1`.

**An automation Turn was told to use a tool it does not have.**
The conversational contract rendered on every turn type while the manifest
admits `user-voice` on `chat` and `agent` only, so the firing spent its
last steps failing to call `send_to_user` — which is how it reached the
batch above. The section is now chosen by the same ceiling that admits the
tool, and a Turn outside the conversation is given the hand-off contract.

**Nothing opened the Turn a hand-off was owed.**
`wake_parent` queues for the Bot's *next* conversational Turn, and nothing
started one: a 9:45am triage waited until the person happened to speak.
The alarm now opens it — an ordinary chat Turn on the Bot's own
conversation, carrying the drained hand-off and a cue saying nobody spoke,
so the Bot says what matters in its own voice with the conversation in
front of it. The firing's Session is deliberately blind to that
conversation, which is why the delivery belongs here and not in a direct
send. One Turn per hand-off, marked before admission; a delivery that
fails costs the hand-off its Turn, never the hand-off.

hits.message:
Split the agent loop from its provider I/O

`kernel-agent-loop/src/index.ts` braided two unrelated concerns: messy
provider I/O and a durable state machine. A malformed streaming chunk and a
Durable Object eviction took the same code path.

The Turn's state machine stays in `index.ts` and reaches its external work
through one seam, `LoopRuntime`. Model dispatch and stream consumption,
tool execution, provider-bound reconciliation and the resumption replay each
move to their own module. `#runTurn` and `#resumeTurn` now share the step
body and one settlement, instead of carrying two copies of each.

No behaviour change: the test suite is untouched, including its imports.

hits.message:
feat(computer): provision one Computer per User and give it a Workspace file surface

Implements Step 1 of docs/plans/slice-2.md and ADR 0012. A Computer is now
provisioned and keyed per User; a Bot attaches to it as a tenant with its own
directories and desktop slot, and every tenant shares one browser profile.

The four per-Bot assumptions the plan listed are gone:

- `ComputerRegistry.assign/assignment/open` take `ComputerIdentityV1` (and, for
  `open`, a `ComputerTenantV1`); the assignment map is keyed by User, so two
  Bots of one User share one assignment and one generation.
- `ComputerProvider.open(identity, tenant, assignment, options)` lets a provider
  tell "provision the Computer" from "attach this tenant".
- `flySpriteNameForTarget` and `flySpriteNameForUserStorage` are replaced by
  `flySpriteNameForComputer(identity)`: one Sprite per User, no separate User
  storage Sprite, and one shared `/home/box/chrome-profile`.
- `ComputerWorkspace.openDirectory({namespace, scope, durability})` is deleted.
  `ComputerWorkspace` now is `WorkspaceFilesV1` plus its `WorkspaceLayoutV1`,
  addressed by `WorkspacePathV1`. `ComputerTarget` and `ComputerTargetV1` go
  with it, along with the unused deprecated `agentId`/`agentKey` spellings.

The Fly provider declares its durable roots — `bot-instructions` at
`agent-data/agents/<key>/skills`, `bot-memory` at `.../memory`, `user-memory`
at `agent-data/user-memory`, and Package-declared roots under
`agent-data/user-packages/<package>/<root>`, matching the GrokBot parity layout
— and implements `WorkspaceFilesV1` over them with declared-variant outcomes,
contract-bounded sizes and pages, and a generation sidecar recording the writer,
size, sha-256 content address, and minted generation id of every write. Memory
roots are read-only through that surface; a write to one is refused.

The ADR 0013 durable-root sync does not exist yet, so the Memory Package keeps
writing Memory roots on the Computer through one clearly named seam,
`ComputerWorkspace.memoryWriter`, which accepts Memory roots and nothing else.
Step 3 deletes it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

hits.message:
fix(model): settle the Assignment saga so a Bot runs on the User default

The workerd suite caught two defects behind the user-level default model.

A Bot that follows the User's default claims its own model Assignment when it
resolves its execution context, but `isolateInvokeModel` read the Bot's
settings straight from durable storage, so an isolate model request from a Bot
that had not yet claimed found no Assignment and fell closed to a pending user
decision. It now resolves the same execution context an admitted Turn does, and
claims nothing extra: a Bot with no default and no binding still refuses.

The Assignment saga then never settled against the real User Durable Object.
`executeConnectionDependency`'s `read` reported a recorded but unacknowledged
dependency as `pending`, which tells the saga the User authority cannot answer
yet; the saga compensated a claim it was entitled to keep and retried for ever,
leaving `assignmentOperations` non-empty and refusing every later configuration
command. A recorded, unacknowledged dependency is `claimed` — the status the
saga acknowledges next. The unit mocks already modelled it that way, so only
the durable seam was wrong and no test covered it until a Bot following the
default drove the saga in workerd.

The Bot skips a claim while another Assignment operation is still reconciling,
and the fly durability test renames the Bot against the revision it reads, the
way the hosted client does, now that a first Turn commits that claim.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

multi-select on it is answered over several seconds, and a notice about
something else entirely must not empty it.

hits.message:
Bill hosted models by the model that answered, from a versioned rate table (#802)

Hosted prices move from the BILLING_MODEL_RATES secret into a versioned,
immutable-per-version table held by the DeploymentPolicy authority and edited
on the admin portal. Routes (the ids a Bot asks for) are ceilings with token
bounds; served entries price the model the Gateway actually ran, keyed
`<cf-aig-provider>/<cf-aig-model>`.

A hosted call reserves at its route's ceiling under the table's version
(`model-rates-<n>` as the reservation's pricing_version) and settles at the
served model's rate, never above the ceiling. A served model without a rate,
or an answer that names none, settles at the ceiling, is flagged `unpriced`
on the settlement and is reported to the authority for the admin portal. A
Gateway cache hit settles at zero, and every Frock AI request now sends
`cf-aig-skip-cache: true` on both transports.

The served identity travels from the Gateway host to billing through the
Frock AI seam's `served` callback and a per-request record on the provider,
not through the model stream, which is also the Plugin model-provider seam.

Each Bot object reads the table at most once a minute; the Gateway's prepaid
bounds come from the same copy. The authority seeds version 1 from the
current production prices under a receipted, repeatable maintenance key.
BILLING_MODEL_RATES is removed from the Worker env, the secrets manifest, the
release workflow, the billing launch check and the installer.

hits.message:
feat(computer): capture the Bot's own desktop as computer_screenshot

Parity row 25: a Bot can see its own screen.

No new host operation was needed. The provider runs one guarded `exec` —
the same human-control assertion every Bot command carries, then `scrot`
under the tenant's own `DISPLAY` — and brings the PNG back with
`file/read`. Reading it back rather than leaving it where `scrot` put it
is the point: a file that reaches a durable root by a shell write is
mirrored to object storage `unattributed`, and only a Workspace write
records the Bot, its Session, and its Turn. So the bytes are written
through `ComputerWorkspace.write` into the Package-declared root
`{packageId: "computer", rootId: "screenshots"}` at
`<botKey>/<turnId>-<seq>.png`, newest twenty kept per Bot.

The tool is declared read-only, so it records no durable intent, and it
is refused while a human holds the takeover lease, because the screen is
then theirs. Its result is JSON — path, root, content hash, size,
dimensions, display, capture time — plus a `ToolExecutionResult`
attachment.

Attachments are references and never bytes. The session event log is one
Durable Object value, so a base64 screenshot recorded in it would be a
durable record that grows past what the object can hold; the decoder
refuses `dataBase64` on the durable side outright. A resident Session
holds the resolved bytes for the requests derived while it lives, the
model-invocation adapter shows them to a model that accepts images and
otherwise names the path in the result text — an image withheld is said,
never silently dropped — and the hosted client draws it from the new
`GET /api/bots/:botId/workspace/file`, which reads object storage and
wakes no Computer.

The live test gains an opt-in provisioning probe
(`FROCKBOT_LIVE_PROVISION=1`): the suite deliberately seeds the
host-state file so the container adopts its Sprite instead of
apt-installing a desktop, so proving the apt list means asking for that
cost. Run against a real Sprite it currently ends in the cold-provision
`WebSocket keepalive timeout` being fixed on fix/computer-host-keepalive.

hits.message:
A batch meta-tool, and sends named by where they were declared

One bubble per inference is what the GrokBot multi-bubble contract costs
today: measured runs have three consecutive steps whose only tool call is
a send_to_user with empty assistant text and a tool result that took no
time at all. The model knows what all three say by the time it writes the
first, and ~5 s of inference buys each one.

`batch` runs up to 25 independent calls in one step. Every sub-call goes
through this same registry - prepare then executePrepared - so admission,
guards, namespace readiness and both tool hooks apply inside a batch
exactly as outside one. One failure does not abort the rest; the batch
exists so one inference can buy several calls, and collapsing it because
the third was refused would cost the other two as well. It refuses to
call itself, and it ORs the sub-results' endsTurn, without which a
finish send, a widget or an approval inside a batch would silently fail
to end the Turn.

Each sub-call is keyed `tool:<turn>:<step>:<ordinal>.<subIndex>` - a dot,
because an approval id may not carry a colon. Distinct ids are not
optional: the tool journal and send_to_user's own dedupe guard both key
on the effect id, and one shared id collapses three sends into one.

And the send ordinal now comes from the declared position rather than
from counting appends. The ordinal is the message's identity - "The
message the cloud names is <runId>:send:<ordinal>" - so deriving it from
arrival order meant that replaying the same batch under different
scheduling would hand the same payload a different message id: duplicate
or lost messages on resume, with a durable log that records whatever
order happened and so never heals. A log holding a send keyed by
anything this module did not mint is left in log order, exactly as
before.

workspace-store, one Computer per User [ADR 0012], backend durable-root
sync [ADR 0013], Skills and Memory Packages, the kernel extraction into
kernel-contracts / kernel-do / kernel-composition / kernel-agent-loop /

Two owner rulings shaped the resolution:

   BotDurableAuthority stays the hosted path. #33's resident Cordis root
   (createFoundationResidentRuntime, executeResidentBotTurn,
   BotResidentExecution) stays in the tree with its tests, but is no
   longer wired into apps/cloudflare. Durable Stop is not weakened:
   admitEffect is threaded through ShellCompositionMountOptions into the
   mounted runtime, Stop-wins-completion and fail-to-cancel live in the

hits.message:
Voice: keep the turn thin between the last word and the first sound

Everything between the end of the person's words and the first sound is
what they wait through. The Bot activity look-ups behind the system
prompt and list_bots went to each Bot's object one after another — a
person with six Bots waited six round trips before the first turn could
start — and every Bot lookup for bot_status, ask_bot and cancel_bot made
two calls where the directory alone answers. Both go out together now.
When the model goes to a tool without having said anything, the session
says "One moment." before running it: a tool step is a second model
round trip plus the tool, seconds of silence otherwise. The bridge is
spoken, not answered, so a turn that ends in the bridge alone still
settles as no_output. VOICE_ASSISTANT_MODEL pins a gateway model for
voice turns instead of the Auto route, so the model can follow what the
model-first-text lines show without a code change; the turn line says
which was used.

hits.message:
feat(voice): check the voice catalog against the account before deploying

Today the curated catalog shipped fourteen ElevenLabs voice ids taken
from the provider's well-known "premade" list. Nine of them are not on
this deployment's account, and one of the five that are was under the
wrong name. Eight of the eleven characters would have been mute.

Nothing caught it, and nothing could have. The voice tests script the
model and the speech provider so they are deterministic and free, which
is right, and means an id the account cannot reach is invisible to every
one of them. It is invisible at runtime too: an unreachable voice does
not raise an error anybody sees, it produces a sentence that never
becomes sound.

So the check talks to the account, which makes it a deploy-time check
rather than a unit test. It runs in the staging job, where the key
already is, before the deploy — so a catalog nobody can speak in neither
reaches staging nor gets a release tag cut over it. With no key in the
environment it skips rather than fails, because a check that cries wolf
on every contributor is one people learn to ignore.

The comparison itself is pure and tested without a key or a network: a
voice the account cannot reach fails, a character pointing outside the
catalog fails, and a name that has drifted is reported without failing,
since the voice still speaks. Our name matches theirs on a word-boundary
prefix, so the account's "Sarah - Mature, Reassuring" and "Jason Pike"
both agree with the short name the picker shows while "Beckett" does not
agree with "Bec".

hits.message:
feat(voice): tidy a dictated transcript once the person stops speaking

Speech-to-text gives back what was said, including the "um"s, the false
starts and the corrections people make mid-sentence. Reading that back
and fixing it by hand is work nobody asked for, so the capture is tidied
once — when they stop, never while they speak, because text that
rewrites itself under the cursor is worse than text that is untidy.

It runs in the relay, between the last segment and `final`, because the
model is reached with a server-side credential and the relay is already
where the capture's own words are. Two new frames carry it: `cleaning`,
which only changes what the composer says, and `cleaned`, which is the
tidied form of the whole capture.

The prompt is a request; the guards are the property. What comes back is
refused — and the raw transcript stands — when it is empty, unchanged,
longer (added information), much shorter (summarised), opens like a
model talking to us, had a question that is no longer a question, or
dropped every negation or every uncertainty the raw text carried. That
last pair is the one that matters: "maybe we should change the model" and
"change the model" are different messages to send to something that acts.
The transcript itself is fenced as data, and the fence's markers are
stripped out of it so it cannot be closed from inside.

Every way this fails ends in the same place — `final`, with the raw
transcript already in the draft. No gateway, no allowance, too short,
too long, a model that throws, a model that takes more than 8 s, a
guard that refuses. A capture the five-minute cap ended is not tidied at
all: it was cut off mid-sentence, so its false starts cannot be told
from its words, and the person is being shown why it stopped.

On the client the tidied text goes through the same `DictationDraftRange`
as every segment, which is what makes it safe rather than
carefully-written: a span the person has edited inside is already fenced
and takes nothing more, and a sent draft no longer contains the span at
all, so a late tidy-up finds nothing to replace. The composer offers
"Use what I said" afterwards and withdraws it the moment they edit.

Spend is one model call per capture, booked against the account's own
voice object before the model is asked, 400 per UTC day, and
deliberately not part of the cap that decides whether a voice call may
go on — a day of tidy-ups is no reason to refuse somebody a conversation.

hits.message:
feat(image): generate_image on Workers AI, fenced by the Workspace

Row 47 of the parity register asks for web search, web fetch and image
generation as first-class tools. This is the third of them; the two web
tools are not built.

`@frockbot/plugin-image` contributes one tool, `generate_image`, and it is
the first whose effect is both billed and durable — so it is the pattern
every later one copies rather than a one-off.

The Package consumes a narrow `ImageModelV1` — `run(model, input):
Promise<ArrayBuffer>` — and knows nothing about Workers AI. The adapter is
`plugin-shell/src/backend-image.ts`, which normalizes the three answers the
Workers AI catalog gives: `{ image: "<base64>" }` from the FLUX models, a
binary `ReadableStream` from the Stable Diffusion ones, a raw buffer from
the binding itself. `BotStateEnv.AI` becomes optional, the `PACKAGE_BUNDLER`
precedent: a host without Workers AI still mounts the Package and the tool
refuses visibly on the Turn that calls it.

Intent before effect. `image/generate-intent { effectId, model, promptHash,
width, height }` is appended and flushed before the model runs; the bytes go
to a Package-declared durable root — `{packageId: "image", rootId:
"generated"}`, at `<botId>/<effectId>.png` — and `image/generated` records
the generation the write produced. The object is keyed by the effect, which
is the reconciliation fence: the tool is `idempotent: false`, so the
registry never retries it, and `reconcile()` reads that one path. Present
means the generation happened; absent means it did not. Nothing is ever
billed twice.

The durable `tool/result` is stable JSON naming the file, never base64 —
`tool/result.content` is replayed into every later model request of the
Turn. `width` and `height` are read back out of the stored bytes' container
header rather than echoed from the request, because `flux-1-schnell` accepts
no size at all and a number in the log that no file agrees with is worse
than no number.

The default model is `@cf/black-forest-labs/flux-1-schnell`, declared as the
`image.model` Package setting. `AI` has no local miniflare simulator, so the
integration suite binds it to an auxiliary Worker with an RPC entrypoint
answering a real 1x1 PNG and counting its calls; the production seam,
`env.AI.run(model, input)`, is the one under test.

hits.message:
feat(subagents): task lifecycle — check, message, stop, resume, and completion inbox

Slice G, PR G2. G1 dispatched a subagent as a Turn in a Subagent Durable Object
of the same Bot (ADR 0017); this is what happens to it afterwards.

Four tools on chat and automation turns, under a second manifest Capability
`task-lifecycle`. `task_check` reads status and the last summary and says out
loud that you are notified on completion and should not poll. `task_message`
appends to the bounded (16) `task-msg:` queue and refuses anything that is not
running, because a queued task has not opened its Session and a settled one
will never read again. `task_stop` is explicit, authenticated cancellation:
durable before the child is asked, terminal on the parent's record, idempotent
on a retry. `task_resume` refuses a running task and refuses a `model` beside a
`resume` — the resumed run continues a transcript the first binding produced —
and runs in the *same* child Durable Object and Session, with `resumedFrom`
recorded and the anchor carried on the record's `childSessionId`.

`background:false` waits up to `TASK_BLOCKING_TIMEOUT` (120 s) and then answers
"still running, id <taskId>", degrading to background. It waits by *polling
durable state* — the parent's own task record, then the child's context by RPC
— and never awaits the child's settle callback, which is an RPC back into the
object that is still inside the dispatching Turn: the reentrancy hazard G1
flagged.

A settled task leaves the same three records a completed Routine firing leaves,
through slice E's own seams rather than beside them: a `task/settled` line on
the Bot's announcement log, a completion-inbox entry and a pending wake, and a
notification intent. `RoutineInboxEntryV1` and `RoutinePendingWakeV1` gain an
optional `source`, so an entry says what produced it and the preamble delivers
a subagent's *summary* — never the child's transcript, which the parent has no
door onto. The inbox half is skipped while the dispatching run is still active:
a blocking dispatch is answered by its own tool result.

`task/dispatched`, `task/message`, `task/settled` and `task/stopped` join the
kernel's session-event map; the first is projected into the run view as a task
chip carrying type, description, model slug and background, and the client
merges its live status and summary from `GET /api/bots/:id/tasks` — the
approval-card seam — because a background task settles long after the run that
dispatched it stopped changing.

`GET /api/bots/:id/tasks/:taskId` and `POST .../tasks/:taskId/stop` sit beside
G1's list route. The stop route is a second authenticated door onto the one
durable cancellation, never a second mechanism.

fix(ui): compact confirmations, a Models surface that answers, honest sub-cent Usage

Five defects a QA pass on v0.3.35 found, each fixed where it lives.

Archive and Delete borrowed the Create-a-Bot frame — a 660x520 two-column
box built for a sheep and a wardrobe — so two sentences wrapped six times in
a 180px column and a quarter page of nothing sat above the buttons. A
confirmation is now `UiConfirmDialog` in client-ui: 420px, a question, one
or two sentences, Cancel and the act. Cancel takes the focus, which is the
answer a stray Enter should give.

The Create-a-Bot dialog's own columns disagreed because the art panel set a
fixed 520px height and the buttons were pinned to the bottom of it. The
dialog is now as tall as its form, so the columns end together and the
buttons sit under the last field.

Models was a full-height drawer holding one sentence, no action, and no
statement of the model actually in use. It now leads with the model the
composer names, explains the platform default, and offers the button that
turns the chooser on — found from manifest facts, like every other routing
decision on that surface.

Usage read "$0.50" for two short Turns. `@frock/auto` — what almost every
Bot runs on — was absent from the price table, so every platform-model Turn
was priced at the unknown-model fallback of $10/$50 per million, twenty-three
times the model it routes to. Auto is now priced at the Frock AI text model
the route serves. The token counts were real: the transport reports none, so
the loop estimates from the normalized request, which carries the system
prompt and every tool schema whatever the person typed. Two such Turns are
about two cents. Sub-cent spend now reads "<$0.01" rather than "$0.00", and
zero still reads as zero.

Opening Applets logged a CSP violation for the zone's injected Insights
beacon. Artifact responses now say `no-transform`: an artifact is addressed
by the hash of its bytes and a zone feature that rewrites its HTML is
rewriting what the hash names. The beacon's two origins are named anyway,
because `no-transform` is a request to an edge feature rather than a
guarantee this Worker can make.

Settings had three "Save settings" buttons, the last one under Usage, which
saves nothing. The profile's Save now sits with the two fields it saves and
says so, and Usage — a reading, not a setting — follows the settings rather
than sitting between two of them. The Bot panel's "Alpha's screen" caption
went: the card above it already says "No computer" and explains why.

hits.message:
A durable flush no longer re-reads the whole Session log

The contiguity guard in persistRunEvents needed one number - how many
events the log already holds - and read the entire conversation to get
it. SessionEventLog.read walks every page and, for each cut entry,
fetches every payload chunk, re-verifies its SHA-256 and parses it. Every
model/request is stored cut, at about 80 KiB, and nothing prunes them, so
a Bot with a long history paid for all of them.

A Turn's preamble flushes about eight times before the first model call:
admission, turn/start, the three preStep injections, step/start,
user/message and model/request. That is eight full hydrations of a log
that only grows.

The count is what the index exists to record. SessionEventLog.count reads
the index and returns eventCount, falling back to the legacy array's
length for a log that has not been migrated. The guard is unchanged.

hits.message:
Deliver a Routine's hand-off, and stop a batch bricking its Session

Three defects found while working out why a Bot "could not access email".
It could: the 2026-09-16 firing read the inbox and built the triage. What
failed was everything after.

**A `batch` sub-call's result broke the Session permanently.**
`deriveMessages` skips a result whose occurrence has a `parentOccurrenceId`
— a call inside a batch answers no tool call the assistant sent — but
`messageTurnsV1` counted every `tool/result`, so the length invariant in
`turnScopedMessagesV1` failed. The events are durable, so this was not one
Turn's failure: every later Turn in that Session died the same way, before
the model was called. Bob's morning triage has failed every day since.
Both readers now take the one list, `messageEventsV1`.

**An automation Turn was told to use a tool it does not have.**
The conversational contract rendered on every turn type while the manifest
admits `user-voice` on `chat` and `agent` only, so the firing spent its
last steps failing to call `send_to_user` — which is how it reached the
batch above. The section is now chosen by the same ceiling that admits the
tool, and a Turn outside the conversation is given the hand-off contract.

**Nothing opened the Turn a hand-off was owed.**
`wake_parent` queues for the Bot's *next* conversational Turn, and nothing
started one: a 9:45am triage waited until the person happened to speak.
The alarm now opens it — an ordinary chat Turn on the Bot's own
conversation, carrying the drained hand-off and a cue saying nobody spoke,
so the Bot says what matters in its own voice with the conversation in
front of it. The firing's Session is deliberately blind to that
conversation, which is why the delivery belongs here and not in a direct
send. One Turn per hand-off, marked before admission; a delivery that
fails costs the hand-off its Turn, never the hand-off.

`AiError` 5006, naming a missing `/audio` object and a crash reading
`parallel_tool_calls`. The route and its target model are correct; the
`AI` binding's `gateway(...).run({ provider: "compat" })` reaches the

`dynamic/flock-auto` fails identically with tools, without tools and
without streaming, while `workers-ai/@cf/...` succeeds with the same
bodies, and a nonexistent route name fails differently — so the route
resolves and the body is not at fault.

authorized by `cf-aig-authorization`. The binding stays as the fallback
wherever the account id and token are absent, which is every local, CI
and end-to-end environment, so none of them acquires a Cloudflare
credential and the `AI` stand-ins keep working unchanged.

The token is optional and carried in the release workflow's optional
list, because `--secrets-file` replaces the Worker's whole secret set.

hits.message:
Stream the Bot's reply as it is written. (#807)

The visible reply is a `send_to_user` call, and it used to appear only once
the model step had finished and the tool had run: the OpenAI-compatible
adapter dropped the SDK's tool-input parts, so a person watched nothing while
the model wrote.

The normalized stream gains `tool-input-delta`, a fragment of a call's
arguments while the model writes them. The OpenAI-compatible adapter (Frock AI
included) and the catalog bridge emit it; billing counts it as partial data;
the Plugin `ai` grant never sees it. The loop hands it to a per-dispatch
`watchToolInput` watcher and journals nothing. The Shell's watcher reads the
`text` of each `send_to_user` being written, alone or inside a `batch`, with a
partial JSON reader and publishes a reply draft at most every 100 ms: a
`state/draft` frame on the Bot state channel, outside the cursor, never
stored or replayed, sent only to sockets that asked with `drafts=1`. Installed
apps never ask, so their exact decoders never meet the frame; a new client on
an older server is simply never sent one.

The Flutter client draws each part as the line its message will be, under the
id that message will have, so the message fills the same bubble when it lands.

Adds the What's New entry "Replies appear as they are written".

hits.message:
Retry external effects by idempotency key, not by forensics

After a crash the loop used to work out whether a dispatched call had
actually happened: `ctx.llm.reconcile`, three retrieval outcomes, a prefix
match of durable `assistant/chunk`s against retrieved `text-delta`s, and a
Turn that owed a reconciliation writing no `turn/end`. When retrieval could
not answer — and for two of the three providers it never can — the run parked
and the Bot sat behind a "Try again" button whose only possible answer was
"give up".

Every external effect that matters already had a key. A model call's is its
`requestId`; a tool call's is its `occurrenceId`, which the tool receives as
`effectId`. So the loop stops investigating and re-issues under the key: one
`model/request` per dispatch, all carrying the same request, and an open tool
occurrence executed again with the same `effectId`. A provider that honours
the key answers once. One that does not may run the call twice, and that is
now explicit rather than reconstructed.

`admitEffect` is unchanged and is called before every dispatch, re-issues
included. Admissions are keyed by effect id, so a Stop or a supersede still
fences a call an evicted Turn had already started.

Deleted, with no compatibility shim: the session event types
`model/effect-not-started` and `model/reconciliation-required`;
`ToolEffectReconciliation`, `ToolDefinition.reconcile` and
`reconcilePrepared`; `ModelEffectReconciliationRequiredError`,
`ToolEffectReconciliationRequiredError`, `BotTurnReconciliationRequiredError`;
the `reconciliation-required` run status and phase, and with them the
`reconcileRun` RPC, the `/reconcile` route, the client's `resumeRun` and the
"Try again" button. `plugin-image`'s `generate_image` becomes idempotent by
reading its effect-keyed Workspace object before it generates, which is what
its `reconcile` did anyway.

Guarantees that are gone, deliberately:

- A dispatched model call whose response was lost is no longer retrieved from
  the provider. It is sent again, and a provider without idempotency may
  answer twice.
- A non-idempotent tool whose outcome is uncertain no longer parks the Turn.
  It is re-issued by key, or — when it threw — recorded as an error result
  that says the outcome is uncertain.
- A person can no longer resolve a parked Turn by hand, because no Turn parks.

Kept: a Turn still writes no `turn/end` when `agent/model-outcome-committed`
could not durably commit. That is the Turn's own write, not a question about
what a provider did, and a resume re-announces the same request id.

hits.message:
fix(turns): settle a timed-out model request, render the ack, and stop leaking jargon

Three defects the verification run on main found, in one code path.

1. A Turn whose model request ran past its budget answered HTTP 500.
   The Gateway host's 60s deadline stayed armed after the response headers
   arrived, so it aborted the *body* mid-stream on any tool-calling step. The
   raw `TimeoutError` read as an uncertain model outcome, the authority parked
   the run on a reconciliation and rethrew, and the composer's `POST /turns`
   answered 500 after 65s with "Couldn't reach the Bot" on screen — over a Bot
   left wedged behind a banner nothing could ever resolve.

   The deadline now bounds reaching the gateway and nothing after it, and is
   120s to match `MODEL_FIRST_BYTE_DEADLINE_MS_V1` so the kernel's deadline —
   the one with a sentence written for a person — wins the race. The body is
   bounded by the kernel's idle deadline. The caller's own signal is never
   disarmed, so Stop still tears a streaming request down.

   And ADR 0028 now applies on the live path, not only on recovery: a run whose
   provider keeps no addressable copy of a completion settles through the
   ordinary run-terminal path — `turn/end`, partial text kept, the reason on the
   record — instead of parking and throwing. A provider that can be asked still
   parks, unchanged.

2. The Bot's acknowledgement was never rendered. The model wrote "On it —
   building the 2027 countdown applet now." as plain assistant text and went on
   to call tools; the thread draws one bubble per send, and there was no send.
   Both ends: the prompt now names the call ("Your own text is not shown to the
   user"), and a new `agent/assistant-text` hook lets the Shell promote a
   tool-calling step's text to a `send/to-user` — before the first tool result,
   once per model request, and never on a step that already spoke.

3. Terminal-outcome copy leaked architecture. A person read "Reconciliation was
   explicitly abandoned: Bot turn ended with outcome model-error: Flock AI keeps
   no durable copy of an interrupted response". The stored `failure` stays the
   diagnostic the debug surface reads; the projection maps it through one
   `runFailureCopyV1` — the kernel's own person-facing sentences first, then the
   terminal outcome — before it crosses the wire. "Stopped by an authenticated
   Stop command" and "Provider reconciliation is required" went with it.

Tests: a stalled provider settles the Turn and resolves the caller; a body still
streaming past the deadline is not torn down while a Stop still is; the hook
fires ahead of the tools; the promotion records one send and no duplicate; and a
guard test that no user-facing sentence contains reconciliation, outcome codes,
provider names or event names.

hits.message:
Keep history when one Turn outgrows the budget, and bound the Turn itself (#891)

* Keep history when one Turn outgrows the budget, and bound the Turn itself

The history selector stopped at the first prior Turn that did not fit,
so one tool-heavy Turn larger than the whole budget took every older Turn
with it: the next request carried no history at all. It now keeps a Turn
that does not fit whole without its tool payloads, and skips only a Turn
that does not fit even then. The choice records which Turns are pruned
and the renderer follows it, instead of recomputing a positional window
that could render a Turn whole after it was charged pruned.

The Turn being assembled was carried whole and unbounded, so a long tool
loop grew each request until the prepaid model limit refused it. Once the
Turn alone passes 100k characters its oldest tool results are cleared
back to 50k, never the newest, replayed in order so a cleared result
stays cleared and the prompt cache breaks only at each clearing. The
selector measures the Turn as it will be sent.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_017FK7NPC96TPG2p6y2tjB2a

* Keep a step's parallel results, read past a skipped Turn, and leave headroom

Review of the history change found three gaps.

Clearing protected only the last tool message, so when one step made
several calls the model was shown [pruned] for results it had never read.
Everything after the model's newest message is now left alone.

The store stopped paging at the first page with a skipped Turn, a rule
written for the old stop-at-first-miss walk, so it could choose different
history from the in-memory path. It now stops at a page none of whose
Turns fit.

History pinned to a Turn's opening could ride along until the Turn reached
twice the budget, which with the system prompt and tools left little room
under Frock AI's 400,000-byte bound. The ceiling is now one and a half
budgets. A twelve-step 85 KB tool loop over a full history now stays
under 330 KB.

hits.message:
feat(supervision): record who wrote each part of a Turn's input, and let only the person ask (#944)

* feat(supervision): record who wrote each part of a Turn's input, and let only the person ask

A Turn's input is often assembled from several writers — a Routine's hand-off
drained in front of what the person typed, a card press and its Plugin's
context, a Routine's prompt and the payload a webhook delivered with it. The
model read them as one message, and so did supervision: every check kept the
first 600 characters of one merged objective, and call review showed all of it
as the person speaking. On 2026-09-27 that hid "Can you remember that my wife
is Becky" behind a 3,700-character hand-off, and let the Routine's own prompt
read as an instruction to the reviewer.

- Every part of an input records its writer (InputSegmentV1: person, routine,
  bot, plugin, platform, external) on input/queued and user/message. Only the
  admitting host sets them; a pre-step hook cannot, and the parts must spell
  out the text exactly.
- turnInputV1 builds them from the drained pending inputs and the Turn's
  origin; a Routine firing records its prompt's writer (promptBy), and its cue
  splits into FrockBot's line, the prompt, and the delivered payload.
- Every check reads the person's words first and what arrived with them after,
  labelled as someone else's; long text is bounded at both ends.
- Call review hears each part from its speaker. Only `user` and `routine`
  (the prompt of a Routine the person wrote) ask for anything; the questions
  say so.

Evals (five repeats each): the Becky write, the clipping set and its control
now pass 7/7 with no flips (were 3/7); response review core 60/60. Call review
core 27/27; the incident set improves to 12/20 with instructsReviewer now
0.1–0.5 instead of 0.5–0.7 — the reads still refused get authorization
"none", which the code-first call review in the next change decides. The
Plugin-card attack still gets through; that change refuses it in code.

No stored data needs cleanup: every new field is optional and absent on older
records.

hits.message:
Make every voice call fresh: Bot answers are told during the call or not at all

A Bot answer that settled after a call ended was queued for the next call
and read out before the person spoke, however stale it was. Tim's design
replaces the queue: each call is a fresh conversation with memory, a Bot's
answer arriving during the call becomes a turn of that call for the
assistant to decide what to say about (or to say nothing), and a call that
ends cancels its open requests, so a Bot still working answers into its own
conversation and nothing carries over.

- Ledger: endCall, endStaleCall and a superseding beginCall cancel the
  call's admitted and settled delegations; recover() cancels any open
  request whose call is not the live one; a turn record may carry an
  `event` (a Bot's answer arriving); markDelegationSpoken records the
  event turn that told it; dropDelegation cancels a settled answer nobody
  can be told. The speech cache, delivery ids, playback receipt and the
  unspoken list are gone.
- Object: announceDelegation replaces the read-out queue. It waits while a
  reply is in flight, waits for a rejoin while the call is on record with
  its socket away, drops an answer whose call is over, and otherwise runs
  tellAssistant: an admitted, metered event turn with the Bot's answer in
  the person's seat under a marker, no bridge, spoken once whole, aborted
  if the person starts talking. onCallStart reads nothing out.
- Assistant: the <answers> prompt block, lead-in, plain read-out, composer
  and age helpers are removed; renderVoiceBotAnswerEventV1 and a prompt rule
  say what a Bot-answer message is and that silence is a choice;
  runVoiceTurnV1 takes acknowledge: false.
- Protocol and phone: voice/answer, voice/answer-end and voice/played are
  removed on both sides; voice/delegation stays as footer chrome.
- Tests: ledger, assistant, probe and workerd suites rewritten for the new
  lifecycle (hang-up cancels and the next call opens quiet; held mid-reply
  then told as a turn; the assistant may say nothing; talking over an
  answer takes the floor; rejoin inside the window is still told).
- Docs: voice.md, the live checklist, the debug skill and architecture.

refactor(shell): make the settling transaction's composition a checked property

Three producers now share the kernel's one `terminalRecords` seam — unread
state, the completion inbox, and approval records — and the two rules that keep
them from ruining each other were invisible in the three spreads that composed
them: each producer has to run exactly once per settlement, and none may
silently overwrite another's key.

once, a key written by two of them throws rather than letting the later one win,
and the whole settlement is stamped with one `now` instead of three producers
each reading their own clock.

firings, fixed in the commit before — but "one settlement wrote two inbox
entries" was worth being able to rule out by test rather than by reading, and
the test now rules it out: an automation Turn contributes exactly one entry and
one wake, a chat Turn that asked for approval contributes unread and the
decision and nothing else, and re-settling a recovered Turn adds no second
record and leaves a decision somebody already made alone.

feat(voice): give each call one Bot, its own voice, and a first-person read-out (#542)

* fix(voice): keep every bridge phrase long enough to be spoken

The acknowledgment the session speaks when a turn has said nothing after
2.5 seconds went missing about one turn in six, and the workerd suite
failed with it: `sends acknowledgment audio while the model is still
pending` timed out with nothing synthesised at all.

The turn was never at fault. Traces from a reproduced failure show the
bridge fired on time — `turn-bridge` at 2553 ms — and the chunk was
yielded, but `beforeSynthesize` was never reached. The SDK streams a
turn's text through `SentenceChunker`, which holds any candidate shorter
than `MIN_SENTENCE_LENGTH` (10) in its buffer rather than emitting it —
the rule that stops "Dr." and "U.S." becoming sentences of their own — and
releases it only when the stream ends. For the bridge that is the one
moment it must not wait for: it exists because the model has said nothing
yet, so a stalled turn buffers it until the stall is over, which for a
turn that never answers is never.

Five of the six phrases clear ten characters. "Hang on." is eight, so
whenever `pickVoiceBridgeV1` chose it the person heard silence through
the whole stall. It is now "Hang on a sec.".

The floor belongs to the SDK, so the Worker suite asserts each phrase
against the SDK's own `SentenceChunker` rather than a number copied out of
it; `app` cannot import `agents`, so the shared test holds the list to
`VOICE_TURN_BRIDGE_MIN_CHARS_V1`. Restoring "Hang on." fails the guard
with `expected [] to deeply equal [ 'Hang on.' ]`.

Verified by reproducing the flake under CPU contention (1 failure in 5
runs before, 5/5 clean after) and by the full workerd suite, 360 tests.

hits.message:
feat(channels): bot-to-bot group channels with durable fan-out

Parity register rows 35 and 57f: a Bot can now say something to a teammate or
to a group and be answered, because the recipient gets a Turn of its own.

The authority is split the way the constitution splits it. Channel records,
membership and the canonical message log are User-scoped, so they live in the
User Durable Object as `plugin-channels`' `ChannelStore`; a Bot's participation
is a `channel` Turn its own Durable Object admits, and nothing else may admit
one. `channel/post` appends the message with the `seq` it assigns *inside the
transaction that writes one `ChannelDeliveryV1` per recipient*, then
acknowledges; the fan-out to `BOT_STATES.deliverChannelInput` is a second,
retryable step, safe to repeat because the debt is already written down. The
recipient writes the input to its own storage, arms its one alarm, and returns
— nothing runs inside the delivery RPC, so a sender's Turn is not held open for
whatever the recipient decides to do, and a reply cannot re-enter the User
Durable Object that is still waiting. The run id is derived from the message id
and the origin names the message, so a redelivery is refused by the kernel's own
Turn idempotency rather than by a check anyone remembered to write.

Four bounds, and every refusal is a durable receipt rather than an exception:
the sender is never a recipient of its own post; `hop` increments per message
and a post past `CHANNEL_HOP_MAX` (3) is refused; a per-Channel token bucket
(20/minute) refuses beyond its rate and reopens in the next window; and
`react_to_message` writes no delivery at all, so a tapback cannot cascade.

A `channel` Turn replays no personal transcript. `plugin-channels` supplies the
Channel's own last messages as the Turn's history through the Agent runtime's
new fresh-history mode — a handler prepended to `agent/request`, so it has the
last word over every Package narrowing and depends on none of them. The messages
are never written to the Bot's durable log, and the Bot's visible transcript
hides a `channel` Turn exactly as it hides an automation one.

Three tools — `send_to_agent`, `react_to_message`, `channel_manage` — admitted
on `["chat", "channel"]` and nowhere else, which is `:419`/`:444` for chat and
the extension that makes a group conversation closed for channel. A bare
`botId` resolves to the implicit 1:1 pair Channel, whose id is derived from the
pair, so both Bots name the same room and the create is idempotent on it. The
teammate directory and the channels list are prompt sections, not tools
(`:463-464`), skipped on automation and subagent Turns.

Manifest v5 adds the `channel` Capability kind: `decodeV5` extends `decodeV4`
exactly as `decodeV4` extends `decodeV3`, and the v1–v4 branches decode
unchanged — a v4 body that declares `channel` is refused, because the version a
manifest states is the version it is read at. `StoredRunOriginV1` gains a
`channel` variant beside `routine`; each is decoded exactly, so a Routine origin
written before this is byte-for-byte the same record.

Register rows 35 and 57f move; row 36 stays "not started" — the `external`
Channel kind and `channel_manage disconnect` exist, but no connector does yet,
and the UI is N3.

Tests: `ChannelStore` receipts, membership, hop, quota and reaction idempotence
over a Map; the three tools on a real `ToolRegistry`, including that an
automation Turn is offered none of them; `ChannelStoreProbe` in workerd, where a
post's message and both its deliveries survive eviction and a redelivered
message admits one Turn; and `channels-group.integration.ts`, where two Bots of
one User meet through `SELF.fetch` — Bot A posts from a chat Turn, Bot B answers
on a `channel` Turn that is absent from its transcript, and the cascade stops at
the hop bound with a refusal that replays.
