hits.message:
feat(routines): a firing the conversation never sees, and the inbox it lands in

A Routine fired, and the whole conversation could see it. This is the half
that makes a firing what GrokBot calls "a fresh subagent turn under the same
agent id, not a turn inside the user's chat": invisible to the transcript,
starting from nothing, and reaching its User through one durable record
instead of speaking.

Three separations do it, and none of them partitions the kernel's log. The
Bot Durable Object still keeps one ordered event log — reconstruction rests
on that — and every rule here is Package policy over it, which is what the
constitution already says about what enters a model request.

`plugin-shell/src/history.ts` is the prompt-history rule, applied on the
existing `agent/request` waterfall. A chat Turn's request carries only the
Turns whose `turn/admission` says `turnType: "chat"`; an automation Turn's
carries its own Turn and one pointer line naming the parent conversation —
how many Turns it has, that none of it has been copied, and that
`wake_parent` is the only way back. The filter runs on the derived messages
rather than on the seeded events, because the log's sequence is contiguous by
kernel rule: the Turn is seeded with the whole history so its own events keep
their place, and only the request is narrowed. Memory is untouched, because
"the parent agent's shared durable memories are available" and Memory is a
prompt section, not history.

`listRuns` and the run lookup filter to the same marker, absent meaning chat,
so every run recorded before turn admission existed stays visible. An
automation run is reachable only through the Routine's run log, and
`GET /api/bots/:id/routines/:routineId/runs/:runId` is that door: what the
firing did, with no model requests, no tool inputs and no payloads.

An automation Turn has no voice, so its outcome is written in the same
transaction that settles it, through the `terminalRecords` hook unread state
already rides — the Shell composes both, and neither policy knows about the
other. A hand-off writes a `RoutineInboxEntryV1` bounded at 100, a
`PendingBotInputV1` of kind `wake` bounded at 16 carrying GrokBot's
`quietOrigin.automation`, and a notification intent. A completion without one
writes the inbox entry alone and notifies nobody — the row's silent landing.
A failure writes neither, because `completeStoredRun` is the hook's only
caller.

`PendingBotInputV1` is wider than Routines on purpose: `{ kind: "wake" } |
{ kind: "approval", approvalId, decision }`, the second decoded with no
producer, so approval cards add a producer rather than a second queue.

It drains at exactly two points. The Bot's next admitted chat Turn moves the
queue into a `routine-drain:<runId>` receipt in one transaction and prefixes
the hand-offs to that Turn's input, ahead of the person's own words; the
receipt is what makes a recovered Turn reproduce the same `model/request`
instead of draining twice, and `run.input` stays what the person typed. The
alarm is the other point: an intent written in the settling transaction
cannot be lost, but a client that was not connected can miss it, so a wake
whose entry is still unread is re-notified once, recorded on the wake.

`GET/POST /api/bots/:id/routines/inbox` lists and acknowledges — an explicit
command, never a side effect of reading, so a background poll cannot clear a
badge — and `RoutineInboxBadge.vue` fills the shell's header slot, because a
completion that never spoke has nowhere else to appear.

Register rows 18 and 19b move to landed; 19 stays partial and now says the
confirmation card is the only thing left of it.

feat(subagents): typed Task dispatch into Subagent Durable Objects

Slice G, PR G1. A Bot dispatches a subagent as a Turn, not as an agent: ADR
0017 splits one Bot across two Durable Objects, and this is the dispatch half
of that split.

The parent Bot Durable Object is the authority. It mints the `TaskRecordV1`,
checks the bounds, pins the Composition generation and the model binding,
holds the desktop-lease intent, and records the one terminal outcome. The
Subagent Durable Object — the same `BotState` class in the same `BOT_STATES`
namespace, named `<userId>:<botId>#task:<taskId>` — is only an execution host:
it runs one `subagent` Turn on its own Session and settles back to the parent.

New package `@frockbot/plugin-subagents`: `TaskRecordV1` and its exact-key
codecs, the storage keys, the bounds, the per-User slot reservation, the model
slug catalog, the `Task` tool and the `<available_subagent_models>` prompt
section, and the `GET /api/bots/:id/tasks` gateway Contribution.

`StoredRunV1.admission.origin` gains a second kind, `{kind:"subagent", taskId,
parentRunId}`, with its own exact-field branch; a chat Turn's fingerprint bytes
are unchanged. `PromptAssemblyContext` gains `turnType`, so a section can
render what the Turn may actually do — an automation or subagent turn is shown
exactly one model slug.

Intent before effect: the task record, the active key, the index row and the
`computerUse` lease intent are durable, and both bounds have answered, before
any Subagent Durable Object is addressed. Settling is idempotent on the task
id, and an unanswered task is reconciled — never re-dispatched — on the
parent's own alarm.

hits.message:
Connect apps through one first-party layer, and give every Bot their tools

Connected apps is `app/connect`: a `connect` Package with one hosted-grant
Connection Type per curated app (Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive,
GitHub, Slack, Notion), so each app is its own Connectors row and connecting
once gives every Bot the app. The provider behind it is the deployment's own
backend, named nowhere a person reads; it is app code rather than a plugin,
because plugin machinery is for untrusted code.

Connect is the existing `authorize` press. The User Durable Object finds or
creates the provider's managed auth config, mints the sign-in link and writes
the Connection in `authorizing`; a public return page says to come back and
touches no object; the next settings read settles the Connection to `ready`
or `failed` through a read bootstrap. Disconnect deletes the account upstream
with revocation. `ModelOAuthCommandV1` gained `connectionTypeId` for a Package
with several types, and the Connectors frame names a row by its type when a
Package declares more than one.

For each ready Connection a Turn mounts one Tool Namespace named for the app
— `gmail`, `gmail-2` for a second account — carrying only the app's important
tools, pinned per Turn. Nothing is in the prompt for an app nobody connected.
Execution carries the deployment key and the account id off the Connection's
safe metadata, so no credential is leased or logged; a failure after dispatch
is reported as an unknown outcome rather than retried.

`COMPOSIO_API_KEY` and `COMPOSIO_WEBHOOK_SECRET` are optional production
secrets, forwarded by both workflows. The harness answers the provider's host
with a stub, and `connect-apps.integration.ts` walks the row, the hand-off,
the settle, the return page, a Bot's tool call and the disconnect through the
gateway. Triggers as a Routine kind are the next cut.

- `/api/ps` and `/api/embed` answer 401 even for a valid key; they are
  unsupported on Cloud and cannot serve as a probe.

So any key validated, the Connection reached `ready` with a full catalog,
and the User only learned the key was bad when a Turn ended `model-error`.
That happened in production today.

`OllamaCloudClient.probeInference` now issues the cheapest authenticated
call: `POST /api/chat` with `stream:false` and `options.num_predict:1`,
measured at `prompt_eval_count: 68`, `eval_count: 1`,
`done_reason: "length"` — about 70 tokens. 401/403 is a definitive
rejection carrying Ollama's own error text; other non-2xx carry status and
text; the assistant content is never parsed or retained. Validation on
create and rotate is now `listModels` AND `probeInference`, against
`gpt-oss:20b` when discovered (cloud model names are bare, with no `:cloud`
suffix) and otherwise the first discovered model. A probe failure sets
`validationStatus: "failed"`, which already flows to the Connection's
`failure`. The periodic catalog refresh stays metadata only and does not
probe.

The measured matrix is recorded in `docs/research/ollama-cloud-auth.md`.

hits.message:
Bootstrapping a new Package's npm trust is one command

Trusted publishing needs a placeholder and a trusted publisher before a
name can be published by the workflow, and that is true of every new
Package, not only the first — a workspace added under `packages/` fails
the next tag's publish step on its own name until it is bootstrapped.
`scripts/bootstrap-npm-trust.ts` already knew what to do; reaching a
usable npm session was the part done by hand each time.

`bun run bootstrap:npm-trust` now does it. The wrapper provisions npm
11.15.0 or later into `node_modules/.cache` when the installed npm is
older, because that is what `npm trust` requires and it is newer than
most Node installations ship, then signs in and shows the plan.

Underneath, the run had to get shorter and louder.

Shorter, because every authenticated npm call demands its own one-time
password against a session that expires in minutes. The old pass asked
`npm trust list` about all sixty-four packages, spending that session on
prompts about packages that needed nothing and expiring before it
reached the two that did. It now acts only on names the registry is
missing — `npm view` is public, so finding them costs nothing — and asks
npm nothing about the rest. A package the registry already has was
published by the workflow, which is only possible if it is trusted.

Louder, because npm asks for that password by printing a URL and waiting
on a browser. Capturing its output hid the question: the run died with
EOTP and the URL redacted, reading as a rejected credential rather than
something nobody was shown. Publishing, deprecating and trusting now
inherit the terminal; only the probes whose output is parsed stay
captured.

The one case the narrowing gives up is a placeholder published by a run
that failed before trusting it, which leaves a package npm has that the
workflow still cannot publish. Naming packages bootstraps them anyway,
and the failure that strands one says so.

hits.message:
feat(voice): tidy a dictated transcript once the person stops speaking

Speech-to-text gives back what was said, including the "um"s, the false
starts and the corrections people make mid-sentence. Reading that back
and fixing it by hand is work nobody asked for, so the capture is tidied
once — when they stop, never while they speak, because text that
rewrites itself under the cursor is worse than text that is untidy.

It runs in the relay, between the last segment and `final`, because the
model is reached with a server-side credential and the relay is already
where the capture's own words are. Two new frames carry it: `cleaning`,
which only changes what the composer says, and `cleaned`, which is the
tidied form of the whole capture.

The prompt is a request; the guards are the property. What comes back is
refused — and the raw transcript stands — when it is empty, unchanged,
longer (added information), much shorter (summarised), opens like a
model talking to us, had a question that is no longer a question, or
dropped every negation or every uncertainty the raw text carried. That
last pair is the one that matters: "maybe we should change the model" and
"change the model" are different messages to send to something that acts.
The transcript itself is fenced as data, and the fence's markers are
stripped out of it so it cannot be closed from inside.

Every way this fails ends in the same place — `final`, with the raw
transcript already in the draft. No gateway, no allowance, too short,
too long, a model that throws, a model that takes more than 8 s, a
guard that refuses. A capture the five-minute cap ended is not tidied at
all: it was cut off mid-sentence, so its false starts cannot be told
from its words, and the person is being shown why it stopped.

On the client the tidied text goes through the same `DictationDraftRange`
as every segment, which is what makes it safe rather than
carefully-written: a span the person has edited inside is already fenced
and takes nothing more, and a sent draft no longer contains the span at
all, so a late tidy-up finds nothing to replace. The composer offers
"Use what I said" afterwards and withdraws it the moment they edit.

Spend is one model call per capture, booked against the account's own
voice object before the model is asked, 400 per UTC day, and
deliberately not part of the cap that decides whether a voice call may
go on — a day of tidy-ups is no reason to refuse somebody a conversation.

Five defects a QA pass on v0.3.35 found, each fixed where it lives.

Archive and Delete borrowed the Create-a-Bot frame — a 660x520 two-column
box built for a sheep and a wardrobe — so two sentences wrapped six times in
a 180px column and a quarter page of nothing sat above the buttons. A
confirmation is now `UiConfirmDialog` in client-ui: 420px, a question, one
or two sentences, Cancel and the act. Cancel takes the focus, which is the
answer a stray Enter should give.

The Create-a-Bot dialog's own columns disagreed because the art panel set a
fixed 520px height and the buttons were pinned to the bottom of it. The
dialog is now as tall as its form, so the columns end together and the
buttons sit under the last field.

Models was a full-height drawer holding one sentence, no action, and no
statement of the model actually in use. It now leads with the model the
composer names, explains the platform default, and offers the button that
turns the chooser on — found from manifest facts, like every other routing
decision on that surface.

Usage read "$0.50" for two short Turns. `@frock/auto` — what almost every
Bot runs on — was absent from the price table, so every platform-model Turn
was priced at the unknown-model fallback of $10/$50 per million, twenty-three
times the model it routes to. Auto is now priced at the Frock AI text model
the route serves. The token counts were real: the transport reports none, so
the loop estimates from the normalized request, which carries the system
prompt and every tool schema whatever the person typed. Two such Turns are
about two cents. Sub-cent spend now reads "<$0.01" rather than "$0.00", and
zero still reads as zero.

Opening Applets logged a CSP violation for the zone's injected Insights
beacon. Artifact responses now say `no-transform`: an artifact is addressed
by the hash of its bytes and a zone feature that rewrites its HTML is
rewriting what the hash names. The beacon's two origins are named anyway,
because `no-transform` is a request to an edge feature rather than a
guarantee this Worker can make.

Settings had three "Save settings" buttons, the last one under Usage, which
saves nothing. The profile's Save now sits with the two fields it saves and
says so, and Usage — a reading, not a setting — follows the settings rather
than sitting between two of them. The Bot panel's "Alpha's screen" caption

feat(skills): managed and plugin-borne Skills, ordered and capped

A Turn's Skill catalog now draws from three live sources instead of one,
and two of them are deliberately not durable-root files.

Managed Skills are four first-party SKILL.md documents compiled into the
plugin-skills artifact — add-connector, export-bot-template,
import-bot-template, learn-from-demonstration, mirroring GrokBot's
read-only managed-skills/ set, with bodies written for FrockBot's own
tools. Their generation is their content hash, and the artifact set hash
the Turn's Composition pins is what makes that reproducible. They are
read-only in the strongest available sense: there is no write path to an
artifact at all, so skill_write refuses scope "managed" and "plugin" with
GrokBot's own wording, "managed skills are not editable this way".

Plugin-borne Skills are an index over the Catalog entries the User has
installed, read from the entry document at the generation each install
pinned and never copied into any root. An uninstall therefore removes
them on the next Turn with nothing to delete and no copy to go stale.
CatalogEntryV1.skills gains an optional, bounded body so the entry
document is the one place a plugin Skill's recipe lives.

Neither source is a Workspace file, so neither meets
isLoadableSkillSourceV1 and AGENTS.md's rule about instruction roots is
untouched: both are a Package contributing prompt content, admitted by an
explicit act of the User. The predicate still decides every question it
decided before, about every file it decided it for.

Assembly is deterministic and bounded: bot then user then managed then
plugin, by ref within a source, under SKILL_CATALOG_CAPS_V1
{ bot: 40, user: 40, managed: 8, plugin: 24, totalBytes: 16_384 }. Refs
are globally unique so ordering shadows nothing, and a name two sources
share is qualified by its ref in the rendered block, which now also
carries source and by. Every drop is an over-source-cap SkillRefusalV1 in
skill/injected.refusals, as is a malformed bundled document or a Catalog
that could not be read — refusals, never a thrown Turn. skill_load and
invocation both resolve managed/<slug> and plugin/<packageId>/<slug>; the
bare path stays accepted for one release.

The user-global root is not here. It needs a new WorkspaceRootV1 kind and
an amendment to the constitution's "the Bot's own instruction root"
sentence, which is a decision rather than code. The user slot exists in
the ordering, the caps and the ref codec, and is always empty.

hits.message:
feat(search): put the transcript index behind a route and a search overlay

The second half of parity register row 52. PR 1 built the index; this makes it
reachable.

`GET /api/search` and `POST /api/search/rebuild` are the Search Package's
gateway Contribution, on the same host as Flock's `/api/bots` and for the same
reason: the gateway is where an authenticated `userId` exists. The route owns
no state. It turns the query string into the same exact `SearchQueryV1` every
other caller uses — an unexpected parameter is a refusal, not something
quietly ignored — asks the User Durable Object, and joins the live Bot
directory so each group carries the Bot's current name, avatar and archived or
hidden label rather than a copy the index made when the row was written.

Grouping is its own pure module and its own test surface. It is also the only
place a deep link is built, so no client assembles one out of parts it might
get wrong.

`SearchOverlay.vue` registers on the shell's client surface registry, opens
from a header control or Cmd/Ctrl-K, and debounces at 200 ms. Results are
grouped by Bot in rank order; each hit switches the active Bot and scrolls to
the `turn-<runId>` anchor the turn renderer now carries — one anchor per Turn,
on its first visible line, because giving the prompt and the reply the same id
would put the same anchor in the document twice. When the Turn is further back
than the loaded page the reader is left on the right Bot and told so.

Five states are rendered distinctly: nothing typed, nothing found, rebuilding,
truncated, and failed. A blank panel that could mean any of them is the one
outcome the surface must not produce.

The shell touches are two lines of template and one computed: a
`frockbot.header-actions` outlet, declared in the Shell manifest, and the
anchor id.

Two deliberate limits. A Bot's generated sheep avatar is drawn only by the
Flock Package's own client components, which it does not export, so a group
shows an uploaded avatar by URL and a monogram otherwise rather than reaching
into another Package's client internals. And a rebuild re-projects an archived
Bot's rows: archiving deletes no Turn, the conversation is still there, and
`includeArchived` is what asks for them.

Tests: 20 more unit tests (query-string decoding, route behaviour, grouping,
client DTO round-trip and rejection) and `search.integration.ts`, where Alice
sees only her turns grouped across two Bots, Bob sees none, an archived Bot is
excluded and then opted into, a rebuild reproduces the page, and a deep link
resolves to a real run through the run-lookup route.

fix(turns): settle a timed-out model request, render the ack, and stop leaking jargon

Three defects the verification run on main found, in one code path.

1. A Turn whose model request ran past its budget answered HTTP 500.
   The Gateway host's 60s deadline stayed armed after the response headers
   arrived, so it aborted the *body* mid-stream on any tool-calling step. The
   raw `TimeoutError` read as an uncertain model outcome, the authority parked
   the run on a reconciliation and rethrew, and the composer's `POST /turns`
   answered 500 after 65s with "Couldn't reach the Bot" on screen — over a Bot
   left wedged behind a banner nothing could ever resolve.

   The deadline now bounds reaching the gateway and nothing after it, and is
   120s to match `MODEL_FIRST_BYTE_DEADLINE_MS_V1` so the kernel's deadline —
   the one with a sentence written for a person — wins the race. The body is
   bounded by the kernel's idle deadline. The caller's own signal is never
   disarmed, so Stop still tears a streaming request down.

   And ADR 0028 now applies on the live path, not only on recovery: a run whose
   provider keeps no addressable copy of a completion settles through the
   ordinary run-terminal path — `turn/end`, partial text kept, the reason on the
   record — instead of parking and throwing. A provider that can be asked still
   parks, unchanged.

2. The Bot's acknowledgement was never rendered. The model wrote "On it —
   building the 2027 countdown applet now." as plain assistant text and went on
   to call tools; the thread draws one bubble per send, and there was no send.
   Both ends: the prompt now names the call ("Your own text is not shown to the
   user"), and a new `agent/assistant-text` hook lets the Shell promote a
   tool-calling step's text to a `send/to-user` — before the first tool result,
   once per model request, and never on a step that already spoke.

3. Terminal-outcome copy leaked architecture. A person read "Reconciliation was
   explicitly abandoned: Bot turn ended with outcome model-error: Flock AI keeps
   no durable copy of an interrupted response". The stored `failure` stays the
   diagnostic the debug surface reads; the projection maps it through one
   `runFailureCopyV1` — the kernel's own person-facing sentences first, then the
   terminal outcome — before it crosses the wire. "Stopped by an authenticated
   Stop command" and "Provider reconciliation is required" went with it.

Tests: a stalled provider settles the Turn and resolves the caller; a body still
streaming past the deadline is not torn down while a Stop still is; the hook
fires ahead of the tools; the promotion records one send and no duplicate; and a
guard test that no user-facing sentence contains reconciliation, outcome codes,
provider names or event names.
